sections.heading: Master Repository — All Constitutional Articles
sections.content:
> **Repository:** Articles Master Bank for Active Recall & Rapid Revision
> **Total Articles:** 51 Key UPSC Articles
> **Format:** Numerical Order with Collapsible Active Recall Answers

---

sections.heading: Article 2 — Admission or Establishment of New States
sections.content:
**Part:** Part I (The Union and its Territory)

**Heading:** Admission or establishment of new States

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: Part I — External Territorial Arrangement
* **Core Provision**: Parliament may by law admit into the Union, or establish, new States on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit.
* **Admission vs Establishment**: *Admission* = Adding pre-existing self-contained unit (pre-existing identity). *Establishment* = Creating/demarcating new territory where none existed before.
* **Practical Status**: **Useless (never used in India's history)** — Per *Re Berubari Union (1960)*, admission requires prior acquisition via sovereign power under international law (Special Majority under Art 368). Since Special Majority subsumes Simple Majority, Art 2 simple majority route is never directly invoked.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 3 — Formation of New States and Alteration of Areas, Boundaries or Names
sections.content:
**Part:** Part I (The Union and its Territory)

**Heading:** Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: Part I — Internal Territorial Arrangement
* **5 Key Powers**: Parliament may by law (a) Form or Abolish a state/UT, (b) Merge states/UTs, (c) Alter boundaries, (d) Increase or diminish area, (e) Change the name of any State.
* **Two Pre-conditions for Bill Introduction**:
  1. **Recommendation of President**: Political phrase for *Government Initiative* (only a Public Member / Home Minister can introduce).
  2. **Opinion of Concerned State Legislature**: Must be referred by President (conventionally 30 days). The opinion is **non-binding** on Parliament/President (reasons: National interest primacy, nature of 'opinion', and Ambedkar's no-free-will doctrine).
* **UT Exception**: If only UTs are involved (e.g. Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu merger), pre-conditions are **NOT required** (Centre-UT relationship is purely Unitary).
* **Passing Majority**: **Simple Majority** in both Houses (justified by principle of administrative convenience of the Centre).

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 4 — Laws under Articles 2 and 3 and Schedules I & IV
sections.content:
**Part:** Part I (The Union and its Territory)

**Heading:** Laws made under articles 2 and 3 to provide for the amendment of the First and the Fourth Schedules and supplemental, incidental and consequential matters

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: Part I — Consequential Constitutional Amendments
* **Article 4(1)**: Any law enacted under Art 2 or 3 shall contain provisions for the amendment of **Schedule I** (Names of States/UTs) and **Schedule IV** (Allocation of Rajya Sabha seats).
* **Article 4(2)**: No such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of **Article 368** (passed by **Simple Majority**).
* **Protection of Art 4 Rule**: Protection applies ONLY when Art 2 or 3 is in action. If Schedule IV is amended directly without Art 2/3 action, **Special Majority under Art 368** is mandatory.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 13 of the Indian Constitution
sections.content:
**Part:** Part III (Fundamental Rights)

**Heading:** Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

**Key Provisions:**
*   Declares that all laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of the Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of Part III, shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void.
*   The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by Part III and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void.
*   Provides the basis for **Judicial Review**. Laws can be declared *ultra vires* (beyond powers) if they violate Fundamental Rights.

**Relevance:** Frequently invoked when challenging legislative or executive actions (like the CAPF Act) that allegedly violate constitutional provisions or fundamental rights.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 14 — Right to Equality
sections.content:
Show Answer * **Category**: Fundamental Rights (Part III) * **Core Concept**: Prohibits arbitrary State action and discriminatory exemptions without a rational nexus. Guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. * **Supreme Court Precedent**: Any executive exemption power must satisfy the *Intelligible Differentia* & *Rational Nexus* tests (*E.P. Royappa vs State of Tamil Nadu*). * **Context**: SC warned that ad-hoc designation of specific case categories without rational classification risks violating equal protection. * **Personal Laws & Section 82 BNS Scrutiny (Aug 2026):** Supreme Court examined petitions challenging Section 2 of Shariat Act 1937 under Article 14 for creating arbitrary exemptions permitting polygamy for Muslim men while non-Muslims face up to 7 years imprisonment under Section 82 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) for bigamy.
---

sections.heading: Article 15 — Prohibition of Discrimination on Grounds of Religion, Race, Caste, Sex or Place of Birth
sections.content:
> **Part:** III — Fundamental Rights > **Subject:** Right to Equality
Show Answer * **Category**: Fundamental Rights (Part III) — Specific Application of Article 14 * **Article 15(1)**: The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds **only** of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them. * **Article 15(2)**: Horizontal application — No citizen shall be subjected to any disability, liability, restriction or condition regarding access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment, or the use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads, and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds. * **Article 15(3)**: Special provisions for **women and children** (protective discrimination / affirmative action). * **Article 15(4)**: Added by 1st Constitutional Amendment Act 1951 — Special provisions for advancement of Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (SEBCs), SCs, and STs. * **Article 15(5)**: Added by 93rd Constitutional Amendment Act 2005 — Reservation in educational institutions. * **Article 15(6)**: Added by 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act 2019 — Up to 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS). * **Current Affairs & Gender Justice Link (Aug 2026):** Section 2 of Shariat Act 1937 challenged before Supreme Court for violating Article 15 by permitting polygamy for Muslim men while subjecting non-Muslims to criminal liability under Section 82 BNS (bigamy up to 7 years), creating religion- and sex-based discrimination against women.
---

sections.heading: Article 16 — Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: Fundamental Rights (Part III)
* **Article 16(3)**: **Only Parliament** has the exclusive power to prescribe residence requirements for public employment. State Legislatures do NOT have this power.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 19 — Right to Freedom
sections.content:
Show Answer * **Category**: Fundamental Rights (Part III) * **Article 19(1)(a)**: Guarantees Freedom of Speech and Expression (source of Right to Information). SC in Aug 2026 DPDP Act hearing noted journalists are not a "special category" with unreserved access to personal data over privacy laws. * **Article 19(2)**: Restricts 19(1)(a) on 8 grounds: (i) Sovereignty & Integrity of India, (ii) Security of State, (iii) Friendly relations with foreign States, (iv) Public Order, (v) Decency or Morality, (vi) Contempt of Court, (vii) Defamation, (viii) Incitement to an offence. In blasphemy and hate speech jurisprudence (Section 295A IPC / Section 299 BNS), courts have cautioned against the 'Heckler's Veto' and pre-emptive censorship. Per the 2016 Madras HC ruling (Perumal Murugan case), the constitutional mandate is to protect free expression against mob censorship, requiring speech restrictions to satisfy a direct 'spark in a powder keg' test (Shreya Singhal / S. Rangarajan) rather than penalizing rational critique or progressive social reform. * **Article 19(1)(b)**: Guarantees citizens the right to assemble peaceably and without arms. SC in NEET protest FRS hearing (Aug 2026) highlighted that indiscriminate biometric surveillance and facial recognition at demonstration sites must be tested for impermissible "chilling effect" on peaceful democratic assembly. * **Article 19(3)**: Restricts 19(1)(b) on 2 specific grounds only: **(i) Sovereignty and integrity of India, or (ii) Public order**. * **Article 19(1)(c)**: Guarantees citizens the right to form associations, unions, or non-governmental organizations (NGOs), including the right to function and seek funding. * **Article 19(4)**: Restricts 19(1)(c) on 3 specific grounds: **(i) Sovereignty & Integrity of India, (ii) Public Order, or (iii) Morality**.
---

sections.heading: Article 21 — Right to Life and Personal Liberty
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: Fundamental Rights (Part III)
* **Environment**: The Supreme Court has interpreted the Right to Life to encompass the right to a clean, pollution-free, and healthy environment.
* **Due Process**: SC cautioned against imposing rigid, statutory trial deadlines (e.g., in complex paper leak cases) because rushed trials compromise the right to a fair trial and defense preparation.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 21A
sections.content:
**Subject:** Right to education.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

*   **Context:** The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 25 — Freedom of Conscience and Free Profession, Practice and Propagation of Religion
sections.content:
> **Part:** III — Fundamental Rights
> **Subject:** Right to Freedom of Religion

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text (Summary)
sections.content: Subject to public order, morality and health, all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion.

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
- Part of **Articles 25–28** which collectively guarantee **Right to Freedom of Religion**.
- Gives every individual (not just citizens) the right to be **religious** as well as to be an **atheist**.
- This is a right of **individuals/Indians**, NOT a state policy.
- **Critical distinction (from Lecture 3):** "Secular" in the Preamble is an **Ideal for India** (the state), NOT for Indians. Indians have the FR to be religious under Art. 25–28.
- Subject to reasonable restrictions: public order, morality, health, and other provisions of Part III.

sections.heading: Relevance to Secularism
sections.content: - Western Secularism = separation of religion from politics (state has NO relation with religion). - Indian/Eastern Secularism = complex triangular relationship between Religion, Individual, and State — the state does not separate itself from religion but treats all religions equally. - Art. 25 ensures individuals can freely practice their religion while the state remains neutral/equidistant. - **Personal Laws & ERP Test (Aug 2026):** Article 25 is expressly subject to other provisions of Part III (Articles 14, 15, 21). Polygamy under Section 2 of Shariat Act 1937 is permissible/customary but not an Essential Religious Practice (ERP), making it subject to State regulatory power for social welfare and gender reform under Article 25(2)(b). - **Article 25(2)(b) & Social Reform Supremacy (Aug 2026):** Article 25(2)(b) explicitly saves the State's power to provide for social welfare and reform. As Dr. B.R. Ambedkar declared in the Constituent Assembly (Dec 2, 1948), religion cannot claim an expansive veto over progressive social legislation or personal law reform. Consequently, state anti-superstition enactments (e.g., Sati Act 1987, Maharashtra Act 2013, Karnataka Act 2017) and rationalist critiques of dogma take constitutional precedence over subjective religious hurt feelings under penal laws. ---

sections.heading: Article 33 of the Indian Constitution
sections.content:
**Part:** Part III (Fundamental Rights)

**Heading:** Power of Parliament to modify the rights conferred by this Part in their application to Forces, etc.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

**Key Provisions:**
*   Parliament may, by law, determine to what extent any of the rights conferred by Part III shall, in their application to:
    *   (a) the members of the Armed Forces; or
    *   (b) the members of the Forces charged with the maintenance of public order; or
    *   (c) persons employed in any bureau or other organisation established by the State for purposes of intelligence or counter intelligence; or
    *   (d) persons employed in, or in connection with, the telecommunication systems set up for the purposes of any Force, bureau or organisation referred to in clauses (a) to (c),
    *   be restricted or abrogated so as to ensure the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

**Relevance:** Significant when dealing with rules, regulations, and acts affecting the fundamental rights, service conditions, and unionization of Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), Police, and Armed Forces.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 39(b) — DPSP: Distribution of Material Resources
sections.content:
> **Part:** IV — Directive Principles of State Policy
> **Subject:** Equitable distribution of material resources of the community

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text
sections.content: The State shall, in particular, direct its policy towards securing that the ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good.

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
- Falls under **Socialistic Provisions** of the Constitution.
- Aims at **equitable distribution of resources** — not equal distribution, but fair distribution that serves the common good.
- Reflects **Marxian element** within India's Democratic Socialism.
- Read with [Article 39(c)](Article_39c.md) for the complete socialistic directive.
- **Not justiciable** (being a DPSP) but fundamental in governance.

sections.heading: Relevant Cases
sections.content:
- **Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973):** Socialistic directives form part of the Constitution's core values.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 39(c) — DPSP: Prevention of Concentration of Wealth
sections.content:
> **Part:** IV — Directive Principles of State Policy
> **Subject:** No concentration of wealth and means of production

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text
sections.content: The State shall, in particular, direct its policy towards securing that the operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment.

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
- Falls under **Socialistic Provisions** of the Constitution.
- Aims at preventing **concentration of wealth** — ensuring that the economic system does not create extreme inequality.
- Reflects **Marxian element** within India's Democratic Socialism.
- Read with [Article 39(b)](Article_39b.md) for the complete socialistic directive.
- Particularly relevant in the context of **LPG reforms (1991)** — privatization creates concentration of wealth, which this Article seeks to prevent through state policy.
- **Not justiciable** (being a DPSP) but fundamental in governance.

sections.heading: Relevant Context
sections.content:
- Marx's core concern: The bourgeois (owner class) grows at the cost of the proletariat (working class) → concentration of wealth = injustice.
- India's Democratic Socialism addresses this through welfare schemes, progressive taxation, and regulatory frameworks rather than abolishing private property.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 43 — DPSP: Living Wage, Conditions of Work & Participation of Workers
sections.content:
> **Part:** IV — Directive Principles of State Policy
> **Subject:** Living wage, etc., for workers

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text
sections.content: The State shall endeavour to secure, by suitable legislation or economic organisation or in any other way, to all workers, agricultural, industrial or otherwise, work, a living wage, conditions of work ensuring a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities and, in particular, the State shall endeavour to promote cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas.

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
- Falls under **Socialistic Provisions** of the Constitution.
- Mandates **participation of workers in management of factories** — a direct socialistic provision.
- Workers' participation ensures: better working conditions, fair working hours, leisure, safety, security, insurance, fair wages, holidays, etc.
- All of these collectively represent a **minimum standard of living** → establishes a **welfare state**.
- Reflects **Gandhian Socialism** — empowering grassroot people, bottom-up approach, cottage industries.
- **Not justiciable** (being a DPSP) but fundamental in governance.

sections.heading: Socialistic Significance
sections.content: - When workers participate in management, they raise issues about their welfare → this is democratic socialism in action. - The provision bridges the gap between the bourgeois (owners) and proletariat (workers) without abolishing private property. - **Labour Codes & Modern Jurisprudence (Aug 2026):** Article 43 and Article 43A provide the constitutional bedrock for India's 4 Labour Codes (Wage Code 2019, IRC 2020, Social Security Code 2020, OSH Code 2020). The SC 9-judge bench (Aug 2026) reaffirmed that while modern economic efficiency requires interpreting the Industrial Relations Code 2020 on a clean slate without the 1978 Bangalore Water Supply judicial burden, the constitutional mandate to ensure living wage, safety, and dispute recourse remains paramount. ---

sections.heading: Article 43A — DPSP: Participation of Workers in Management of Industries
sections.content:
> **Part:** IV — Directive Principles of State Policy
> **Subject:** Participation of workers in management of industries
> **Added by:** 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text
sections.content: The State shall take steps, by suitable legislation or in any other way, to secure the participation of workers in the management of undertakings, establishments or other organisations engaged in any industry.

sections.heading: Key Constitutional Points
sections.content:
* Added by the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976** under the Indira Gandhi administration, reflecting the socialistic commitments inserted into the Preamble.
* Falls under the **Socialistic Principles** of Part IV (DPSPs).
* **Industrial Democracy:** Elevates the status of workers from mere wage earners/factors of production to partners in the industrial and economic decision-making process.
* Complements **Article 43** (Living wage and decent standard of life) and **Article 39(b)/(c)** (Prevention of wealth concentration and equitable distribution of resources).
* **Not justiciable** in courts (Article 37) but fundamental in the governance of the country and acts as a guiding light for labour legislation.

sections.heading: Landmark Jurisprudence & Contemporary Relevance
sections.content: * **1978 Bangalore Water Supply Case (Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer):** Expansively defined 'industry' under Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 using the 'triple test' to protect workers' collective bargaining rights in educational institutions, hospitals, and municipalities. * **Supreme Court 9-Judge Bench Verdict (Aug 2026):** Held that the 1978 Bangalore Water Supply expansive definition of 'industry' will NOT apply to the new Industrial Relations Code (IRC), 2020. Section 2(p) of IRC 2020 must be interpreted on a 'clean slate' according to its own text and context, while the 1978 triple test continues to govern pending industrial disputes. ---

sections.heading: Article 44 — Uniform Civil Code for the Citizens
sections.content:
> **Part:** IV — Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) > **Subject:** Liberal-Intellectual Principles
Show Answer * **Category**: Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) — Non-justiciable in court (Article 37) but fundamental in governance. * **Text**: "The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India." * **Core Objective**: To replace fragmented, community-specific personal laws relating to marriage, divorce, maintenance, inheritance, adoption, and succession with a single common set of civil laws for all citizens regardless of religion. * **Landmark Judicial Precedents**: * **Shah Bano Case (1985)**: SC observed that Article 44 had remained a "dead letter" and urged the state to enact a UCC to facilitate national integration and gender justice. * **Sarla Mudgal Case (1995)**: SC held that religious conversion cannot be used to escape monogamy laws and reiterated the constitutional necessity of enacting a UCC. * **Shayara Bano Case (2017)**: SC struck down instant triple talaq (*talaq-e-biddat*), reinforcing that gender equality in personal laws is integral to constitutional morality. * **Current Affairs Link (Aug 2026):** Supreme Court examined petitions seeking universal application of Section 82 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS - bigamy punishable up to 7 years) and codification of Muslim Personal Law, reinforcing the progressive spirit of Article 44 towards gender-just matrimonial laws. * **21st Law Commission Stand (2018)**: Stated UCC is "neither necessary nor desirable at this stage", but strongly advocated reforming discriminatory provisions within each personal law.
---

sections.heading: Article 45
sections.content:
**Subject:** Provision for early childhood care and education to children below the age of six years.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

*   **Context:** The State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 46
sections.content:
**Subject:** Promotion of educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

*   **Context:** The State shall promote with special care the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections of the people, and, in particular, of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, and shall protect them from social injustice and all forms of exploitation.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 47 of the Indian Constitution
sections.content:
**Part:** Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy)

**Heading:** Duty of the State to raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living and to improve public health

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

**Key Provisions:**
*   The State shall regard the raising of the level of nutrition and the standard of living of its people and the improvement of public health as among its primary duties.
*   In particular, the State shall endeavour to bring about **prohibition of the consumption except for medicinal purposes of intoxicating drinks and of drugs which are injurious to health**.

**Relevance:** Forms the constitutional basis for anti-drug initiatives (like 'Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat'), liquor prohibition laws in various states, and public health policies addressing substance abuse.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 48A — Protection of Environment & Wildlife
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV)
* **Core Concept**: Directs the State to endeavor to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 50 — Separation of Judiciary from Executive
sections.content:
> **Part IV — Directive Principles of State Policy**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text
sections.content:
**50. Separation of judiciary from executive.**

The State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.

---

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
*   **Nature:** This is a **Directive Principle of State Policy (DPSP)** — non-justiciable, meaning it cannot be enforced through courts, but it is fundamental in governance.
*   **Significance:** This is the **only explicit reference to Separation of Powers** in the Indian Constitution.
*   **Purpose:** Ensures that the judiciary operates independently from the executive, particularly at the lower court level where magistrates historically had both executive and judicial functions.
*   **Implementation:** The Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC, now BNSS) provisions for separation of judicial and executive magistrates implement this directive.
*   **Current Status:** Separation has been largely achieved — Judicial Magistrates function under the High Court, while Executive Magistrates function under the State Government (District Administration).

---

sections.heading: UPSC Relevance
sections.content:
*   Prelims: SoP is both implicit and explicit in the Constitution — Art. 50 is the explicit provision.
*   Mains: Discuss how the Indian model of SoP differs from the American (watertight) model; Art. 50 as a DPSP vs. enforceable right.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 51A(g) — Duty to Protect Environment
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A)
* **Core Concept**: Mandates that it is the duty of every citizen of India to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 54 — Election of President (Electoral College)
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: Part V (The Union Executive)
* **Electoral College Composition**:
  1. Elected members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha).
  2. Elected members of Legislative Assemblies (MLAs) of the States.
  3. Elected members of Legislative Assemblies of UTs of Delhi and Puducherry (**70th CAA 1992**).
* **Exclusions**: Nominated members of Parliament/Assemblies, all MLCs, and UT of J&K (not yet incorporated into Art 54).

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 55 — Manner of Election of President & Vote Values
sections.content:
Show Answer * **Category**: Part V (The Union Executive) * **Core Principle**: Uniformity among States and Parity between States and the Union. * **System**: Proportional Representation by Single Transferable Vote (PR-STV) via secret ballot. * **Vote Value Formulas**: * **1 MLA Vote** = $\frac{\text{State Population}}{\text{Total Elected MLAs}} \div 1000$ * **1 MP Vote** = $\frac{\text{Total Value of All MLA Votes}}{\text{Total Elected MPs}}$ * **1971 Census Freeze**: Population is frozen to the 1971 Census until the first census after 2026 (**84th CAA 2001**).
---

sections.heading: Article 71 — Matters Relating to Presidential / VP Elections
sections.content:
Show Answer * **Category**: Part V (The Union Executive) * **Exclusive Jurisdiction**: Supreme Court of India alone inquires into and decides election disputes. Decision is final. * **Vacancy Bar (Art 71(4))**: Election cannot be questioned on the ground of any vacancy in the Electoral College. * **Locus Standi**: Only a candidate or 20+ electors can challenge (*Act of 1952*). * **Art 71(2) Non-Invalidation Rule**: If election is declared void by SC, official acts done prior to declaration remain valid.
---

sections.heading: Article 72 — Power of President to Grant Pardons, etc.
sections.content:
> **Part V — The Union, Chapter I — The Executive**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text
sections.content:
**72. Power of President to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases.**

(1) The President shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence—

   (a) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is by a Court Martial;

   (b) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends;

   (c) in all cases where the sentence is a sentence of death.

(2) Nothing in sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall affect the power conferred by law on any officer of the Armed Forces of the Union to suspend, remit or commute a sentence passed by a Court Martial.

(3) Nothing in sub-clause (c) of clause (1) shall affect the power to suspend, remit or commute a sentence of death exercisable by the Governor of a State under any law for the time being in force.

---

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
*   **Nature:** This is an **executive power** of the President, NOT a judicial function. The President does not sit as a court.
*   **Reason for this power:** The judiciary cannot track how a prisoner has reformed in jail — the executive (through its administrative machinery) can.
*   **Types of clemency powers:**
    *   **Pardon:** Completely absolves the conviction and sentence.
    *   **Commutation:** Substituting one form of punishment for a lighter form.
    *   **Remission:** Reducing the period of sentence without changing its character.
    *   **Respite:** Awarding a lesser sentence in place of one prescribed, on special grounds.
    *   **Reprieve:** Temporary suspension of sentence (especially death sentence) to allow time for appeal.
*   **Scope:** Extends to **all cases** under Union law + all **Court Martial** cases + all **death sentences** (even under State law).
*   **Governor's parallel power:** Article 161 grants similar (but narrower) power to the Governor of a State.

---

sections.heading: UPSC Relevance
sections.content:
*   Prelims: Difference between Pardon, Commutation, Remission, Respite, Reprieve.
*   Mains: Debate on whether the President's pardoning power is subject to Judicial Review (Epuru Sudhakar case, Kehar Singh case).

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 74
sections.content:
**Subject:** Council of Ministers to aid and advise President.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

*   **Context:** States that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 75
sections.content:
**Subject:** Other provisions as to Ministers (Union).

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

*   **Context:** The Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President and the other Ministers shall be appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister. Includes provisions on collective responsibility.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 81 — Composition of Lok Sabha
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: The Union Legislature (Part V)
* **Core Concept**: Defines the composition of the Lok Sabha. Currently capped at **543 elected members** based on the 1971 Census figures.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 82 — Delimitation Commission
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: The Union Legislature (Part V)
* **Core Concept**: Mandates the readjustment of seats and territorial constituencies after every decennial census by a **Delimitation Commission**.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 102
sections.content:
**Subject:** Disqualifications for membership (Parliament).

sections.heading: Article 105 — Powers, Privileges, etc. of the Houses of Parliament and of the Members and Committees thereof
sections.content:
> **Part:** V — The Union
> **Chapter:** II — Parliament
> **Subject:** Parliamentary Privileges

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text (Summary)
sections.content:
- Freedom of speech in Parliament — no MP shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given in Parliament.
- No person shall be liable in respect of the publication of any report, paper, votes or proceedings under the authority of either House.

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
- Provides **Parliamentary Privilege** to MPs.
- Whatever MPs say **on the floor of the house**, or whatever they give/do not give on the floor of the house, **cannot be questioned in any court of law**.
- **However:** To maintain the sanctity of judges and judiciary, MPs **cannot discuss the conduct of judges** on the floor of the house.
- They can discuss **judgments** freely (e.g., discussing Kesavananda Bharati, Golaknath, etc.) but not the **personal conduct** of judges.

sections.heading: Relevance to Checks & Balances (Lecture 3)
sections.content:
- Parliamentary privilege is an instrument through which the Legislature maintains its autonomy.
- The restriction on discussing judicial conduct maintains the **Doctrine of Mutual Respect** between organs.
- Contempt of Court: If someone **obstructs justice** → contempt. But merely discussing/critiquing a judgment is NOT contempt.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 111 — Assent to Bills & Presidential Veto Powers
sections.content:
Show Answer * **Category**: Part V (The Union Legislature) * **President's 3 Options**: Declare Assent, Withhold Assent (**Absolute Veto**), or Return for Reconsideration (**Suspensive Veto**). * **Mandatory Assent**: If a returned Ordinary/Financial Bill is re-passed by Parliament (Simple Majority), President *must* give assent. * **Money Bill Bar (Art 111 Proviso)**: President CANNOT return a Money Bill for reconsideration (no suspensive veto); can only Assent or Withhold. * **Constitutional Amendment Bills**: Assent is mandatory under Art 368(2) (**24th CAA 1971**); no veto power. * **Pocket Veto**: Indefinite non-action due to absence of constitutional time limit.
---

sections.heading: Article 123 of the Indian Constitution
sections.content:
**Part:** Part V (The Union)

**Heading:** Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

**Key Provisions:**
*   If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require.
*   An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament.
*   Every such Ordinance shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament and shall **cease to operate** at the expiration of **six weeks** from the reassembly of Parliament (or if resolutions disapproving it are passed by both Houses, upon the passing of the second of those resolutions).
*   Maximum life of an Ordinance: **6 months and 6 weeks**.

**UPSC Relevance:**
*   Ordinances are the **3rd type of law** in the "Laws of Land" classification.
*   They are **temporary laws** made by the **Executive** (unlike ordinary laws made by Legislature).
*   The President acts on the **aid and advice** of the Council of Ministers (Article 74).

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 124 — Establishment and Constitution of Supreme Court
sections.content:
> **Part V — The Union, Chapter IV — The Union Judiciary**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text (Key Clauses)
sections.content:
**124. Establishment and constitution of Supreme Court.**

(1) There shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, of not more than seven other Judges.

(2) Every Judge of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with such of the Judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Courts in the States as the President may deem necessary for the purpose and shall hold office until he attains the age of sixty-five years:

Provided that in the case of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of India shall always be consulted.

---

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
*   **Original sanctioned strength:** CJI + 7 = 8 judges (1950).
*   Parliament has power to **increase** the number of judges by law (Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956).
*   **Current strength (2026):** CJI + 33 = 34 judges (proposed to increase to 38).
*   **Appointment:** By the President, after consultation with CJI and other SC/HC judges → evolved into the **Collegium System** (Three Judges Cases: 1981, 1993, 1998).
*   **NJAC (National Judicial Appointments Commission)** — established by 99th Amendment + NJAC Act 2014, struck down by SC in 2015 as unconstitutional (violated judicial independence).
*   **Retirement age:** 65 years for SC judges; 62 years for HC judges.
*   **Qualifications:** Must be a citizen of India + (a) Judge of HC for 5 years, or (b) Advocate of HC for 10 years, or (c) Distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President.

---

sections.heading: UPSC Relevance
sections.content:
*   Prelims: Sanctioned strength, Collegium system, NJAC case.
*   Mains: Debate on Collegium vs. NJAC; judicial independence vs. accountability; pendency crisis.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 142 — Supreme Court Plenary Jurisdiction
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: The Union Judiciary (Part V)
* **Core Concept**: Empowers the Supreme Court with extraordinary plenary jurisdiction to pass any decree necessary for doing **"complete justice"** in any cause or matter pending before it.
* **Key Supreme Court Precedents**:
  * *Prem Chand Garg (1962)*: SC held that an order under Article 142 cannot directly violate express Fundamental Rights.
  * *Union Carbide (1991)*: SC ruled that plenary powers under Article 142 are not limited by statutory prohibitions in general laws.
  * *SC Bar Association (1998)*: Clarified that Article 142 is **supplementary**, not supplanting existing statutory law; it cannot bypass express statutory prohibitions of Parliament.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 213 of the Indian Constitution
sections.content:
**Part:** Part VI (The States)

**Heading:** Power of Governor to promulgate Ordinances during recess of State Legislature

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

**Key Provisions:**
*   If at any time, except when the Legislative Assembly of a State is in session (or where there is a Legislative Council, except when both Houses are in session), the Governor is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require.
*   An Ordinance so promulgated shall have the same force and effect as an Act of the State Legislature.
*   Every such Ordinance shall be laid before the State Legislature and shall **cease to operate** at the expiration of **six weeks** from the reassembly of the Legislature.

**UPSC Relevance:**

sections.heading: Article 262 — Adjudication of Disputes Relating to Waters of Inter-State Rivers or River Valleys
sections.content:
> **Part XI — Relations Between the Union and the States, Chapter II — Administrative Relations**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text
sections.content:
**262. Adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter-State rivers or river valleys.**

(1) Parliament may by law provide for the adjudication of any dispute or complaint with respect to the use, distribution or control of the waters of, or in, any inter-State river or river valley.

(2) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may by law provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of any such dispute or complaint as is referred to in clause (1).

---

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
*   **Purpose:** Provides the constitutional basis for resolving inter-State water disputes.
*   **Clause (2) — Bar on SC jurisdiction:** Parliament can exclude the SC and all courts from adjudicating water disputes — a significant exception to judicial review.
*   **Implementing legislation:** **Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956** — provides for the constitution of Water Disputes Tribunals.
*   **Major Tribunals constituted:**
    *   Godavari Water Disputes Tribunal (1969)
    *   Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal (1969)
    *   Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal (1969)
    *   Ravi-Beas Water Tribunal (1986)
    *   **Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (1990)** — award in 2007, modified by SC in 2018.
    *   Mahadayi Water Disputes Tribunal (2010)
*   **Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA):** Constituted in 2018 by the Centre to implement the SC's order on Cauvery water sharing.
*   **Inter-State River Water Disputes (Amendment) Bill, 2019:** Proposes a single permanent tribunal replacing multiple ad-hoc tribunals.

---

sections.heading: UPSC Relevance
sections.content:
*   Prelims: Article 262 provisions, major tribunals, CWMA.
*   Mains: Centre-State relations in water governance; cooperative federalism challenges; SC's role despite Art. 262(2) bar.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 275 — Grants-in-Aid from the Union to Certain States
sections.content:
> **Part XII: Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits — Chapter I (Finance)**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Constitutional Provision
sections.content:
* **Text:** Sums as Parliament may by law provide shall be charged on the **Consolidated Fund of India** in each year as grants-in-aid of the revenues of such States as Parliament may determine to be in need of assistance.
* **Purpose:** Equalization of public services across states with uneven revenue capabilities or special needs (e.g. Tribal welfare, Hill States, demographic disadvantages).
* **Finance Commission Role (Article 280(3)(b)):** The Finance Commission makes recommendations to the President regarding the principles governing grants-in-aid under Article 275.

sections.heading: Key Types of Grants under Article 275
sections.content:
1. **Revenue Deficit Grants (RDG):** Given to States experiencing a gap between revenue expenditure and revenue receipts post-tax devolution.
2. **Sector-Specific Grants:** Targeted funding for health, education, agriculture, etc.
3. **State-Specific / Disaster Relief Grants:** Allocated based on special geographical or demographic challenges.

sections.heading: Cross-References
sections.content:
* **Article 280:** Finance Commission recommendations on Article 275 principles.
* **Article 282:** Discretionary Grants (Outside Finance Commission recommendations).
* **Linkage:** `Fiscal Federalism` $\leftrightarrow$ `16th Finance Commission` $\leftrightarrow$ `Equalization Grants`

</details>

sections.heading: Article 279A — Goods and Services Tax Council (GST Council)
sections.content:
> **Part XII: Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits — Chapter I (Finance)**
> *Inserted by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016.*

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Constitutional Provision
sections.content:
* **Nature:** Joint forum of the Centre and the States constituted by the President within 60 days of enforcement of 101st Amendment.
* **Composition:**
  * Chair: **Union Finance Minister**
  * Members: Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue/Finance + State Finance Ministers / designated Ministers.
* **Voting Mechanism:**
  * Decisions require a **3/4th weighted majority** of members present and voting.
  * Union Government vote weightage = **1/3rd** of total votes cast.
  * All State Governments combined vote weightage = **2/3rds** of total votes cast.

sections.heading: Mandate & Recommendations
sections.content:
* Recommends GST rates, exemptions, threshold limits, model GST laws, and principles of place of supply.
* *Supreme Court Ruling (Union of India v. Mohit Minerals, 2022):* GST Council recommendations are **not binding** on Union and States, but possess persuasive value promoting **cooperative federalism**.

sections.heading: Key Interlinks
sections.content:
* **Article 246A:** Special provision with respect to goods and services tax.
* **Article 269A:** Levy and collection of GST in course of inter-State trade/commerce (IGST).
* **Linkage:** `Fiscal Federalism` $\leftrightarrow$ `GST Collections` $\leftrightarrow$ `101st Amendment`

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 280 — Finance Commission
sections.content:
> **Part XII: Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits — Chapter I (Finance)**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Constitutional Provision
sections.content:
* **Nature:** Quasi-judicial, constitutional body constituted by the **President of India** every 5 years (or earlier).
* **Composition:** Chairman + 4 other members appointed by the President. Qualifications determined by Parliament (Finance Commission Act, 1951).

sections.heading: Key Functions & Mandates
sections.content:
1. **Vertical Devolution (Art 280(3)(a)):** Distribution of net proceeds of taxes between Union and States.
2. **Horizontal Devolution:** Allocation between States of their respective shares of tax proceeds.
3. **Grants-in-Aid Principles (Art 280(3)(b)):** Principles governing grants-in-aid of revenues under **Article 275**.
4. **Local Bodies Grants (Art 280(3)(bb) & (c)):** Measures to augment State Consolidated Funds to supplement Panchayat and Municipality resources (added by 73rd & 74th Amendments).

sections.heading: Key Historical Context & 16th FC
sections.content:
* **16th Finance Commission (FC-16):** Chaired by **Arvind Panagariya** (Constituted Dec 2023; Report covering 2026–31 period).
* **Key Interlinks:** `Vertical Devolution` $\leftrightarrow$ `Horizontal Devolution` $\leftrightarrow$ `Article 275` $\leftrightarrow$ `Fiscal Federalism`

</details>

sections.heading: Article 300A — Right to Property (Constitutional Right)
sections.content:
> **Part:** XII — Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits
> **Subject:** Persons not to be deprived of property save by authority of law

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text
sections.content: No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Originally:** Right to Property was a **Fundamental Right** under Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31.
- **44th Amendment Act, 1978** (Janata Party Government): Converted Right to Property from a **Fundamental Right** to a **Constitutional Right** under Art. 300A.
- This **reduced its status** — it is no longer enforceable under Art. 32 (right to constitutional remedies) but can be enforced under Art. 226 (HC writ jurisdiction).
- **Significance for Socialism:** The existence of Right to Property (even as a constitutional right) proves India is NOT a Marxian-socialist state (which requires NO private property).
- India's Democratic Socialism is **flexible** — allows private property while aiming for equitable distribution through [Art. 39(b)](Article_39b.md) and [Art. 39(c)](Article_39c.md).

sections.heading: Historical Context
sections.content:
- Indira Gandhi's government had issues with Right to Property as a FR because it obstructed land reform legislation.
- The Janata Party government (post-Emergency) amended it to balance individual rights with state's welfare objectives.

</details>

---

sections.heading: Article 312 of the Indian Constitution
sections.content:
**Part:** Part XIV (Services Under the Union and the States)

**Heading:** All-India Services

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

**Key Provisions:**
*   Provides for the creation of one or more All India Services (including an all-India judicial service) common to the Union and the States.
*   The Rajya Sabha must pass a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting declaring that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest to do so.
*   The Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and the Indian Police Service (IPS) are deemed to be services created by Parliament under this article.

**Relevance:** Highly relevant in matters concerning the Indian Police Service (IPS) and their deputation or leadership roles across various Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) and state police departments.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 324 — Superintendence, Direction and Control of Elections
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text (Simplified)
sections.content:
1. The **superintendence, direction and control** of the preparation of electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to Parliament and to the Legislature of every State and of elections to the offices of President and Vice-President shall be **vested in the Election Commission of India (ECI)**.
2. The Election Commission shall consist of the **Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)** and such number of other **Election Commissioners** as the President may from time to time fix.
3. When any other Election Commissioner is so appointed, the **CEC shall act as the Chairman** of the Election Commission.
4. The conditions of service of the CEC and other ECs shall be determined by the President by rule — provided that the CEC shall not be removed except in like manner and on like grounds as a **Judge of the Supreme Court** (i.e., by impeachment under Article 124(4)).
5. The President (or Governor at State level) shall, when so requested by the EC, make available such staff as may be necessary for the discharge of its functions.

sections.heading: Key Points for UPSC
sections.content:
*   ECI is an **independent constitutional body** (not a statutory or executive body).
*   **Plenary powers:** Article 324 gives the EC wide, residuary powers over the entire election process — from preparation of electoral rolls to the conduct and supervision of elections.
*   The EC's powers under Article 324 include the power to:
    *   Prepare and revise electoral rolls.
    *   Notify election schedules.
    *   Enforce the Model Code of Conduct.
    *   Order re-polls, countermand elections.
    *   Register and de-register political parties.
*   **Landmark Case — Mohinder Singh Gill v. CEC (1978):** SC held that Article 324 gives the EC residuary power to act in situations not covered by specific legislation, to ensure free and fair elections.
*   **Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023:** Changed the appointment mechanism — Selection Committee now comprises PM, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by PM.

sections.heading: Article 326 — Elections to the House of the People and to the Legislative Assemblies of States to Be on the Basis of Adult Suffrage
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text (Simplified)
sections.content: The elections to the **House of the People (Lok Sabha)** and to the **Legislative Assembly of every State** shall be on the basis of **adult suffrage**; that is to say, every person who is a **citizen of India** and who is **not less than 18 years of age** on such date as may be fixed by or under any law made by the appropriate Legislature, and is not otherwise disqualified under the Constitution or any law on grounds of non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime, or corrupt or illegal practice, shall be entitled to be **registered as a voter** at any such election.

sections.heading: Key Points for UPSC
sections.content:
*   **Universal Adult Suffrage (UAS):** India adopted UAS from its very first general election in 1951–52 — a radical democratic choice given that many Western democracies took centuries to extend suffrage universally.
*   **Voting age was reduced from 21 to 18 years** by the **61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988** (during Rajiv Gandhi's government).
*   **Disqualification grounds:** Non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime, corrupt or illegal practice.
*   The preparation and revision of **electoral rolls** under this Article is supervised by the Election Commission under [Article 324](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_324.md).
*   **Part XVI** of the Constitution (Articles 324–329) deals with elections.

sections.heading: Article 368 of the Indian Constitution
sections.content:
**Part:** Part XX (Amendment of the Constitution)

**Heading:** Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

**Key Provisions:**
*   Notwithstanding anything in the Constitution, Parliament may, in exercise of its **constituent power**, amend by way of **addition, variation, or repeal** any provision of the Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.
*   **Procedure:**
    1.  An amendment can be initiated only by the introduction of a **Bill** (Constitution Amendment Bill — CAB) in **either House of Parliament** (not in State Legislatures).
    2.  The Bill must be passed by a majority of the total membership of each House AND by a majority of **not less than two-thirds** of the members present and voting.
    3.  For **federal subjects** (provisions affecting Centre-State relations), the Bill must also be ratified by **not less than one-half of the State Legislatures**.
    4.  When the Bill is passed and ratified (if required), it shall be presented to the President, who shall give his **assent** to the Bill. The Constitution shall thereupon stand amended.
*   **No Bill can be introduced by a private member** — it must be a Government Bill or can be introduced by any member.

**UPSC Relevance:**
*   Central to the concept of the Constitution being **organic in nature** (Living Document).
*   Represents the **Constituent Legislative Power (CLP)** of Parliament — distinct from Ordinary Legislative Power (OLP).
*   JLN's philosophy: *"Stagnancy leads to irrelevancy"* → legally codified by Dr. Ambedkar under Art. 368.
*   India is **both rigid and flexible** depending on the subject:
    *   Federal subjects → 2/3 Parliament + 1/2 States → **Rigid**
    *   Non-federal subjects → 2/3 Parliament only → **Flexible**
*   **106 amendments** passed so far (106th Amendment: Women's reservation in legislative bodies).

**Related Doctrines:**
*   **Basic Structure Doctrine** (*Kesavananda Bharati Case, 1973*): Parliament can amend any provision but cannot alter the **basic structure** of the Constitution. (To be covered in future lectures.)

</details>

sections.heading: Article 111: Assent to Bills & Presidential Veto Powers
sections.content:
> **Tags:** `[GS-2: Executive & Legislature - Legislative Powers of President, Part V Chapter 2]`
> **Last Updated:** 2026-08-17
> **Related Notes:** [Polity_Lec2_AbheyKumar_President.md](../GS_Polity_VR_Notes/Polity_Lec2_AbheyKumar_President.md)

sections.heading: Active Recall Questions
sections.content:
What are the three constitutional choices of the President when an Ordinary Bill is presented for assent under Article 111? 1. **Declare Assent:** Bill becomes an Act (law). 2. **Withhold Assent (Absolute Veto):** Bill dies immediately and permanently. (Exercised on advice of CoM — e.g., *PEPSU Appropriation Bill 1954*, *MP Salaries Bill 1991*). 3. **Return for Reconsideration (Suspensive Veto):** Bill is sent back with/without presidential recommendations.
What happens if Parliament passes a returned Bill again? - If the Bill is passed again by both Houses (with or without amendment) by a **Simple Majority**, the President **"shall not withhold assent therefrom"** (assent becomes mandatory). - Example: *MP Prevention of Disqualification Bill, 2006* returned by Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam, re-passed by Parliament, and subsequently assented.
Can the President return a Money Bill for reconsideration under Article 111? - **NO (Article 111 Proviso):** The proviso to Article 111 explicitly states that the President may return the bill *"if it is not a Money Bill"*. The President has **NO power of suspensive veto over Money Bills**. For a Money Bill, the President can only either give Assent or Withhold Assent.
Does the President have any veto power over Constitutional Amendment (CA) Bills? - **NO:** Under the **24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971** amending Article 368(2), when a CA Bill is presented, the President **"shall give his assent"**. The President cannot withhold, return, or pocket a CA Bill.
What is a "Pocket Veto" and where does it originate? - Article 111 does NOT prescribe any time limit within which the President must declare his decision. - By keeping the bill pending indefinitely on his desk without declaring assent, withholding assent, or returning it, the President exercises an informal **Pocket Veto** (e.g., Zail Singh and the *Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986*).

sections.heading: Article 123 of the Indian Constitution
sections.content:
**Part:** Part V (The Union)

**Heading:** Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament

<details>

**Key Provisions:**
*   If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require.
*   An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament.
*   Every such Ordinance shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament and shall **cease to operate** at the expiration of **six weeks** from the reassembly of Parliament (or if resolutions disapproving it are passed by both Houses, upon the passing of the second of those resolutions).
*   Maximum life of an Ordinance: **6 months and 6 weeks**.

**UPSC Relevance:**
*   Ordinances are the **3rd type of law** in the "Laws of Land" classification.
*   They are **temporary laws** made by the **Executive** (unlike ordinary laws made by Legislature).
*   The President acts on the **aid and advice** of the Council of Ministers (Article 74).

</details>

sections.heading: Article 124 — Establishment and Constitution of Supreme Court
sections.content:
> **Part V — The Union, Chapter IV — The Union Judiciary**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text (Key Clauses)
sections.content:
**124. Establishment and constitution of Supreme Court.**

(1) There shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, of not more than seven other Judges.

(2) Every Judge of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with such of the Judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Courts in the States as the President may deem necessary for the purpose and shall hold office until he attains the age of sixty-five years:

Provided that in the case of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of India shall always be consulted.

---

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content: * **Original sanctioned strength:** CJI + 7 = 8 judges (1950). * Parliament has power to **increase** the number of judges by law (Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956). * **Current strength (2026):** CJI + 33 = 34 judges (proposed to increase to 38). * **Appointment:** By the President, after consultation with CJI and other SC/HC judges → evolved into the **Collegium System** (Three Judges Cases: 1981, 1993, 1998). * **NJAC (National Judicial Appointments Commission)** — established by 99th Amendment + NJAC Act 2014, struck down by SC in 2015 as unconstitutional (violated judicial independence). * **Retirement age:** 65 years for SC judges; 62 years for HC judges. * **Qualifications:** Must be a citizen of India + (a) Judge of HC for 5 years, or (b) Advocate of HC for 10 years, or (c) Distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President. * **Judges Cases Matrix (Evolution of Collegium):** * **First Judges Case (1981 — *S.P. Gupta*):** Executive primacy; 'Consultation' does not mean concurrence. * **Second Judges Case (1993 — *SCAORA*):** Judicial primacy established; collective opinion of CJI + 2 senior-most judges; 'Consultation' = Concurrence. * **Third Judges Case (1998 — *Special Reference 1 of 1998*):** Expanded to 5-member collegium (CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges) for SC appointments and transfers. * **Fourth Judges Case (2015 — *NJAC Case*):** 99th CAA 2014 & NJAC Act struck down (4:1) for violating Judicial Independence as part of the Basic Structure. * **Transparency & Accountability Jurisprudence (Modern Debates):** * **Justice Ujjal Bhuyan's Observation (2026):** Openness in the collegium process is essential to strengthen public confidence and ensure merit as the governing principle. * ***CPIO vs Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019):*** 5-Judge Bench held the Office of the CJI is a "Public Authority" under Section 2(h) of the RTI Act, 2005; judicial independence is not a shield against transparency. * ***MediaOne Judgment (2023):*** SC held sealed-cover secrecy is "antithetical to a transparent and accountable system", highlighting the need to avoid opacity in judicial appointments. * ***Umadevi Doctrine (2006):*** SC ruled that public appointments under Articles 14 & 16 must follow open, transparent procedures rather than backdoor methods. * **Global Models:** UK Judicial Appointments Commission (publicly advertised vacancies & structured interviews) and South Africa Judicial Service Commission (public nominations & televised interviews). ---

sections.heading: UPSC Relevance
sections.content:
*   Prelims: Sanctioned strength, Collegium system, NJAC case, Qualifications, RTI applicability.
*   Mains: Debate on Collegium vs. NJAC; judicial independence vs. accountability; transparency and eligibility matrix; "Uncle Judges" syndrome; comparative appointment models (UK JAC / South Africa JSC).

</details>

sections.heading: Article 13 of the Indian Constitution
sections.content:
**Part:** Part III (Fundamental Rights)

**Heading:** Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

**Key Provisions:**
*   Declares that all laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of the Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of Part III, shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void.
*   The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by Part III and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void.
*   Provides the basis for **Judicial Review**. Laws can be declared *ultra vires* (beyond powers) if they violate Fundamental Rights.

**Relevance:** Frequently invoked when challenging legislative or executive actions (like the CAPF Act) that allegedly violate constitutional provisions or fundamental rights.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 14 — Right to Equality
sections.content: Show Answer * **Category**: Fundamental Rights (Part III) * **Core Concept**: Prohibits arbitrary State action and discriminatory exemptions without a rational nexus. Guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. * **Supreme Court Precedent**: Any executive exemption power must satisfy the *Intelligible Differentia* & *Rational Nexus* tests (*E.P. Royappa vs State of Tamil Nadu*). * **Context**: SC warned that ad-hoc designation of specific case categories without rational classification risks violating equal protection. * **Personal Laws & Section 82 BNS Scrutiny (Aug 2026):** Supreme Court examined petitions challenging Section 2 of Shariat Act 1937 under Article 14 for creating arbitrary exemptions permitting polygamy for Muslim men while non-Muslims face up to 7 years imprisonment under Section 82 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) for bigamy.

sections.heading: Article 142 — Supreme Court Plenary Jurisdiction
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: The Union Judiciary (Part V)
* **Core Concept**: Empowers the Supreme Court with extraordinary plenary jurisdiction to pass any decree necessary for doing **"complete justice"** in any cause or matter pending before it.
* **Key Supreme Court Precedents**:
  * *Prem Chand Garg (1962)*: SC held that an order under Article 142 cannot directly violate express Fundamental Rights.
  * *Union Carbide (1991)*: SC ruled that plenary powers under Article 142 are not limited by statutory prohibitions in general laws.
  * *SC Bar Association (1998)*: Clarified that Article 142 is **supplementary**, not supplanting existing statutory law; it cannot bypass express statutory prohibitions of Parliament.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 148 — Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text & Constitutional Provisions (Simplified)
sections.content:
1. **Establishment & Appointment:** There shall be a Comptroller and Auditor-General of India (CAG) who shall be appointed by the **President by warrant under his hand and seal**.
2. **Tenure & Removal:** The CAG shall only be removed from office in **like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court** (i.e. under Article 124(4) on proved misbehaviour or incapacity via special majority in both Houses of Parliament).
3. **Oath:** The CAG takes an oath before the President in accordance with the **Third Schedule**.
4. **Post-Retirement Ineligibility:** The CAG is **not eligible for further office** either under the Government of India or under the Government of any State after retirement (guarantees constitutional independence).
5. **Administrative Expenses:** The administrative expenses of the CAG's office, including all salaries, allowances, and pensions, shall be **charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India** (not subject to parliamentary vote).

sections.heading: Key Points for UPSC Prelims & Mains
sections.content:
* **Guardian of Public Purse:** Dr. B.R. Ambedkar termed the CAG as *"the most important officer under the Constitution of India"* and one of the four bulwarks of the democratic system (alongside SC, UPSC, and ECI).
* **Term of Office:** 6 years or up to 65 years of age, whichever is earlier (prescribed by CAG's DPC Act, 1971).
* **Salary & Conditions of Service:** Determined by Parliament by law (equal to that of a Supreme Court judge) and cannot be varied to CAG's disadvantage after appointment.
* **Audit Mandate:** Audits all receipts and expenditures from the Consolidated Fund of India and each State/UT with Legislative Assembly, Contingency Funds, and Public Accounts.

sections.heading: Article 149 — Duties and Powers of the Comptroller and Auditor-General
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text & Constitutional Provisions (Simplified)
sections.content:
* The CAG shall perform such duties and exercise such powers in relation to the **accounts of the Union and of the States** and of any other authority or body as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament.
* **Governing Legislation:** Enacted under this article, the **Comptroller and Auditor-General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 (DPC Act)** governs the audit mandate.

sections.heading: Key Points for UPSC
sections.content:
* **Three Types of Audits Conducted:**
  1. **Financial Audit / Regularity Audit:** Verifying that accounts are properly kept and financial statements present a true and fair view.
  2. **Compliance Audit / Legality Audit:** Ensuring that expenditure conforms to the laws, rules, and budgetary sanctions enacted by the legislature.
  3. **Performance / Value for Money (VFM) Audit:** Assessing the Economy, Efficiency, and Effectiveness (3 Es) of government programmes and schemes (e.g. Green India Mission, MGNREGS, Defense procurements).
* **Audit of Bodies/Authorities:** Substantially financed bodies, government companies under the Companies Act, and statutory corporations whose acts provide for CAG audit.
* **Separation of Accounts from Audit:** In 1976, accounting was separated from auditing at the Union level (CGA under Ministry of Finance prepares accounts; CAG only audits). At State level, CAG still handles both compilation of accounts and audit in most States.

sections.heading: Article 15 — Prohibition of Discrimination on Grounds of Religion, Race, Caste, Sex or Place of Birth
sections.content:
> **Part:** III — Fundamental Rights > **Subject:** Right to Equality
Show Answer * **Category**: Fundamental Rights (Part III) — Specific Application of Article 14 * **Article 15(1)**: The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds **only** of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them. * **Article 15(2)**: Horizontal application — No citizen shall be subjected to any disability, liability, restriction or condition regarding access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment, or the use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads, and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds. * **Article 15(3)**: Special provisions for **women and children** (protective discrimination / affirmative action). * **Article 15(4)**: Added by 1st Constitutional Amendment Act 1951 (post-*State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan*) — Special provisions for advancement of Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (SEBCs), SCs, and STs. (`MST-073` **held** 11 Sep Ghost Recall. `CSE-2023-Q34` **held** 12 Sep evening: 1st Amendment = the one widely believed to overcome FR judicial interpretations.) * **Article 15(5)**: Added by 93rd Constitutional Amendment Act 2005 — Reservation in educational institutions (aided or unaided, except minority educational institutions under Art 30). * **Article 15(6)**: Added by 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act 2019 — Up to 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS). * **Current Affairs & Gender Justice Link (Aug 2026):** Section 2 of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937 challenged before Supreme Court for violating Article 15 by permitting polygamy for Muslim men while subjecting non-Muslims to criminal liability under Section 82 BNS (bigamy up to 7 years), creating religion- and sex-based discrimination against women.

sections.heading: Article 151 — Audit Reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text & Constitutional Provisions (Simplified)
sections.content:
1. **Union Accounts:** The reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India relating to the accounts of the Union shall be **submitted to the President**, who shall cause them to be **laid before each House of Parliament**.
2. **State Accounts:** The reports of the CAG relating to the accounts of a State shall be **submitted to the Governor of the State**, who shall cause them to be **laid before the Legislature of the State**.

sections.heading: Key Points for UPSC
sections.content:
* **Laying in Legislature:** CAG does not submit reports directly to Parliament/Legislature; reports are submitted to the Executive Head (President/Governor) who is constitutionally obligated to lay them before the respective Houses.
* **Role of Public Accounts Committee (PAC):**
  * Once laid on the table of Parliament, CAG audit reports are referred to the **Public Accounts Committee (PAC)** for detailed examination.
  * The CAG acts as a **"friend, philosopher, and guide"** to the PAC during committee scrutiny.
* **Impact of Performance Audits:** Highlights systemic administrative deficiencies, scheme convergence gaps, resource leakages, and cost overruns (e.g., CAG Performance Audit on Green India Mission 2026, 2G spectrum, Coal allocation).

sections.heading: Article 16 — Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: Fundamental Rights (Part III)
* **Article 16**: Equality of opportunity in **public employment**.
* **Article 16(3)**: **Only Parliament** has the exclusive power to prescribe residence requirements for public employment. State Legislatures do NOT have this power. (`MST-074` **held** 11 Sep Ghost Recall.)
* **Article 16(4)**: State may reserve posts for backward classes inadequately represented.

sections.heading: Update — 10 September 2026 (UPSC CSE Prelims 2023)
sections.content:
`CSE-2023-Q40` **missed** (`MST-069`). SC has held that reservation under **16(4)** can be limited by **Article 335** for maintenance of efficiency of administration. **Article 335 does not define** “efficiency of administration.” Class still: 16(4) = public-employment reservation for SC/ST/OBC. **Held 12 Sep evening.**

sections.heading: Article 161 — Power of Governor to Grant Pardons, etc.
sections.content:
> **Part VI — The States, Chapter II — The Executive**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text
sections.content:
**161. Power of Governor to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases.**

The Governor of a State shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends.

---

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
*   **Parallel to Article 72** — but narrower in scope.
*   **Scope:** Only offences under **State law** (matters within State executive power).
*   **Cannot pardon death sentence:** Unlike the President, the Governor CANNOT pardon a death sentence. Only the **President** can pardon death sentences (Art 72(1)(c)).
*   **Can commute death sentence:** Governor CAN commute death → life imprisonment (changes nature, not removes conviction).
*   **No Court Martial jurisdiction:** Unlike the President (who is Supreme Commander of Armed Forces), Governor has no power over Court Martial sentences.
*   **Court hierarchy irrelevant:** Whether the sentence was passed by High Court, Supreme Court, or any court — if the offence is under State law, Governor has jurisdiction. Court hierarchy does not matter.

---

sections.heading: President (Art 72) vs Governor (Art 161) Comparison
sections.content:
| Feature | President (Art 72) | Governor (Art 161) |
|---------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Law scope | Union law | State law |
| Court Martial | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |
| Death sentence — Pardon | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |
| Death sentence — Commute | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |
| Applicable courts | All courts | All courts |
| Discretion word | NOT in constitution | Explicitly in Art 163 |

---

sections.heading: UPSC Relevance
sections.content: * Prelims: "Governor cannot pardon death sentence" — TRUE. "Governor has no mercy powers" — FALSE (common trap). * Mains: Compare mercy powers of President vs Governor; discuss whether Governor's clemency power is subject to judicial review. * **UPSC Trap:** "Governor cannot pardon" does NOT mean Governor has zero mercy powers. Governor can commute, remit, respite, reprieve — Governor specifically cannot **pardon death sentence** but can **commute** it (death → life).

sections.heading: Article 162 — Executive Power of a State
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

* **Category**: The State Executive (Part VI)
* **Core Concept**: The executive power of a State extends to the matters with respect to which the Legislature of the State has power to make laws. (e.g., used by states to argue their power to grant jobs via executive action).

</details>

sections.heading: Article 163
sections.content:
**Subject:** Council of Ministers to aid and advise Governor.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

*   **Context:** States that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Chief Minister at the head to aid and advise the Governor in the exercise of his functions, except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 164
sections.content:
**Subject:** Other provisions as to Ministers (States).

<details>

*   **Context:** The Chief Minister shall be appointed by the Governor and the other Ministers shall be appointed by the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister. Includes provisions on collective responsibility to the State Legislative Assembly.
