sections.heading: Article 172 — Duration of State Legislatures
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text (Simplified)
sections.content:
1. **Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha):** Every Legislative Assembly of every State, unless sooner dissolved, shall continue for **five years** from the date appointed for its first meeting and no longer and the expiration of the said period of 5 years shall operate as a dissolution of the Assembly:
   * **Proviso (National Emergency):** While a Proclamation of Emergency (Article 352) is in operation, the said period may be extended by Parliament by law for a period not exceeding **one year at a time** and not extending beyond **six months** after the Proclamation has ceased to operate.
2. **Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad):** The Legislative Council of a State shall **not be subject to dissolution**, but as nearly as possible **one-third of the members** thereof shall retire as soon as may be on the expiration of every second year in accordance with the provisions made by Parliament by law.

sections.heading: Key Points for UPSC
sections.content: * **Exact Mirror of Article 83 at State Level:** Legislative Assembly has a 5-year tenure; Legislative Council (in bicameral states) is a permanent body with 1/3rd members retiring every 2 years. * **Premature Dissolution:** The Governor has the power to dissolve the Legislative Assembly under [Article 174(2)(b)](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_174.md), normally on the aid and advice of the Chief Minister/Council of Ministers. * **Extension Mechanism:** Note that only **Parliament by law** (not the State Legislature itself) can extend the tenure of a State Legislative Assembly during a National Emergency under Article 352. * **One Nation One Election (ONOE) Implication:** Any attempt to synchronise State Assemblies with Lok Sabha requires amending Article 172(1) — introducing provisions for early dissolution of ongoing terms or truncated midterm assemblies serving only the remainder of the 5-year national cycle. Requires ratification by ≥50% of State Legislatures under Article 368(2) proviso.

sections.heading: Article 19 — Right to Freedom
sections.content: Show Answer * **Category**: Fundamental Rights (Part III) * **Article 19(1)(a)**: Guarantees Freedom of Speech and Expression (source of Right to Information). SC in Aug 2026 DPDP Act hearing noted journalists are not a "special category" with unreserved access to personal data over privacy laws. * **Article 19(2)**: Restricts 19(1)(a) on 8 grounds: (i) Sovereignty & Integrity of India, (ii) Security of State, (iii) Friendly relations with foreign States, (iv) Public Order, (v) Decency or Morality, (vi) Contempt of Court, (vii) Defamation, (viii) Incitement to an offence. In blasphemy and hate speech jurisprudence (Section 295A IPC / Section 299 BNS), courts have cautioned against the 'Heckler's Veto' and pre-emptive censorship. Per the 2016 Madras HC ruling (Perumal Murugan case), the constitutional mandate is to protect free expression against mob censorship, requiring speech restrictions to satisfy a direct 'spark in a powder keg' test (Shreya Singhal / S. Rangarajan) rather than penalizing rational critique or progressive social reform. * **Article 19(1)(b)**: Guarantees citizens the right to assemble peaceably and without arms. SC in NEET protest FRS hearing (Aug 2026) highlighted that indiscriminate biometric surveillance and facial recognition at demonstration sites must be tested for impermissible "chilling effect" on peaceful democratic assembly. * **Article 19(3)**: Restricts 19(1)(b) on 2 specific grounds only: **(i) Sovereignty and integrity of India, or (ii) Public order**. * **Article 19(1)(c)**: Guarantees citizens the right to form associations, unions, or non-governmental organizations (NGOs), including the right to function and seek funding. * **Article 19(4)**: Restricts 19(1)(c) on 3 specific grounds: **(i) Sovereignty & Integrity of India, (ii) Public Order, or (iii) Morality**.

sections.heading: Article 2: Admission or Establishment of New States
sections.content:
> **Tags:** `[GS-2: Constitution - Part I Union & Territory, External Arrangement]`
> **Last Updated:** 2026-08-17
> **Related Notes:** [Indian_Polity_Constitution.md — Lecture 05](../GS_Polity_VR_Notes/Indian_Polity_Constitution.md)

sections.heading: Active Recall Questions
sections.content:
<details><summary>What does Article 2 empower Parliament to do?</summary>

- Parliament by law can **admit** into the Union or **establish** new states as per conditions it deems fit.
- Article 2 deals with **external arrangement** — territory **outside** India.
</details>

<details><summary>What is the difference between "Admission" and "Establishment" under Art 2?</summary>

- **Admission:** Adding a **self-contained unit** (pre-existing territory with its own identity) to India. The territory had an identity before joining.
- **Establishment:** Creating/demarcating a **new territory** where none existed before, and adding it to India. India itself creates the identity.
- **Analogy:** A student taking *admission* at Vajiram (pre-existing identity) vs. Vajiram *establishing* a new branch (created from scratch).
</details>

<details><summary>Has Article 2 ever been used in India's history? Why/Why not?</summary>

- **No.** Article 2 has **never been used**.
- **Reason:** Per Re Berubari Union (1960), to admit territory, you must first **acquire** it. Acquiring requires **special majority** (sovereign power under international law). Since special majority automatically subsumes simple majority (needed for admission), acquiring takes care of admission in one step.
- Therefore, Art 2 became **USELESS** (not meaningless — the provision exists but circumstances prevent its use).
- Sikkim and Goa were NOT admitted under Art 2 — they were **acquired** first.
</details>

<details><summary>Does Article 2 require the pre-conditions (President's recommendation & State opinion)?</summary>

- **No.** Art 2 does NOT require the pre-conditions that Art 3 requires.
- Pre-conditions (Recommendation of President + Opinion of State) apply only to Art 3 Bills.
</details>

<!-- 2026-08-17: Created from Polity Lecture 05 — Art 2 Admission vs Establishment, External Arrangement, USELESS not meaningless (Berubari Union reasoning). -->

sections.heading: Article 20 — Protection in Respect of Conviction for Offences
sections.content:
> **Part III: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35)**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Constitutional Provisions & 3 Guarantees
sections.content:
1. **Article 20(1) — Protection Against Ex-Post Facto Law:**
   * No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of commission.
   * Applies **only to criminal laws**, not civil liabilities or tax laws.

2. **Article 20(2) — Protection Against Double Jeopardy (*Nemo Debet Bis Vexari*):**
   * No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the **same offence** more than once.
   * Protection applies only before a **court of law or judicial tribunal**. Departmental or administrative proceedings do not attract Article 20(2).

3. **Article 20(3) — Protection Against Self-Incrimination:**
   * No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.
   * Extends to oral and documentary evidence. Does not cover physical evidence (blood samples, thumb impressions).

sections.heading: Key Recent Judicial Ruling & Statutory Distinctions
sections.content: * **PMLA vs Predicate Offence (Karnataka HC 2026):** Prosecution under PMLA after conviction for a predicate/scheduled offence does NOT violate Article 20(2) or Sec 300 CrPC, because money laundering under PMLA is an independent statutory offence. * **PMLA & Acquittal Trap (Aug 2026 MCQ):** While a person cannot be prosecuted under PMLA if they are finally acquitted of the predicate offence (as proceeds of crime cease to exist), this protection is NOT strictly due to Article 20(2) Double Jeopardy. Double jeopardy under Art 20(2) only protects against being prosecuted for the *same* offence twice; PMLA and predicate offences are distinct in law. * **Article 20(2) vs Section 300 CrPC / BNSS (*Autrefois Acquit* vs *Autrefois Convict*):** Article 20(2) strictly requires the person to have been *both prosecuted and punished* (*autrefois convict*). If merely acquitted, Article 20(2) offers no constitutional protection. However, **Section 300 CrPC / BNSS provides broader statutory protection** by barring a retrial for the same offence even after a previous acquittal (*autrefois acquit*).

sections.heading: Non-Suspendable Feature
sections.content: * Under **Article 359** (as amended by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978), **Article 20 and Article 21 CANNOT be suspended** even during a National Emergency under Article 352.

sections.heading: Key Interlinks
sections.content:
`Fundamental Rights` $\leftrightarrow$ `Article 21` $\leftrightarrow$ `Double Jeopardy` $\leftrightarrow$ `PMLA 2002` $\leftrightarrow$ `BNSS Sec 337 / CrPC Sec 300`

</details>

sections.heading: Article 21 — Right to Life and Personal Liberty
sections.content: Show Answer * **Category**: Fundamental Rights (Part III) * **Environment**: The Supreme Court has interpreted the Right to Life to encompass the right to a clean, pollution-free, and healthy environment. * **Due Process**: SC cautioned against imposing rigid, statutory trial deadlines (e.g., in complex paper leak cases) because rushed trials compromise the right to a fair trial and defense preparation. * **Right to Privacy vs. RTI**: Puttaswamy (2017) established Right to Privacy under Art 21 to protect citizens against State incursion. SC (Aug 2026) is hearing petitions challenging Sec 44(3) DPDP Act for turning privacy on its head by shielding State/public officers from RTI disclosure under Sec 8(1)(j) RTI Act. * **Nuclear Disasters & Absolute Liability**: In SHANTI Act 2025 hearing (Aug 2026), SC held that statutory liability caps cannot restrict Constitutional Courts under Art 32/226 from awarding suitable compensation against legal torts violating Right to Life (Art 21), upholding the Absolute Liability principle (M.C. Mehta). * **Biometric Surveillance & Proportionality**: In NEET protest FRS hearing (Aug 2026), SC held that police deployment of Facial Recognition Systems (FRS) and automated biometric surveillance at public demonstrations must satisfy the 4-prong Proportionality Test under Article 21 (Legality, Legitimate Aim, Suitability, Necessity/Least Intrusive Means, and Balancing) to prevent indiscriminate mass profiling. * **Dignified Livelihood & Minimum Wages**: In MGNREGA / VB-G RAM G Act proceedings (Aug 2026), SC considered the nexus between Article 21 (dignified existence / Olga Tellis livelihood) and statutory minimum wages, reaffirming that economic distress forcing labour below minimum wages violates dignity and transitions into Article 23 forced labour. * **Hazardous Mining & Ecological Buffer Rights**: In Meghalaya uranium mining resolution and Kaziranga ESZ debates (Aug 2026), Article 21's guarantee to a pollution-free and hazard-free environment was reinforced alongside Sixth Schedule tribal customary land sovereignty (SC Dimasa 2019) and ecological buffer protection under EPA 1986. * **Marital autonomy (Sep 2026):** SC (CJI Surya Kant / Justice Joymalya Bagchi, 9 Sep 2026) recognised a married woman’s individual autonomy and that involuntary sex in marriage makes her a victim, but asked whether courts can prosecute husbands for ‘rape’ while IPC 375 / BNS 63 still exempt marital rape. Full lock: `CA-260910-03`.

sections.heading: Article 213 of the Indian Constitution
sections.content:
**Part:** Part VI (The States)

**Heading:** Power of Governor to promulgate Ordinances during recess of State Legislature

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

**Key Provisions:**
*   If at any time, except when the Legislative Assembly of a State is in session (or where there is a Legislative Council, except when both Houses are in session), the Governor is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require.
*   An Ordinance so promulgated shall have the same force and effect as an Act of the State Legislature.
*   Every such Ordinance shall be laid before the State Legislature and shall **cease to operate** at the expiration of **six weeks** from the reassembly of the Legislature.
*   The Governor cannot promulgate an Ordinance without **instructions from the President** if a Bill containing the same provisions would require the previous sanction of the President under the Constitution.

**UPSC Relevance:**
*   State-level counterpart of Article 123 (President's Ordinance power).
*   Part of the 3rd type of law in the "Laws of Land" classification — Ordinances made by Executive.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 21A
sections.content:
**Subject:** Right to education.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

*   **Context:** The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 23 — Prohibition of Traffic in Human Beings and Forced Labour
sections.content:
> **Part:** III — Fundamental Rights (Right against Exploitation)
> **Subject:** Prohibition of traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text
sections.content:
(1) Traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour are prohibited and any contravention of this provision shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.
(2) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from imposing compulsory service for public purposes, and in imposing such service the State shall not make any discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class or any of them.

sections.heading: Key Points & Constitutional Scope
sections.content:
* **Available Against Both State and Private Individuals:** Unlike many fundamental rights that operate only against State action, Article 23 protects individuals against both the State and private entities.
* **Positive Injunction on State:** Imposes an obligation on the State to eradicate practices of human trafficking, *begar*, bonded labour, and forced labour.
* **Exceptions [Clause (2)]:** The State can impose compulsory public service (e.g., military conscription or disaster response), provided no discrimination is made based *only* on religion, race, caste, or class (gender is not listed in Clause 2, allowing gender-specific compulsory services if rational).

sections.heading: Landmark Judicial Precedents & Evolution
sections.content: * **People's Union for Democratic Rights (PUDR) v. Union of India (1982) [Asiad Workers Case]:** * Supreme Court held that "force" under Article 23 is not restricted to physical violence or legal coercion. * **Economic Compulsion:** When poverty, hunger, or destitution forces a worker to accept remuneration below the statutory minimum wage, it constitutes **"forced labour"** within the meaning of Article 23. * **Sanjit Roy v. State of Rajasthan (1983):** * SC struck down provisions of the *Rajasthan Famine Relief Works Employees Act* that allowed paying famine-affected workers less than the minimum wage. * Held that the State cannot take advantage of the helpless condition of citizens struck by drought or famine to extract labour below statutory minimum wages. * **Rural Work & Minimum Wages Scrutiny (Aug 2026):** In the MGNREGA / VB-G RAM G Act hearing (Aug 2026), the Supreme Court examined the argument that rural work provided below statutory minimum wage floors violates Article 23, reaffirming that economic vulnerability cannot be leveraged by the State to dilute wage entitlements. * **Delink from Minimum Wages Act, 1948 (Sep 2026 CA):** MGNREGA notified wages were delinked from the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 from 2009, so scheme wages need not equal the statutory minimum — the *Sanjit Roy* / *PUDR* Article 23 floor is the constitutional argument against that gap.

sections.heading: Article 246
sections.content:
**Subject:** Subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

*   **Context:** Deals with the division of legislative powers between the Union and the States (Union List, State List, and Concurrent List in the Seventh Schedule).

sections.heading: Article 25 — Freedom of Conscience and Free Profession, Practice and Propagation of Religion
sections.content:
> **Part:** III — Fundamental Rights
> **Subject:** Right to Freedom of Religion

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text (Summary)
sections.content: Subject to public order, morality and health, all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion.

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
- Part of **Articles 25–28** which collectively guarantee **Right to Freedom of Religion**.
- Gives every individual (not just citizens) the right to be **religious** as well as to be an **atheist**.
- This is a right of **individuals/Indians**, NOT a state policy.
- **Critical distinction (from Lecture 3):** "Secular" in the Preamble is an **Ideal for India** (the state), NOT for Indians. Indians have the FR to be religious under Art. 25–28.
- Subject to reasonable restrictions: public order, morality, health, and other provisions of Part III.

sections.heading: Relevance to Secularism
sections.content: - Western Secularism = separation of religion from politics (state has NO relation with religion). - Indian/Eastern Secularism = complex triangular relationship between Religion, Individual, and State — the state does not separate itself from religion but treats all religions equally. - Art. 25 ensures individuals can freely practice their religion while the state remains neutral/equidistant. - **Personal Laws & ERP Test (Aug 2026):** Article 25 is expressly subject to other provisions of Part III (Articles 14, 15, 21). Polygamy under Section 2 of Shariat Act 1937 is permissible/customary but not an Essential Religious Practice (ERP), making it subject to State regulatory power for social welfare and gender reform under Article 25(2)(b). - **Article 25(2)(b) & Social Reform Supremacy (Aug 2026):** Article 25(2)(b) explicitly saves the State's power to provide for social welfare and reform. As Dr. B.R. Ambedkar declared in the Constituent Assembly (Dec 2, 1948), religion cannot claim an expansive veto over progressive social legislation or personal law reform. Consequently, state anti-superstition enactments (e.g., Sati Act 1987, Maharashtra Act 2013, Karnataka Act 2017) and rationalist critiques of dogma take constitutional precedence over subjective religious hurt feelings under penal laws.

sections.heading: Article 262 — Adjudication of Disputes Relating to Waters of Inter-State Rivers or River Valleys
sections.content:
> **Part XI — Relations Between the Union and the States, Chapter II — Administrative Relations**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text
sections.content:
**262. Adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter-State rivers or river valleys.**

(1) Parliament may by law provide for the adjudication of any dispute or complaint with respect to the use, distribution or control of the waters of, or in, any inter-State river or river valley.

(2) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may by law provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of any such dispute or complaint as is referred to in clause (1).

---

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
*   **Purpose:** Provides the constitutional basis for resolving inter-State water disputes.
*   **Clause (2) — Bar on SC jurisdiction:** Parliament can exclude the SC and all courts from adjudicating water disputes — a significant exception to judicial review.
*   **Implementing legislation:** **Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956** — provides for the constitution of Water Disputes Tribunals.
*   **Major Tribunals constituted:**
    *   Godavari Water Disputes Tribunal (1969)
    *   Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal (1969)
    *   Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal (1969)
    *   Ravi-Beas Water Tribunal (1986)
    *   **Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (1990)** — award in 2007, modified by SC in 2018.
    *   Mahadayi Water Disputes Tribunal (2010)
*   **Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA):** Constituted in 2018 by the Centre to implement the SC's order on Cauvery water sharing.
*   **Inter-State River Water Disputes (Amendment) Bill, 2019:** Proposes a single permanent tribunal replacing multiple ad-hoc tribunals.

---

sections.heading: UPSC Relevance
sections.content:
*   Prelims: Article 262 provisions, major tribunals, CWMA.
*   Mains: Centre-State relations in water governance; cooperative federalism challenges; SC's role despite Art. 262(2) bar.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 275 — Grants-in-Aid from the Union to Certain States
sections.content:
> **Part XII: Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits — Chapter I (Finance)**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Constitutional Provision
sections.content: * **Text:** Sums as Parliament may by law provide shall be **charged on the Consolidated Fund of India** in each year as grants-in-aid of the revenues of such States as Parliament may determine to be in need of assistance. * **UPSC Prelims Mandatory Distinction:** Statutory grants under Article 275 are **CHARGED EXPENDITURE** upon the Consolidated Fund of India (non-votable by Parliament). In contrast, Discretionary Grants under Article 282 are subject to annual parliamentary appropriation and voting. * **Purpose:** Equalization of public services across states with uneven revenue capabilities or special needs (e.g. Tribal welfare, Hill States, demographic disadvantages). * **Finance Commission Role (Article 280(3)(b)):** The Finance Commission makes recommendations to the President regarding the principles governing grants-in-aid under Article 275.

sections.heading: Key Types of Grants under Article 275
sections.content:
1. **Revenue Deficit Grants (RDG):** Given to States experiencing a gap between revenue expenditure and revenue receipts post-tax devolution.
2. **Sector-Specific Grants:** Targeted funding for health, education, agriculture, etc.
3. **State-Specific / Disaster Relief Grants:** Allocated based on special geographical or demographic challenges.

sections.heading: Cross-References
sections.content:
* **Article 280:** Finance Commission recommendations on Article 275 principles.
* **Article 282:** Discretionary Grants (Outside Finance Commission recommendations).
* **Linkage:** `Fiscal Federalism` $\leftrightarrow$ `16th Finance Commission` $\leftrightarrow$ `Equalization Grants`

</details>

sections.heading: Article 279A — Goods and Services Tax Council (GST Council)
sections.content:
> **Part XII: Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits — Chapter I (Finance)**
> *Inserted by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016.*

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Constitutional Provision
sections.content:
* **Nature:** Joint forum of the Centre and the States constituted by the President within 60 days of enforcement of 101st Amendment.
* **Composition:**
  * Chair: **Union Finance Minister**
  * Members: Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue/Finance + State Finance Ministers / designated Ministers.
* **Voting Mechanism:**
  * Decisions require a **3/4th weighted majority** of members present and voting.
  * Union Government vote weightage = **1/3rd** of total votes cast.
  * All State Governments combined vote weightage = **2/3rds** of total votes cast.

sections.heading: Mandate & Recommendations
sections.content:
* Recommends GST rates, exemptions, threshold limits, model GST laws, and principles of place of supply.
* *Supreme Court Ruling (Union of India v. Mohit Minerals, 2022):* GST Council recommendations are **not binding** on Union and States, but possess persuasive value promoting **cooperative federalism**.

sections.heading: Key Interlinks
sections.content:
* **Article 246A:** Special provision with respect to goods and services tax.
* **Article 269A:** Levy and collection of GST in course of inter-State trade/commerce (IGST).
* **Linkage:** `Fiscal Federalism` $\leftrightarrow$ `GST Collections` $\leftrightarrow$ `101st Amendment`

</details>

sections.heading: Article 280 — Finance Commission
sections.content:
> **Part XII: Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits — Chapter I (Finance)**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Constitutional Provision
sections.content:
* **Nature:** Quasi-judicial, constitutional body constituted by the **President of India** every 5 years (or earlier).
* **Composition:** Chairman + 4 other members appointed by the President. Qualifications determined by Parliament (Finance Commission Act, 1951).

sections.heading: Key Functions & Mandates
sections.content:
1. **Vertical Devolution (Art 280(3)(a)):** Distribution of net proceeds of taxes between Union and States.
2. **Horizontal Devolution:** Allocation between States of their respective shares of tax proceeds.
3. **Grants-in-Aid Principles (Art 280(3)(b)):** Principles governing grants-in-aid of revenues under **Article 275**.
4. **Local Bodies Grants (Art 280(3)(bb) & (c)):** Measures to augment State Consolidated Funds to supplement Panchayat and Municipality resources (added by 73rd & 74th Amendments).

sections.heading: Key Historical Context & 16th FC
sections.content:
* **16th Finance Commission (FC-16):** Chaired by **Arvind Panagariya** (Constituted Dec 2023; Report covering 2026–31 period).
* **Key Interlinks:** `Vertical Devolution` $\leftrightarrow$ `Horizontal Devolution` $\leftrightarrow$ `Article 275` $\leftrightarrow$ `Fiscal Federalism`

</details>

sections.heading: Article 282 — Discretionary Grants by the Union or States for Public Purposes
sections.content:
> **Part XII: Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits — Chapter I (Finance)**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Constitutional Provision
sections.content: * **Text:** The Union or a State may make any grants for any public purpose, notwithstanding that the purpose is not one with respect to which Parliament or the Legislature of the State, as the case may be, may make laws. * **UPSC Prelims Mandatory Distinction:** Article 282 is a general spending power provision. Grants made under Article 282 are **DISCRETIONARY** and completely outside the statutory recommendations of the Finance Commission under Article 280. * **Key Trap Detail:** Unlike Article 275 (which is charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India and non-votable), Article 282 grants are **VOTED EXPENDITURE** subject to annual parliamentary/state assembly appropriation. * **Historical Usage:** Article 282 was heavily utilized by the Union government to transfer massive capital and revenue funds for Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) planned by the erstwhile Planning Commission, overshadowing statutory transfers under Article 275.

sections.heading: Cross-References
sections.content:
* **Article 275:** Statutory Grants-in-aid (Charged on Consolidated Fund of India).
* **Article 280:** Finance Commission recommendations.
* **Linkage:** `Fiscal Federalism` $\leftrightarrow$ `Centrally Sponsored Schemes` $\leftrightarrow$ `Planning Commission vs NITI A`

</details>

sections.heading: Article 3: Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States
sections.content:
> **Tags:** `[GS-2: Constitution - Reorganization of States, Federalism, Part I]`
> **Last Updated:** 2026-08-17
> **Related Current Affairs:** [[2026-08-13_Current_Affairs]] (Kerala Name Change)
> **Related Notes:** [Indian_Polity_Constitution.md — Lecture 05](../GS_Polity_VR_Notes/Indian_Polity_Constitution.md)

sections.heading: Active Recall Questions
sections.content:
What are the 5 powers of Parliament under Article 3? - Parliament by law can: 1. **Form** or **Abolish** a state 2. **Merge** two or more states 3. **Alter the boundaries** of states 4. **Increase or Decrease** (diminish) the areas of a state 5. **Change the name** of a state - Note: In this Article, **"states" includes Union Territories**.
What are the TWO pre-conditions for introducing an Article 3 Bill? 1. **Recommendation of President** — a political phrase meaning **Government Initiative** (only a Public Member, specifically the Home Minister, can introduce the Bill) 2. **Opinion of Concerned State(s)** — the proposal must be sent to the affected State for its opinion (by convention, **30 days** given). The opinion is **NOT binding** on the Centre.
Why is the State's opinion under Art 3 NOT binding? 1. **Primacy of national interest over regional interest** — Constitution empowers Parliament, not States 2. **Nature of opinion** — opinion = views, which are inherently non-binding 3. **Ambedkar's reasoning** — "There is no element of free will in India." If binding, no princely state would have joined India - Sending proposal to State = **Federal feature**; Not listening = **Unitary bias**
When are Art 3 pre-conditions NOT required? - When **only UTs** are involved (without touching any State) - Example: Merger of Dadra & Nagar Haveli with Daman & Diu (both UTs) — pre-conditions NOT needed - Reason: UTs are the Centre's own territory → Centre-UT relationship is **unitary**
What is the procedure for altering the name of a State under Article 3? - A Bill contemplating such a change can be introduced in the Parliament **only with the prior recommendation of the President**. - Before recommending the Bill, the President must refer the same to the **State Legislature concerned** for expressing its views within a specified period. - The President (or Parliament) is **not bound** by the views of the State Legislature. - The Bill is passed by a **simple majority** in Parliament. - **Current Affair (Aug 2026):** For example, the Kerala Assembly passed a resolution in 2024 to change its name to *Keralam*. Subsequently, the Union government introduced and the Rajya Sabha passed the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026 to effect this change.
How does Article 3 apply to demands for separate Statehood (e.g. Gorkhaland)? - Under **Article 3(a)**, Parliament has the exclusive power to create a new State by separating territory from an existing State (e.g., carving Gorkhaland out of West Bengal). - **Procedure:** 1. The Bill can be introduced **only on the prior recommendation of the President**. 2. The President refers the Bill to the **State Legislature (West Bengal Assembly)** for its views within a specified time limit. 3. The views or resolutions of the State Legislature are **NOT binding** on the President or Parliament. 4. Under **Article 4(2)**, the Bill is passed by a **Simple Majority** of Parliament (not deemed an amendment under Article 368). - **Current Affair (Aug 2026 — Gorkha Permanent Political Solution):** Following decades of agitation and the failure of statutory bodies (Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council 1988 & Gorkhaland Territorial Administration 2011), the Union Ministry of Home Affairs constituted a high-level committee chaired by former Deputy NSA Pankaj Kumar Singh to draft modalities for a permanent constitutional solution (examining Art 3 Statehood/UT vs Sixth Schedule/Art 371 Asymmetric Autonomy).

sections.heading: Article 300A — Right to Property (Constitutional Right)
sections.content:
> **Part:** XII — Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits
> **Subject:** Persons not to be deprived of property save by authority of law

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text
sections.content: No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Originally:** Right to Property was a **Fundamental Right** under Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31.
- **44th Amendment Act, 1978** (Janata Party Government): Converted Right to Property from a **Fundamental Right** to a **Constitutional Right** under Art. 300A.
- This **reduced its status** — it is no longer enforceable under Art. 32 (right to constitutional remedies) but can be enforced under Art. 226 (HC writ jurisdiction).
- **Significance for Socialism:** The existence of Right to Property (even as a constitutional right) proves India is NOT a Marxian-socialist state (which requires NO private property).
- India's Democratic Socialism is **flexible** — allows private property while aiming for equitable distribution through [Art. 39(b)](Article_39b.md) and [Art. 39(c)](Article_39c.md).

sections.heading: Historical Context
sections.content:
- Indira Gandhi's government had issues with Right to Property as a FR because it obstructed land reform legislation.
- The Janata Party government (post-Emergency) amended it to balance individual rights with state's welfare objectives.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 312 of the Indian Constitution
sections.content:
**Part:** Part XIV (Services Under the Union and the States)

**Heading:** All-India Services

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

**Key Provisions:**
*   Provides for the creation of one or more All India Services (including an all-India judicial service) common to the Union and the States.
*   The Rajya Sabha must pass a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting declaring that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest to do so.
*   The Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and the Indian Police Service (IPS) are deemed to be services created by Parliament under this article.

**Relevance:** Highly relevant in matters concerning the Indian Police Service (IPS) and their deputation or leadership roles across various Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) and state police departments.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 323A — Administrative Tribunals
sections.content:
> **Part XIV-A: Tribunals (Inserted by 42nd Amendment Act, 1976)**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Constitutional Provisions & Scope
sections.content:
* **Article 323A:** Empowers **Parliament ONLY** to establish administrative tribunals for adjudication of disputes relating to recruitment and conditions of service of public servants (Union, State, local authorities, public corporations).
* **Key Features:**
  * Can be established ONLY by Parliament (not State Legislatures).
  * Only ONE central administrative tribunal (CAT) and state administrative tribunals (SATs) can be set up under Art 323A.

sections.heading: Article 323A vs Article 323B Distinction
sections.content:
| Parameter | Article 323A | Article 323B |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Subject Matter** | Public Service matters ONLY | Specific matters (Taxation, Foreign Exchange, Industrial/Labour, Land Reforms, Ceiling on Property, Elections, Foodstuffs) |
| **Establishing Authority** | Established **ONLY by Parliament** | Established by **Parliament OR State Legislatures** (within legislative competence) |
| **Hierarchy** | Single hierarchy of tribunals | Multiple tribunals can be created |

sections.heading: Land Mark Judgments & Recent Legislation
sections.content: * **L. Chandra Kumar Case (1997):** SC ruled that power of judicial review of High Courts under Art 226/227 and Supreme Court under Art 32 is part of **Basic Structure**. Decisions of tribunals are subject to appeal before Division Bench of High Court. * **Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 & 2026 Bill:** SC invalidated key provisions of 2021 Act for violating separation of powers. Parliament passed **Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026** establishing the **National Tribunals Commission (NTC)** (HQ: New Delhi, Chairperson: Retd SC Judge/HC CJ + 4 Members: 2 Judicial, 2 Technical) for uniform selection and oversight.

sections.heading: Key Interlinks
sections.content:
`Part XIV-A` $\leftrightarrow$ `Article 323B` $\leftrightarrow$ `L. Chandra Kumar` $\leftrightarrow$ `National Tribunals Commission` $\leftrightarrow$ `Separation of Powers`

</details>

sections.heading: Article 324 — Superintendence, Direction and Control of Elections
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text (Simplified)
sections.content:
1. The **superintendence, direction and control** of the preparation of electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to Parliament and to the Legislature of every State and of elections to the offices of President and Vice-President shall be **vested in the Election Commission of India (ECI)**.
2. The Election Commission shall consist of the **Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)** and such number of other **Election Commissioners** as the President may from time to time fix.
3. When any other Election Commissioner is so appointed, the **CEC shall act as the Chairman** of the Election Commission.
4. The conditions of service of the CEC and other ECs shall be determined by the President by rule — provided that the CEC shall not be removed except in like manner and on like grounds as a **Judge of the Supreme Court** (i.e., by impeachment under Article 124(4)).
5. The President (or Governor at State level) shall, when so requested by the EC, make available such staff as may be necessary for the discharge of its functions.

sections.heading: Key Points for UPSC
sections.content: * ECI is an **independent constitutional body** (not a statutory or executive body). * **Plenary powers:** Article 324 gives the EC wide, residuary powers over the entire election process — from preparation of electoral rolls to the conduct and supervision of elections. * The EC's powers under Article 324 include the power to: * Prepare and revise electoral rolls. * Notify election schedules. * Enforce the Model Code of Conduct. * Order re-polls, countermand elections. * Register and de-register political parties. * **Landmark Case — Mohinder Singh Gill v. CEC (1978):** SC held that Article 324 gives the EC residuary power to act in situations not covered by specific legislation, to ensure free and fair elections. * **Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023:** Changed the appointment mechanism — Selection Committee now comprises PM, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by PM. * **Electoral Machinery Hierarchy (RPA 1950):** ECI (Art 324) → Chief Electoral Officer (CEO — State/UT level, Sec 13A) → District Election Officer (DEO — Sec 13AA) → Electoral Registration Officer (ERO — Assembly level, Sec 13B) → Assistant ERO → Booth Level Officer (BLO — polling station door-to-door enumeration). * **Electoral Roll Revision Mechanics (SIR vs SSR):** *Special Summary Revision (SSR)* runs annually based on voluntary claims across 4 qualifying dates; *Special Intensive Revision (SIR)* involves 100% door-to-door physical enumeration by BLOs to purge ghost/duplicate voters and map urban ASD (Absent, Shifted, Dead) electors. * **Mandatory Safeguard Against Deletion (Rule 21A, Registration of Electors Rules 1960):** An ERO cannot summarily delete an elector's name from draft rolls; a formal inquiry, individualized show-cause notice, and opportunity of being heard are statutory pre-requisites.

sections.heading: Related Articles
sections.content:
*   [Article 325](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_325.md) — No person to be ineligible for electoral roll on grounds of religion, race, caste, or sex.
*   [Article 326](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_326.md) — Elections on the basis of adult suffrage.
*   [Article 329](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_329.md) — Bar to interference by courts in electoral matters.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 326 — Elections to the House of the People and to the Legislative Assemblies of States to Be on the Basis of Adult Suffrage
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text (Simplified)
sections.content: The elections to the **House of the People (Lok Sabha)** and to the **Legislative Assembly of every State** shall be on the basis of **adult suffrage**; that is to say, every person who is a **citizen of India** and who is **not less than 18 years of age** on such date as may be fixed by or under any law made by the appropriate Legislature, and is not otherwise disqualified under the Constitution or any law on grounds of non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime, or corrupt or illegal practice, shall be entitled to be **registered as a voter** at any such election.

sections.heading: Key Points for UPSC
sections.content: * **Universal Adult Suffrage (UAS):** India adopted UAS from its very first general election in 1951–52 — a radical democratic choice given that many Western democracies took centuries to extend suffrage universally. * **Voting age was reduced from 21 to 18 years** by the **61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988** (during Rajiv Gandhi's government). * **Disqualification grounds:** Non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime, corrupt or illegal practice. * The preparation and revision of **electoral rolls** under this Article is supervised by the Election Commission under [Article 324](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_324.md). * **Part XVI** of the Constitution (Articles 324–329) deals with elections. * **Four Rolling Qualifying Dates (Election Laws Amendment Act 2021):** Citizens turning 18 qualify for registration on 4 dates annually — January 1, April 1, July 1, and October 1 (amending Section 14(b) of RPA 1950, replacing single Jan 1 date). * **Statutory Claims & Objections Forms:** **Form 6** (New registration/inclusion), **Form 7** (Objection to entry / request for deletion), and **Form 8** (Correction of particulars, transposition, shifting of residence, PwD marking). * **Jurisprudence on 'Right to Vote':** Held as a statutory right created by RPA 1951 (*N.P. Ponnuswami 1952*, *Kuldip Nayar 2006*), but reaffirmed as an intrinsic democratic constitutional facet flowing from Article 326 in *PUCL (2013 - NOTA)* and *Anoop Baranwal (2023)*.

sections.heading: Related Articles
sections.content:
*   [Article 324](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_324.md) — Superintendence, direction and control of elections vested in ECI.
*   [Article 325](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_325.md) — No person ineligible for electoral roll on grounds only of religion, race, caste, or sex.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 33 of the Indian Constitution
sections.content:
**Part:** Part III (Fundamental Rights)

**Heading:** Power of Parliament to modify the rights conferred by this Part in their application to Forces, etc.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

**Key Provisions:**
*   Parliament may, by law, determine to what extent any of the rights conferred by Part III shall, in their application to:
    *   (a) the members of the Armed Forces; or
    *   (b) the members of the Forces charged with the maintenance of public order; or
    *   (c) persons employed in any bureau or other organisation established by the State for purposes of intelligence or counter intelligence; or
    *   (d) persons employed in, or in connection with, the telecommunication systems set up for the purposes of any Force, bureau or organisation referred to in clauses (a) to (c),
    *   be restricted or abrogated so as to ensure the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

**Relevance:** Significant when dealing with rules, regulations, and acts affecting the fundamental rights, service conditions, and unionization of Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), Police, and Armed Forces.

</details>

sections.heading: Article 343 — Official Language of the Union
sections.content:
> **Part XVII: Official Language — Chapter I (Language of the Union)**

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Constitutional Provisions
sections.content:
* **Article 343(1):** The Official Language of the Union shall be **Hindi in Devanagari script**. The form of numerals to be used for official purposes of the Union shall be the international form of Indian numerals.
* **Article 343(2):** Provided that for a period of 15 years from the commencement of the Constitution (until 1965), the **English language** shall continue to be used for all official purposes of the Union.
* **Article 343(3):** Empowers Parliament to provide by law for the continued use of English beyond 15 years (enacted via **Official Languages Act, 1963**).

sections.heading: Historical Compromise & Language Policy
sections.content: * **Munshi-Ayyangar Formula:** Framed in Constituent Assembly by K.M. Munshi and N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar to reconcile pro-Hindi and non-Hindi proponents. Retained English alongside Hindi. * **Supreme Court Observations (2026):** Challenged the false binary of English vs Indian languages. SC noted English in India has evolved into an administrative, legal, and academic instrument of Indian expression. * **CBSE three-language (10 Sep 2026 paper):** Centre told SC it “has an issue” with treating English as indigenous/native; possible one-time Class 6 reprieve from a mandatory CBSE Class 10 third-language paper. That hearing is `CA-260910-01`, not a change to Article 343 text. * **Census 2011 Data:** ~129 Million English speakers in India (~260,000 mother tongue speakers; 46M 2nd language; 83M 3rd language). Estimated 180M-250M at present. Sahitya Akademi recognizes English as a language of Indian literature.

sections.heading: Key Interlinks
sections.content:
`Part XVII` $\leftrightarrow$ `Official Languages Act 1963` $\leftrightarrow$ `8th Schedule` $\leftrightarrow$ `Article 344` $\leftrightarrow$ `Article 351`

</details>

sections.heading: Article 356 — Provisions in Case of Failure of Constitutional Machinery in States (President's Rule)
sections.content:
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

sections.heading: Text (Simplified)
sections.content:
1. If the President, on receipt of a report from the Governor of a State or **otherwise**, is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution, the President may by Proclamation:
   * (a) Assume to himself all or any of the functions of the Government of the State and all or any of the powers vested in or exercisable by the Governor.
   * (b) Declare that the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of **Parliament**.
   * (c) Make incidental and consequential provisions, including suspending in whole or in part the operation of any provisions of this Constitution relating to any body or authority in the State (except High Courts).
2. Any such Proclamation may be revoked or varied by a subsequent Proclamation.
3. Every Proclamation shall cease to operate at the expiration of **two months** unless approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament (by **Simple Majority**).
4. If approved, it continues for **six months** at a time, up to a maximum period of **three years** (subject to 44th Amendment conditions for extensions beyond one year: National Emergency in operation + EC certificate that elections cannot be held).

sections.heading: Key Points for UPSC
sections.content: * **Grounds for Imposition:** 1. *Article 356:* Failure of constitutional machinery (Governor's report or 'otherwise'). 2. *Article 365:* Failure of State to comply with, or to give effect to, any directions given by the Union Executive. * **High Court Powers Protected:** The President **cannot** assume the powers of the State High Court or suspend any constitutional provisions relating to High Courts (Article 356(1) proviso). * **Parliamentary Approval & Majority:** * Must be approved within **2 months** by both Houses by a **Simple Majority** (contrast with Article 352 which requires Special Majority within 1 month). * **Landmark Case — S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994):** * Proclamation under Article 356 is subject to **Judicial Review**. * The State Legislative Assembly should **not be dissolved immediately** upon proclamation; it can only be dissolved **after Parliament approves** the proclamation. Until then, it can only be kept under **suspended animation**. * Floor test on the floor of the House is the **sole constitutional test** to determine majority support. * Secularism and Federalism are part of the **Basic Structure** of the Constitution. * **One Nation One Election (ONOE) Misuse Trap:** Holding a fallen state assembly in perpetual suspended animation under Article 356 until the next synchronized national election date directly violates the Bommai guidelines, as President's Rule cannot be used as an administrative tool for electoral calendar alignment.

sections.heading: Related Articles
sections.content:
* [Article 352](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_352.md) — Proclamation of Emergency (National Emergency).
* [Article 355](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_355.md) — Duty of the Union to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance.
* [Article 365](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_365.md) — Effect of failure to comply with directions given by the Union.
* [Article 172](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_172.md) — Duration of State Legislatures.

</details>
