sections.heading: 4. Fast-Track Special Courts (FTSCs) & Structural Justice Reforms
sections.content: > **Tags:** `[GS-2: Judiciary - Pendency, Fast-Track Courts & Right to Fair Trial]` · `[GS-2: Governance & Judicial Reforms]`

sections.heading: Context & Background
sections.content:
- Prime Minister announced fast-track courts for paper leak cases under the **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024**.
- Delhi High Court constituted a specialized fast-track court at the **Rouse Avenue Courts Complex** to hear exam leak cases.

sections.heading: Critical Assessment of Fast-Track Special Courts (FTSCs)
Major Challenges Identified
sections.content:
| Challenge Area | Detailed Analysis |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Resource Reallocation Trap** | FTSCs reassign existing judges and courtrooms rather than expanding total judicial capacity. This shifts judicial backlog onto regular court dockets (total trial court pendency: **~4.8 Crore cases**, 74% criminal). |
| **Operational Bottlenecks** | Severe shortage of trained Public Prosecutors and cyber/digital forensic laboratory support. |
| **Article 21 (Due Process)** | Supreme Court cautioned against imposing rigid, statutory trial deadlines. Rushed trials in complex paper leak cases (voluminous chargesheets, hundreds of witnesses) compromise the right to a fair trial and defense preparation. |
| **Article 14 (Equal Protection)** | SC warned that ad-hoc designation of specific case categories without rational classification or institutional expansion risks violating equal protection. |

sections.heading: Mains Utility / Way Forward for Judicial Reform
sections.content:
1. **Capacity Expansion over Reallocation:** Increase the baseline judge-to-population ratio (India has ~21 judges per million vs. 50 recommended by Law Commission 120th Report).
2. **Investigative & Forensic Strengthening:** Modernize forensic science laboratories (FSLs) and establish a dedicated cadre of trained prosecutors before prescribing tight trial timelines.
3. **Procedural Discipline:** Enforce strict limits on frivolous adjournments under Section 309 of CrPC / Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).

sections.heading: Lecture 01 — 6 August 2026
sections.content:
*Date added: 2026-08-06*
*Lecture date: 2026-08-06*

> **Source:** Vajiram & Ravi — **BS Sir** | Economy Lecture 01 | Class Notes + Transcript

---

sections.heading: Section A: Two Branches of Economics
sections.content:
*Context: "Indian Economy is like studying economics for our country called India. Most of the questions that you get in GS are around Indian economy only."*

Economics has **two fundamental branches**:

---

sections.heading: 1. Microeconomics (Micro = Small)
sections.content:
*   **Definition:** The study of **economic behaviour from an individual perspective**.
*   **Individuals** here = **Consumers** + **Producers**.
    *   **Consumers** → those who **buy** Goods & Services (G&S).
    *   **Producers** → those who **produce & sell** G&S.
*   G&S are consumed because they provide **utility** (satisfaction).

##### Goods vs Services
| | Goods | Services |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | **Tangible** — can see/feel physically | **Intangible** — consumed but cannot be shown physically |
| Examples | Food items, notebooks, pens, books | Transportation, communication, software |

---

sections.heading: Demand for a G/S
sections.content:
*   **Definition:** Relationship between **quantity demanded** of a G/S and **its price**.
*   **Quantity demanded** = Different quantities of a G/S that a **consumer is willing to buy** (at different prices).

##### Law of Demand

> **Quantity demanded** of a G/S is **inversely related** to its price, **keeping other factors constant**.

*   Two parts:
    1.  **Inverse relationship** — Higher price → lower quantity demanded; Lower price → higher quantity demanded.
    2.  **Ceteris paribus** ("keeping other factors constant") — Other factors = factors other than price that can impact quantity demanded.
        *   Example of other factor: **Income of the consumer**.
*   *Context: "When you went to buy rice expecting ₹100/kg but found ₹200/kg, you bought only half a kg. That is the inverse relationship."*

---

sections.heading: Supply of a G/S
sections.content:
*   **Definition:** Relationship between **quantity supplied** of a G/S and **its price**.
*   **Quantity supplied** = Different quantities of a G/S that a **producer is willing to sell**.

##### Law of Supply

> **Quantity supplied** of a G/S is **directly related** (positively related) to its price, **keeping other factors constant**.

*   Two parts:
    1.  **Direct relationship** — Higher price → producer willing to sell more (more profit/revenue); vice versa.
    2.  **Ceteris paribus** — Other factors = factors other than price that can impact quantity supplied.
        *   Example: **Input prices** (seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, water/irrigation inputs).
*   *Context: "Producers would be happier if they get higher price — which is reflected in the law of supply."*

---

sections.heading: Market / Market Mechanism
sections.content:
*   **Definition:** A mechanism under which the **market forces of demand and supply interact** to result in the **market price** of a G/S.
*   Demand & Supply are also called **market forces**.
*   Physical markets (vegetable market) and **digital markets** (Amazon, Big Basket) are both examples — digital markets are considered *better* examples because of larger number of buyers/sellers.

##### Market Economy

*   **Definition:** Economy where **almost all economic sectors** (e.g., Agriculture, Industries, etc.) **follow market mechanism** — i.e., prices determined through demand & supply.
*   India is **NOT** a market economy. India is a **Mixed Economy** since the **1950s** (Five-Year Plans).

##### Mixed Economy (India)

*   **Definition:** An economy where there is a **combination of both** the role of **Government** and the role of **Market** in different economic sectors.
*   Also described as: Mix of **Capitalist** (market emphasis) and **Socialist** (government emphasis) economic principles.
*   **Till 1991** → Greater role of **Government** (lesser role of market).
*   **Post-1991** → Greater role of **Market** (lesser role of government).
    *   *1991* = Year of **severe economic crisis** in India (Balance of Payment crisis). After 1991, many changes were brought — government reduced its direct role, market role increased. Still increasing decade by decade.
*   *Context: "Unless you know what is market, you can't understand Indian economy — that is the reason I did demand, supply, market in the very first section."*
*   **Examples of Government role still present:**
    *   **MSP** (Minimum Support Price) — Government determines prices for many crops, not market.
    *   Price regulation in certain industries (e.g., Khadi shops).
    *   Government is considered the **opposite** of market — it regulates/fixes prices.

---

sections.heading: Change in Demand for a G/S
sections.content:
*   **Definition:** Change in **quantity demanded** of a G/S **at all possible prices**.
    *   Different from Law of Demand (which links one quantity to one price level). Here: at **all** prices, quantity demanded changes.
*   **Two types:**
    1.  **Increase in Demand** → ↑ in Qty demanded of a G/S at **all possible prices**.
    2.  **Decrease in Demand** → ↓ in Qty demanded of a G/S at **all possible prices**.
*   **Cause:** Due to **change in other factors** (income, festivals, pandemics, etc.).
*   **Examples:**
    *   ↑ Income → ↑ Demand (more confidence, buy costlier products).
    *   Festival season → ↑ Demand for fruits (no matter what price, more quantity demanded).
    *   COVID pandemic → ↑ Demand for sanitizers/masks; post-pandemic → ↓ Demand.

---

sections.heading: Change in Supply of a G/S
sections.content:
*   **Definition:** Change in **quantity supplied** of a G/S **at all possible prices**.
*   **Two types:**
    1.  **Increase in Supply** → ↑ in Qty supplied at all prices — always due to **lower cost of production** (lower input prices, lower taxes, etc.).
    2.  **Decrease in Supply** → ↓ in Qty supplied at all prices — always due to **higher cost of production** (higher input prices, higher taxes, etc.).
*   **Cause:** Due to **change in other factors**.
*   **Example:** Fertilizer becomes costlier (due to West Asia crisis → petroleum products costlier → fertilizer costlier) → ↓ Supply of agricultural products → producer will sell less even at higher prices because higher input price neutralizes higher selling price.

---

sections.heading: Combined Relationships (Winding up Micro)
sections.content:
| Scenario | Effect on Market Price |
|---|---|
| ↑ Demand for G/S + **same Supply** | → **Higher** Market Price of G/S (and vice versa) |
| ↑ Supply of G/S + **same Demand** | → **Lower** Market Price of G/S (and vice versa) |

*   **Example (Demand ↑):** Rising income levels → producers aware consumers can pay more → higher market prices. Festival season → fruits costlier.
*   **Example (Supply ↑):** Good monsoon → ↑ supply of agricultural products → lower market prices. *Context: "Good monsoon expected → food prices relatively stable — they are talking about the same thing."* Bad monsoon/drought → ↓ supply → higher prices.

> **Note:** Direct microeconomics questions in UPSC are less common but not impossible. Don't go into more detail beyond this. The tools (demand–supply analysis) will be reused in other topics: demand & supply of money, foreign currency exchange rate, etc.

---

sections.heading: 2. Macroeconomics (Macro = Large)
sections.content:
*   **Definition:** The study of **economic aggregates and their behaviour**.
*   **Aggregate** = Adding up / summing up. Whenever we aggregate something in economics → macroeconomics.

##### Examples of Economic Aggregates

| Aggregate | Examples | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **National Income** | GDP, GNP, etc. | GDP Growth Rate (e.g., 7% p.a. = for each ₹100 of G&S produced last year, ₹107 this year) |
| **Aggregate Prices / Price Index** | CPI (Consumer Price Index), WPI (Wholesale Price Index) | Higher Agg. Prices = **Inflation**; Lower Agg. Prices = **Deflation** (less common) |

*   **Behaviour** = Are aggregates going up or coming down? At what rate?
*   Macroeconomics is **directly more important** for GS exam. Micro is interesting but direct questions are less common.

---

sections.heading: Section B: References & Strategy for UPSC Economy
References
sections.content:
| # | Reference | How to Use |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NCERT — Indian Economic Development** | **Background reading** — read like a story book, ignore data (outdated). Finish within a month. Read once more before Mains. *Latest edition only.* |
| 2 | **NCERT — Introductory Macroeconomics** | Do **selectively** — only chapters related to topics. **Older edition** recommended (simpler language, better chapter division for GS). Avoid NCERT on Microeconomics. **Avoid graphs & numericals.** |
| 3 | **Institute reference books** (Yellow/Orange books) | Use same way as macro NCERT — refer chapter-wise per topic. |
| 4 | **Handouts** from teachers | Short (2–5 pages) but CRISP. For **BS Sir's** classes: **Class notes + Handout = Full class notes** (not optional). |
| 5 | **Current Affairs (Dynamic Part):** | |
| | — Institute material (monthly booklets, student portal, YouTube channel) | Minimum current affairs coverage. |
| | — **Newspapers** — Editorials + Economy articles (NOT business articles) | Develop a habit. Repetition = stronger recall. |
| | — **Economic Survey** (selected parts) | Published by MoF, Feb. Summary of last year's economic performance. Do for exam year only. **Do NOT do entirely.** |
| | — **Annual Budget** (selected parts) | Published by MoF, Feb. Forward-looking: how govt plans to spend/generate revenue. More important for **Mains** than Prelims. |

##### Newspaper Reading — Economy vs Business Articles

| Economy Articles (READ ✅) | Business Articles (SKIP ❌) |
|---|---|
| Macroeconomic developments: GDP growth, industrial growth, inflation | Which company made how much profit |
| Sector-level articles: Banking, Agriculture, Infrastructure | Company mergers/acquisitions |
| Policy explanations: Monetary policy, RBI decisions | What CEO is saying |
| Share market **concepts** (when relevant) | Daily share price movements |

*   Focus on **concepts over figures**. Don't mug up data from Day 1.
*   *Context: "You will never get a question like 'What was GDP growth of India in Q2 of 2025-26?'"*

sections.heading: Strategy

sections.heading: Section C: Topic 1 — National Income Accounting (Basic Macroeconomic Concepts)
Four Types of Economic Sectors & Their Roles
sections.content:
| # | Sector | Definition / Role |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Firms (Companies)** | **Producers** of different types of G&S. Includes both private sector & public sector enterprises (SAIL, ONGC, etc. are firms, NOT government). Examples: car-making companies, software companies, fertilizer companies. |
| **2** | **Households (HHs)** | **Groups of consumers** with **similar consumption habits** (≈ family). All of us are household members. Similar food, furniture, services consumed within a family unit. |
| **3** | **Government** (Centre, States, UTs, Local) | **Four Roles:** |
| | | **(i)** As **buyer of G&S** — just like households, govt purchases goods/services for official use. |
| | | **(ii)** As **provider of services** — public administration, defence, etc. (Services where market mechanism literally cannot be applied → hence govt provides them even in market economies. This is why market economy definition uses "**almost** all sectors".) |
| | | **(iii)** **Welfare role** — Govt provides **subsidies** (discounted inputs, e.g., subsidized fertilizers to farmers), **infrastructure** (roads, schools, hospitals). |
| | | **(iv)** **Levies & collects taxes** — Govt decides who pays what tax and then collects it. **Main source of revenue** for the government. |
| **4** | **Financial Sector** | Acts as an **intermediary** between **surplus fund sectors** and **deficit fund sectors**. Best example: **Banks** — accept savings from surplus sectors, provide loans to deficit sectors. *(Note: Financial sector is technically a part of Firms — banks are also companies providing banking services. Separated here because of the unique & important role.)* |

##### Surplus vs Deficit Fund Sectors

| | Surplus Fund Sector | Deficit Fund Sector |
|---|---|---|
| **Meaning** | Revenue > Expenditure (have more than they need) | Expenditure > Revenue (have less than they need) |
| **Contribution** | **Savings** | **Loans / Borrowings** |

##### Savings & Borrowing Rankings

| Rank | Top Savers (contribute to savings) | Top Borrowers (depend on loans) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Households** (top savers) | **Firms** (main loan takers — need capital for production) |
| 2 | Firms | Government (3 of 4 roles involve spending; only taxes generate revenue) |
| 3 | Government (least saver — typically spends more than it earns → always in deficit) | Households (least borrowers) |

*   *Context: "Government typically spends more money than what it earns. So government is always in deficit. Therefore in savings, government contribution is the least."*

---

sections.heading: Circular Flow of Income & Expenditure
sections.content:
*   **Definition:** Reflects **interrelationships** between different **economic sectors**.
*   We start with a **Two-Sector Model** (Firms ↔ Households) — captures ~80–85% of major circular flow. Government (taxes, subsidies) and External Sector (exports, imports) are added later.

---

sections.heading: Real Flow (Without Prices / Adjusted for Prices)
sections.content:
Figure: Real flow — Firms supply final G&S to households; households supply factors of production to firms. No prices involved.

* **Firms → HHs:** Final Goods & Services (e.g., final cars produced by car-making firm go to households for consumption). "Final" because whenever a household gets a G/S from a firm, it is always **final**. * **HHs → Firms:** Factors of Production / Factor Inputs (e.g., household members provide **labour** — work in car-making companies/factories). Labour = simplest example; also capital, etc. (to be done in next class). * **Key Insight:** Both sectors are **mutually dependent** — "Circular flow is like democracy in economics. No one is superior or inferior." Companies depend on us for factor inputs; we depend on them for final G&S. ---

sections.heading: Nominal / Monetary Flow (With Prices)
sections.content:
Figure: Nominal flow — the same two-sector loop measured in money: firms pay factor payments to households, households return PFCE to firms.

* **Firms → HHs:** **Factor Payments** (what firms pay for factors of production → to households). * Also called: **Factor Cost** (from firm's perspective — part of production cost) = **Factor Income** (from household's perspective — it is their income/salary). * *Context: "When I get salary from the institution — for the institution it is factor cost, but for me it is factor income. Same thing, perspective change."* * Example: Wages paid by car company to workers. * **HHs → Firms:** **Private Final Consumption Expenditure (PFCE)** — expenditure made by households when they consume final G&S. * *"Private"* here refers to **households** (as opposed to government). * Examples: Buying a book, food item, metro ticket — all PFCE. ##### Real vs Nominal — Summary | | Real Flow | Nominal / Monetary Flow | |---|---|---| | **Meaning** | Without prices / adjusted for prices | With prices / monetary value included | | **Firms → HHs** | Final G&S | Factor Payments (Factor Cost / Factor Income) | | **HHs → Firms** | Factors of Production (Factor Inputs) | Private Final Consumption Expenditure (PFCE) | ##### PYQ Reference * **Prelims question:** "Which of the following represent the **real sectors** in an economy?" * A farmer **producing** a crop → **Real** (no price involved, just production). * A loan given by a bank → **Nominal** (loans always in monetary value). * A farmer **selling** his crop in APMC Mandi → **Nominal** (the moment price comes in → nominal). * *Context: "You will be lucky if you get such a question — believe me. And you can't afford to make mistakes there."* ---

sections.heading: 4 Types of Factors of Production
sections.content:
1. **Land:** Natural resources used as input to production (e.g., plot of land, water, minerals).
   - **Factor Payment:** Rent.
2. **Labour:** Human resource inputs to production.
   - **Factor Payment:** Wages.
3. **Capital:** Long-term, man-made resource inputs to production (e.g., machineries, factories).
   - **Factor Payment:** Interest.
   - Capital is often the **costlier factor** due to its **lumpy nature** (can't be divided easily — either a machine is bought as a whole or not at all).
   - Firms need bank loans to buy capital. These loans are sourced from savings, which are mostly done by households (HHs) in expectation of earning interest.
4. **Entrepreneurship:** Risk-taking ability in production (e.g., launching a new product).
   - **Factor Payment:** Profits. (Top-level management or founders take the risk and earn profits beyond standard wages).

---

sections.heading: National Income (NI) Definition
sections.content: Total money value (**Quantity × Price**) of all final goods and services produced by the residents of the country over a given period (e.g., 1 year).

sections.heading: 2 Types of NI (on the basis of Money Value)
sections.content:
1. **Nominal NI (NI at current prices):**
   - Values current year's production at **current year's prices**.
   - Formula: `Sum of (Quantities of final G/S produced in current year × Price in current year)`
   - **Limitation:** Nominal NI can increase solely due to higher prices (inflation), even if real production is declining.

2. **Real NI (NI at constant prices):**
   - Values current year's production at **base year's prices**.
   - Formula: `Sum of (Quantities of final G/S produced in current year × Price in Base Year)`
   - **Real NI is a better indicator** for comparing NI/growth because it has "less surprises" and adjusts Nominal NI for inflation.
   - `Real NI = Nominal NI / NI Deflator` (The deflator is a measure of inflation).

sections.heading: Understanding Base Year
sections.content:
- Base year is a reference year from the past used to calculate Real NI.
- **Rules for selecting a Base Year:**
  1. It should be a **Normal year** (with minimal economic/geographical surprises, e.g., NO drought years, NO pandemic years like 2021).
  2. It should neither be **too new** (inflation can't be properly analyzed if it's too close) nor **too old** (many new types of goods/services may not be valued correctly). Ideally, it should be revised every 7–8 years, with a minimum 3-year gap.
- **Current Base Year for India:** **2022-23** (Revised from 2011-12, implemented since 2026 based on the recommendation of the **Vishwanath Goldar Committee**).

---

sections.heading: Types of Goods based on usage
sections.content:
- **Intermediate Goods:** Goods used up in the production of other goods/services.
- **Final Goods:**
  1. **Consumer Goods:** Used for final consumption by Households (HHs) or Government.
  2. **Capital Goods:** Used by firms to produce other G/S **without** loss in its identity over a short term.
- *Note:* The same good can be a final good for one entity (e.g., Household buying an item) and an intermediate good for another (e.g., a firm using it to produce something else).
- To calculate NI, we **only include the value of final goods/services** to avoid **double-counting**. Note: Sale of second-hand goods is not included.

sections.heading: Depreciation of Fixed Capital
sections.content:
- Gradual loss in the value of capital goods due to normal wear & tear, obsolescence (mainly due to technological development), etc.
- It reduces the ability of capital to produce new goods.
- **Provisions for Depreciation:** Firms keep aside a part of the capital value every year so that new capital can be bought after complete depreciation.

sections.heading: Gross vs Net NI
sections.content:
- **Gross NI:** NI not adjusted for depreciation of fixed capital.
- **Net NI:** NI after adjusting for depreciation of fixed capital.
- `Net NI = Gross NI - Depreciation of Fixed Capital`

---

sections.heading: 3 Types of Expenditures on Final Goods
sections.content:
1. **PFCE (Private Final Consumption Expenditure):** Expenditure on new final consumer goods by Households.
2. **GFCE (Government Final Consumption Expenditure):** Expenditure on new final consumer goods by the Government.
3. **GFCF (Gross Domestic Fixed Capital Formation):** Expenditure on new final capital goods by firms, government, or households (e.g., Purchase of new houses by HHs is considered infra development/capital formation).

sections.heading: Gross Domestic Capital Formation (GDCF)
sections.content: - GDCF reflects improvement in productivity across different sectors and is a crucial determinant of longer-term economic growth. - **Official MoSPI/CSO Formula:** `GDCF = GFCF + Change in Stocks + Net Acquisition of Valuables` - **Component 1 — GFCF (Gross Fixed Capital Formation):** Investment in machinery, equipment, buildings, infrastructure, and residential housing. - **Component 2 — Change in Stocks (Closing Stocks - Opening Stocks):** Net addition to raw materials, semi-finished, and finished inventory held by enterprises. - **Component 3 — Net Acquisition of Valuables:** Net purchases of gold, silver, precious stones, and artwork held as store of value (explicitly included in India's National Income Accounts). - **Synonyms:** GDCF is also known as Investment Expenditure, Capital Expenditure (CapEx), or simply Capital Formation. ---

sections.heading: ECO-02-05: Residents of a Country
sections.content: NI measures the output produced by the **residents** of the country. There are 2 types of residents (Resident Individuals & Institutions, though mostly discussed are individuals):

sections.heading: 1. Resident Individuals
sections.content:
Individuals who **ordinarily reside** in a country and their **centre of economic interest** lies in that country.

- **Employment / Tourist Rule:**
  - If an individual resides in a foreign country for **up to 1 year** for employment or tourism, they remain a resident of their **home country**.
  - If they reside in a foreign country for **more than 1 year** for employment, they become a resident of the **foreign country (host country)**.
- **Diplomats / Government Employees:** Government employees working in another country (e.g., diplomats) are **always** residents of their home country, regardless of duration.
- **Students:** Students studying abroad (even for 3-5 years) remain residents of their home country because their centre of economic interest (fees, expenditure) is funded by parents in the home country.
- **Citizenship vs Residency:**
  - Nationals (citizens) of a country can be non-residents.
  - Non-nationals (foreigners) of a country can be residents.

---

sections.heading: ECO-02-06: GVA at Basic Prices & Production vs Product Taxes
sections.content: * **Formula Hierarchy:** `GVA at Basic Prices = GVA at Factor Cost + Production Taxes - Production Subsidies` * `GDP at Market Prices = GVA at Basic Prices + Product Taxes - Product Subsidies` * **UPSC Prelims Crucial Trap:** * **Production Taxes/Subsidies:** Independent of actual volume of production (e.g., Land Revenue, Stamp Duty, Registration Fee, Payroll Tax, Profession Tax). * **Product Taxes/Subsidies:** Directly dependent on volume per unit of product (e.g., GST, Excise Duty, Custom Duty, Sales Tax, Service Tax). Fertilizer subsidy to *farmers* is production; to *fertilizer companies* is product. * Full class: **Lecture 04 — 2 September 2026** below. ---

sections.heading: ECO-03-01: Resident Institutions & Subsidiary Rules
sections.content: NI calculation depends on understanding **who** is producing (residents vs non-residents). In addition to Resident Individuals (covered in Lecture 2), there are **Resident Institutions**.

sections.heading: 2. Resident Institutions
sections.content:
*   **Definition:** Institutions (e.g., firms/companies) that are **registered in a country** and **mainly owned** by resident individuals of that country are **Resident Institutions** of that country.
*   Two key criteria (generally same, but in exception — go by registration/incorporation):
    1.  **Where** the company is registered (incorporated).
    2.  **Who** owns it (shareholders).

sections.heading: Examples (Automobile Sector)
sections.content:
| Company | Resident for India? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Tata Motors** | ✅ Yes | Registered in India, owned by Indian residents |
| **Mahindra, Bajaj** | ✅ Yes | Same logic as above |
| **Ford** (USA) | ❌ No | Foreign company manufacturing in India without independent subsidiary |
| **Renault** (France) | ❌ No | French company |
| **Suzuki Motors** (Japan) | ❌ No | Japanese parent company |
| **Hyundai Motors Korea** | ❌ No | Parent company based in Korea |
| **Hyundai Motors India Ltd** (subsidiary) | ✅ Yes | **Independent subsidiary** detached from parent, registered in India |
| **Apple, Samsung** (smartphones) | ❌ No | Non-resident — producing in India but not registered as Indian subsidiary |

> **Key Rule:** When a foreign company sets up an **independent subsidiary** in India (e.g., Hyundai Motors India Ltd), that subsidiary is treated as an **Indian Resident Institution**, detached from the parent company. The parent remains a foreign resident.

> **UPSC Exam Note:** If a question involves resident institution classification, sufficient information will be provided. Focus on understanding the principle (registration/incorporation + ownership).

---

sections.heading: Gross National Product (GNP)
sections.content:
> **Definition:** Total money value of all final goods and services **produced by the residents** of a country, over a period, **without adjusting for depreciation** of fixed capital.

*   GNP definition = exact copy of National Income definition + "without adjusting for depreciation" (because **Gross**).
*   GNP is considered the **ideal/conceptual measure** of National Income.
*   **WHO** produces → Residents → GNP answers the question "**Who** is producing?"

sections.heading: Net National Product (NNP)
sections.content:
> **Definition:** Same as GNP but **after adjusting for depreciation** of fixed capital.

*   `NNP = GNP - Depreciation`
*   NNP is considered the **best way** to measure national income (adjusting for depreciation is ideal).
*   Practically, depreciation is hard to calculate accurately → GNP is more commonly used.

sections.heading: Converting between Gross & Net
sections.content:
*   **Gross → Net:** Change "without" to "after" adjusting for depreciation.
*   In national income: **Gross** = without adjusting for depreciation; **Net** = after adjusting for depreciation.

---

sections.heading: Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
sections.content:
> **Definition:** Total money value of all final goods and services produced **in the Domestic Territory** of a country, over a period, **without adjusting for depreciation** of fixed capital.

*   The **only difference** from GNP: Replace "by residents" → "in the Domestic Territory".
*   GDP answers: **WHERE** is production taking place?

sections.heading: Domestic Territory (DT)
sections.content:
**DT of a country includes territories under the political control of the country:**

1.  **Geographical map** of India (entire landmass + territories).
2.  **Territorial waters** — up to **12 nautical miles**.
3.  **Government offices outside the country** — Embassies, Consulates, and other government offices abroad.
4.  Any **economic activity** happening outside the geographical map but under India's political control (e.g., Indian-operated ships outside territorial waters).

> **Note:** **Disputed areas** are NOT counted in GDP calculation.

---

sections.heading: ECO-03-04: GDP vs GNP — Core Difference
sections.content:
| | **GNP** | **GDP** |
|---|---|---|
| **Core Question** | **WHO** produces? | **WHERE** is it produced? |
| **Answer** | Residents | Domestic Territory |
| **Includes non-resident production in India?** | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| **Includes resident production abroad?** | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |
| **Complexity** | More complex (resident concept has many nuances) | Simpler (just count within geographical map) |
| **Conceptually better?** | ✅ Yes | Used more in practice |

**Overlap:** If someone is an Indian resident AND produces in Indian DT → counted in **BOTH** GDP and GNP.

**Example:** Apple produces smartphones in India → counted in **GDP** (production in Indian DT) but **NOT in GNP** (Apple is not an Indian resident).

---

sections.heading: Who calculates GDP in India?
sections.content:
*   **NSO (National Statistical Office)** — the office responsible for GDP calculation.
*   NSO comes under **MOSPI (Ministry of Statistics and Program Implementation)** under the **Government of India**.

sections.heading: How NSO calculates GDP
sections.content:
NSO divides the economy into **3 types of producing sectors** and calculates their contributions separately:

1.  **Primary Sector**
2.  **Secondary Sector**
3.  **Tertiary Sector (Services)**

---

sections.heading: ECO-03-06: Primary Sector
sections.content:
> **Definition:** A sector that converts **natural resources into commodities** (value-added goods).

**Commodities** = goods where value has been added from the raw/natural state.

sections.heading: Components of Primary Sector:
sections.content:
| # | Sub-Sector | Details |
|---|---|---|
| (i) | **Agriculture & Allied Sectors** | Crop production (food & non-food crops). Allied = Horticulture, **Animal Husbandry** (dairy, poultry), Food Processing |
| (ii) | **Forestry** | Self-explanatory |
| (iii) | **Fishery** | Self-explanatory |
| (iv) | **Mining & Quarrying** | **Mining** = minerals extraction; **Quarrying** = stone, sand extraction |

> **UPSC Trap:** Many think Mining is Secondary sector (because it seems industrial). But Mining uses **natural resources** → it is **Primary Sector**. This was tested in a PYQ (match-the-column: Primary/Secondary/Tertiary).

> **Why Primary?** All these activities use natural resources (seeds, soil, water, minerals, stones) and convert them into value-added commodities.

---

sections.heading: ECO-03-07: Secondary Sector
sections.content: > **Definition:** A sector that converts **commodities into other commodities** (inputs are already value-added; further value is added).

sections.heading: Components of Secondary Sector:
sections.content:
| # | Sub-Sector | Details |
|---|---|---|
| (i) | **Manufacturing** | Converting commodities through physical/chemical/electrical processes into other commodities. Examples: Steel-making, car-making, fertilizer industry. Has 2 sub-types: **Registered** & **Unregistered** |
| (ii) | **Construction** | Construction of buildings, establishments, factories. Uses commodities (bricks, cement, concrete, steel) → produces another commodity (building/factory) |
| (iii) | **Public Utilities** | **Electricity, Gas, and Water Supply**. Not physical commodities but their production **can be quantified** (gigawatts, million metric tons, etc.). Included following international convention |

---

sections.heading: Registered Manufacturing (= Organized Manufacturing)
sections.content:
*   Includes manufacturing units **registered with the Factories Act, 1948**.
*   Alternatively: units with **10 or more hired workers**.
*   **Link:** Any unit with ≥10 hired workers is **legally required** to register under Factories Act.
*   Since they are legally registered → they are **legally bound to provide data** on final goods, intermediate goods, etc.
*   **Value-Added Method** is used to calculate their GDP contribution (because data is available).

sections.heading: Unregistered Manufacturing (= Unorganized Manufacturing)
sections.content:
*   Includes manufacturing units **NOT registered** with the Factories Act.
*   Units with **less than 10 hired workers**.
*   Typically: household-based manufacturing, very small-scale units.
*   **Data availability is a problem** → Value-Added Method cannot be easily used.

> **Why this distinction matters:** Different methods of GDP calculation are used for each type (because of data availability differences).

---

sections.heading: Organized Sector of India
sections.content:
> **Definition:** Includes **all enterprises** (any type of economic activity — manufacturing, construction, services, etc.) with **10 or more hired workers**.

*   Broader than "Registered Manufacturing" — includes services too (e.g., Infosys is organized sector even though it's a service provider).
*   Registered/Organized Manufacturing is a **subset** of the Organized Sector.

sections.heading: Unorganized Sector of India
sections.content: > **Definition:** Includes **all enterprises** with **less than 10 hired workers**.

sections.heading: Key Statistics:
sections.content:
| Metric | Organized Sector | Unorganized Sector |
|---|---|---|
| **GDP Contribution** | **55–60%** (higher) | ~40–45% |
| **Employment Contribution** | ~20% | **~80%** (dominant) |
| **Average Wages** | Higher | **Lower** |
| **Quality of Employment** | Better | **Poor** |

> **Why lower average wages in unorganized sector?** Through circular flow logic: A sector contributing only ~40–45% to GDP but hiring ~80% of workers → wages divided by larger number → lower average wages → poor quality of employment.

> **UPSC Relevance (Employment topic):** One of the problems of Indian employment = large share is of poor quality, because most jobs come from unorganized sector which contributes less to GDP.

sections.heading: Why Agriculture is mostly Unorganized
sections.content:
*   Most agricultural production uses **family labor** (not hired workers).
*   Even when workers are hired, rarely ≥10.
*   The word **"hired"** is key — family workers are NOT hired workers.
*   Yet **data availability** for primary sector is good because **government is actively involved** (MSP policy, APMCs, e-marketing initiatives).

---

sections.heading: ECO-03-10: Tertiary Sector / Services
sections.content:
> **Definition:** A sector that does **NOT produce commodities** but provides **services**.

*   Examples: Transport, Communication, Storage, Public Administration, Education, Health, Banking, Financial Services, etc.
*   Contributes **more than 50% of GDP** in India.
*   Services **cannot be quantified** like goods (unlike even public utilities like electricity which can be measured in gigawatts).
*   This quantifiability problem → **Value-Added Method cannot be used** for services → **Income Method** is used instead.

---

sections.heading: ECO-03-11: Value-Added Method (Method 1 of GDP Calculation)
sections.content: > **Definition:** Calculates GDP as the **sum of Gross Value Added (GVA)** by different producing sectors.

sections.heading: GVA Formula:
sections.content:
> **GVA = Value of Gross Output of Final Goods & Services − Value of Gross Output of Intermediate Goods & Services**

*   Essentially: **Final Value − Intermediate Value** = Value Addition.
*   Subtracting intermediate goods avoids **double counting** in GDP.
*   We take the value addition by each producer and keep adding → gives GDP.

sections.heading: Where is Value-Added Method used in India?
sections.content:
| Sector | VA Method Used? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary Sector** | ✅ Yes | Government actively involved → good data on final/intermediate goods (despite being largely unorganized) |
| **Registered Manufacturing** | ✅ Yes | Legally registered → legally bound to provide data |
| **Unregistered Manufacturing** | ❌ No | Data not easily available (small/household units) |
| **Services/Tertiary** | ❌ No | Cannot quantify services; use Income Method instead |
| **Construction** | ❌ No | Uses Income Method |

> **Key insight:** VA Method works well when there is **better data on final and intermediate goods** — which exists for Primary sector (due to govt involvement) and Registered Manufacturing (due to legal obligation).

---

sections.heading: ECO-03-12: Income Method (Method 2 of GDP Calculation)
sections.content: > **Definition:** Calculates GDP as the **sum of factor incomes** generated in producing final goods and services.

sections.heading: Why Income Method works (Logic via Circular Flow):
sections.content:
*   If more goods/services are produced → more factors of production are employed → more factor income generated.
*   Factor income = wages, rent, interest, profits (W, R, I, P).
*   Factor incomes **reflect value addition** to production (workers add value → earn wages; land adds value → earns rent; capital adds value → earns interest; entrepreneur adds value → earns profit).
*   **Plan B logic:** If we can't capture GDP at the production stage (value-added), we capture it at the income stage (factor incomes), because they are correlated.

sections.heading: (i) Compensation of Employees (CoE)
sections.content:
> **CoE = Wages & Salaries paid by employers to employees + Other benefits by employers to employees**

*   **Other benefits include:**
    *   **Social Security** → Pension, Insurance, Provident Fund (PF)
    *   **Allowances** → HRA (House Rent Allowance), other allowances
*   CoE = practical extension of "wages" as a factor payment. Workers get more than just wages in practice.

sections.heading: (ii) Operating Surplus (OS)
sections.content:
> **OS = Sum of incomes from Property (Rent) + Savings (Interest) + Entrepreneurship (Profits)**

*   Essentially: All factor incomes **other than wages/CoE** combined together.
*   Rent + Interest + Profits = Operating Surplus.

sections.heading: (iii) Mixed Income of Self-Employed (MI)
sections.content:
> **MI = Sum of all factor incomes (W, R, I, P) of self-employed persons who do NOT maintain accounts.**

*   **Self-employed who maintain accounts** (doctors, CAs, lawyers, start-up owners) → their income is captured in CoE or OS.
*   **Self-employed who do NOT maintain accounts** (newspaper vendors, tea vendors, rickshaw pullers, auto drivers, small book shop owners) → cannot separate their income into wages, rent, interest, profit → their **total overall income** is taken as Mixed Income.
*   **Why "Mixed"?** Because it mixes all types of factor income without classification.
*   Majority of India's self-employed do not maintain accounts → MI is a crucial component.

sections.heading: Income Method is used for:
sections.content:
*   **All Services / Tertiary Sector** (cannot quantify output → capture factor incomes instead)
*   **Unregistered Manufacturing** (data not available for VA method)
*   **Construction sector**

---

sections.heading: Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)
sections.content:
> **NFIA = (Factor incomes brought by Indian residents for providing factor inputs abroad) − (Factor incomes taken out by foreign residents for providing factor inputs in Indian DT)**

*   **Example of positive component:** Indian software engineer works in USA for 6 months → brings back part of income to India → added to NFIA.
*   **Example of negative component:** South Korean engineer earns in India → takes income back to South Korea → deducted from NFIA.

sections.heading: The Key Formula:
sections.content:
> ## **GNP = GDP + NFIA**

This is the **most accurate way** to differentiate GDP and GNP.

sections.heading: NFIA for India: **NEGATIVE**
sections.content:
*   **Net COE from abroad → Positive** for India (Indian skilled professionals bring salaries back from abroad).
*   **But Net Profits → Strongly Negative** (dominant factor).
*   **Reason:** Significant **profit outflows** by non-resident companies (MNCs / FDI companies) from Indian Domestic Territory.
    *   Examples: Samsung, Apple produce in India → profits go back to home countries.
    *   Non-resident companies **dominate** sectors like smartphone manufacturing, automobiles, etc.
*   **Result:** Profit outflows **overwhelm** salary inflows → NFIA is **negative** overall.

sections.heading: Implication: **GNP < GDP for India**
sections.content:
*   Since NFIA is negative → adding a negative number to GDP → GNP is **smaller** than GDP.
*   **One reason India officially uses GDP** (not GNP): GDP gives a **higher number** (partly political — makes the economy look bigger).
*   **Other reasons:** GDP is **easier to calculate** (domestic territory is simpler than resident concept).

---

sections.heading: Net Remittances
sections.content:
> **Definition (Way 1):** Net COE brought by Indian residents from abroad **+** Net transfers made by Non-Residents (NRIs) to India from abroad.

> **Definition (Way 2 — Simpler):** Net **inflows of money in foreign currencies** to **Indian households** from abroad.

*   **India is the LARGEST remittance receiver in the world** (rare area where India beats China in international context).

sections.heading: NFIA vs Net Remittances — NOT the same
sections.content:
| | **NFIA** | **Net Remittances** |
|---|---|---|
| Includes **Net COE from abroad** | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes (overlapping part) |
| Includes **Rent, Interest, Profit** (cross-border) | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |
| Includes **Transfers by NRIs** (non-residents) | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| Part of National Income? | Part of GNP calculation | Generally **NOT** part of NI (except the COE overlap) |

> **Venn Diagram:** The overlapping part = Net COE from abroad. Everything else is unique to each.

> **No contradiction:** India can be the **largest remittance receiver** yet have **negative NFIA** because profit outflows (counted in NFIA but NOT in remittances) overwhelm the salary inflows.

> **Key UPSC rule:** No part of remittance can be part of **GDP**. In **GNP**, only the net COE component (the overlap) is included.

---

sections.heading: ECO-03-15: Expenditure Method (Method 3 of GDP Calculation) — Demand Side of GDP
sections.content: > **Definition:** Calculates GDP as the **sum of expenditures by all sectors** on domestically produced goods and services.

sections.heading: The GDP Formula (Expenditure Method):
sections.content:
> ## **GDP = C + I + G + NX**

| Symbol | Full Form | Meaning | Sector |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C** | **PFCE** (Private Final Consumption Expenditure) | Expenditure on final consumer goods by **Households** | Households |
| **I** | **Investment Expenditure** (GDCF) | Expenditure on capital goods — **mainly by firms**, also by government (infrastructure) and households (new houses) | Firms (mainly) |
| **G** | **GFCE** (Government Final Consumption Expenditure) | Government expenditure on final consumer goods | Government |
| **NX** | **Net Exports** = Exports − Imports | Expenditure by **External Sector** | External Sector |

sections.heading: External Sector
sections.content: > Includes **non-domestic sectors** (any firm, household, or government NOT belonging to India) + **International Organizations** (World Bank, IMF, etc. — always external for every country).

sections.heading: Why subtract Imports?
sections.content:
*   **Imports are NOT part of Indian GDP** (produced in other countries).
*   But C, I, and G **all include expenditure on imports** (hidden within them).
    *   **C example:** You buy clothes — a T-shirt may be made in Bangladesh = import hidden in C.
    *   **I example:** Companies buy imported machinery = import hidden in I.
    *   **G example:** Government buys imported defense products = import hidden in G.
*   Since imports cannot be separated at the C/I/G level in day-to-day life → we **subtract total imports at the end** to filter out non-GDP components.

sections.heading: NX for India: **NEGATIVE**
sections.content:
*   India's Imports > Exports → NX is negative → NX **pulls down** GDP.
*   Positive contributors: C (largest at **55–60% of GDP**), I (second), G (third).

---

sections.heading: Primary Use in India
sections.content:
Expenditure method is used in India **mainly for policy making** (not primarily for GDP calculation).

**Logic:** If GDP = C + I + G + NX, then increasing any component → higher GDP → higher economic growth.

sections.heading: Policy Links from Expenditure Method:
sections.content:
| Component | How to increase? | Policy Area |
|---|---|---|
| **C** (Consumption) | More income to households → more employment → more spending | **Employment Policy** |
| **I** (Investment) | Promote investment in industries, agriculture, infrastructure | **Investment Promotion**, FDI policy |
| **G** (Govt Expenditure) | Fiscal policy — taxation, subsidies | **Fiscal Policy** (e.g., reducing GST rates) |
| **NX** (Net Exports) | Promote exports, reduce import dependency | **Export Promotion Policy** |

sections.heading: C & I are interrelated:
sections.content:
*   **C → I:** Higher consumption → larger market → signal for producers to invest more (more demand → more factories).
*   **I → C:** More investment → more factories → more jobs → more income → more consumption.
*   **Ideal:** This self-fueling cycle keeps GDP growing.
*   **During crisis** (e.g., COVID): Neither C nor I increases → **unique role of Government** (G) through fiscal policy becomes critical.

sections.heading: Monetary Policy (RBI)
sections.content:
*   Also impacts GDP through similar channels.
*   Details covered in Money & Banking topic.

sections.heading: Mains PYQ Application — "How can X lead to higher economic growth?"
sections.content:
**Example: How can MSMEs lead to higher economic growth?**

1.  **More potential to increase Investment (I):** MSMEs are smaller → historical investment came from large industries → future potential lies more in MSMEs (large industries reach saturation).
2.  **More Labour Intensive → higher C:** MSMEs hire more workers (textiles, leather, food processing) → more employment → more consumption expenditure → higher GDP.
3.  **Export Potential → higher NX:** Some MSMEs have significant export potential (textiles especially) → increase in exports → higher GDP.

sections.heading: Savings & Economic Growth
sections.content:
*   **How savings help:** Savings → finance Investment (through financial intermediaries: banks channel surplus funds to deficit fund sectors) → higher I → higher GDP.
*   **Conceptual tension:** Savings is opposite of consumption (more saving = less spending). Could savings reduce C and lower GDP?
*   **Answer: Generally No.** Savings are done **only after** basic consumption needs (food, clothing, shelter) are met. People don't go hungry to save money in banks. Savings may reduce **luxury consumption** only, which has limited GDP contribution.
*   **Conclusion:** Savings are generally treated as **good for economic growth**.

sections.heading: ECO-05-01: Three valuations — Market Price, Factor Cost, Basic Price
sections.content: **National Income (NI) at Market Price (MP):** inclusive of **all** taxes paid by producers = **Net Production Taxes + Net Product Taxes**. This is the price you actually pay in the market. **NI at Factor Cost (FC):** **neither** net production taxes **nor** net product taxes. Same as **wages + rent + interest + profit (W + R + I + P)** — the **basic cost of production**, the minimum a producer must recover to stay in business. FC **excludes taxes** but **includes subsidies** (because “net tax” = tax − subsidy; dropping tax means adding the opposite). **NI at Basic Price (BP):** **between** FC and MP. Inclusive of **net production taxes only** (not net product taxes). | Valuation | Net production taxes | Net product taxes | |:---|:---:|:---:| | **MP** | Yes | Yes | | **BP** | Yes | No | | **FC** | No | No | **FC < BP < MP.** Traditional view: **FC is better than MP** because FC gives **less importance to transfer payments**. **United Nations System of National Accounts (UN SNA), 2008** recommended **BP**: production taxes are **similar to the basic cost of production** (without stamp duty / land revenue, production is illegal — like unpaid wages). India adopted the BP route from **2015**. FC vs BP is still debated; the rupee gap is small because production taxes are a **tiny** share of India’s tax revenue. **Prelims trap:** BP is **not** “no tax.” It includes **production** taxes, excludes **product** taxes (Goods and Services Tax (GST), excise, customs). ---

sections.heading: ECO-05-02: Production vs product taxes and subsidies
sections.content: **Production taxes / subsidies:** paid or received by producers **in relation to production**, **independent of the volume** of actual output. You can infer that production is happening, not *how much* or *of what*. | | Examples (class) | |:---|:---| | Production **tax** | **Land revenue** (area, not crop); **stamp duty paid by producers** (factory / land / building) | | Production **subsidy** | **Fertilizer subsidy to farmers** (urea bag ≠ wheat quintals) | **Product taxes / subsidies:** paid or received **per unit of product** — **dependent on volume**. Same core idea as **indirect taxes**. | | Examples (class) | |:---|:---| | Product **tax** | **GST**, **excise**, **customs** | | Product **subsidy** | **Fertilizer subsidy to fertilizer companies** (50 t output → subsidy on 50 t) | **Net** = that tax **minus** that subsidy. **Value of a good/service at BP** = amount **receivable** per unit by producers, inclusive of **net production taxes**, **not** net product taxes. Producers actually *receive* MP; BP is a constructed valuation. **Transfers (one-sided payments):** A pays B **without** the same-value good/service returning. Examples: **taxes, subsidies, old-age (social) pensions, scholarships, grants, donations**. NRI transfers (part of remittances) are international transfers. **Two-sided payments:** same-value return. **Private Final Consumption Expenditure (PFCE)**; **factor payments**. **Prelims traps:** (1) Fertilizer to **farmer** = production subsidy; to **company** = product subsidy. (2) **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) / Viksit Bharat — Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-G RAM G)** is **wages for labour**, **not** a transfer. (3) **Service pension** after work = deferred salary (two-sided); **old-age social pension** = transfer. ---

sections.heading: ECO-05-03: India’s GDP steps since 2015
sections.content:
**National Statistical Office (NSO)** under the **Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI)** calculates. **UN SNA recommends**; it does **not** compute India’s GDP.

**Before 2015:** official GDP was **GDP at Factor Cost**. Step 1 used GVA at **MP**, then converted toward FC. Handout has the old steps; class did not drill them.

**Since 2015 — five steps**

1. **Value Added (VA) method** → **Gross Value Added (GVA) at BP** for **primary + registered manufacturing**.  
   `GVA_BP = (gross output of final goods at BP) − (gross output of intermediate goods at BP)`
2. **Other sectors** (unregistered manufacturing, construction, public utilities, **services**): mainly **Income method** (expenditure method for some sub-sectors, e.g. construction) → **GVA at FC**.  
   `GVA_FC = Compensation of Employees (COE) + Operating Surplus (OS) + Mixed Income (MI) + provision for depreciation`  
   Income method is **net** by default; **depreciation** is added to make it **gross**. Step 1 already used *gross* output, so depreciation was inside.
3. Convert: `GVA_BP = GVA_FC + Net Production Taxes`
4. Add all sectors: `GDP_BP = Σ GVA_BP`
5. **Official GDP since 2015:** `GDP_MP = GDP_BP + Net Product Taxes`

Quarterly estimates often **copy registered manufacturing growth onto unregistered** — data lag, not a valuation debate. Black money is **outside** GDP; that is a general limitation.

sections.heading: Criticism of the 2015 method (vs pre-2015)
sections.content:
1. **Overestimates GDP compared with the old method** — because **GDP_MP > GDP_FC**. Comparing 2016 MP with 2014 FC is **technically wrong**.
2. Gives **more weight to transfers**, mainly **product taxes** (GST, excise) — not production taxes.
3. **Product / indirect tax share of total tax revenue** is **higher in developing countries**. Class: India roughly **45–48%** product taxes (direct ~52–55%); developed countries often **~20–30%**. Same UN method **inflates India more** than a rich country. Indirect taxes are often **regressive**; development should raise the **direct-tax** share.

Government defence: **UN SNA recommendation**, not a homemade trick.

---

sections.heading: ECO-05-04: International comparison — MER vs PPP; per capita GDP
sections.content: **Exchange Rate (ER)** (India): units of **₹ needed for US $1**. **Market Exchange Rate (MER)** = **flexible / floating ER** = ER from **demand and supply of dollars in India**. **Importers buy $**; **exporters sell $**. **Internationalisation of the rupee** is a later external-sector point. **GDP at MER:** ₹GDP converted to $ using MER. Class illustration: if MER = ₹90/$, $GDP = ₹GDP × (1/90). Newspaper **“$4 trillion+”** talk is **GDP at MER**. MER is **popular**, not **ideal** for India: **exports are only ~14–15% of GDP**, and MER is an **trade-FX** price. Imports are **not** part of GDP (they are subtracted). **Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)–based ER:** amount of ₹ needed in India to buy the **same Common Consumption Basket (CCB)** that $1 buys in the USA. `PPP-ER (₹/$) = (expenditure on CCB in India, ₹) / (expenditure on CCB in USA, $)` CCB ≈ **essentials** (food, fuels, clothing). History: **Big Mac Index** as a one-good shortcut. | | Use | |:---|:---| | **MER** | International **transactions** (export, import) | | **PPP-ER** | Non-trade comparisons — e.g. **World Bank poverty line $3 / person / day at PPP-ER** | Class numbers (order of magnitude, not to invent precision): for India **MER > PPP-ER** (~**₹80/$** MER vs ~**₹20/$** PPP) because **cost of living is lower** than in rich countries; MER is **higher** for an **import-dependent** country. **GDP at MER < GDP at PPP** (same ₹GDP, smaller divisor at PPP). Class rank: India **6th** at MER (sheet: earlier **4th**); **3rd** at **PPP**. **Per capita GDP = GDP / total population** — **better indicator of economic welfare** than raw GDP. **Prelims trap:** Official Indian GDP since 2015 is **GDP_MP**, not GDP_FC and not GDP_BP. **PPP** is for **welfare / poverty comparison**, not for invoicing exports. **$4 tn** headlines = **MER**. ---

|:---|:---|
| **NI / MP / FC / BP** | National Income / Market Price / Factor Cost / Basic Price |

sections.heading: Section A: Monetary Policy vs Fiscal Policy — The Two Pillars
sections.content:
| | Monetary Policy | Fiscal Policy |
|---|---|---|
| **Hindi Name** | *Mudra Niti* (मुद्रा नीति) | *Rajkoshiya Niti* (राजकोषीय नीति) |
| **Deals With** | Money & Banking | Government's Money ("Ruler's Treasury") |
| **Governed By** | **RBI** | **Government** (Central + State) |
| **Announced** | Bi-monthly (MPC meetings) | **1st February** every year (Union Budget) |

sections.heading: Budget — Historical Context
sections.content:
- **Pre-2000:** Budget presented at **5:00 PM** — convenient for Britishers to print and return same day; no legal basis for this timing
- **Year 2000 (Atal Bihari Vajpayee Govt):** Changed to **11:00 AM** — convenient for Indians
- **Pre-2017:** Budget presented in **March**
- **2017 onwards (Modi Govt):** Shifted to **1st week of February** (specifically 1st February)

---

sections.heading: Section B: Budget — Structure & Classification
sections.content:
> **Budget** = A record of **government receipts and expenditures**

Figure: Budget structure — Receipts and Expenditure, each further classified into Revenue and Capital.

---

sections.heading: B.1 Revenue Receipts
sections.content:
> **Definition — Three Key Characteristics:**
> 1. They **do NOT create liability** for the government
> 2. They are **NOT obtained through selling of government property**
> 3. *(Implicit)* They are **short-term/recurring** in nature

Revenue Receipts are divided into:

sections.heading: (i) Tax Revenue
sections.content:
- **Direct Tax** — Personal Income Tax (PIT), Corporate Tax, MAT (Minimum Alternate Tax), DDT (Dividend Distribution Tax), CGT (Capital Gains Tax), STT (Securities Transaction Tax)
- **Indirect Tax** — GST (on most goods & services), VAT (on 7 excluded items)

sections.heading: (ii) Non-Tax Revenue
sections.content:
| Item | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Fees** | Hospital registration (₹10 ticket at AIIMS — ₹10 × 1 crore patients/month = significant revenue) |
| **Fines** | Traffic challans (no helmet/seat belt — through system, not "under the table") |
| **License** | Driving license, passport, **4G/5G spectrum license** (telecom operators pay huge sums) |
| **Dividend** | Part of profit given to shareholder — Government gets dividends from PSUs/PSEs (ONGC, SBI, etc.) |
| **Escheat** | Amount charged by govt for care-taking work on property due to absence of legal heir |
| **Special Assessment** | Amount charged for developmental activities done in a particular area (e.g., toll tax) |
| **Asset Monetisation** | Giving government property on rent/lease (NOT sale) to earn revenue |

---

sections.heading: B.2 Capital Receipts
sections.content:
> **Definition — Three Key Characteristics (Reverse of Revenue Receipts):**
> 1. They **may have long-term character**
> 2. They **may be obtained through selling of government property**
> 3. They **may create liabilities** for the government

| Item | How it matches the definition |
|---|---|
| **Recovery of Loans** | Long-term character (e.g., India's loan to Sri Lanka — repaid after 10 years) |
| **Disinvestment** | Obtained through selling govt property (e.g., Air India sold to Tata) |
| **Borrowings** | Creates liability (₹1 lakh crore borrowed → must return ₹1.1 lakh crore with interest) |

> **Memory Aid:** Capital receipts = **huge sums** involved. "A capitalist has a good amount of money."

> **UPSC Logic Test:** *"Why is borrowing a Capital Receipt and NOT Revenue Receipt?"*
> Because borrowing **creates liability** → fits Capital Receipt definition. Revenue Receipt definition says "does NOT create liability" → borrowing cannot be kept under Revenue.

---

sections.heading: Dividend
sections.content:
- It is a **part of profit** given to the **share owner**
- **Example:** RBI transferred **~₹3 lakh crore** to Government of India in **2026** as a part of **surplus dividend**, while keeping around **5.6%** of its surplus dividend with itself
- This is based upon **Bimal Jalan Committee's recommendation** (Bimal Jalan = ex-RBI Governor)
- **How RBI earns profit:** Gold purchased at ₹30,000 (2004) now worth ₹1,30,000; foreign bond investments; interest on loans to commercial banks (bank rate, repo rate)
- The Bimal Jalan Committee recommended RBI can keep **5.6% to 5.9%** of total profit with itself, remaining to be transferred to GoI

sections.heading: Escheat
sections.content:
- It is the amount charged by the government for the **care-taking work** done on a property due to the **absence of legal heir**
- **Case 1:** Owner dies, no legal heir present → Govt takes control → When heir appears (after 6 months, 10 years etc.), property handed over after document verification → Govt charges escheat for care-taking period
- **Case 2:** Legal heir is a **minor** → Govt takes control until heir attains age of majority → Charges escheat for care-taking work

sections.heading: Special Assessment
sections.content:
- Amount charged by the government for **developmental activities done in a particular area**
- **Example:** Delhi expanding — forest area (Dwarka) developed into residential area → Government cut trees (with environmental ministry permission, 3× plantation elsewhere), constructed roads, water/permit system, public parks, street lights, police station, metro → Residents of that area pay special assessment
- Also applies as **toll tax** — specific road/bridge constructed → only those crossing it pay, not all residents

sections.heading: Asset Monetisation
sections.content: - **Definition:** Giving government property **on rent or on lease** *(lease = temporary ownership)* — NOT selling - **Key Distinction:** Disinvestment = **selling** govt property (Capital Receipt); Asset Monetisation = **renting/leasing** (Non-Tax Revenue Receipt) - **UPSC Prelims Trap:** Under the National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP), core brownfield infrastructure assets (highways, pipelines, railway tracks) are leased out under structured contractual concession frameworks for a fixed period. Sovereign ownership is strictly retained by the government, and assets revert back. Hence, proceeds from NMP/Asset Monetisation are classified as **Non-Tax Revenue Receipts**, whereas Disinvestment (selling equity/assets permanently) is a **Non-Debt Capital Receipt**. - **Examples:** - National highway monetised → land under highway pillars given to hotels, petrol pumps → ₹15,000 crore earned - Railway land along tracks → given on rent to private parties (go-downs, commercial use) - Govt pipeline (after refinery sold) → given on rent to Ambani/Adani for oil transport - **Target Achievement:** Last year target ₹88,000 crore → achieved ₹93,000 crore - Compare: Disinvestment target ₹1.68 lakh crore → achieved only ₹15,000 crore (opposition to selling) ---

sections.heading: B.4 Revenue Expenditure
sections.content:
> **Definition — Three Key Characteristics:**
> 1. They are to **maintain day-to-day services** of the government to **run the economy**
> 2. They **do NOT reduce liabilities** of the government
> 3. They **do NOT create assets**

Revenue Expenditure is further divided into:

sections.heading: (i) Developmental Revenue Expenditure
sections.content:
- Day-to-day services by the government **in order to run the economy**, like:
  - Health & Education services
  - Transport & Communication services
  - Irrigation & Flood control services
  - Research & Development services
  - Export services
  - A host of services which government provides on a day-to-day basis to **industry, agriculture and various other sectors**

> **Understanding "Developmental":** Teacher's salary in a government school = **Developmental** (directly contributes to skill development/education). Non-teaching staff salary = **Non-developmental** (essential but doesn't directly develop human capital). Similarly, doctor's salary = Developmental; hospital gatekeeper/clerk = Non-developmental.

sections.heading: (ii) Non-Developmental Revenue Expenditure
sections.content:
Comprises expenditure of:
- **Defence**
- **Law & Order**
- **Interest Payment** *(Key concept: interest is "free money" to banks — govt never received the interest amount, only the principal)*
- **Pension**
- **Civil Administration**
- **Subsidies**
- **Grants to States**

> **Critical Distinction — Interest vs Principal:**
> - Government borrows ₹1 lakh crore → constructs roads (development done with **principal**)
> - Interest of ₹10,000 crore paid to bank → **no development** from interest (never received that money)
> - Therefore: **Interest payment** = Non-developmental Revenue Expenditure
> - **Principal repayment** = Capital Expenditure
> - This is why loan repayment is always "**re**payment" (paid back in installments — EMI), not just "payment"

> **School Building vs School Staff:**
> - Government school **building construction** = **Capital Expenditure** (physical asset created — visible)
> - Government school **teacher salary** = **Developmental Revenue Expenditure** (runs day-to-day education)
> - Government school **non-teaching staff salary** = **Non-developmental Revenue Expenditure** (essential but no direct development contribution)

---

sections.heading: B.5 Capital Expenditure
sections.content:
> **Definition (Reverse of Revenue Expenditure):**
> 1. They **may create assets**
> 2. They **may reduce liabilities**

| Item | How it matches |
|---|---|
| **Construction of Roads** | Creates physical asset (e.g., 10,000 km → 70,000 km) |
| **Construction of Airports** | Creates physical asset (78 → 170 airports) |
| **Repayment of Loans** | Reduces liability (principal repaid) |

sections.heading: Classification of Tax — Key Principle
sections.content:
| | Direct Tax | Indirect Tax |
|---|---|---|
| **Nature** | **Directly paid** by the person on whom it is levied | **Indirectly paid** — transferred to another party |
| **Transferability** | **Cannot be transferred** | **Can be transferred** (consumer → seller → govt) |
| **Compulsion** | **Compulsory** — whether you consume or not, must pay | **Conditional** — only when you purchase/consume |
| **Example** | Income Tax (you earn ₹10 lakh, you pay ₹1 lakh tax — you cannot ask someone else to pay it) | GST (you pay fees + GST to Vajiram → Vajiram transfers GST to government) |

> **"Is it Double Taxation?"** — NO! Direct tax + Indirect tax ≠ Double Taxation. Double taxation occurs when the **same type of tax** is levied twice (e.g., income tax charged twice on the same income). Paying income tax on earnings AND GST on purchases is NOT double taxation — one is compulsory, other is conditional/by choice.

sections.heading: C.1 Direct Taxes (Details to be covered in later classes)
sections.content:
| Tax | Full Form | Key Point |
|---|---|---|
| **PIT** | Personal Income Tax | Up to ₹7 lakh: no tax (till last year) → Now **₹12 lakh** (2026 Budget) |
| **Corporate Tax** | Tax on company profits | Separate rates for different company sizes |
| **MAT** | Minimum Alternate Tax | Ensures companies pay minimum tax even with exemptions |
| **DDT** | Dividend Distribution Tax | Tax on dividends distributed by companies |
| **CGT** | Capital Gains Tax | Tax on profit from sale of assets |
| **STT** | Securities Transaction Tax | Tax on stock market transactions |

sections.heading: GST (Goods & Services Tax)
sections.content:
- Introduced: **1st July 2017**
- Slogan: **"One Nation, One Tax"**
- Covers: **All goods and services EXCEPT 7 items**
- GST Rates: **5%, 12%, 18%, 28%** (4 slabs)
- Constitutional Amendment: **101st Amendment Act**

##### GST Structure
- **CGST** (Central GST) — goes to Central Government
- **SGST** (State GST) — goes to State Government
- Always split **equally** (e.g., 18% GST = 9% CGST + 9% SGST)

##### Why "One Nation One Tax"?
> **Under VAT regime:**
> - Item produced in State A at ₹100 + 18% VAT = ₹118
> - Crosses state boundary → Entry tax ₹5 = ₹123
> - Enters municipal area → Octroi ₹2 = ₹125
> - **Tax in State A = ₹18; Tax in State B = ₹25** → Different prices in different states!
>
> **Under GST regime:**
> - Item at ₹100 + 18% GST = ₹118
> - Goes to State B → **still ₹118** (no additional entry tax, octroi etc.)
> - **One Nation, One Tax** (Standardized nationwide)

sections.heading: 7 Items Still Under VAT (NOT under GST)
sections.content:
| # | Item |
|---|---|
| 1 | **Crude Oil** |
| 2 | **ATF** (Aviation Turbine Fuel) |
| 3 | **Petrol** |
| 4 | **Diesel** |
| 5 | **Natural Gas** |
| 6 | **Alcohol** (for human consumption) |
| 7 | **Electricity** |

> **5 Petroleum Products + Alcohol + Electricity = 7 items under VAT**

##### Why Petrol/Diesel Prices Differ Across States
- **Central Excise (CENVAT)** → Same across all states
- **State-Level VAT (SLVAT)** → **Different** in each state
  - Maharashtra: SLVAT = 21% → Petrol at ₹90+
  - Delhi: SLVAT = 21% → Different price
  - Uttarakhand: SLVAT = 14% → Cheaper petrol
- **The entire price difference is because of State VAT, NOT Central tax**
- If petroleum products come under GST (proposed at 30% rate in July 2022): CGST = 15%, SGST = 15% → **same price everywhere**

> **Political Awareness:** "When ANY political party (ruling or opposition) says petrol/diesel price is too high — they are ALSO responsible. SLVAT is in the hands of the State Government. If they want relaxation, they can reduce SLVAT. Both Centre and State levy tax on petroleum."

sections.heading: FRBM Act — Fiscal Responsibility & Budget Management Act
sections.content:
> **Full Form:** Fiscal Responsibility **and** Budget Management Act
> **Core Idea:** It is the **duty of the government** ("fiscal" = government's money) to **responsibly manage** the budget (receipts and expenditures)

| Version | Year | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **Old FRBM Act** | **2003** | Already asked in Mains |
| **New FRBM Act** | **2017** | Current applicable version |

sections.heading: Sri Lanka Case Study — Why FRBM Matters
sections.content:
- **Gotabaya Rajapaksa** became head → **reduced taxes** (revenue fell) + **increased expenditures** (free gas, unemployment allowance, old-age pension)
- **Huge gap** created between revenue and expenditure
- Borrowed from **IMF** → could NOT repay → **defaulted**
- After 1.5–2 years: **economy devastated** — "We do not have money to purchase petroleum products from tomorrow"
- Same people who praised him **forcefully entered his house and looted everything**
- India & China provided emergency loans to help Sri Lanka purchase petroleum

> **Lesson:** Government MUST balance expenditure with revenue. Irresponsible fiscal management → Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Argentina, Afghanistan, Bangladesh — all struggling examples.

sections.heading: India's Fiscal Responsibility Example
sections.content:
- **May 2022:** India reduced petroleum tax by 4% → expected revenue loss ₹1 lakh crore
- **July 2022 (one month later):** Introduced **Windfall Tax** on crude oil → expected recovery ₹96,000 crore
- Similarly: **PM-KISAN** (₹6,000/farmer) increased expenditure → introduced **Krishi Kalyan Cess** (tax on tax)
- **Ayushman Bharat** (₹5 lakh free treatment) increased expenditure → introduced **Health & Education Cess**
- India always **manages the gap** — unlike Sri Lanka

sections.content:

Full lock on `03_Taxation.md` Lecture 7 (cluster **ECO-07**). The ₹96,000 crore offset above stays. Do **not** add a second Day-1 for this pair.

sections.heading: Function
sections.content:
- Whatever **central government collects** as tax from the states goes into a **Divisible Pool**
- Finance Commission recommends **how to divide** this pool between Centre and States
- Rationale: Centre collects from the entire country (more tax revenue) but States have limited area → States need more than their direct collection
- Like a father having more money and giving additional to the child who has less

sections.heading: Finance Commissions Studied
sections.content:
| FC | Period | Key Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **14th FC** | — | Reference taken for comparison |
| **15th FC** | — | Current reference |
| **16th FC** | **1 April 2026 – 31 March 2031** (5 years) | Just started; will be studied in detail |

- **15th FC Devolution:** Centre transfers **41%** of divisible pool to states
- CGST collected ≠ all stays with Centre → part goes to States through devolution → On every item, States effectively get more than Centre

> **Note:** On a ₹100 item with 18% GST: CGST = ₹9 (but part shared with states), SGST = ₹9 (fully with state). Net effect: States get MORE, Centre gets LESS per item.

sections.heading: Section F: Inclusive Growth & Development
sections.content: > **GDP** measures only **quantity** (production value). When we see **quantity + quality** → that is **Inclusive Growth / Development**.

sections.heading: Two Dimensions
sections.content: Figure: Inclusive Growth = quantity + quality, delivered through two dimensions — Physical Development and Human Development.

sections.heading: (a) Infrastructure Development
sections.content:
- **Roads** → Under PMGSY (Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana) / State-level schemes
- **Electricity** → Essential for factories, late-night studies, quality of life
- **Communication** → Internet access bridges urban-rural divide

sections.heading: F.2 Human Development
sections.content:
- **Health** — Hospitals, medical staff, public health services
- **Education** — Schools, colleges, skill development centres

sections.heading: Infrastructure Classification
sections.content:
| Economic Infrastructure | Social Infrastructure |
|---|---|
| Electricity | Education |
| Transportation | Health |
| Communication | Housing |

> **Mains Recurring Question (2018, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025):**
> *"Investment in infrastructure is inclusive growth" — Discuss*

sections.heading: Why Infrastructure > Subsidies (Key Mains Argument)
sections.content:
> **Infrastructure EMPOWERS** people → makes them **independent** → they start their own economic activity
> **Subsidies** make people **dependent** on the government → moment government stops, they suffer

**Three Real-World Examples from Lecture:**

1. **Farmer & Intermediary Example:**
   - Farmer sells at ₹2/kg (cost of production = ₹1.08/kg → negligible profit)
   - Intermediary buys at ₹2, sells at ₹20 in city (₹14/kg profit!) → "Economy of intermediaries, not producers"
   - If **roads** constructed → farmer can directly sell at ₹15-20/kg → permanent solution
   - Government MSP of ₹6/kg is **temporary** (only for one crop) + only 16% farmers know about MSP (SC/SIT report: 84% farmers unaware)
   - **Road construction** = permanent empowerment

2. **Village Worker Example:**
   - Man tried city life: ₹9,000 salary – ₹5,000 rent – ₹3,000 school fees = nothing left → returned
   - After PMGSY **road construction**: got ₹9,000 job in city (40 min bus commute), lives in village (₹1,000 transport + ₹3,000 school fees + ₹1,500 children's transport + ₹300 electricity + ₹200 internet = ₹6,000) → saves ₹3,000/month
   - **Additional income:** Grows vegetables, sells at city market every 7 days = ₹2,600→3,300/month extra
   - Urban schools sending buses to villages because of good roads → children getting quality education

3. **Jacket Factory Example:**
   - 3 Mumbai workers (earning ₹18,000 each, saving ₹1,000-2,000 in expensive city) returned to village
   - Started jacket manufacturing factory using **quality electricity** infrastructure
   - Borrowed ₹50,000 from SBI → repaid → borrowed ₹5 lakh → repaid → now bank offers ₹15-20 lakh
   - Now earning ₹27,000 each in village (more than Mumbai!) + employing 2 workers at ₹10,000 each
   - From **job seekers** to **job creators** — all because of electricity infrastructure

> **China's Proverb:** "Instead of giving fishes to someone, teach them the art of catching fishes — and they will survive for life."

---

sections.heading: GDP ≠ Government Income
sections.content:
- **GDP** = Income of the **people** (farmers, companies, service providers)
- **Government's income** = **Tax** (direct + indirect)
- If GDP = ₹5 trillion and tax = 0, government has NO resources despite high GDP

sections.heading: Tax-to-GDP Ratio — The Real Indicator
sections.content:
| Country | Tax-to-GDP Ratio | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| **India** | ~11% | ₹100 crore GDP → ₹11 crore tax to govt |
| **Sweden** | ~42% | ₹100 crore GDP → ₹42 crore tax → better roads, salary, railways, metro, police, law & order |

- **Developing vs Developed:** Low tax-to-GDP = developing; High = developed
- Migration flows from India → Sweden (for better infrastructure, salary, quality of life) — NOT reverse
- **Agriculture is tax-free** in India → if GDP is mostly agricultural, government gets less revenue → less development capacity
- India's GDP has good mix of agriculture + secondary + tertiary → secondary & tertiary give good tax revenue

> **Comparative Context:** GDP of Maharashtra > GDP of Pakistan. Market cap of Tata > GDP of Pakistan.

---

sections.heading: Section H: UNDP — 5 Human Development Reports
sections.content:
> **Published by:** United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) — **every year**

| # | Index | Full Form | Key Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **HDI** | Human Development Index | Core measure of development |
| 2 | **IHDI / PHDI** | Inequality-Adjusted HDI / Planetary Pressures-Adjusted HDI | Adjusts for inequality & environmental sustainability |
| 3 | **GDI** | Gender Development Index | Gender-based development gaps |
| 4 | **GII** | Gender Inequality Index | **Nobel Prize 2023 — Claudia Goldin** (work on gender inequality) |
| 5 | **MPI** | Multidimensional Poverty Index | Beyond income-based poverty measurement |

> *2025 Mains question was related to these indices.*
