sections.heading: 11. Google tax — Equalisation Levy (ECO-07-03)
sections.content:
**Equalisation Levy (EL)** — sheet *Equalization*; class **Google tax** because it **started** on Google, then all similar platforms.

> EL was aimed at **taxing foreign companies** which had a **significant local client** but were **billing them through their offshore units**, effectively **escaping** the country’s tax system.

In simple words: levied on **revenue** generated by **Google, Twitter (now X), Facebook, YouTube** etc. from **advertisement in India**.

| Lock | Fact |
|:---|:---|
| Rate | **6%** |
| In force | **2016** (proposed **2016–17 Budget**; from **1 April 2016**) |
| Threshold | payment **exceeding ₹1 lakh a year** to a **non-resident** service provider for **online advertisements in India** |

**Class why:** platform licence was for **content**, not for **ads**. Offline hoardings pay a licence; YouTube used the same platform at near-zero extra cost → **unfair**. Two ways to legalise: **licence** or **tax**. Government closed its eyes till **31 March 2016**, then taxed. **Level playing field** with offline ads. **Donald Trump** (first stint) called it a penalty on **American** firms; India: (i) no licence, (ii) the idea is **Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)** — America is a prime OECD member.

**Vocal for local:** advertisement on **Koo** (Indian) — **no** EL; on **X / Twitter** — **yes**. **Permanent establishment** in India → this levy **off**; tax them on **net income** made here, plus jobs.

sections.heading: Update — 13 September 2026 (UPSC CSE Prelims 2018)
sections.content: `CSE-2018-Q08` **missed** (`MST-086`). Official key = **neither**. The 6% Equalisation Levy on non-resident online ads is a **separate levy** from **1 April 2016** (2016–17 Budget) — **not** introduced as a part of the Income-tax Act. Non-resident ad platforms **cannot** claim a home-country **DTAA** credit for it. Class rate / ₹1 lakh threshold / scrap **1 April 2025** **held** (Q7 + flash). **Repeat 2 — 14 Sep evening:** picked **II only** (DTAA credit exists). Key = **III only**. **Held 15 Sep** Ghost Recall. 15-day **30 Sep**.

sections.heading: 11.1 Impact (sheet)
sections.content:
1. **Role of international organisations / forums.** The idea came from the **OECD Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) action plan**. That plan considered EL as an **option to tax digital transactions**.
2. **Prevents / reduces shifting of profits.** Would prevent technology companies from shifting the **majority of their profits** into their own nations **and** offshore to **tax havens** (haven = harbour, not heaven).
3. **Ensuring tax payment by online companies.** Global online businesses taxed for the **considerable income they earn from India**. Incentive to have **permanent establishment** in India and be taxed only on **net income** made here. Also discourages avoiding tax by exploiting **weaknesses in international taxation rules**.

---

sections.heading: 12. Digital Service Tax — Equalisation Levy 2.0 (ECO-07-04)
sections.content:
**Not** a second year of the same tax. **EL 1.0** = **6% on advertisement** revenue. **EL 2.0 / Digital Service Tax (DST)** = **2% on genuine e-commerce business** of **non-resident** platforms.

**Amazon / Flipkart** illustration: commission from sellers/buyers = genuine business; ads on the same site = already under EL 1.0. Offline Apple showroom has rent + staff; online seller can sit with stock in an almirah and **discount**. Same **level-playing-field** logic as **anti-dumping** at the border. **Only** e-commerce companies whose **headquarters are outside India** / **no tangible presence** (no offline business here). **Walmart–Flipkart** and **Amazon** → Trump complaint again. Introduced **1 April 2020** (four years after EL 1.0).

> EL further extended to **e-commerce companies** which were **sourcing their revenues from Indian customers without having tangible presence** here. The amendment to the **Finance Act, 2020** expanded the ambit of EL for **non-resident e-commerce operators** involved in **supply of services**, including **online sale of goods** and **provision of services**, with the levy at **2%**, **effective 1 April 2020**.

**European Union** analogue in class: **GAFA** tax (different name, same family).

sections.heading: 12.1 Impact of DST (sheet — after “effective from 1 April 2020”)
sections.content:
1. **Prolonged international tax-law negotiations.** Agenda: reform international tax law so digital companies were taxed **where economic activities were carried out**. Formally framed **within the OECD BEPS programme**.
2. **Changing international economic order.** **Proliferation of DST** was a **symptom** of that change. Countries such as **India**, which provide **large markets** for digital corporations, seek a **greater right to tax incomes**. (Class: India **3rd** on **Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)** — same L5 lock.)
3. **Adverse impact on foreign e-commerce companies.** Additional tax would **reduce profits**; they **may close operations in India**, which may further hit **investment and employment** (direct + attached). Singur / Tata Nano is **colour** for “don’t drive the plant out” — not a DST fact.

sections.heading: 12.2 Why both levies were scrapped
sections.content:
> To promote **cordial (friendly) trade relationship** with the **USA** and **European Union**, also to **scrap multiple direct-tax structure** in India, and also to stop the **possible exodus** of foreign e-commerce companies, government **scrapped both** the Equalisation Levies on **1 April 2025**.

Class extra (not on the sheet, but dictated): most platforms **took the advertisement licence** → EL 1.0’s original excuse faded; **Indian offline went online** → EL 2.0’s level-playing-field excuse faded; Trump had complained since **2016 / 2020**. **1 April 2025** is the exam date.

---

sections.heading: 13. Base Erosion and Profit Shifting — working toolkit (ECO-07-05)
sections.content:
L5 one-liner stays. Today is the **toolkit**.

**Sheet family:** **CbCR** · **Thin capitalisation** · **Patent box tax regimes** · **GAAR** (GAAR already **Lecture 6** — do not open a second Day-1).

> **BEPS** refers to the strategies used by **Multinational Corporations (MNCs)** to **avoid paying tax** by exploiting the **mismatches and gaps** in the tax rules.

sections.heading: Update — 13 September 2026 (UPSC CSE Prelims 2016)
sections.content:
`CSE-2016-Q60` **held**. BEPS in the news = **curbing tax evasion by multinational companies**. Not mining in backward areas, not biopiracy / genetic resources, not EIA / environmental-cost skip. Class toolkit (CbCR / thin cap / patent box) still sits here.

Mostly prevalent in **intellectual-property-intensive technology** (class: **Google, Apple**) and **life-sciences** (class: **Pfizer**).

**Impact:** nations have lost tax revenue to the tune of **US$100 billion to US$240 billion annually** (OECD). The lost revenue is equivalent to **4–10%** of **total income-tax revenue at the global level**. Class: if a firm leaves a **15%** India for a **10%** Sri Lanka, that **5 points** goes **nowhere** — not to India, not to Sri Lanka. Class also: finance ministers of about **130** nations sat on a **BEPS-avoidance** understanding (do **not** overwrite L5 **139** GMCT members).

sections.heading: 13.1 Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR)
sections.content: Part of the **OECD BEPS action plan**. As per the old **Income-tax Act, 1961, Section 286(2)**, the CbCR is required to be submitted by an **Indian affiliate of a foreign-parented group** **or** an **Indian parent company**, **and also by the destination nation**. Class: Sri Lanka tells India “your firm is trying to land here”; the firm also files; destination + home both report so the shift can be **incentivised to stop** or **blocked** under the avoidance understanding.

sections.heading: 13.2 Thin capitalisation
sections.content:
> A condition where a company is **financed with a high level of debt compared to its own capital**.

Class mechanism (illustration, **not** a statutory 60:40 lock): for a footloose MNC, India wants **most of the project funded by Indian-bank debt**, **own funds in the minority** — **thin** own capital. Banks can then say **pay us before you sell and leave**. Sticky debt = less easy BEPS.

sections.heading: 13.3 Patent box tax regime
sections.content:
Introduced in India by enacting **Section 115BBF** of the **Income-tax Act, 1961**. As per **Finance Act, 2016**, it is a **special, very low corporate-tax regime** used by countries to **incentivise research and development** by **taxing patent income differently from others**.

Class illustration: ordinary corporate rates stay; **if** the firm does **R&D in India** and earns from a **patented** product, that patent income can be taxed at a **much lower** rate (class example **10%**) so the firm does **not** need to leave for a 10% jurisdiction. **Do not** treat 10% as a gazette lock unless a later class numbers the section.

**GAAR** — already Lecture 6. Same sitting’s “measures to avoid BEPS” list; no extra cluster row.

---

sections.heading: 14. Faceless Tax Assessment Scheme (ECO-07-06)
sections.content:
L6 one-liner. Today’s working version.

The **Central government** introduced the faceless assessment scheme to provide **greater transparency, efficiency and accountability** in **income-tax assessments**. It is an attempt to remove **individual tax officials’ discretion** and **potential harassment** for income-tax payers. **All provisions** introduced under this sit under the **old Income-tax Act, 1961**.

- Eliminate the **interface** between **assessing officers** and **taxpayers** (neither knows the other; notice and reply **online**).
- **Optimise utilisation of resources** through **economies of scale** and **functional specialisation**.
- **Main objective:** remove **physical interaction** as much as possible.

Class: cash + a face-to-face meeting is where the bribe lives; opportunity cost of five trips to the ward; “come tomorrow, PAN not visible.” Faceless = only the **genuine demand** survives.

---

L7 one-liner on Border Adjustment Tax as a **countervailing-duty** swap is **not** today’s lock — today’s cousin is **anti-dumping duty**.

sections.heading: 16. Lecture 7 — UPSC Quick Recall
sections.content:
1. Windfall = **surtax** / **special additional excise duty** on **Indian** crude (**₹23,250 / tonne**, July 2022 lock) and on **exports** of ATF / petrol / diesel (**₹15 / ₹13 / ₹10**). **Not** on OPEC. **Cannot** pass to the pump. Review **every 14 days**. **July 2022 → scrapped Dec 2024 → back March 2026**.
2. Land tax = **municipality**, lump-sum, also property / building / house. Land-revenue = **State**, **0.5–1%** on **circle rate**, **5–10 years**, even on a **loss**; **seller**. Professional tax = **State**, lump-sum on professionals; **adjusted** against income tax.
3. **EL / Google tax** = **6%** on **ad** revenue of **non-residents**; **₹1 lakh / year** threshold; **1 April 2016**; OECD BEPS option for digital.
4. **DST / EL 2.0** = **2%** on **non-resident e-commerce** without **tangible presence**; **Finance Act 2020**, **1 April 2020**. **Both ELs scrapped 1 April 2025** (USA/EU, multiple DT, exodus).
5. BEPS = MNC strategies exploiting **gaps** in tax rules; OECD loss **US$100–240 bn / year** = **4–10%** of global income-tax revenue. **CbCR** = **s.286(2)** ITA 1961. Thin cap = **high debt / thin own capital**. Patent box = **s.115BBF**, **Finance Act 2016**. **GAAR** = L6.
6. Faceless = no officer–taxpayer **face**; ITA 1961; transparency / efficiency / accountability. **Vivad / Sabka / BAT / e-Bikray / GST extras = Lecture 8.**

sections.heading: 17. Vivad Se Vishwas — Direct Tax (ECO-08-01)
sections.content:
Introduced **2019** to resolve **Direct Tax** disputes. Announced with the object of **settling Direct Tax disputes**.

It benefits **both**:

- the **government** — **timely revenue**;
- the **tax payer** — brings down **uncertainty** and **litigation costs**.

Sheet margin: *Vivad Se Vishwas Tax — DT*. Prelims split: this name is the **direct-tax** scheme.

---

sections.heading: 18. Sabka Vishwas — Indirect Tax (ECO-08-01)
sections.content:
Announced with the object of settling **pending disputes of service tax and Central excise duty** which are **now subsumed under GST**.

Sheet heading *Sabka Vishwas scheme — IT* here means **Indirect Tax**, **not** Income Tax. Two names so Prelims can split **DT / IDT**.

**Two components of the scheme:**

1. **Dispute resolution** — aimed at the **legacy cases** of Central excise duty and service tax now subsumed under GST, and **pending in litigation at various forums**.
2. **Amnesty** — offers an opportunity to tax payers to **pay the outstanding tax** and be **free of any other consequences under the law**.

**Under both schemes** there will be **total waiver of interest / penalty** and **immunity from prosecution**.

---

sections.heading: 19. Border Adjustment Tax vs ADD vs CVD (ECO-08-02)
sections.content:
**Duty vs tax (class lock):** **duty** = tax on **goods**. **Tax on services** from **1 April 1994** (service tax). Do not swap.

NITI Aayog members suggested imposing **Border Adjustment Tax (BAT)** on **imports** to provide a **level playing field** to **domestic industries**.

**BAT** is a duty **proposed** to be imposed on **imported goods in addition to the customs duty**, levied at the **border**. **Proposed, not introduced.** Class: it might **replace anti-dumping duty (ADD)** or **part** of it — that is the cousin, **not** a live levy.

**Destination principle:** BAT follows the rule that you tax a product **based on the location of its sale to the final consumer**, rather than on the **location of production or origin**.

| Instrument | Class lock |
|:---|:---|
| **Anti-Dumping Duty (ADD)** | Foreign firm **excess production** / sells **below own-country price**. Today’s BAT cousin. |
| **Countervailing Duty (CVD)** | Foreign **subsidy**. L7 parked line “BAT replaces CVD” is **wrong for today**. |
| **Border Adjustment Tax (BAT)** | Extra border duty on imports **on top of customs**, destination-based, **proposed**. |

**Impact (class):**

- **Macro:** if imports fall, a country can **cut the trade deficit**.
- If the country is a **major export market** for many **developed** countries, the tax plan will have a **serious adverse effect** on them after implementation.
- BAT may render **some firms less profitable**. If prices are **forced upward**, they may lose **competitiveness** versus **substitutes** or **locally made similar product**.

Class warning: BAT is **not** a licence to tax imports **above** the domestic rate. The NITI pitch is a **true World Trade Organization (WTO) level playing field**, not a hidden tariff hike.

---

sections.heading: 20. SMA → NPA → ARC → SARFAESI (ECO-08-03)
sections.content:
**Loan** splits **secured** (collateral / mortgage) vs **unsecured**.

| Clock | Label |
|:---|:---|
| **0–89 days** overdue | **Special Mention Account (SMA)** |
| **90 days** onward | **Non-Performing Asset (NPA)** |

**NPA buckets (class):**

| Bucket | Window |
|:---|:---|
| **Substandard** | **90 days – 1 year** |
| **Doubtful** | **> 1 year – 3 years** |
| **Lost** | **> 3 years** (banks “wash their hands”) |

**Asset Reconstruction Company (ARC):** Reserve Bank of India (RBI) licence. Buys the NPA. Class board example: years **90 / 91 / 92**.

**Gross NPA story (class numbers):** **10.67% (2014)** → **14% (2018)** → **~1.70–1.72%** now.

**M.S. Verma Committee** (ex-State Bank of India chairman — “who knows the pain of NPA better than SBI?”) → **SARFAESI Act, 2002**. Banks may **sell mortgaged / collateral property** to recover a bad loan. **Public Sector Banks (PSBs) only** on the e-auction story that follows.

---

sections.heading: 21. e-Bikray → BAANKIT (ECO-08-04)
sections.content:
**e-Bikray** = **Electronic Banking Revenue Auction Yojana**. Launched **February 2019** by the **Finance Minister**. **PSBs only.**

It is an **e-auction platform**: **single-window** access to information on properties put up for e-auction, plus a facility to **compare similar properties** across all PSB e-auction sites. It is for those **mortgaged properties whose loans have become NPA** — **not** “any property.”

It provides **navigational links** to all PSB e-auction sites, a **property search** feature, and **single-window** access to information on the property up for e-auction through **photographs, videos, and Google Map** address.

The platform also helps the **buyer** to **verify ownership** (bank e-auction sites often listed a property already selected). Search by **state / district / bank-wise** details.

**Indian Banks Auctions Mortgage Properties Information (IBAPI).** The e-Bikray / BankNet platform is linked to IBAPI. IBAPI is an initiative of the **Indian Banks Association (IBA)** under the policy of the **Department of Financial Services**, **Ministry of Finance**, which causes mortgage properties to be auctioned **online** and also **banks alerting** with Public Sector Banks.

**Replacement:** e-Bikray was replaced with **BAANKIT** (**e-bank asset auction network**) on **3 January 2025** (transcript lock). Sheet 4 wrote **3 January 2021** — year slip; do not mix the two.

---

sections.heading: 22. VAT, ITC and inverted duty (ECO-08-05)
sections.content:
**Value Added Tax (VAT)** is a common form of an **indirect tax levied on goods**. It is paid to the government by the producers **at every stage in the supply chain**. VAT is applicable only on goods **sold within a particular state**, which means the **buyer and seller need to be in the same state**. (You may belong to Tamil Nadu and buy petrol in Delhi — both legs of that sale are in **Delhi**.)

**VAT in India:** tax charged on the **gross margin at every stage** in the sale of goods. Tax is assessed and collected at **each point**, starting from the **manufacturer** until the product reaches the **retailer**.

It is a tax **only on value addition**, and **only on goods**, **not on services**. Services had a separate **service tax**.

**Timeline (class):**

| Year | Lock |
|:---|:---|
| **1986** | India, on the recommendations of the **L.K. Jha Committee** (same committee that recommended **Minimum Support Price (MSP)** in **1964**). |
| Suggestion | **Manufacturing Value Added Tax (MANVAT)** |
| Introduced | **Modified Value Added Tax (MODVAT)** at **8%, 16% and 24%** |
| **2000** | **Yashwant Sinha** Finance Minister. MODVAT replaced by **Central Value Added Tax (CENVAT)** at a **single 16%**. |
| **2004** | **Central excise duty** included **Input Tax Credit (ITC)** in CENVAT. **State sales tax** included ITC → **State-Level VAT (SLVAT / SVAT)**. |

**ITC (class):** manufacturer / service provider is **not** the final consumer. Tax paid on **inputs** is **credited** on the GST portal and set off against tax collected on output. Only the **net** is deposited. Final-consumer purchases (director’s home AC, own-room TV) get **no** credit.

**Cascading** = past taxes **carried forward** until ITC. Class numerical: value added ₹100 + ₹50 + ₹50 = ₹200; 10% VAT → government gets **₹10 + ₹5 + ₹5 = ₹20** — tax **only on production / value addition**, not on the already-taxed earlier stage.

**Inverted duty structure:** arises when **taxes on output are lower than taxes on input**, creating an **inverse accumulation of Input Tax Credit** which **in most cases has to be refunded**. Class purpose: so a rate-cut announcement (e.g. bikes **28% → 18%** from **22 September 2025**) does **not** freeze production for two months while dealers wait — government refunds the **input–output gap**.

---

sections.heading: 23. Need of GST, dual structure, zero-rated, e-way (ECO-08-06)
sections.content:
**Need of GST.** Despite having VAT, people were paying several additional taxes: **service tax, additional excise duty, countervailing duty, entertainment tax, entry tax, octroi** etc. Apart from this there was a **lack of proper coordination** between Centre and States in the **fixation of indirect tax**.

So, in order to **scrap the multiple indirect-tax structure**, to introduce a **national-level VAT**, and to ensure proper Centre–State coordination in fixation of indirect taxes, government **replaced VAT with GST in July 2017**.

**Already locked on SS Sir L1** (do not restudy): 1 July 2017; One Nation, One Tax; CGST + SGST equal; seven items still under VAT.

**New on this sitting:**

**Union Territory Goods and Services Tax (UTGST):** Union Territory **with** a legislative assembly → treat like **SGST**. Union Territory **without** a legislative assembly → **only UTGST**.

**Dual structure:**

- Goods and services **produced and consumed in the same State** → **CGST + SGST** collected (18% on ₹100 → ₹9 + ₹9).
- Produced in **one State**, consumed in **another** → **Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST)** collected **first**, then divided in **equal proportions** between the **Centre** (as CGST) and the **consumer State** (as SGST).

**SGST amount is always shared with the consumer State in India**, because GST is a **destination-based tax**.

**Zero-rated status (exports):** Government of India does **not** levy GST on **exportable items**, but exporters can get the **ITC refund**. Since the entire process of export involves **zero GST**, exportable items in India have **zero-rated status**. **Imported items still attract GST** (class: in the form of IGST). Aim: make Indian exports **cheaper / more competitive** abroad.

**E-way bill:** an **electronic document** generated on the **GST portal**, **GST app**, or even through **SMS**, evidencing the **movement of goods 10 km away** from the **point of sale or point of production**, valued **more than ₹50,000**. Earlier **only inter-State**; later **intra-State** also, still measured from the point of production/sale (within 10 km the seller can still verify). Aim: seamless transport — invoice, weight, bill number travel with the consignment.

**GST tree on the sheet (names only today):** dual structure; destination-based; e-way bill; zero-rated status; **National Anti-Profiteering Authority (NAA)**; GST Council; compensation scheme; ITC / inverted duty; **GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT)**; **Reverse Charge Mechanism (RPM)**. Council / compensation / GSTAT / RPM = **next class**.

To bring any of the remaining seven VAT items under GST, class: **75% voting** in the GST Council.

---

sections.heading: 24. GST rates from 22 September 2025, NAA → CCI (ECO-08-07)
sections.content:
**Before 22 September 2025** (sheet **22/9/25**; transcript once slipped to 2026 — lock the **sheet**): four slabs **5%, 12%, 18%, 28%**.

**28%** held **luxury** (cars, bikes, private jets etc.), **sin goods** (tobacco, cigarettes, pan masala; **alcohol ×** — still under VAT), and **demerit goods** (petrol, diesel — **also ×**, still under VAT). Class mnemonic: **sin goods = internal pollution**; **demerit goods = external pollution**.

**GST compensation cess** sat **on top** of 28% (class range **1–22%** of **value**, not tax-on-tax). Example: Mercedes = price + 28% + 22%. **Cess scrapped from 22 September 2025.**

**22 September 2025 onwards:** **two** working slabs **5%** and **18%**, plus a **special rate of 40%** on fewer items. **99.99%** of items sit in 5 / 18. **All former 12% items move to 5%** (class examples: drip irrigation, sprinkler).

| Now 18% (class examples) | Now special **40%** |
|:---|:---|
| **ACs**, **refrigerators**, **TVs beyond 32 inch** (earlier 28%) | Petrol cars **> 1200 cc** and **> 4 m** length |
| Petrol cars **upto 1200 cc** and **4 m** length | Diesel cars **> 1500 cc** |
| Diesel cars **upto 1500 cc** | Bikes **> 350 cc** |
| Bikes **upto 350 cc** | **Sin goods**; **aerated drinks** |

**Sin goods extra:** class — **12–30% additional tax** on top of 40% (not a cheapening vs the old 28% + cess stack). **Alcohol / petrol / diesel remain outside GST** until the Council votes them in; **when** they come they would sit at the **maximum** rate.

Government bet: lower rate → **more quantity** purchased → revenue held up by volume, not by a higher rate.

**National Anti-Profiteering Authority (NAA).** Constituted by the **Central government** after GST, to analyse whether **ITC credit** availed by any **registered person**, or a **reduction in tax**, is **passed on to the consumers**, and the public is protected from **random price increase** for self-interest **in the name of GST**. Class story: vegetable thali 18% → 5%; some sellers raised the base price so the bill stayed ₹118. Penalty / **six-month** licence suspension / permanent cancellation if not corrected. **For five years 2017–2022.** **In 2022 NAA was subsumed under the Competition Commission of India (CCI).**

**GST Council** — heading on the sheet; **not taught today**. Next class.

---

sections.heading: 25. Lecture 8 — UPSC Quick Recall
sections.content:
1. **Vivad 2019 = Direct Tax** disputes. **Sabka = service tax + Central excise** now under GST. Sheet *IT* on Sabka = **Indirect Tax**, not Income Tax. **Both:** waiver of **interest / penalty** + **immunity from prosecution**. Sabka = **dispute resolution** (legacy cases, various forums) + **amnesty** (pay outstanding tax, no other consequences).
2. **BAT** = proposed extra **border** duty on imports **on top of customs**, **destination**-based (sale to final consumer, not origin). NITI pitch = **level playing field**. Cousin to replace = **ADD**, not **CVD**. Duty = goods; service tax from **1 April 1994**.
3. **SMA 0–89 days**; **NPA from 90 days**: substandard **90d–1y** / doubtful **1–3y** / lost **>3y**. Gross NPA **10.67% (2014) → 14% (2018) → ~1.70–1.72%**. **SARFAESI 2002** from **M.S. Verma** (ex-SBI). **ARC** buys NPA (RBI licence).
4. **e-Bikray** Feb **2019**, FM, **PSBs only**, mortgaged NPA properties. **IBAPI** = IBA + Department of Financial Services. Replaced by **BAANKIT 3 January 2025** (sheet wrote 2021).
5. VAT = goods, **same State**, every stage of the chain. **L.K. Jha 1986** (same MSP 1964 committee) → suggest **MANVAT** → **MODVAT 8/16/24** → **2000 CENVAT 16%** (Yashwant Sinha) → **2004 ITC** in CENVAT and **SLVAT**. **Inverted duty** = output tax **<** input tax → ITC pile, **usually refunded**.
6. GST July **2017** scraps the VAT-plus-many-cesses stack. **Same State = CGST+SGST**; **inter-State = IGST first**, then **equal** split with the **consumer** State. **UT without assembly = UTGST**. Exports = **zero-rated** (no GST + **ITC refund**); **imports still GST**. **E-way:** portal / app / SMS; **10 km** from sale or production; value **> ₹50,000**.
7. From **22 September 2025**: slabs **5% + 18%** + special **40%**; **compensation cess scrapped**; old **12% → 5%**. Small petrol **≤1200 cc / 4 m**, diesel **≤1500 cc**, bikes **≤350 cc** = **18%**; beyond that, sin goods, aerated drinks = **40%**. **NAA** Centre, 2017–22, then **CCI**. **GST Council / GSTAT / RPM / compensation scheme = next class.**

sections.heading: Lecture 02 — 3 September 2026
sections.content:
> **Date of Lecture:** 3 September 2026  
> **Date Added:** 2026-09-03  
> **Faculty:** **Shyam Sundar Sir (SS Sir)** — continues Fiscal Policy from **Lecture 01, 22 August 2026** (`02_Fiscal_Policy_Budget_and_Syllabus_Overview.md`). That class listed the six deficits and named the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act; today is the working formulas, 1997 shift, and FRBM targets.  
> **Source:** Vajiram & Ravi class + audio transcript + 6 handwritten notebook pages (dated **3/9/26**)  
> **Also relevant for:** Prelims (deficit identities, FRBM numbers), GS-III (fiscal consolidation, crowding out, debt)

**How to read class shortcuts:** full form on first use. Glossary at the end. Do not invent a number the sheet / class did not give.

L01 already has Sri Lanka / windfall-tax as *why FRBM matters*. Do not re-drill that story here.

---

sections.heading: 1. Budget Deficit vs Fiscal Deficit (ECO-06-01)
sections.content:
**Revenue Expenditure (RE) + Capital Expenditure (CE)** = total expenditure.  
**Revenue Receipts (RR) + Capital Receipts (CR)** = total receipts.

| | Formula (class) | What it captures |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Budget deficit** | Total exp − Total receipt = **(RE + CE) − (RR + CR)** | Gap after **all** receipts, **including borrowing**. Pre-1997 India used this and then *made the gap look zero* after the year ended. |
| **Fiscal deficit** | Total exp − Total receipt **except borrowing** = **(RE + CE) − (RR + CR except borrowing)** | How much the government **must borrow**. Announced **in advance** so others can help close the gap (tax, disinvestment, better spending). |

**Capital receipts** in class: (a) **recovery of loans**, (b) **disinvestment**, (c) **borrowing**. For fiscal deficit, **(c) is dropped**. Recovery + disinvestment = **CR except borrowing** = **non-debt CR**.

Class logic: telling the country the gap **after** the year is over is useless — economists cannot suggest better ways to close it. Fiscal deficit is the **roadmap**.

**Ways and Means Advances (WMA):** sheet “Ways & Means bill” — **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** can lend to the **Government of India (GoI)** for **90 days**.

---

sections.heading: 2. Before 1997: Monetised Deficit and Deficit Financing (ECO-06-02)
sections.content:
Before **1997**, GoI tried to make the **budget deficit look zero** by:

1. **Printing currency** = **monetised deficit**. Class: **most inflationary** way to finance government spending. Extra cash in pockets (freebies, cash transfers) raises **demand** with **no extra supply** → inflation. Class illustrations of how bad printing can get: **England ~11.7%** (highest in 40 years, about three years back); **Pakistan 27%**; **Sri Lanka 68%**; **Argentina 292%** (and a Venezuela figure on the sheet trail — do not mix them). Inflation **kills purchasing power** even if the nominal salary is unchanged.
2. **Borrowing from RBI** — unsold government bonds parked with RBI as security; RBI was administratively bound to fund the gap (plus the **90-day** WMA window).

**Deficit financing** (sheet) = those two **plus** borrowing from financial institutions (**World Bank**, **Asian Development Bank (ADB)**, **New Development Bank (NDB)**, etc.) **plus** issuing **government bonds**.

**From 1997** (Sukhamoy Chakravarty Committee): GoI **almost stopped** printing and RBI-window financing. It now **relies on market-based financial institutions** (banks, markets) to fund the deficit. World Bank / ADB-type loans are for **capital / developmental** use, not for cash freebies — so **printing-based promises run hotter** than **borrowing-based** ones.

---

sections.heading: 3. Market Borrowing: Crowding Out, Prices, Inflation Band (ECO-06-03)
sections.content:
Higher **fiscal deficit** = higher **borrowings**. Borrowing is **not bad** if it funds **productive** use and **asset creation**. Class: **in India it is mostly non-developmental revenue expenditure.**

**Implications of financing the deficit through market-based institutions**

1. **Crowding out.** Government borrows large against **government securities**. Banks are left with **less** to lend the **private** sector. Opposite picture in class: if banks are flush, they cut the rate and **crowd in** small investors.
2. The **borrowing rate of interest** rises (interest = **price of money**). Higher cost can be **passed to consumers** as higher prices.
3. Because the borrowing is largely for **non-developmental RE**, **income and demand** are transferred **without corresponding output** → **inflation risk**.

**India’s inflation target (margin):** **4% ± 2** → band **2–6%**. Class: should not go below **2** or above **6**.

---

sections.heading: 4. Revenue Deficit, Credit Rating, Primary Deficit (ECO-06-04)
sections.content:
**Revenue Deficit (RD) = RE − RR.**

High borrowing → high **interest burden**. Interest is paid from **revenue receipts**, so **RE − RR widens**. Financing **non-developmental RE** by borrowing **hurts the sovereign credit rating**; the **next** foreign loan comes **dearer**.

Agencies class named: **Standard & Poor’s, Moody’s, Fitch** — together **>96%** of world rating business; S&P + Moody’s **>80%**. Better rating = country’s **trust**; class recalled an upgrade **BBB− → BBB** with a **positive** outlook (do not invent the year).

**Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payment** (sheet wrote “interest rate payment” = **interest payment**).

It shows the **direction** of the fiscal deficit. **Low primary deficit is not a healthy sign** if it means **almost the entire fiscal deficit is interest on old loans** — little left for roads, rails, airports, welfare. Class contrast: a large fiscal deficit with **small** interest share can still be going into **capital / developmental** spending.

---

sections.heading: 5. Effective Revenue Deficit — Pranab Mukherjee, 2012 (ECO-06-05)
sections.content:
**Effective Revenue Deficit** = **RD − grants to states for production / asset creation** (developmental RE). Introduced by **Pranab Mukherjee** as Finance Minister in **2012**.

It tries to show the **net / real adverse impact** of the revenue deficit: take total RD, **subtract** the grants that are **meant** for productive activity (even if they sit in the revenue account). Class: still **not** the headline number the Budget treats as the main RD — **knowledge surface** only. One concept was **introduced**; another was **recommended but not accepted** (PSBR sits in that second bucket).

---

sections.heading: 6. PSBR and Off-Budget Borrowing (ECO-06-06)
sections.content:
**Public Sector Borrowing Requirement (PSBR)** = **gross fiscal deficit** of **Centre + States** (and the borrowing that finances it) **+ independent borrowings by Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)** = **off-budget borrowings**.

Class: when we say “India’s fiscal deficit is x%” we usually mean the **Centre only**. Combine Centre + States and the number is **much larger** (class said **more than 10%** in that illustration — do not treat as a current official print). **Indian Oil** example: asked the Centre for **₹70,000 crore**; Budget support **₹10,000 crore**; remaining **₹60,000 crore** borrowed outside = off-budget.

Based on **C. Rangarajan** and **Bimal Jalan** committee recommendations (sheet: “Vimal”; same Jalan as the RBI surplus committee in L01). **Not accepted** as the headline deficit. **16th Finance Commission** (from **1 April 2026**): class — **off-budget borrowings to stop**.

---

sections.heading: 7. Old FRBM Act 2003 (Vijay Kelkar) (ECO-06-07)
sections.content:
**Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act** — passed **2003**, path from **2004–05 to 2008–09** (five years). **Vijay Kelkar Committee.**

**Fiscal consolidation** = reduce the deficit by **rationalising expenditure** on one side and **raising revenue** on the other. Aim: government **responsible, accountable, transparent** in fiscal exercise.

| Target (old FRBM) | Path | By 2008–09 |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Revenue deficit** | Down **0.5%** of GDP **each year** | **Zero** (does **not** mean expenditure zero — revenue must rise to match) |
| **Fiscal deficit** | Down **0.3%** of GDP each year | **Not more than 3% of GDP** |

**Not achieved.** Targets were reset / extended (class: 2012, then 2014); **effective revenue deficit** and a **macroeconomic framework** entered the story; **N.K. Singh Committee** formed **May 2016**, report **early 2017**, to ask why the path failed.

---

sections.heading: 8. N.K. Singh Committee — New FRBM Path (ECO-06-08)
sections.content:
Sheet: **old FRBM 2004** vs **new FRBM 2017 / 2022–23 / 2023–24**.

1. **Revenue deficit:** bring down from **2.1% of GDP (2017)** by **0.25% each year** so that by **2022–23** RD is **not more than 0.8% of GDP**.
2. **Fiscal deficit:** reduce to **3% by 2017–18**, **stay at 3% for the next three years**, then cut **0.2% each year** so that by **2023–24** FD is **not more than 2.5% of GDP**.
3. **Escape route:** **±0.5%** around the **annual fiscal-deficit target**. Economy **does well** → policymakers may **cut** the target by **0.5%** (right time to trim subsidies / raise tax). Economy **does not** → may **raise** it by **0.5%**. A **range**, not a single point — so the government need not freeze salaries and halt roads in Q4 just to hit a point target (class: **Himachal Pradesh** salary-stop illustration).
4. **Fiscal Council** — autonomous body for coordination of **monetary and fiscal policy**, **Centre and States**, and **direct + indirect tax** fixation (GST has a split logic; **VAT** on petrol etc. does not).

**Debt:** bring **total outstanding debt** from **70% of GDP** (**49% Centre + 21% States**) to **60%** (**40% Centre + 20% States**). Sheet margin: **2019 → 67%**. Class: 2019 was a **better** fiscal year; pandemic blew the path (do not treat later % as a drill unless re-taught).

sections.heading: Update — 13 September 2026 (UPSC CSE Prelims 2018)
sections.content:
`CSE-2018-Q09` **held**. Statement 1 = NK Singh path: general government **60%** by **2023** = **40% Centre + 20% States**. Statement 2 **fails** — it **swaps** the starting split (Centre **49%**, States **21%**, not the reverse). Statement 3 = **Article 293**: a State **must** take the Centre’s consent to raise a loan if it owes the Centre outstanding liabilities. Key = **1 and 3 only**.

**Rename:** FRBM → **Debt Management and FRBM Act and Rules**.

**Way forward (class)**

- National consensus on **non-developmental RE**. **Economic Times 2022:** state subsidies should **not exceed 1% of Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP)**.
- More **capital expenditure / infrastructure**. **Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD):** **80%** of rural government expenditure on **subsidies**, only **20%** on infrastructure.
- Better **data** to assess subsidies and tax.
- **Fiscal prudence** with development: **debt-to-GDP can be higher** if it finances **developmental RE and CE**, **not** non-developmental RE. Class: US internal debt-to-GDP cited as **~130%** — the issue is **use and repayment**, not the ratio alone.
- Sheet closed on **Windfall tax** — numbers already in L01 (July 2022 crude).

---

sections.heading: UPSC Cues
sections.content:
- **Budget deficit includes borrowing; fiscal deficit excludes it.** Non-debt CR = recovery + disinvestment.
- **Monetised deficit = printing = most inflationary.** Stopped as the main plug from **1997 (Chakravarty)** → **market** finance.
- Market finance → **crowding out** + higher interest + inflation if the money is **non-developmental RE**. India inflation **4% ± 2**.
- **Low primary deficit ≠ healthy** if it is all **old interest**.
- **Effective RD (Mukherjee, 2012)** = RD minus **state grants for assets**. **PSBR** = Centre + State FD + **PSU off-budget**; **16th FC: stop off-budget**.
- Old FRBM: RD **0.5%/yr → 0**; FD **0.3%/yr → 3%** by **2008–09**. NK Singh: RD **2.1 → 0.8** by **2022–23**; FD **3% then 2.5% by 2023–24**; escape **±0.5%**; debt **70 → 60**.

---

sections.heading: 1. Environment vs Ecosystem (ENV-01-02)
sections.content:
**Environment** = our **surroundings**. It is made of:

| Class shortcut | Full form | Examples in a forest |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **l.f. / biotic** | **Living factors** (life forms) | Plants, animals |
| **n.l. / abiotic** | **Non-living** components | Air, water (surface + groundwater), landforms, nutrients in soil |

An **ecosystem** is not just a bag of those parts. It is an **entity** whose parts **interact**. Plants ↔ animals (food + pollination); plants ↔ air/water/nutrients (photosynthesis); animals ↔ oxygen, water, landforms (habitat); soil fertility ↔ flora and fauna; even abiotic–abiotic links exist.

**Orographic / relief rainfall** (school geography, used here only to show abiotic–abiotic linkage): moisture-laden winds hit a mountain → **windward** side wet → **leeward** side dry. Water resources of a forest therefore depend on rainfall, which often depends on **landforms**.

Because of these two-way associations the forest becomes **self-sustaining** — it can support life on its own — and that is what qualifies it as an ecosystem.

> **Dictated definition:** An ecosystem is a **functional unit** composed of a **biotic community** integrated with its **physical non-living environment** through the **flow of energy** and the **flow of nutrients**.

- **Functional unit** — every ecosystem *performs* functions (energy flow + nutrient flow).
- **Biotic community** — all living components taken together.
- **Integrated with** — associated / linked with the abiotic setting.

**A.G. Tansley** (Arthur George Tansley) coined the concept of ecosystem.

| Classification | Meaning | Examples |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Terrestrial** vs **aquatic** | Land-based vs water-based | Forest, grassland, desert vs river, lake, ocean |
| **Natural** vs **artificial** | Wild vs **human-managed** | Forest vs cropland / aquarium |
| Simple vs complex | Complexity generally rises with **size** | A pond is simpler to map than a large forest |

---

sections.heading: 2. Trophic Structure and the 10% Rule (ENV-01-03)
sections.content:
**Trophic** from Greek *trophos* = food / nourishment. > **Trophic structure** = hierarchical arrangement of **biotic** components of an ecosystem based on **feeding relationships**. Abiotic components are **not** in this diagram. The hierarchy is read off **food chains and food webs**. Simple forest chain: plants → deer (herbivore) → tiger (carnivore) → vulture/hawk (scavenger on remains). Energy flow follows the **two laws of thermodynamics**: (1) solar energy is converted into **chemical** energy (neither created nor destroyed); (2) that chemical energy is transferred **unidirectionally** from a lower trophic level (**T.L.**) to the next higher one — it does **not** cycle back as energy. **10% rule:** generally only **up to ~10%** of energy at a given trophic level is transferred to the next. Ecological efficiency is low → food chains are **short** (generally **4**, at most **5** trophic levels — never 14–15).

Figure: Trophic structure is always drawn as a tapered pyramid because of the 10% rule — never a cuboid or a sphere.

---

sections.heading: 3. Nutrients and Biogeochemical Cycles (ENV-01-04)
sections.content:
Nutrients = **elements** that are the building blocks of carbohydrates, fats, proteins.

| | Needed in | Examples (class) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Macronutrients** | Large quantities | **C** Carbon, **H** Hydrogen, **N** Nitrogen, **O** Oxygen (sheet also flagged **P** Phosphorus in the margin) |
| **Micronutrients** | Small quantities | **Cu** Copper, **Zn** Zinc, **Fe** Iron |

They sit in four **reservoirs** (storage pools) of the planet — **atmosphere, lithosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere** — in different chemical forms, and they **move cyclically**. Energy flow is **unidirectional**; nutrient flow is **cyclical**. That cycling, driven by the flow of energy, is a **biogeochemical (B.G.C.) cycle**. Syllabus cycles: **carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus** (NCERT last unit — read all three).

Energy flow is a **one-way street**. Nutrient flow is a **closed loop** — the element leaves a reservoir and **must return** to it. That is why the class sketches are drawn as **cycles**, not chains.

sections.heading: Carbon cycle
sections.content:
Carbon starts as **CO₂ (carbon dioxide) in the atmosphere** and **returns as CO₂** — same form in, same form out. Read the diagram **clockwise**: the ring is the cycle.

Figure: Carbon is a cycle because the blue return arrow brings CO₂ home. Energy cannot do this — it only goes up the trophic pyramid.

sections.heading: Nitrogen cycle
sections.content:
Plants **cannot** use atmospheric **N₂ (nitrogen gas)** directly. Usable soil forms: **NO₃⁻ (nitrate)** and **NH₄⁺ (ammonium)**. Read **clockwise**: fixation → uptake → death. The **blue arc** is denitrification — that closes the cycle. The short orange arrow is **decomposition** feeding ions back into the soil pool (an inner loop, not a shortcut through the hub).

Figure: Nitrogen is a cycle because of the thick blue arc — denitrification. The orange line is a side-loop that returns N to the soil, not a second trip through the centre.

| Bacterium | Role as taught | Extra precision | |:---|:---|:---| | ***Rhizobium*** | In **root nodules of legumes**; **symbiotic** (mutually beneficial) | True N₂-fixer | | ***Azotobacter*** (class audio: “acetobacter”) | Free-living fixer | True N₂-fixer | | ***Nitrosomonas***, ***Nitrobacter*** | Help put N into a **usable** soil form | **Nitrification** (ammonium → nitrate), not fixation | | ***Pseudomonas*** | **Denitrification** — complex N back to **N₂** gas → atmosphere | **Closes the cycle** | **Decomposition** (school definition): chemical breakdown of **complex dead organic matter** into simpler organic and inorganic matter (bacteria + fungi). In both cycles it is the step that **unlocks** the element from dead litter so it can move to the next reservoir.

sections.heading: Gaseous vs sedimentary cycles (ENV-01-05)
sections.content:
| Type | Major reservoir | Examples | How the nutrient enters the cycle |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Gaseous** | **Atmosphere** | Carbon (as **CO₂**), Nitrogen (as **N₂**), hydrological cycle (water vapour) | Already in the air |
| **Sedimentary** | **Earth's crust only** (rocks) | **Phosphorus**, **Sulphur / Sulfur** | Released from rock |

- **Phosphorus:** **weathering** is the **only** release path.  
- **Sulphur:** **weathering + volcanism** (high-T lava → **SO₂ / sulphur dioxide** out of the volcano).

**Prelims trap (class):** “Weathering of rock is the **main** source of release” → **phosphorus**. Drop the word *main* and both **P and S** become correct. UPSC repeats by changing **one word**.

---

sections.heading: 4. Ecological Productivity (ENV-01-06)
sections.content:
**Biomass** ≈ body weight of an organism. **Production** = gain in body weight over time. **Productivity** = **rate** of biomass production.

> Ecological productivity = rate of biomass production by the biotic components of an ecosystem. Two types: **primary** (producers) and **secondary** (consumers).

**Unit of primary productivity:** **grams per metre square per year** (g m⁻² yr⁻¹) — production ÷ **area of the ecosystem (E.S.)**. Whenever a question says only “productivity”, it means **primary** productivity.

sections.heading: Gross vs net primary productivity
sections.content:
- **GPP (Gross Primary Productivity)** = rate at which **solar energy is captured** by producers during **photosynthesis**.
- While capture is happening, part of that energy is used in **respiration** or lost as heat in **transpiration**. Together these are **respiration losses (~20% of GPP)**.
- **NPP (Net Primary Productivity)** = rate at which the **leftover** energy is used by producers for their own biomass. **NPP = GPP − respiration losses ≈ 80% of GPP**.

**PAR (Photosynthetically Active Radiation)** = the slice of **insolation** (incoming solar radiation) that can support photosynthesis.

| Quantity | Share (class figures — learn the **range**) |
|:---|:---|
| **GPP** | **2–10% of PAR** |
| Respiration losses | **~20% of GPP** |
| **NPP** | **~80% of GPP** = **1.6–8% of PAR** (audio said “1.628%”; that is 80% of the *lower* bound 2% — the sheet’s **1.6 to 8%** is the full range) |

sections.heading: Secondary productivity
sections.content: Rate of biomass production by **consumers** (T.L. II, III, IV). Practically: change in consumer body weight over a year ÷ area. It **depends on** primary productivity; numerical tables of ecosystem productivity need **not** be memorised.

sections.heading: Controls on terrestrial primary productivity (ENV-01-07)
sections.content:
Three major environmental controls, acting **simultaneously**:

1. **Temperature**
2. **Availability of water**
3. **Availability of nutrients**

Primary productivity is **positively correlated** with all three — but **no single factor is “the” control**. Warmer / wetter / more nutrients → generally higher NPP, so **lower latitude > higher latitude** and **lower elevation > higher elevation** *other things equal*. **Sahara** is hot yet poor in NPP because **soil moisture** is the **limiting factor**. If any one control goes too low, it caps productivity.

**Amazon rainforest (Brazil) vs Sahara:** visible biomass is the everyday indicator of NPP.

---

sections.heading: 5. Biodiversity — Three Levels (ENV-01-08)
sections.content:
> Biodiversity = **totality of genes, species and ecosystems** over the planet (*bio* = life, *diversity* = variety).

| Level | Definition |
|:---|:---|
| **Genetic diversity** | Variety of genes within the individuals of a **population of a given species** (the variable part of that species’ **gene pool**) |
| **Species diversity** | **Species richness** (how many kinds) **+ species evenness** (relative abundance of their populations) |
| **Ecosystem diversity** | Variety of ecosystems in a **region** (India as a region: Thar desert, alpine grassland, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands…) |

**Why evenness matters:** because of the 10% rule, higher trophic levels support **smaller populations**. Long-term balance needs a **proportion**, not just a species count. Do **not** memorise ratios — they vary and even ecologists rarely compute them.

sections.heading: Genetic diversity → survival (the Mains articulation)
sections.content:
Higher genetic diversity **expands the range of tolerance** to environmental stresses (moisture, heat, pests, weeds, disease) → improves **resilience and adaptability** → **better chance of survival** of the species. Prelims can be a bubble; **Mains needs this sentence written out**.

---

sections.heading: 6. Project Tiger and Genetic Diversity in the Wild (ENV-01-09)
sections.content:
This is the **applied** side of genetic diversity.

| Item | Detail |
|:---|:---|
| Started | **1973**, **centrally sponsored scheme** |
| Implementing agency | **NTCA (National Tiger Conservation Authority)** — a **statutory** authority under **MoEF&CC (Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change)** |
| Phases | First **50 years** done; **second phase** now running |
| Last census | **3,682** tigers |
| 2006 baseline | **1,411** — population has more than doubled; rising **since 2006** |
| Global rank | **Tiger capital of the world** — **>70%** of world tigers; **only** one of 13 tiger-range countries where numbers are **consistently rising** |

Conservationists now watch **two** things: **headcount** (anti-poaching / anti-trafficking has been strong) **and genetic diversity**. Some landscapes show diversity **declining or plateauing**.

sections.heading: Similipal Tiger Reserve (T.R.), Odisha (ENV-01-10)
sections.content:
Largest tiger reserve of Odisha. Famous for **pseudo-melanistic** tigers: **black stripes become wider and start to merge**, so black dominates over gold — but it is **not fully black**. Full black would be **melanistic**. This is an **aberration of appearance**, **not a disease**. **Cause chain taught in class:** 1. Human demand for land (agriculture, mining, industry, settlements) → **deforestation**. 2. One large forest becomes **islands** of forest. 3. **Habitat loss** = area shrinks. **Habitat fragmentation** = remaining patches are **geographically disconnected**. 4. Wildlife **mobility falls** (human footprint in between; a leopard in a city is called “conflict”, not ecology). 5. Isolated groups **breed among themselves** → **inbreeding** → rare genes (e.g. pseudo-melanism) become locally common, **overall genetic diversity falls**. **Policy response mentioned:** **wildlife corridors** reconnect fragmented habitats and reduce inbreeding.

Figure: Similipal-type problem — disconnected forest islands, not one continuous tiger landscape.

---

sections.heading: 7. High Primary Productivity ↔ High Biodiversity (ENV-01-11)
sections.content:
**Positive correlation:** high NPP at T.L. I → more energy to transfer → more species **and** larger populations at every level → higher biodiversity. These ecosystems dominate newspaper Environment copy; **detail in later lectures**. Sheet wrote “10% / 30% North & South” for latitudes — the lecture said **degrees**, not percent.

| Ecosystem | What it is | Where |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Equatorial rainforest** | Tropical **evergreen** forest | **~10° N–S**. Example: **Amazon**, South America |
| **Mangrove forest** | Tropical evergreen forest of the **intertidal zone** (between high-tide and low-tide lines on the coast) | **~30° N–S**. Largest: **Sundarbans** (India + Bangladesh) |
| **Coral reef** | **Marine** ecosystem | **~30° N–S**. Largest: **Great Barrier Reef**, Australia |
| **Wetlands** | Most technical — full definition later | **Wular Lake** (Kashmir), **Sambhar Lake** (Rajasthan), **Chilika** (Odisha), **Loktak** (Manipur), **Kanwar Lake** (Bihar, from the sheet), **Vembanad** (Kerala, from the lecture) |

**Prelims habit:** “sequence of ecosystems in **decreasing productivity**” → default = **primary** productivity = production ÷ **area**. A huge ocean can have large *total* production but **low productivity per unit area**.

---

sections.content:
| Shortcut on the sheet | Full form |
|:---|:---|
| **Env.** | Environment / Environmental |
| **l.f.** | Living factor (biotic) |
| **n.l.** | Non-living (abiotic) |
| **R.F.** | Rainfall (orographic / relief rainfall) |

sections.heading: UPSC Cues & PYQ Connections
sections.content:
- Ecosystem = **functional unit** (energy + nutrients), coined by **A.G. Tansley**.
- Energy **unidirectional + 10% rule** vs nutrients **cyclical (B.G.C.)**.
- **NPP = GPP − R**; GPP = 2–10% of **PAR**; NPP ≈ 80% of GPP.
- Terrestrial NPP controls: **T + water + nutrients**, simultaneous; Sahara = water-limited.
- Biodiversity = genes + species (richness **and** evenness) + ecosystems.
- High genetic diversity → **range of tolerance → resilience → survival**.
- **Project Tiger 1973** / **NTCA** statutory under **MoEF&CC**; **3,682** vs **1,411 (2006)**; **>70%** world share.
- **Similipal:** pseudo-melanism ≠ disease; **habitat fragmentation → inbreeding**.
- **P vs S:** weathering is the **main/only** source for **phosphorus**; sulphur also **volcanism**.
- High-NPP, high-biodiversity set: equatorial rainforest, mangrove, coral, wetland.
- Productivity questions = **primary**, **per unit area**.

---

sections.heading: Lecture 2 — Climate Change and Climate Action
sections.content:
> **Date of Lecture:** 29 August 2026 (Lecture 2)  
> **Date Added:** 2026-08-29  
> **Source:** Vajiram & Ravi class lecture + audio transcript + 7 handwritten notebook pages  
> **Also relevant for:** Prelims Environment, GS-III (climate change, pollution, conservation), GS-II (international institutions), Essay  
> **How to read class shortcuts:** full form on first use, then the short form. Glossary at the end.  
> **Data rule from class:** climate numbers in the exam come from **IPCC** (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) or **WMO** (World Meteorological Organization) — not random news figures.

---

sections.heading: 1. What Climate Change Is (ENV-02-01)
sections.content:
**Weather** = the meteorological mix at a place *now* (insolation, temperature, cloud, humidity, wind, rainfall).

**Climate** = the **average of weather over at least ~30 years**.

> **Climate change** is a **significant variation in the mean state of climate** (temperature, precipitation, wind, etc.) lasting **at least a decade or more**.

A one-year spike is **not** climate change. The deviation must be **consistent** (~10 years+).

sections.heading: 1.1 Natural vs anthropogenic
sections.content:
Earth’s 4.5-billion-year history has many **natural** climate shifts (solar input, axial tilt, land–water layout — Geography will do these). Example: **Pleistocene** glaciation ended ~10,000–11,000 years ago; **Holocene** interglacial (relatively warmer) began.

The 21st-century environmental concern is **not** that natural cycle. It is **human-caused** — **anthropogenic climate change**. Qualify that claim with a scientific body, not with opinion.

sections.heading: 1.2 IPCC — the citing machine for Mains
sections.content:
| Item | Content |
|:---|:---|
| **What** | **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)** — scientists from governments worldwide (including India) |
| **Set up** | **1988**, jointly by **UNEP** (United Nations Environment Programme) and **WMO** |
| **Product** | Periodic **Assessment Reports (AR)**, generally every **~6 years** |
| **AR1** | **1990** — already said anthropogenic climate change is happening (this is why Rio 1992 could act) |
| **AR6** | Volumes through **2022–23** (typically four volumes) |

> **As per IPCC (AR6):** human activities have caused a **global average temperature rise of 1.1 °C** compared with **pre-industrial** levels.

Class illustration (not a figure to over-memorise): if pre-industrial mean was ~13.5 °C, present mean is ~14.6 °C.

Simplest indicator of climate change = **global warming** (temperature rise). IPCC also talks of extremes as **“climate on steroids”** — not new disasters, but **more frequent and more intense** ones. Tropical cyclones still need ~**27 °C** sea-surface temperature to form; climate change does not *invent* cyclones, it **loads** them.

---

sections.heading: 2. Two Causes: More GHGs and Smaller Sinks (ENV-02-02)
sections.content:
**Causes of present climate change**

1. **Increased emissions of greenhouse gases (GHGs).**
2. **Shrinking carbon sinks** and **land-use change**.

Both trap a **greater amount of heat** in the **Earth-atmosphere system**.

sections.heading: 2.1 Greenhouse effect (needed, not the villain)
sections.content:
Sun → **short-wave** radiation heats the surface. The surface emits **long-wave terrestrial radiation**. **Water vapour** and **CO₂** (carbon dioxide) trap that long-wave radiation. That **greenhouse effect** is one reason Earth is warm enough for life (~13–14 °C). The problem is **too much** of it after the industrial revolution.

Natural GHGs: water vapour (most important natural), CO₂, ozone, methane. After industrialisation the energy base is **fossil fuels — coal, oil and gas**.

sections.heading: 2.2 Carbon dioxide — the headline number
sections.content:
| | Pre-industrial | Now |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **CO₂** | **280 ppm** (parts per **million** — the audio said “billion”; the sheet is ppm) | **~420 ppm** |

- Present CO₂ is **150% of pre-industrial** (420 / 280).
- **420 ppm is the highest in ~8 lakh (800,000) years.** For most of that span the planet held CO₂ near 280 ppm; the jump is in ~200 industrial years.

**Anthropogenic CO₂ sources:** combustion of fossil fuels in **power, heavy industry** (cement, fertiliser, steel), **transport**.

sections.heading: 2.3 Scale of human emissions (handout / IPCC–WMO table)
sections.content:
- Humanity’s total annual GHG emissions ~ **59 Gt** (gigatonnes).
- **Gas-wise (lecture):** ~**75% CO₂**, ~**18% methane (CH₄)**, ~**5% nitrous oxide (N₂O)**; rest **F-gases** (fluorinated gases, e.g. chlorofluorocarbons — later lecture).
- **Sector-wise (lecture):** **energy ~ three-fourths**; **agriculture ~12%** (second); then industry; landfill; land-use / shrinking sinks.

---

sections.heading: 3. Methane, Landfills and Swachh Bharat (ENV-02-03)
sections.content:
**Methane (CH₄)** is measured in **ppb** (parts per **billion**), not ppm. Present concentration = **260% of pre-industrial**.

**Anthropogenic sources**

| Source | Why methane |
|:---|:---|
| **Agriculture** | **Paddy** (flooded, anaerobic) + **livestock** (enteric fermentation) |
| **Coal, oil and gas extraction** | Methane trapped in pore spaces is released when the field is opened |
| **Landfill sites** | Unsegregated **legacy waste**; **anaerobic** decay → CH₄ |

**Aerobic** decay (with oxygen) → **CO₂**. **Anaerobic** (no oxygen) → **CH₄**. Methane is highly flammable; landfill fires in the **pre-monsoon dry** months are hard to kill because CH₄ keeps forming. **Kochi** landfill fire is the news example; **Deonar** (Mumbai) and **Ghazipur** (Delhi) are the named dumps.

sections.heading: 3.1 Why Indian cities leak methane
sections.content:
Urbanisation → more consumption → more solid waste.

| | What class said |
|:---|:---|
| **Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM) 1.0** | **Open Defecation Free (ODF)** — largely achieved |
| **SBM 2.0** | **Solid waste management:** door-to-door collection → **segregation at source** → **treatment** |
| **Economic Survey (class)** | Collection **>90%**; scientific treatment only **~20%**. The rest (~80%) → landfills |

**Indore model** (Mains has asked Indore vs Delhi): source segregation by citizens; near-100% collection; **GPS-enabled** vans; **bio-CNG** (compressed natural gas) plants for wet/biodegradable waste; **waste-to-energy** (high temperature, limited oxygen) for non-bio. Indore stays #1 on Swachhata rankings.

**Delhi (typical metro):** collection exists; **source segregation is weak**; **treatment capacity is short** → hills of **legacy waste** at the periphery.

---

sections.heading: 4. Nitrous Oxide, NOx and GHG vs Air Pollutant (ENV-02-04)
sections.content:
**NOx** = nitrogen oxides, three species formed together: | Gas | Formula | GHG? | |:---|:---|:---| | Nitric oxide | NO | No (directly) | | **Nitrous oxide** | **N₂O** | **Yes** — now **125% of pre-industrial** | | Nitrogen dioxide | NO₂ | No (directly) | **Sources of all three:** (1) **burning fossil fuels** — N₂ and O₂ do not react at room temperature; they do at **combustion** temperatures → power, industry, transport (same sectors as CO₂); (2) **agriculture** — **nitrogen fertilisers**: urea, **DAP** (diammonium phosphate), NPK. **Trap (class true/false):** *“All types of NOx emissions are responsible for present global warming.”* **True** — N₂O is a GHG **directly**; **all three** help form **tropospheric ozone (O₃)**, which **is** a GHG. So NO and NO₂ are **indirect**. **Tropospheric ozone** = GHG **and** air pollutant (toxic). Do **not** use GHG and air pollutant as synonyms. > **Air pollutant:** an atmospheric **contaminant** (solid, liquid or gas) that poses a **health hazard** to humans and other life forms — a **toxin** in the air.
**PM2.5 / PM10** (particulate matter): diameter **≤ 2.5 / ≤ 10 microns**. Invisible; stay suspended; enter lungs and blood; can **carry** other toxins (SO₂, CO). **Not GHGs.** Dust you *see* in a sunbeam is **not** PM2.5. ---

sections.heading: 5. Carbon Sinks, Ecological Degradation, Oceans as Heat Sponges (ENV-02-05)
sections.content:
> **Carbon sink:** a mass atmospheric-carbon reservoir that **absorbs carbon from the atmosphere and stores it for a long duration**. Forests and other ecosystems; oceans (dissolved CO₂ / seawater). **Sequestration** = absorption.

**Land-use change** (deforestation) and **ecological degradation** shrink those sinks.

> **Ecological degradation:** a **consistent decline in primary productivity** of an ecosystem, which then hurts human / economic well-being.

| Driver | What degrades |
|:---|:---|
| Forest fire | Forest (a sink can flip into a **source**) |
| Marine pollution | Ocean (photosynthetic capacity falls) |
| Soil erosion | Land / soil |
| Coral bleaching | Coral reef (technical mechanism = later class) |

**Before industry:** natural CO₂ sources (volcanoes, wildfire) **balanced** natural sinks → ~280 ppm held for ages.

**After industry:** sources **explode** *and* sinks **shrink** → more GHGs → more greenhouse effect → more heat in the Earth-atmosphere system.

Oceans have **high specific heat**. Atmosphere and ocean sit at an interface, so most extra heat does **not** stay only in air.

> **As per IPCC: more than 90% of the excess heat has been absorbed by the oceans.** Oceans are the **heat sinks / heat sponges** of the planet. That stored heat is why **thermal expansion** and marine impacts follow.

---

sections.heading: 6. UNFCCC, COPs, Mitigation and CCS / CCUS (ENV-02-06)
sections.content:
**1990 AR1** gave the science. **1992 United Nations Conference on Environment and Development**, Rio de Janeiro (**Rio Summit**, Brazil) adopted the **United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)**. **In force 1994**. Aim: **internationally coordinated climate action** through **mitigation and adaptation**. India was a party.

| Term | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| **Convention** | International **agreement** on a common agenda |
| **Adopted** | Final text acceptable to all is ready (1992 for UNFCCC) |
| **Ratification** | Countries sign on; **~two-thirds** ratification → **comes into force** (1994) |
| **Party** | A country that has joined |
| **COP** | **Conference of the Parties** — parties meet regularly |

**COPs of UNFCCC:** first **1995**. Held **every year** except **2020** (pandemic). **COP 30 — 2025**. Next class starts **COP 3, Kyoto, 1997**.

sections.heading: 6.1 Mitigation
sections.content:
> Aim of **climate mitigation:** **reduce and stabilise atmospheric concentration of GHGs** (the class picture: try to walk CO₂ from **420 ppm back toward 280 ppm**).

Three methods in this lecture:

1. **Substitute fossil energy** with **non-fossil** — **renewables and nuclear**.
2. **Afforestation** (grow the sink).
3. **Geological sequestration** = **Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS)**.

**CCS:** capture CO₂ at a **point source** (e.g. thermal power plant) so it never enters the air; **pressurise** and **inject** it into empty pore space of **depleted oil and gas fields** / other sub-surface sedimentary rock; cap with an **impermeable** layer.

If some of the captured CO₂ is also **used** in industry, the name becomes **Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (CCUS)**. Utilisation / recycling of carbon = **next lecture**. Prelims has already asked CCUS.

**Hard truth from class:** however hard we mitigate, we **cannot** return to pre-industrial GHG levels **in this century**. Climate change is a **lived reality** → adaptation is not optional.

> Aim of **climate adaptation:** **modify human ways of life** to **minimise negative impacts** of climate change on **human systems**.

---

sections.heading: 7. Impacts: Disasters, Sea Level, SIDS (ENV-02-07)
sections.content:
**1. Increased intensity and frequency of climatic disasters** — tropical cyclones, **GLOFs** (glacial lake outburst floods), cloudbursts, floods, drought, heatwaves, forest fire. Climate change does **not create** cyclones; it makes them **more often and more severe**. Human cost: mortality, livelihood, food, poverty, trauma (class pointed to a unfolding Nepal disaster as a development-setback example).

**2. Sea-level rise (SLR)** — as per **IPCC**, average annual rate **3–4 mm**; **cumulative rise by end-century more than a metre**.

**Consequences of SLR**

1. More **coastal erosion** by waves and tides (loss of fertile delta farmland).
2. **Seawater intrusion** → **groundwater salinisation** of coastal habitats (water **quality** falls; Himalayan glacier melt after mid-century also hits **quantity** in Indus–Ganga–Brahmaputra).
3. Worse **coastal flooding** in cyclones and tsunamis.
4. **Coastal land submersion.** Highest risk: **low-elevation coastal zones (LECZ)** and **Small Island Developing States (SIDS)**.

> **LECZ:** coastal land with elevation **up to 10 m above mean sea level**.

**SIDS** (sovereign, small, island, developing): **Maldives, Mauritius, Fiji, Tonga, Tuvalu, Solomon Islands, Papua New Guinea (PNG)** — some face **whole-country** submergence.

**Major causes of SLR (cryosphere + ocean)**

1. Faster melting of the **cryosphere**: Arctic sea ice, Greenland ice cap, Antarctic ice sheet, mountain snow and glaciers (class also listed high-latitude / Alaskan ice).
2. **Thermal expansion** of oceans (the 90% heat sponge).

sections.heading: 8. Migration, Biodiversity, Health, Equity, Climate-Smart Agriculture (ENV-02-08)
sections.content:
**Environmental / climatic migration:** **distressed displacement** of people because of environment-related stress.

**Biodiversity / ecological hits:** climate change → intense heatwaves → forest fire (California, Australia); coral bleaching; habitat loss (polar bear); other stresses.

**Agriculture:** thermal stress + moisture stress in **Kharif and Rabi**. Class caution: India can still be **food-grain self-sufficient** even while climate hits yields — do not collapse every agri sentence into “food security collapse”.

**Human health**

- **Direct:** heatwave → heat stress / heat stroke.
- **Indirect:** climate → agriculture → food; climate → water → health.

Climate change **undercuts Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)**. Impacts are **disproportionate**: **developing countries and Least Developed Countries (LDCs)**, and **marginalised** groups inside countries.

| | Developed | Developing / LDCs |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Emissions | High (growth ↔ emissions) | Lower / often negligible (Nepal, Fiji, PNG) |
| Livelihood mix | Secondary, tertiary, quaternary — less weather-tied | **Agriculture, forestry, fisheries** — directly climate-tied |
| Coping capacity | Money, tech, institutions, **Early Warning Systems (EWS)** | Weak. Himalayan cloudburst EWS needs hundreds of **Doppler weather radars**; India could afford **<10** even with ministry funding. 1980s **African drought** = early documented climate-linked drought in the tropics |

Same split **inside India: rich vs poor**. Rich emit more, sit in non-farm jobs, can still buy food when prices spike. Poor / farmers / tribals / fishers emit less and absorb the hit.

**Two adaptation buckets in this lecture**

1. **Efficient disaster management** (EWS, Doppler radars, funding).
2. **Climate-smart agriculture (CSA)** — **FAO** (Food and Agriculture Organization) idea: an agri-system that **copes with climate impacts** (more **resilient**), **raises productivity and income**, and **cuts GHG emissions** from farming.

Examples: **Direct Seeded Rice (DSR)** (cuts paddy **CH₄** vs flooded transplanting); **millets** / drought-resilient varieties; **micro-irrigation — drip and sprinkler** (flood irrigation has low water-use efficiency; Himalayan-fed north faces tighter water).

---

sections.heading: UPSC Cues
sections.content:
- Climate = ~30-year weather average; climate change = **≥ decade** shift. **Anthropogenic**, cite **IPCC**.
- **IPCC 1988 = UNEP + WMO.** AR1 1990; AR6 2022–23; **+1.1 °C**.
- Two engines: **GHG up + sinks down**. CO₂ **280 → 420 ppm**, **8 lakh-year** high, **150%** of pre-industrial. CH₄ **260%** (ppb). N₂O **125%**.
- **CO₂ and water vapour = GHG, not air pollutants.** **SO₂ and PM = pollutants, not GHGs.** Overlap: **CH₄, trop. O₃, CFCs**.
- Only **N₂O** among NOx is a GHG; all NOx still warm via **trop. ozone**.
- **SBM 1.0 = ODF; 2.0 = waste.** Collection ~90%, treatment ~20%. Indore vs Delhi / legacy waste / Deonar / Kochi fire.
- Oceans absorb **>90%** of excess heat.
- **UNFCCC** adopted **1992**, in force **1994**; **COP** yearly (no 2020); mitigation = non-fossil + forests + **CCS/CCUS**.
- SLR **3–4 mm/yr**, **>1 m** by 2100; **LECZ ≤ 10 m**; **SIDS** list; cryosphere + thermal expansion.
- **CSA:** DSR, millets, drip/sprinkler. Equity: those who emitted least are hit first.

sections.heading: 2. What Geography Is
sections.content:
- **Etymology:** Geography → *Geo* + *Graphein*. Literally **the description of the Earth**.
- **Origins:** Greeks are **supposed to be** the first geographers of the world.
- **Eratosthenes** coined the word *geography* and defined it as the **study of the Earth as the home of man**.
- That study has three parts: **Nature**, **Man**, and their **Interaction**.
- Class instruction: **enrich the answer with spatial analysis**.

sections.heading: Landscapes, method, two definitions
sections.content:
- **Landscapes:** the assembly / collection of land types. Every landscape is the stage of an eternal fight between **endogenous (endogenic) and exogenous (exogenic)** processes.
- Geography is governed by **method** rather than by a fixed body of facts. That method is **spatial analysis**.
- **Insolation:** incoming solar radiation.
- **Geopolitics:** the geographical constellation / context of international politics.

sections.heading: Geography as a spatial science
sections.content:
- Every science attempts to discover an **order** in the apparent **chaos** of Nature.
- **Science is the deadly enemy of uniqueness.**
- Geography, being a **spatial science**, attempts to discover **spatial ordering** in the occurrence of natural and human elements of the Earth's surface.

---

sections.heading: 3. Geodesy and the Earth's Shape
sections.content:
- **Geodesy:** the science that attempts to determine Earth's **size and shape** by surveys and mathematical calculations.

1. Until **1687**, the **spherical-perfection model** was the basic assumption of geodesy.
2. In **1687** Sir Isaac Newton postulated that the round Earth (and the other planets) could **not** be perfectly spherical.
3. Newton reasoned that spin slightly misshapes the Earth: it **bulges at the equator** and is **flattened at the poles** → **oblate spheroid**.
4. Today the Earth is considered a **geoid** — the shape of the Earth is uniquely Earth-shaped.

sections.heading: Update — 9 September 2026 (Test 1 — geoid + IST city)

**IST meridian 82°30′ E (Mirzapur).** Among Bengaluru / Delhi / Kolkata / **Raipur**, **Raipur** is nearest. Delhi and Bengaluru sit near **77° E**; Kolkata near **88° E**. You clicked Delhi (`MST-061`).

| Equatorial diameter (slightly bulging) | ≈ 12,756 km |

The variation is very minute, so **in most practical cases we treat the Earth as a perfect sphere**.

sections.heading: 5. Grid, Greenwich, Latitude and Longitude
sections.content:
Fundamental to geographic analysis is a comprehensive, logical framework to fix the **accurate location** of any spot on the Earth's surface.

The imaginary grid is anchored by the **poles and the equator**, which come from Earth's slight variance from a perfect sphere.

**Earth's axis:** an imaginary line joining the North Pole and the South Pole, passing through the centre.

sections.heading: Why Greenwich was chosen as the prime meridian
sections.content:
Three reasons:

1. The **Royal Observatory at Greenwich** was already in use as a reference.
2. **Dominance of the English Empire.**
3. A convenient choice for the **International Date Line (IDL)**.

sections.heading: Equatorial plane
sections.content: The imaginary plane that cuts the Earth through the middle and divides it into the **Northern Hemisphere** and the **Southern Hemisphere**. In the class diagram, segment **CA** is the equatorial plane.

sections.heading: Latitude
sections.content:
- Angular distance of a place **north or south** of the equator.
- Project a line from point **P** on the surface to the centre **C**. The angle between **PC** and the equatorial plane (**CA**) is the latitude of P.
- Written as **P (latitude, longitude)** or **P (x° N, y° E)**.
- **Range:** 0° to 90° N or S.
- **Parallel:** a line connecting all points of the same latitude. They run parallel to each other.
- The **0° parallel** is the **equator**.

sections.heading: Longitude
sections.content:
- Angular distance of a place **east or west** of the **Greenwich Meridian** (0° meridian / prime meridian).
- **Meridian:** a line joining places of the same longitude.
- **Range:** 0° to 180° E or W.

sections.heading: Time and meridians
sections.content:
- Romans used **meridian** for **12 noon local time** — the moment the sun is highest (shortest shadow).
- All places on a given meridian / longitude have the **same local time**.

---

sections.heading: Great circle
sections.content:
1. Any plane through the **centre** of a sphere bisects it and creates a **great circle** where it meets the surface.
2. A great circle is the **largest** circle that can be drawn on a sphere — the circumference.
3. A given sphere has **infinite** great circles.
4. Of all the parallels, the **equator alone** is a great circle. All other parallels are **small circles**.
5. Each meridian is a **semi-great circle**.
6. An **arc of a great circle** joining any two points on the Earth's surface is always the **shortest route** between them.

sections.heading: Circle of illumination
sections.content:
- The sun illuminates **one half** of the Earth at any given moment.
- The edge of the sunlit hemisphere is the **circle of illumination**.
- It is a great circle that divides the Earth into a **light half** and a **dark half**.

sections.heading: Important parallels
sections.content:
| Parallel | Latitude |
|----------|----------|
| Arctic Circle | 66½° N |
| Tropic of Cancer | 23½° N |
| Equator | 0° |
| Tropic of Capricorn | 23½° S |
| Antarctic Circle | 66½° S |

1. These parallels help us understand the distribution of **insolation** on the Earth's surface.
2. The two tropics are the **farthest limits** of the sun's apparent movement.
3. The two tropics are also the farthest limits of the sun's **vertical** (overhead) position.

- **Tropic** from Latin *tropicus* — the parallel **from where the sun turns**.
- **Solstice:** the sun reaching **farthest** in the given hemisphere.
- **Equinox:** the two days when the sun is overhead at the equator and **all places** have equal day and night.

sections.heading: Seasonality (how the class closed)
sections.content:
1. As Earth revolves around the sun in a year, the relationship between the two keeps changing.
2. **Seasonality** is the consequence of that changing relationship.
3. Seasonality shows up as the **changing length of a day**.
4. Day length depends on **how the circle of illumination cuts the Earth into two halves**.
5. The circle of illumination is always a great circle, so it always cuts the Earth in half — but it does so **differently at different times of the year**.
6. The **equator** is the only parallel cut evenly all year → **12 hours day and 12 hours night** every day.
7. All other parallels are cut unevenly, except on the two **equinox** days.
8. Seasonal variation in day length is **0 at the equator** and **increases as latitude increases**.

**Day-length rules (DS):**

- **(a)** Higher the latitude, **longer** the summer day.
- **(b)** Higher the latitude, **shorter** the winter day.

| Temperate | 23½° – 66½° N, and 23½° – 66½° S |
| Polar | Area around the poles (no exact measure) |
| Sub-polar | Higher latitudes just outside the Arctic and Antarctic Circles |

In a broader view the whole Earth's surface is three parts:

| | Zone | Meaning |
|---|------|---------|
| (a) | Tropical | Lower latitudes |
| (b) | Temperate | Middle latitudes |
| (c) | Polar | Higher latitudes |
