sections.heading: Lecture 10 — 13 September 2026
sections.content:
> Notebook dated **13/9/26**. Tenth climatology class. Continues Lecture 9’s Hadley one-cell. Today is **William Ferrel (1856)** — **three-cell / tricellular model** of **tropospheric air circulation (TAC)**. Sheet spelling **Ferrell**; class audio **Farrell** — same scholar already named in Lecture 8. **Parked (next class, ~45 min):** draw the three cells on the left of the globe; *why* the four distinct belts rise or sink; then **break both assumptions** to get closer to real TAC. Audio runs to class close.

**How to read class shortcuts:** **TAC** = tropospheric air circulation; **ELPB / STHPB / TLPB / PHPB** = equatorial low / subtropical high / temperate low / polar high pressure belts; **PGF** = Pressure Gradient Force. Full forms on first use.

**Already in Lectures 6–9 — do not restudy as a new topic:** GAPD = combined heat + rotation (L9); cell = 3-D closed loop (L9); PGF 90° to isobars, Coriolis right NH / left SH, friction near the surface (L8); Hadley 1735 parked rotation and was rejected (L9); SW monsoon ≈ three-fourths of India’s rain (L8). Cluster for *this* sitting is **GEO-13**.

**Yellow Book** *Atmospheric Circulation* (Ch 13) is **not uploaded**. This class is the exam default. Do not paste a book chapter here.

---

sections.heading: 38. Quotes from this class
sections.content:
> Essay / Ethics more than Geography facts. Vision / action already sat on Lecture 9.

- "God sleeps in the minerals, awakens in plants, walks in animals and thinks in Man."
- "Vision without action is a daydream. Action without vision is a nightmare."
- "The wisdom of the wise is an uncommon degree of common sense."
- "Forests precede people, deserts succeed them."
- "Don't let your future be held hostage by the past."

---

sections.heading: 39. Why Ferrel, and the two-part journey (GEO-13-01)
sections.content:
Hadley **1735** was the first attempt at TAC. He **knew** rotation mattered (later named Coriolis) but **parked** it — heat first. That **oversimplified** the model. Science then waited **more than 100 years**.

**William Ferrel, 1856** — second attempt. **Accepted.** Whatever later books and newspaper circulation items use (El Niño / La Niña, monsoon, cyclones, jets) is built **on Ferrel**, not on Hadley’s whole model. Class: today’s lecture **plus the next** are the foundation for the rest of the atmosphere syllabus.

**Three-cell / tricellular:** **three** cells **in each hemisphere** — lower, middle, and high latitudes — not Hadley’s one cell per hemisphere.

Background is the same as Hadley: TAC correlates with **GAPD**, and GAPD is the **combined effect of the Sun’s heat and Earth’s rotation / Coriolis**.

sections.heading: 39.1 Three major considerations
sections.content:
| # | Consideration | Kind |
|:---:|:---|:---|
| **i** | **Uniform Earth surface** — either **continent or ocean** (class: land or water). Avoids differential heating from specific heat and **albedo**. | **Assumption** |
| **ii** | **Rotating Earth** — **Coriolis effect is being considered**. Hadley’s blunder is not repeated. | **Fact** |
| **iii** | **Sun overhead at the equator** all the time = **equinox** position (Lecture 2). Holds the moving “bulb” still so the heating picture can be finished. | **Assumption** |

Two of the three are assumptions → today’s picture is **simplified**.

sections.heading: 39.2 Two parts of the topic (margin lock)
sections.content:
| | What | When |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Part 1** | Ferrel’s model = a **simplified** picture of TAC based on **uniform surface** + **Sun’s equinox position** | **This class** (winds + belts; cells parked) |
| **Part 2** | Attempt to reach **as close as possible** the real complexity of TAC by **breaking the two assumptions one by one** (surface is not uniform; Sun moves between the tropics → heat, pressure, winds, weather shift) | **Next class** |

Need the real atmosphere: tropical cyclones, monsoon benefit, aircraft safety.

---

sections.heading: 40. Pressure belts (GEO-13-02)
sections.content:
Because the surface is taken as **uniform**, the same latitude has the **same** low or high **all around the world**. That latitudinal strip is a **pressure belt**.

> The term **pressure belt** refers to a **latitudinal region** with **uniform** low or high pressure **throughout the world**.

**From Hadley (heat, non-rotating, now made uniform):** equatorial **low** everywhere → **Equatorial Low Pressure Belt (ELPB)**; polar **high** everywhere → **Polar High Pressure Belt (PHPB)** in **each** hemisphere.

**From rotation (observed in nature; Ferrel takes it in):** two **more** belts **in each hemisphere**, on an **average** around **30°** and **60°**. “Average” because the Sun is held at the equator today. Next class the Sun moves → heat shifts → **belts shift** (NH summer / June, Sun near Tropic of Cancer → belts a few degrees **north**; NH winter / Sun near Tropic of Capricorn → **south**).

| Average latitude | Pressure (today = **relative** low vs high — not “how low”) | Class name | Other valid name |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Equator | Low | **Equatorial Low Pressure Belt (ELPB)** | — |
| ~**30°** N/S | High | **Subtropical High Pressure Belt (STHPB)** | — |
| ~**60°** N/S | Low | **Temperate Low Pressure Belt (TLPB)** | **Subpolar** Low Pressure Belt (**G.C. Leong**) |
| Poles | High | **Polar High Pressure Belt (PHPB)** | — |

**Why two names at 60°:** when belts shift **north** (NH summer) that belt sits in a **subpolar** latitude; when they shift **south** (NH winter) it sits in a **temperate** latitude. Class uses **temperate** because the reference book uses **subpolar**, so both stay in view. Do **not** treat one as wrong.

**Seven belts on the globe; four distinct types** to explain next class: equatorial low, subtropical high, temperate low, polar high.

**Prelims trap:** do **not** analyse a belt with **heat alone**. Subtropical areas are “hot” → a heat-only student predicts **low** pressure — the belt is **high**. Subpolar / temperate areas are “cold” → heat-only predicts **high** — the belt is **low**. That inversion is the point of taking **rotation** with heat.

---

sections.heading: 41. Combined effect first; thermally vs dynamically (GEO-13-03)
sections.content:
**Golden statement (best; cannot be improved):** every belt on this diagram is the **combined effect of heat and Earth’s rotation**. Try to explain any belt with **one** factor and the analysis is wrong.

**Broader / school language (allowed, not best):**

| Belts | Broad label | Class reason |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Equatorial low + polar high | **Thermally induced** | **More** to do with the Sun’s heat. They were already in Hadley’s **non-rotating** picture. |
| Subtropical high + temperate / subpolar low | **Dynamically induced** | **More** to do with **Earth’s rotation**. They appear once rotation is taken. |

**Lock:** thermally induced belts still have “colours” of rotation; dynamically induced belts still have “colours” of heat. Combined effect remains the answer if UPSC asks for the **best** statement. Matches `MST-002` (subpolar / temperate low is **not** thermally induced).

---

sections.heading: 42. Three cells named; three surface winds drawn (GEO-13-04)
sections.content:
**Named today, drawn next class** (left of the globe is reserved):

| Latitudes | Cell (class name) | Why that name |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Lower / tropical | **Hadley cell** | Hadley first showed lower latitudes as the **powerhouse** |
| Middle | **Ferrel cell** | Ferrel’s original work on mid-latitude (North American) circulation |
| High / polar | **Polar cell** | Location |

A **cell** (Lecture 9): surface HP → LP, rise at LP, tropopause lid, diverge aloft, sink at HP. The **surface** limb of each cell is **wind** = **horizontal** movement of air.

| Cell’s surface wind | Where it lives on the globe |
|:---|:---|
| **Trade winds** (or **trades**) | Tropical / lower latitudes |
| **Westerlies** | Middle latitudes |
| **Polar easterlies** | Polar / high latitudes |

Together they are the world’s **three wind systems**. Almost every later topic comes back to this diagram.

sections.heading: 42.1 Global analysis drops friction
sections.content:
Near-surface air is under **three** forces (Lecture 8): **PGF, Coriolis, friction**. Today’s picture is **global**. **Friction is a local force** (each tree / building / vehicle on Pusa Road has its own) **and a minor force**. Books also draw planetary winds with **PGF + Coriolis only**.

> In our **global** analysis of winds, we do **not** consider **frictional force**, as it is a **local** force (it is a **minor** force too).

**Margin:** wind is the **horizontal** movement of air, **but shown on the vertical frame** of the board / notebook. Same trap later for **ocean currents**. Do not “dance with the page” after two months and say air only moves up the sheet.

sections.heading: 42.2 How the arrows are drawn
sections.content:
**PGF** tries to take air **high → low** across the isobars at **90°** (broken arrow). **Coriolis** then deflects it — **right of the wind** in the **Northern Hemisphere**, **left of the wind** in the **Southern Hemisphere** (thick arrow = both forces). Right/left = of the **wind**, not of the student.

**Do not** draw *more* deflection in higher latitudes on this **static** diagram. Coriolis also depends on **speed**. A fast tropical parcel can out-deflect a slow mid-latitude parcel. Static diagram = **nature** of deflection only (right / left). Amount = later, separately.

**What the arrows already show (Lecture 9 language):** equatorial low = zone of **convergence**; subtropical high = zone of **divergence**; temperate low = another **convergence**.

sections.heading: 42.3 Fronts at the temperate low (preview, not today’s cyclone chapter)
sections.content:
Air from the **polar** side is **cold and dry**. Air from the **subtropics** is **warm and moist**. At ~**60°** they **meet and do not mix** (“like dissolves like”). Norwegian scientists around the **First World War** called that transition a **front**. Some fronts later become **temperate cyclones** — frequent, **not** the destructive tropical type; they are why **middle latitudes have the highest weather variability**. **India lock (coming classes):** temperate cyclones travel from Europe / Atlantic / Mediterranean / West Asia toward the India–Afghanistan–Pakistan meeting zone. We call them **Western Disturbances** (west + disturbance = monsoon / cyclone-type change). They come **more in winter**. Compensation for the **Western Himalaya** — **Himachal Pradesh** and **Jammu and Kashmir (J&K)** — which the summer monsoon does not reach well (higher latitude **and** altitude vs the eastern Himalaya): **snowfall**. Also some rain on **Punjab, Haryana, Delhi** (good for **rabi** / wheat); polar air → **cold wave**; sometimes **hail**. Equatorial convergence is **similar** (warm, moist) air — fronts are **generally not** an equatorial feature.

Figure (copy notes): Names on the right, as on the sheet. Arrows sit on the globe (easterlies west; westerlies east; trades into the equator). Blue = high, red = low. Left dashed box = Hadley / Ferrel / Polar cells, parked. Broken PGF vs thick final arrow is how the sheet was built; this print keeps the final winds.

---

sections.heading: 43. Naming winds; insolation; trades vs school books (GEO-13-04 continued)
sections.content:
> As per convention, **wind is always named in terms of its direction of origin**.

On today’s static globe: tropical NH arrows look **north-east**; tropical SH **south-east**.

**Insolation** is the **ultimate driving force** for wind (Sun’s energy first creates pressure differences; rotation complicates the path). Wind is a **by-product of insolation**.

**Seasonal variation of insolation increases as we go higher in latitude** → **winds become more and more variable** as we go higher. Lower latitudes: **relative** constancy (not absolute — India is still hot in both solstices; Europe / North America winters are dark).

**Result in the lower latitudes:**

- Winds in the lower latitudes are the **most consistent of all planetary winds**.
- They **generally** blow with **good speeds** and in **relatively constant** directions.
- Because of that consistency they became the **winds of world commerce** in the ancient past (sailors = traders; no engine) → **trade winds**, or simply **trades**.
- **North-east trades** and **south-east trades** on the diagram.

**School trap:** school books write **same speed and constant direction throughout the year** so a child sees *why* the name “trade.” Class language is **relative**: **most consistent, but they do vary.** They do **not** always come from the north-east / south-east. Scientists still find they **generally appear to come from the east** → at this level, **trades = easterlies**. A school child will ask “which hemisphere?” and answer NE or SE. Do not.

**Good speed** (class, to a question): more Sun + non-uniform real surface → stronger differential heating → stronger **PGF**. (Today’s *model* surface is uniform; the speed remark is about the real tropics.)

sections.heading: 43.1 South Asian summer — monsoon is a transformation of the trades
sections.content:
If the school picture were a law, tropical–subtropical **India** would have **north-east trades all twelve months**. Class analysis: India should have **easterlies** in general. What India actually gets for about **four months** is a massive **south-west** system — the **south-west monsoon** — about **three-fourths** of annual rainfall.

> During summer in **South Asia**, the trade winds change **drastically** and result in the **south-west monsoon**, which brings India about **three-fourths** of its annual rainfall.

Not special air sent for India. Same air that was making the trades. **How** that drastic change happens = many later classes (jets, El Niño, IOD, Madden–Julian Oscillation, Himalaya, Indian Ocean). Do not invent a monsoon theory today. First monsoon explanation class cited: **1690s**; still not “finished” in the 21st century. **120+ years** of South Asian monsoon data: **no two monsoons exactly the same**.

---

sections.heading: 44. Westerlies and polar easterlies (GEO-13-05)
sections.content:
**Middle latitudes:** more seasonal variation of insolation → winds **more variable**. On the static diagram: **south-westerlies** (NH) / **north-westerlies** (SH). In nature they do **not** always come from those quarters. They **generally appear to come from the west** (the north/south component is weaker) → **westerlies**.

**Polar region:** still more seasonal variation → winds **highly variable**. On the diagram they look north-east / south-east, but in nature they are **strongly easterly** (not NE/SE). Trades are already easterlies, so the polar set always takes the prefix **polar easterlies**.

**Why any belt’s wind is what it is:** **dynamics / interaction of PGF and Coriolis** (both change with the situation; the diagram is not nature frozen).

**Polar extra (Prelims-flagged):** polar winds become **strongly easterlies** because of the **stronger Coriolis effect of higher latitudes**. Coriolis **dominates** there (progressive increase with latitude — Lecture 8). Demo: PGF still 90° pole → temperate low; a strong right-turn (NH) pulls the origin more and more **east**.

General question “what decides wind behaviour in all three belts?” → **PGF and Coriolis**. Polar-only “why strongly easterly?” → **stronger Coriolis**.

---

sections.heading: 45. Planetary, prevailing, primary — then secondary and local (GEO-13-06)
sections.content:
| School name | Why |
|:---|:---|
| **Planetary winds** | The three systems are almost **global in extent** |
| **Prevailing winds** | They blow almost **throughout the year** |

**Beyond school:** the three constitute the **primary circulation** of the atmosphere. **Most** of the rest of TAC diversity is a **by-product** of those three.

**Secondary circulations** (also **atmospheric disturbances**): **spatial** (place to place) and **temporal** (at a place, time to time) variations **over** the primary winds. Examples: **cyclones, monsoons**. India’s monsoon = spatial **South Asia** + temporal **June–September** — a change **over the trades**. A Bay of Bengal cyclone = trades changed so far they take a cyclone’s shape — not special destructive air. Temperate cyclones = **Western Disturbances** because they come from the west **and** they are disturbances.

**Besides** primary and secondary: **hundreds of local winds** in different parts of the world at different times of the year — **sometimes** called **tertiary circulation**; school and later classes more often say **local winds**. Class examples: **land and sea breeze**, mountain breeze, **loo** (hot wind of the north Indian plains). Land/sea breeze is **not** a by-product of the three planetary winds in this telling — third category. Class: a **Mains** question this year on local winds; more often a Prelims topic.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  P["Primary = trades + westerlies + polar easterlies"] --> S["Secondary / disturbances: monsoon, cyclones, …"]
  P --> L["Local / tertiary: loo, land–sea breeze, …"]
  T["Trades"] -->|"S Asia summer drastic change"| M["SW monsoon ~3/4 of India’s rain"]
```

Mother-nature analogy (class): three **ingredients** (the planetary winds) → almost the whole **menu** of atmospheric dishes.

**Tropical vs temperate cyclone timing (one line, later classes):** temperate cyclones stronger / more frequent in **winter**; India’s tropical cyclones more often **before or after** the monsoon.

---

sections.heading: 46. Parked for next class
sections.content:
1. Draw **Hadley / Ferrel / polar cells** on the left of today’s globe (~45 min).
2. Re-explain **why** the **four distinct** belts are low or high (rise → LP; sink → HP) — combined effect already stated; next is the practical circulation reason.
3. **Break both assumptions** (surface not uniform; Sun not always at the equator) so the picture moves from **average / simplified** toward real TAC.

Come with this diagram revised. Do not start monsoon mechanics from this sheet.

---

sections.heading: 47. Lecture 10 — UPSC Quick Recall
sections.content:
1. **Ferrel 1856** = **three cells / hemisphere** (tricellular). Accepted; later TAC sits on it. Hadley parked rotation.
2. Three considerations: **uniform surface** (assumption); **rotating Earth / Coriolis** (fact); **Sun at equator / equinox** (assumption).
3. **Pressure belt** = latitudinal strip of **uniform** LP or HP **worldwide** (uniform-surface model).
4. **Seven** belts, **four** types: ELPB, STHPB ~**30°**, TLPB ~**60°** (temperate **or** subpolar / Leong), PHPB. Positions are **averages**.
5. **Best:** every belt = **heat + rotation**. Broadly: eq + polar = **thermally** induced; STHP + temperate low = **dynamically** induced.
6. Global winds: **PGF + Coriolis only**. Friction = local **and** minor. Wind = **horizontal**, drawn on a **vertical** page.
7. **Trades** = most consistent planetary winds **but they vary**; **generally easterlies**. School “always NE/SE, constant all year” is the trap.
8. **South Asian summer:** trades change **drastically** → **SW monsoon** ≈ **3/4** of India’s rain. Same air, not special monsoon air.
9. **Westerlies** generally from the **west**. **Polar easterlies** = prefix **polar**; **strongly** easterly because **Coriolis is stronger** at high latitude.
10. Three winds = **planetary / prevailing / primary**. Most other TAC = **secondary / disturbances** (monsoon, cyclone). **Local winds** ≈ tertiary (**loo**, land–sea breeze). **Cells themselves = next class.**

---

sections.heading: Lecture 1 — Agriculture: Importance, Trade and Commodities
sections.content:
> **Date of Lecture:** 28 August 2026  
> **Date Added:** 2026-08-28  
> **Source:** Vajiram & Ravi class lecture + audio transcript + 4 handwritten notebook pages  
> **Also relevant for:** GS-III / General Studies Paper III (agriculture, food security, subsidies, trade), Prelims (crops, Geographical Indication / GI, missions), Essay  
> **Exam strategy from class:** Do **not** memorise exact figures now — learn the *range* and the *logic*. Data is for Mains colour, not for Prelims trap questions.

**How to read class shortcuts:** the notebook uses short forms for speed. In this note the **full form is given on first use**, then the short form is kept. A glossary is at the end.

---

sections.heading: 0. How to Study This Topic (Book List)
sections.content:
Physical geography (Class XI NCERTs + G.C. Leong principles) is **static** — questions can come straight from the book. Human geography (Class XII: *Fundamentals of Human Geography* + *India: People and Economy*) is **dynamic**. The XII books still use **Census 2001** data; energy chapters were written when renewables were insignificant. Use them only for **definitions** (e.g. Total Fertility Rate). Current facts come from:

| Source | How to use it |
|:---|:---|
| **NCERT** (National Council of Educational Research and Training) **XI & XII** | Concepts and standard definitions only |
| **G.C. Leong** | Pick **one** source per topic (do not double-read overlapping NCERT + Leong chapters) |
| **Yellow Books** | Institute compilation (NCERT + Leong + magazines + newspapers) |
| **Newspapers** | Primary source for class discussions. Make notes **topic-wise**, not date-wise; revise every Sunday |
| **Economic Survey** | Two must-read chapters every February: **Agriculture & Food Management** and **Climate Change & Environment** (read the full chapter, not the summary) |
| **Yojana / Kurukshetra** | Summary is enough if time is short |
| **Down to Earth** | Fortnightly; **do not** read cover to cover — selective, after you know the syllabus |
| **Ashok Gulati** | *Indian Express* Ideas page, **Mondays** — column *"From Plate to Plough"* (high GS-III yield; the lecture audio misheard this as “From Plague to Glow”) |
| **Harish Damodaran** | *Indian Express* Rural Affairs editor — read whenever he writes |

---

sections.heading: 1. Why Agriculture Is Still the Backbone (GEO-05-01)
sections.content:
India is called a farmers' country because almost every layer of life — physical environment, social custom, and the macro-economy — still turns on agriculture.

| Indicator | Figure to remember (range) | Source / year |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Workforce **directly** dependent on agriculture | **~45%** (Economic Survey: **46.2%**) | Latest Economic Survey |
| Direct share in **GDP (Gross Domestic Product)** | **~17%** (less than 20%) | Latest Economic Survey |
| Indirect dependence | Much higher (inputs, agro-industry, rural demand) | — |

The puzzle of the lecture: **how can a sector that gives <20% of GDP still be the backbone?** Because the **macro indicators** — inflation, fiscal deficit, trade — are agriculture-driven even when the GDP share is small.

---

sections.heading: 2. Who Is a Farmer? (GEO-05-02)
sections.content:
There is **no single official definition** of "farmer" in India. That ambiguity has serious implications for **who actually gets subsidies and scheme benefits**.

**M.S. Swaminathan / National Commission on Farmers (early 2000s)** — a farmer should include:

| Category | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| **Owner-cultivator** | Person who **owns arable land** (land fit for cultivation) **and cultivates it** |
| **Tenant farmer** | Cultivates someone else's land and pays **rent in cash** |
| **Sharecropper** (*bataidar*) | Cultivates someone else's land and **shares the harvest** (no cash rent) |
| **Landless agricultural worker** | Daily-wage labour on another's field (e.g. pesticide spraying) |
| **Allied activities** | Dairy, poultry, fisheries, **beekeeping** (pollination raises mustard yield; beekeeper sells honey, beeswax, royal jelly) |
| **Tribal collectors** | Communities gathering **minor forest produce (MFP)** |

> Farming is not only crop cultivation. Allied and forest-based livelihoods sit inside the same "farmer" tent that Swaminathan drew.

---

sections.heading: 3.1 Inflation and Engel's Law
sections.content:
**Engel's Law:** as income rises, the **proportion** of income spent on food **falls** (the rupee amount may still rise). A Delhi earner on ₹10,000/month may spend ~40% on food; a ₹1 crore/month earner cannot spend 40% on food.

That is why **CPI (Consumer Price Index)** gives **maximum weight to food and beverages** — most Indians still spend a large share of income on food. Weak monsoon / **El Niño** (Pacific warming that often weakens the Indian monsoon) → food inflation → headline inflation. Buffer stocks of grain can **soften the blow**.

A common newspaper metric: **cost of thali**.

sections.heading: 3.2 Fiscal deficit and the subsidy chain
sections.content:
Fiscal deficit = expenditure − revenue (the borrowing gap). Government spending splits into:

- **Capital expenditure** — physical infrastructure (Sagarmala, Bharatmala, ports, railways) and social infrastructure (schools, hospitals).
- **Revenue / non-capital expenditure** — salaries and **subsidies**. Being a welfare state, the largest subsidy buckets are **food and agriculture**.

sections.heading: Food subsidy — NFSA / PMGKAY
sections.content:
**NFSA** = **National Food Security Act, 2013**. **PMGKAY** = **Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana** (the free-grain overlay on NFSA from the COVID years; from Jan 2023 the NFSA rice/wheat issue price itself became zero).

| Item | Detail |
|:---|:---|
| Coverage | **~67.5%** of population: **75% rural + 50% urban** ≈ **82 crore** people |
| 2013 NFSA issue price | Rice **₹3/kg**, wheat **₹2/kg** |
| From **January 2023** | Rice and wheat **free** at fair-price shops |
| Priority households | **25 kg / family of five** (5 kg per person) |
| Antyodaya (poorest of poor) | **35 kg / household** of five |
| Economic cost (2024) | Rice **~₹41/kg**, wheat **~₹28/kg** (2025 rice ~₹44/kg) |

**Two purposes of procurement, not one:**

1. **Food security** of consumers who cannot pay economic cost.
2. **Remunerative price for farmers** via **MSP (Minimum Support Price)** — **FCI (Food Corporation of India)** lifts surplus so market price does not crash, then uses grain for the **PDS (Public Distribution System) + buffer stock**. Government often procures *more* than the strategic buffer needs, because that extra lift is what **stabilises farm prices**.

sections.heading: Fertilizer subsidy — urea and DAP
sections.content:
- **Urea** is made from **ammonia** (hydrogen from **methane/natural gas** + nitrogen from air). **~51%** of natural gas is imported, much of it from **West Asia**. Strait of Hormuz / Qatar disruption → gas dearer → urea costlier, but the farmer's retail price is held — so **subsidy balloons** (class example: ~₹1.7 lakh crore → ~₹3.4 lakh crore).
- **~30% of India's natural gas** is used just for fertilizer.
- Pre-2015, some urea used **naphtha** from refining. India is a **net importer of crude** but a **net exporter of petroleum products**.
- **DAP (Diammonium Phosphate)** — **~80% imported** from **China, Morocco, Saudi Arabia, Russia**. Needs phosphoric acid ← rock phosphate + sulphuric acid.
- **Food vs fuel / food vs cars:** China is diverting phosphoric acid into **LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate) EV (Electric Vehicle) batteries**, which are cheaper than lithium-ion — so less DAP/phosphoric acid for India.
- India has a **5-year DAP offtake treaty with Saudi Arabia**, but **landed CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight) price** still rises: Houthi risk in the **Red Sea** and trouble in the **Strait of Hormuz** raise **insurance**; the Cape of Good Hope detour raises **freight**.
- Class prediction: this year **fertilizer subsidy may exceed food subsidy**.

sections.heading: Power subsidy for irrigation
sections.content:
**~64% of irrigated area** is **groundwater**, mostly tubewells — which need electricity.

| Completely free farm power | Heavily subsidised |
|:---|:---|
| Punjab (since 2001), Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu | Bihar, **UP (Uttar Pradesh)**, Rajasthan, **MP (Madhya Pradesh)** |

**NITI Aayog** (*National Institution for Transforming India*) **Fiscal Health Index 2026:** Punjab **last** among 18 major states; Andhra Pradesh also near the bottom — both heavy subsidy states. Tamil Nadu **CM (Chief Minister)**'s white paper on fiscal burden makes the same point: **food + agriculture subsidies strain state finances**.

---

sections.heading: 4. Agri-Trade: Surplus on Exports, Deficit on Three Imports (GEO-05-04)
sections.content:
India has a **merchandise trade deficit**, but an **agricultural trade surplus** (agri exports > agri imports).

| We **export** (net surplus items) | We **import** (and this year may hit a record — El Niño hit) |
|:---|:---|
| Basmati + non-basmati rice | **Edible oils** (~$20 bn / year; **60%** of requirement) |
| Marine / aquaculture products | **Pulses** (India is among the world's largest importers) |
| Buffalo meat (*carabeef* / "buff") | **Cotton** (net importer for the last ~1 year) |
| Tea, coffee, spices, tobacco, **F&V (Fruits and Vegetables)** | — |
| Sugar (when not banned) | — |

**Resource paradox to quote in Mains:**

| India's share of world | Figure |
|:---|:---:|
| Land | **2.4%** |
| Fresh water | **4%** |
| Population | **18%** |
| Livestock | **18%** |
| World's buffaloes | **>50%** |

---

sections.heading: 5. Rice — Largest Area, Producer and Exporter (GEO-05-05)
sections.content:
- Largest **area**, largest **producer**, largest **exporter** — **~40% of world rice trade**, more than Vietnam + Pakistan + Thailand **combined**.
- India was once a **ship-to-mouth** economy; Green Revolution flipped that story.

sections.heading: Basmati vs non-basmati
sections.content:
| | **Basmati** | **Non-basmati** |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Character | **Aromatic**; long grain is secondary | All other varieties |
| Grown for | **Export** (too expensive for most Indians) | Domestic + cheap export |
| Belt | **North-west GI (Geographical Indication) belt:** Punjab, Haryana (biggest market), western **UP (Uttar Pradesh)**, Uttarakhand, **HP (Himachal Pradesh)**, **J&K (Jammu and Kashmir)** | Rest of India |
| Markets | **West Asia is #1** (Iran biggest, then Saudi, **UAE (United Arab Emirates)**, Iraq); also **EU (European Union)** and USA | **Africa** (**DRC / Democratic Republic of the Congo**, Benin, Côte d'Ivoire, Burkina Faso), **Bangladesh, Nepal** |
| Current affair | US tariff threat over "dumping"; US grew **Texmati** (Texas) which failed commercially | — |

**GI (Geographical Indication) fight:** only those seven north-western states can export under the name "basmati". **Madhya Pradesh** grows aromatic rice but must label it "fragrant/aromatic" — farmers do not get the full premium, so MP demands a basmati GI; existing states say that would **dilute** the tag.

sections.heading: Virtual export of water
sections.content:
Rice is water-intensive. In **semi-arid Punjab–Haryana** it is grown on **assured irrigation**, not rainfall. **~5,000 litres of water per kg of rice in Punjab** → exporting 1 kg of rice is a **virtual export of 5,000 litres of water** from a water-stressed country.

---

sections.heading: 6. Marine Products and Aquaculture (GEO-05-06)
sections.content:
- India is the **2nd largest** producer of marine products (China 1st): fish, crustaceans (crab, prawn, shrimp), seaweed.
- Coastline **>11,000 km** (including islands) + inland water — but **maximum output is from aquaculture** (farm ponds + fingerlings), not capture fisheries.
- **Why aquaculture:** **FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN)** says marine stocks are **over-exploited**. **Bottom trawling** takes juveniles (fine mesh) and **bycatch** (turtles). Mechanised fishing made ocean harvest unsustainable.

| Top producing states | Export markets |
|:---|:---|
| **Andhra Pradesh** (esp. East & West Godavari, Krishna) > West Bengal > Gujarat > Tamil Nadu | **EU (European Union)**; **USA = biggest market for Indian shrimp/prawn**; East & **SE (South-East) Asia** (Hong Kong, Singapore) |

---

sections.heading: 7. Buffalo Meat (GEO-05-07)
sections.content:
- India is the **largest producer of buffalo meat** because it holds **>50% of the world's buffaloes**.
- Top states: **Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra**.
- Export is **boneless boxed meat**; bones have other uses. Spent buffaloes (after lactation cycles) are sold — proceeds buy a new calf and **support the dairy economy** even though the trade is politically sensitive.
- Markets: **Egypt, Vietnam, Cambodia, Malaysia**; newer: **Russia, Central Asia, UAE (United Arab Emirates)**.

---

sections.heading: 8. Sugar — Dual Use, Irregular Export (GEO-05-08)
sections.content:
Top cane/sugar states: **UP (Uttar Pradesh) > Maharashtra > Karnataka**. World sugar also comes from **sugar beet**; India is overwhelmingly **cane**. India is the **2nd largest producer** (Brazil 1st) but the **largest consumer**. Export of sugar is **not regular**. Government **banned sugar export until September 2026** (likely to be extended) because: (a) we are the largest consumer; (b) high crude → mills would dump sugar abroad; (c) El Niño / weak monsoon risk to cane.

Figure: Sugarcane is either a food crop (refined sugar + molasses ethanol) or, since 2018, a fuel crop (direct juice-to-ethanol). World sugar prices move one-for-one with crude oil — which is why an export ban appears whenever oil spikes.

**Why sugar is still on PDS (Public Distribution System):** it is the **cheapest source of calories** for manual labourers who cannot afford a high-protein diet. ---

sections.heading: 9. Tea (GEO-05-09)
sections.content:
- **Largest area** under tea; **2nd largest producer** (China 1st). Production **~1,300 million kg** → **~2/3 domestic, ~1/3 export**.
- Tea is **not endemic** to India — introduced by the British.

| Region | Places / notes |
|:---|:---|
| **Assam (~50%)** | Upper Assam: **Dibrugarh, Tinsukia, Lakhimpur, Sivasagar** (where British tea began); also Udalguri, Darrang, Sonitpur |
| **Bodoland link** | Sparse **NE (North-East)** needed labour → British moved workers from **central and eastern India** → demography flipped → local groups became a minority → **Bodoland** demand (**NDFB = National Democratic Front of Boroland**, etc.) |
| **West Bengal (~20–25%)** | **Darjeeling** (**GI / Geographical Indication**; ~6,500+ ft) and the **Duars** (Jalpaiguri, Siliguri, Alipurduar) — *dwar* = **door to the Himalayas** |
| **South** | **TN (Tamil Nadu):** **Ooty / Nilgiris**; Kerala: **Munnar (Idukki), Wayanad**; limited Karnataka |
| **Western Himalaya** | **UK here = Uttarakhand** (not United Kingdom): **Dehradun, Almora**; **HP (Himachal Pradesh):** **Kangra** (GI), **Mandi** |

**Export markets:** Russia, Iran, **CIS (Commonwealth of Independent States)**, China (even though China is the largest producer).

---

sections.heading: 10. Coffee (GEO-05-10)
sections.content:
Quantity is far below tea, but **export value last year exceeded tea** because coffee is a premium crop. Also **not endemic**.

- **Karnataka >70%** of India's coffee. **Coorg / Kodagu** alone **>50%**. **Baba Budan** (a saint from **Yemen**) first planted coffee on the **Baba Budangiri** hills near **Chikmagalur**.
- **Andhra Pradesh:** tribal **Araku Valley**, Visakhapatnam.
- **Odisha:** **Koraput** (borders Andhra).

---

sections.heading: 11. Other Exports (thin surplus)
sections.content:
Fruits & vegetables, spices, tobacco — **high export value but also high imports**, so the surplus is thin.

| Export | Import that offsets it |
|:---|:---|
| Mangoes, pomegranates, onions | Apples, nuts / dry fruits |
| Chilli, coriander, turmeric | **Green cardamom from Sri Lanka** |

---

sections.heading: 12. Why Agri-Imports May Hit a Record — Edible Oils (GEO-05-11)
sections.content:
Headline of the class article: El Niño could push **vegetable oil, pulses and cotton** imports to a new high.

Until **1991** India was fairly comfortable in edible oil. After liberalisation, imports surged. Today **~60% of edible oil is imported** (~**$20 billion**/year).

**Demand side:** population + **middle-class dietary shift** after 1991 — from cereal-heavy poor diets to fat- and protein-rich diets; festival fried food became everyday; restaurant culture. (Palm oil in chips, soaps, cosmetics; biggest food use = **hydrogenated vegetable oil / vanaspati / Dalda**, because it is cheaper than mustard/soy/sunflower.)

**Supply side:** Green Revolution research went into **rice and wheat**, not **oilseeds and pulses**. No comparable **HYVs (High-Yielding Varieties)**. Oilseeds are grown on **unirrigated, poorer land** — exactly the land El Niño hits.

| Oil | Source | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Palm oil** | **Indonesia, Malaysia** | Oil palm is **endemic to equatorial West Africa**, not **SE (South-East) Asia** — Europeans replaced SE Asian evergreen forest with plantations. Indonesia's **biodiesel programme** → less export → **palm price high** |
| **Soybean oil** | Brazil, Argentina | — |
| **Sunflower** | Ukraine, Russia, Argentina | **Ukraine ~80%** of India's sunflower oil |
| **Canola** | Canada | A mustard-family oil |

**NMEO-Oilseeds = National Mission on Edible Oils – Oilseeds (2024, 7 years):** bring imports to **<30%** of requirement by (1) **HYV (High-Yielding Variety) seeds** to farmers and (2) **better procurement** of oilseeds.

---

sections.heading: 13. Pulses (GEO-05-12)
sections.content:
| Status | Pulse | Also called | Import origin (where relevant) |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Self-sufficient** | Gram | Chana / chickpea | — |
| **Self-sufficient** (lecture) | Green gram | Moong | Class notebook listed moong with imports; **spoken lecture said India is now self-sufficient** |
| **Imported** | Red gram | Pigeon pea / **arhar / tur** | **Myanmar** |
| **Imported** | Black gram | Urad | Myanmar / E. Africa |
| **Imported** | Lentil | Masoor (rabi) | **Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique**; also Canada, Russia, Australia |
| **Imported** | Yellow peas | *Peeli matar* | **Canada, Australia, Russia** |

**Mission for Atmanirbharta in Pulses (2025–2031):** HYV seeds + better procurement — same template as the oilseed mission.

---

sections.heading: 14. Cotton — From Exporter to Net Importer (GEO-05-13)
sections.content:
India has the **largest area** under cotton, and used to be a net **exporter**. For the **last ~1 year** it has been a **net importer**.

**Imports:** USA; **Egypt (Giza cotton)**; West Africa (**Burkina Faso, Benin**).

**Growing conditions:** **warm** tropics (Ukraine is Europe's northern limit; **J&K (Jammu and Kashmir)** / Uttarakhand / Himachal cannot grow it); rainfall **50–100 cm** (class notebook wrote 50–100 *mm* — almost certainly a missed zero; the lecture said centimetres) — **not** the heavy-rain east or Kerala.

| Rank / belt | Region |
|:---|:---|
| **1. GJ (Gujarat)** | **Saurashtra / Kathiawar plateau** — Bhavnagar, Surendranagar, Rajkot, Amreli, Porbandar, Junagadh |
| **2. MH (Maharashtra)** | **Vidarbha** — Nagpur, Akola, Amravati, Yavatmal, Chandrapur |
| **3. Telangana** | — |
| Other black-soil belts | **SE (South-East) Tamil Nadu** (Tirunelveli), **Dharwad** (Karnataka), **Malwa — MP (Madhya Pradesh):** Indore, Ujjain, Ratlam, Dhar |
| North | Punjab, **HR (Haryana)**, **RJ (Rajasthan)** |

> **One-line reason production collapsed: Pink Bollworm.** Detail in a later lecture.

---

sections.heading: UPSC Cues & PYQ Connections
sections.content:
- **Workforce vs GDP (Gross Domestic Product) gap** (45% workers, 17% GDP) is the standard "disguised unemployment / structural transformation" Mains hook.
- **No legal definition of farmer** + Swaminathan's inclusive list (tenant, sharecropper, landless, allied, **MFP / Minor Forest Produce**).
- **Engel's Law** → why **CPI (Consumer Price Index)** is food-heavy.
- **NFSA (National Food Security Act) coverage (75/50)** and the **2023 free-grain shift**; economic cost vs issue price.
- **MSP (Minimum Support Price) = price support + PDS (Public Distribution System) + buffer**, not charity.
- **DAP (Diammonium Phosphate) 80% imported**; phosphoric acid → **LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate) batteries**; Red Sea / Hormuz **CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight)** shock.
- **64% irrigation = groundwater**; free power ↔ Punjab's fiscal rank.
- **Agri trade surplus vs three chronic imports** (oil, pulses, now cotton).
- **Rice: 40% of world exports** vs **virtual water** (5,000 L/kg in Punjab).
- **Basmati GI (Geographical Indication) belt** vs **MP (Madhya Pradesh)**'s aromatic rice; **Texmati**.
- **Duars = door to the Himalayas**; Darjeeling & Kangra GI tea.
- **Baba Budan / Yemen → Chikmagalur coffee**; Araku, Koraput.
- **Palm oil not native to SE (South-East) Asia**; Indonesia biodiesel.
- **NMEO-Oilseeds (National Mission on Edible Oils – Oilseeds, 2024)** and **Mission for Atmanirbharta in Pulses (2025–31)**.
- **Pink bollworm** as the cotton-import trigger.

---

sections.heading: Lecture 2 — Agriculture: Society, Climate and Stubble
sections.content:
> **Date of Lecture:** 30 August 2026  
> **Date Added:** 2026-08-30  
> **Source:** Vajiram & Ravi class lecture + audio transcript + 4 handwritten notebook pages  
> **Continues:** 28 August lecture (`04_Agriculture_Importance_Trade_and_Commodities.md`) — that class was *economic* importance; this one is *social* importance, then how agriculture and climate change (CC) cut both ways  
> **Also relevant for:** GS-I (society, urbanisation, migration), GS-III (agriculture, climate, air pollution), GS-II (land reforms, Other Backward Classes / OBC politics), Essay  
> **How to read class shortcuts:** full form on first use, then the short form. Glossary at the end.

**Read with this lecture:** **Harish Damodaran** (rural affairs; class flagged his El Niño / climate-migration pieces). *The Hindu*, 23 July 2026 — India’s paddy fields among the world’s methane hotspots. Punjab **Direct Seeding of Rice (DSR)** area up **36%** to **over 4 lakh hectares** in **Kharif 2026**.

---

sections.heading: 1. Festivals Sit on the Harvest (GEO-07-01)
sections.content:
A large share of Indian custom is agricultural. Class examples (memorise as a map, not a list of “culture facts”):

| Festival | Region | What it marks |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Baisakhi** (sheet: Baishakhi) | North-West India | **Wheat** harvest — wheat is the staple there |
| **Bihu** (incl. **Magh Bihu**) | Assam | Harvest festival |
| **Pongal** | Tamil Nadu (**TN**) | Harvest festival |
| **Harela** | **Uttarakhand (UK)** — *not* the United Kingdom | Sowing *before* the monsoon arrives |

Social *problems* also sit on agri performance: distress migration, feminisation of the farm workforce, farmer suicides. The rest of the note is that chain.

---

sections.heading: 2. Village vs Town, and Why India’s Urbanisation Hurts (GEO-07-02)
sections.content:
**Census 2011** (last completed census): **~68–69% rural**, **~31% urban**. India is urbanising fast (metros, rural out-migration). The **United States (US)** and **Western Europe (EU / European Union)** are already **>80% urban** — that is *not* India’s problem. India’s problem is **distress / duress migration**: people leave because agriculture does not pay, not because a factory has already hired them.

**You cannot have smart cities without smart villages.** New urban infrastructure is never enough if rural distress keeps feeding slums and squatters (class: Delhi dividers near Patel Nagar / Connaught Place; slums of Delhi and Mumbai filled by migrants, not “old Delhi-born” poor).

sections.heading: 2.1 There is no official definition of a “village”
sections.content:
Not population. Not administration. Not a primary-health-centre test. **Dhanbad** is a **town** even though coal mining is a *primary* activity — so “primary vs secondary vs tertiary” does not define village vs town.

Official papers rarely say *gaon* / *gram*. The working term is **mauza** = **revenue village**: the **smallest territorial unit for collecting land revenue**. For all practical purposes, that *is* a village in India.

sections.heading: 2.2 Two kinds of town (Prelims lock)
sections.content:
| Type | Defined by | Rule |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Statutory town** | **Administration** | If a **municipal corporation / municipal council**, **cantonment board**, or **town area committee** governs the place, it is a town — *regardless* of population, density, occupation or infrastructure |
| **Census town** | **Population criteria** (Census of India) | Must satisfy **all three** conditions below |

**Census-town triple (all three):**

1. Population **≥ 5,000**
2. Density **≥ 400 persons / km²**
3. **≥ 75% of males** (not of total population) in **non-agricultural** work (any other primary / secondary / tertiary job is fine)

Eastern **Uttar Pradesh (UP)**, **Bihar**, **West Bengal (WB)** villages are often large *and* dense — they already pass (1) and (2). **Criterion 3** is what usually separates town from village.

---

sections.heading: 3. Agriculture Is a Climate Bet (GEO-07-03)
sections.content: Agri is high-risk **without** high-gain. A farmer is betting on climate even where irrigation exists.

sections.heading: 3.1 Punjab wheat, March 2022 — grain shrink
sections.content:
**Punjab** is among India’s better-off agri regions (irrigation + machines). In **2022** the harvested **wheat grain was smaller** → lower yield. Scientists: **March heatwave** during **grain filling** (panicles filling).

Wheat is **rabi**: sown **October–November**, harvested **March–April**. Apparent sun moves from equator toward Cancer from March → summer arrives **earlier in the peninsula**, **mid-May peak in North India**.

| Region | Typical wheat harvest |
|:---|:---|
| **Madhya Pradesh (MP)**, **Maharashtra (MH)** | mid-**March** |
| **Punjab** | first week of **April** |
| **Himachal Pradesh (HP)** | last week of **April** |

Class analogy (no formula): on a hot afternoon, sprinting spends energy on **sweating / cooling**, so less energy is left for the sprint. A wheat plant does the same via **transpiration**. High March heat → more cooling cost → **less energy for grain filling** → **smaller grain**. Irrigation did not save the farmer.

sections.heading: 3.2 Climate can hit you from another continent
sections.content:
- **El Niño** — Pacific warming that often **weakens the Indian monsoon**. A Pacific event, Indian farm incomes.
- **Desert locusts, 2020** (lockdown March–April pictures; Punjab, **Haryana (HR)**, **Rajasthan (RJ)**). Trigger: **exceptionally heavy 2019 rain in East Africa** → waterlogging → locust boom → swarms moved north via **Iran–Pakistan**. **UN FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization):** a **1 km** swarm (~**40 million** insects) can eat in a day what **~35,000 people** eat. Climate event in East Africa, crop loss in North-West India.

sections.heading: 3.3 Meteorological drought becomes agricultural drought
sections.content:
Where irrigation is thin, a monsoon failure is not only “less rain” — it is **crop failure**. No rural industry → the only exit is the city. Unskilled distress migrants become **urban poor** (slums, congestion, squatters) instead of rural poor.

**Climate migration** (class article): people *do not want* to move. Two belts named:

| Belt | Where | Hook |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Marathwada (MH)** | around **Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar**, **Beed**, **Jalna**, **Aurangabad** belt | sugar / drought / later also farmer-suicide geography |
| **Bundelkhand** | **UP:** Hamirpur, Banda, Mahoba, Jhansi, Jalaun, Lalitpur. **MP:** Panna, Tikamgarh, Chhatarpur, Datia, Damoh | drought-prone; class: many Rajendra Nagar domestic workers are from here. **Panna (MP):** **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** — progressively less rain, rising heat. Estimate: Bundelkhand mean **+3.5 °C by 2100** |

---

sections.heading: 4. Feminisation of Agriculture (GEO-07-04)
sections.content: **Meaning (class, lock this):** *not* “more women than men in the field”. It means the **share of women in the agri workforce is rising** compared with the past — because **young males migrate** and women stay on the farm.

sections.heading: 4.1 Sex ratio explains the map
sections.content:
**Sex ratio (India)** = **females per 1,000 males**.

**Census 2011:** India **943** (books / some government sites print **940** — class: **both acceptable**). **Rural 949**. **Urban 929**.

Migration is **age-selective** and **sex-selective**. Young men move more easily (jobs). Young women face safety / family resistance (class: Delhi’s image). The old rarely move for a career. Result:

- **Urban:** adverse sex ratio → weaker gender sensitivity; in extreme form, crime against women
- **Rural:** relatively more women left behind → they work the fields → **feminisation**

sections.heading: 4.2 Three exam challenges
sections.content:
| Challenge | Class figure / fact |
|:---|:---|
| **Exploitation** | Women paid less than men for the same work. Extreme: **forced hysterectomies / tubal cutting** of women sugarcane workers in **Marathwada (MH)** so a contractor couple stays “productive” through the **October–April/May** crushing season (~**7–8 months**). In **UP** the *farmer* harvests and carts cane to the mill; in **MH** the **mill** must harvest and transport — so mills hire contractors → couples. Domestic *and* foreign press have covered this |
| **Workforce vs title** | Women ≈ **60%** of agri **workforce**; **< 15%** of **land titles** in women’s names → they enter as **landless workers**, not owner-cultivators |
| **Machines not designed for women’s work** | Productivity needs technology (the **Green Revolution** started with **Norman Borlaug**’s **high-yielding variety (HYV)** wheat in Mexico). **Tractors** exist for **ploughing** — culturally reserved for **men** in most of India. **Tea-leaf plucking** is largely women’s work — almost no machine. Machines are built for whoever has **purchasing power**, and that is concentrated with men |

sections.heading: 4.3 Credit trap when the husband has left
sections.content:
The wife needs seed / fertiliser / pesticide **credit**. **Institutional** route: scheduled commercial bank, **Regional Rural Bank (RRB)**, cooperative — cheap, because **Priority Sector Lending (PSL)** forces a farm quota (including small/marginal farmers). Bank still wants **collateral**. Land is in the *husband’s* name, and he is in the city. Formal “no-collateral” small loans are often blocked in practice.

**Farm-loan waivers** (class: **TN**, **MH** extensions) create a **moral hazard**: the honest repayer is punished; the strategic defaulter is rewarded before elections → more deliberate default → banks stop lending → women go to the **village moneylender**. North India class rate: **2–3% per month** = **24–36% per annum** vs a bank’s ~**0.5%** (class contrast). Two failed monsoons + that interest → public humiliation / violence → **suicide**.

---

sections.heading: 5. Farmer Suicides — Not a “Backward-State Only” Story (GEO-07-05)
sections.content:
**National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB):**

| Window | Figure (class) |
|:---|:---|
| **1995–2015** | **> 3 lakh** farmer suicides. After the 2015 report hit Parliament, the government **stopped publishing** the series for **three years** |
| **2023** | **10,786** — **cultivators + landless agricultural workers** |

**Maharashtra** has high per-capita income and is still the worst belt: class **~35–40%** of India’s farmer suicides, concentrated in **Marathwada** and **Vidarbha** (link yesterday’s **cotton / pink bollworm** map).

**Tamil Nadu** has industry + social security + a well-irrigated **Cauvery** delta — and a **drought-prone south-east**.

sections.heading: Why south TN can starve in a “normal monsoon” year
sections.content:
Most of India: **June–September South-West (SW) monsoon**. The peninsula splits the SW into an **Arabian Sea** branch and a **Bay of Bengal** branch. The **Bay branch bypasses far-south / south-east TN**. **Maximum TN rain is October–November–December from the North-East (NE) monsoon** (winds that have picked up moisture over the Bay).

**2016:** all-India **SW monsoon normal**, agri output good — **TN** had one of the **worst droughts of the century**, **~65% rainfall deficit** (class: if NE rain is 100 cm, that year ~**35 cm**). Farmers then protested at **Jantar Mantar** (half-clad, dead rats in the mouth, skeletal remains of suicide victims). Class point: urban India often does not even *count* this as a social problem.

---

sections.heading: 6. Agriculture as Empowerment — Land, Green Revolution, OBCs (GEO-07-06)
sections.content:
Not only problems. Agri has also **empowered**.

**1793 Permanent Settlement** (Cornwallis) → **zamindari**. After Independence, **land reforms**: abolish zamindari, take surplus land, give it to the tiller — reading **Directive Principles** on preventing concentration of wealth (**Articles 39(b) and 39(c)**).

Land is not only an economic asset; it carries **social / emotive** value.

**Intermediate caste groups** (never the ritual top, never the most oppressed; numerical majority and *dominant* in their pockets) were often the **biggest land-reform beneficiaries**:

| Pocket | Dominant intermediate group (class) |
|:---|:---|
| Western TN (Erode, Coimbatore, Nilgiris) | **Kongu Vellala Gounder** |
| Southern **Karnataka (KA)** | **Vokkaligas** |
| **Andhra Pradesh (AP)** | **Reddys** |
| **Telangana (TG)** | **Khammas** |
| **Gujarat (GJ)** | **Patels / Patidars** |
| Parts of **UP** and Bihar | **Yadavs** |
| Western UP, Punjab, HR | **Jats** |

Sequence class wants for **GS-I / GS-II**:

1. Land reform → **social** power (they already had numbers)
2. **Green Revolution** (Punjab, HR, western UP, coastal Andhra, Cauvery west) → **economic** power
3. Numbers + money → **political** power: rise of **state-level parties** from the **late 1960s / early 1970s** = the **OBC (Other Backward Classes)** political wave. **No coincidence** that this is also the GR window.

**Rudolph & Rudolph:** **“bullock capitalists”** — rich peasants who rode land reform + GR.

---

sections.heading: 7.1 Greenhouse, then the Earth
sections.content:
A parked car / a glass-walled **greenhouse** (or a **polyhouse**) lets heat in and slows its escape → inside warmer than outside. **Greenhouse gases (GHGs)** — **carbon dioxide (CO₂)**, **methane (CH₄)**, **nitrous oxide (N₂O)**, **sulphur hexafluoride (SF₆)**, water vapour — do something similar to Earth. More GHGs → more trapped heat → **global warming**.

**Physics (class, no LaTeX):** a **hot** body radiates at a **short** wavelength; a **cooler** body at a **longer** wavelength. The Sun is extremely hot → **short-wave** insolation crosses the air and **heats the land**. The land is cooler → **long-wave** radiation heats the air above. Warm air expands, rises → **low pressure** → winds (high → low) → moisture → rain. Change temperature → change pressure → change wind → change precipitation = **climate change**.

**Climate change** = change in **temperature, wind and precipitation** of an area **over a period of time**.

It *has* been **natural** (glacial / interglacial cycles): change in **axial tilt**, change in the **elliptical orbit**, **sunspot** cycles. **Present-day speed** is **anthropogenic** (human GHG rise).

sections.heading: 7.2 Who emits, and why the tropics are hit harder
sections.content:
Class shares (order-of-magnitude, for Mains colour):

| Source | Share of GHGs (class) |
|:---|:---|
| Transport | ~**13%** |
| Industry | ~**21%** |
| **Agriculture + land-use change** (**UN FAO**) | **~18%** |

Any climate shift hits **agri more than most other sectors**. The hit is **more pronounced in the tropics** than in the temperate zone:

1. **More people** (eastern India, tropical China, South-East Asia) → more food demand.
2. Tropics already farm **~12 months** (kharif + rabi). Temperate Canada may have **~8 months** under snow; **+2 °C** can *lengthen* that season (snow 4 months → 2). Tropics get **heatwaves**, not a longer season.
3. Tropical countries are **poorer** — fewer drought-resistant / flood-tolerant seeds, less irrigation, almost no climate-controlled farming. A ₹100/kg onion shock hits the poor, not a Delhi rich household.

Faulty agri practices also *cause* the GHGs. Two big ones in this lecture: **flooded paddy** and **livestock**. Third: **stubble burning**.

---

sections.heading: 8. Flooded Paddy vs Direct Seeding of Rice (GEO-07-08)
sections.content:
India has the **largest area** under paddy and is the **largest rice producer** — so it is also a **top methane source** from rice (*The Hindu*, 23 July 2026). Class: paddy fields ≈ **10% of world CH₄**.

**The problem is not rice. The problem is the transplantation method.**

sections.heading: 8.1 Transplantation (the common method)
sections.content:
1. Sow seed in a **nursery** (raised bed in one corner).
2. **Plough** and **flood** the main field; **puddle** (break soil aggregates to fines). **Water-holding capacity is inversely proportional to grain size** — sand drains, clay holds.
3. After ~**30 days**, seedlings ~**15 cm** → workers transplant **two seedlings per hill** in rows.
4. Field stays flooded. Rice makes **aerenchyma** and can live **waterlogged ~7–8 days**. **Weeds cannot**. Water = **natural herbicide**.
5. Dead weeds decompose. Standing water = **no oxygen** → **anaerobic** bacteria → **CH₄**.

Also: heavy **labour** (Punjab / HR / western UP rice depends on migrants from eastern UP, Bihar, Bengal — workers are scarce even at high wages); **25–30 irrigations**; class already gave **~5,000 litres of water per kg of Punjab rice**; **groundwater** collapse.

**System of Rice Intensification (SRI)** is **not** DSR — class: a hybrid (very early, two-leaf transplant). Do not mix them in Prelims.

sections.heading: 8.2 Direct Seeding of Rice (DSR)
sections.content:
Seed drill on a tractor puts seed **straight into the main field**. No nursery, no transplant labour. **Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD):** never flood. Keep the field wet. Clay **swells when wet, cracks when dry** — cracks = time for the next irrigation. **~15 irrigations** instead of 25–30. Crop **matures 7–10 days earlier**. **No standing water → no transplant-style methane pulse.** **Kharif 2026:** Punjab DSR area **+36% to >4 lakh ha** — **El Niño** year, June–July rain deficit, plus a government push (new seed varieties in a later “seeds” lecture). **Challenge that keeps DSR unpopular:** **weeds**.
---

sections.heading: 9. Livestock Methane and “Non-Veg Milk” (GEO-07-09)
sections.content:
Cattle release **more methane than paddy fields** (class). Four-chamber stomach; **enteric fermentation** (anaerobic digestion; class named the gut bacteria). Most CH₄ leaves as **belching**, not as dung.

Why is a “natural” gut process counted as **anthropogenic**?

1. **Numbers:** **artificial insemination** and veterinary care → more cattle than a natural herd.
2. **Diet:** high-protein / hard-to-digest feed raises milk *and* methane.

Milk depends on **breed + diet**.

| Animal (class) | Daily milk (order of magnitude) |
|:---|:---|
| Indigenous (**Gir**, **Sahiwal**) | ~**3.5 L** even for a good animal |
| Cross-bred (India) | ~**7–8 L** |
| **Jersey / Brown Swiss** in India | ~**13–14 L** |
| Same exotic types in **Israel / US** | up to ~**35–36 L** |

Gap is largely **feed**. **“Non-veg milk”** (news when **USAID** pressure to open India’s dairy market): US / Israeli farms mix **intestines** and **blood meal** (dried blood) into feed. India: **~8 crore** small/marginal farmers with **1–2 backyard animals** vs US mega-herds (scale + price shock). Hindu ritual use of milk is a second political block if the cow was fed meat.

---

sections.heading: 10. Stubble Burning (GEO-07-10)
sections.content: **October–November smog** in Delhi is *partly* **paddy stubble** from Punjab / HR / western UP. Class will **not** die on the year-round share. Article cited: stubble ≈ **14% of Delhi–NCR PM2.5 (Particulate Matter 2.5)** *across the year* — **small for the year, large in those two months**.

sections.heading: 10.1 Why the farmer burns
sections.content:
This belt grows **rice as a commercial crop** (basmati for export; non-basmati almost entirely lifted by the **Food Corporation of India (FCI)** / state agencies — not eaten locally). **Wheat** is the staple. **~90%** of paddy and wheat is cut by a **combine harvester** (harvest + thresh) — it takes only the **ear**, leaves **hard, silica-rich non-basmati stems**. Transplanting put **2–3 seedlings per hill**, so the stubble is a clump.

**Window:** rice harvested ~**1 November** → wheat must be **drilled by ~15 November** (after that, cold kills germination) = **~15 days**. A normal seed drill **cannot** push through standing stubble. Migrant labour has already gone home.

Burning is free, instant, and **sanitises** the field (monsoon fungi, pests, reptiles). **Myth:** ash adds nutrients. Class: some nutrients are added, **more are destroyed** → **net loss**.

sections.heading: 10.2 Why winter makes it a Delhi problem
sections.content: In winter the Sun is toward **Capricorn** → land cold → air above **dense and sinking**. Summer burning would loft the plume. Winter burning parks **oxides of carbon / nitrogen / sulphur + particulate** in the **breathing layer**. Calm winter air compounds it.

sections.heading: 10.3 Solutions that work only if the calendar allows
sections.content: **Pusa bio-decomposer** (**Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) / Pusa**): capsules → spray → stubble becomes manure in **~30 days**. **Delhi** has used it with success. **Punjab / HR** usually have only **~15 days** — the capsule is too slow. Why not transplant earlier and harvest by mid-October? - **2001 Punjab:** **8 hours free farm power** → farmers tried **two rice crops a year** in a **semi-arid** state that cannot grow even one rice crop on rainfall alone → **groundwater crash**. - **2009:** Punjab and HR laws — **no paddy transplant before 15 June ± 5 days** (held through **2024**). That late start → late harvest → no 30-day decomposer window. **Variety trap** | Variety | Who | Duration | Yield (class) | |:---|:---|:---|:---| | **Pusa-44** | **IARI** under **Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR)**, ~**1993–94** | **150–160 days** (~**130 days after** a 30-day nursery) | up to **~6,000 kg/ha** | | **PR-121, 122, 126, 128** | **Punjab Agricultural University (PAU), Ludhiana** | e.g. **PR-128 ≈ 120 days** | a bit less (~**4,500–5,000 kg/ha**) but **~40 days saved** | Transplant **20 June** + Pusa-44 → harvest **~1 November** → **15-day** wheat window. Swap in **PR-128** → theoretically **~55 days** — enough for Pusa decomposer **or** a **55–60 day moong (green gram)** crop. Many farmers **take the moong**, then still transplant PR rice, and the rice–wheat window **collapses again**. Others stay on Pusa-44. **2025:** Punjab tried to **ban Pusa-44** and refused procurement; farmers brought seed from HR; **High Court** restored the variety. **Happy Seeder / Super Seeder:** cuts stubble, lays it as mulch, drills wheat in one pass. **50–80% capital subsidy** (higher for cooperatives in the class example). Still unpopular: needs a **high-horsepower tractor**, **slow**, **more diesel** — subsidy is one-time, **operating cost** is every season.

sections.heading: 10.4 What actually reduces fires
sections.content:
Lectures do not move farmers. **Haryana has controlled burning better than Punjab** by **paying**:

- Class example: if cutting stubble costs **₹1,500/acre**, pay **₹1,500/acre** for *not* burning → farmer still nets a gain versus fire
- Village that goes from **>80%** burning last year to **zero** this year: **₹1 lakh** to the **gram panchayat** for welfare

Then **give the straw a price**: manure; **second-generation ethanol** (residue, not cereal — contrast first-generation food-to-fuel); **paper** (class: **Trident** mill near **Bathinda**); biopower. **Haryana** puts **balers** at block / village level so transport is cheap.

**Enforce:** fines that are actually **collected** (pre-election write-offs kill the signal). Officers were blocked at village gates → **satellite geotagging**. Farmers adapted: **International Forum for Environment, Sustainability and Technology (IFEST) Stubble Burning Status Report 2025** — fires shifted to **late afternoon / evening**, when the monitoring satellite is not overhead. A claimed **~90% drop** can be a **sensor gap**, not a behaviour change.

**Long-term:** change the **cropping pattern**. **Punjab and Haryana are not made for rice.** Grow what soil and climate can carry without free power and a June-15 law.

**Environment as tragedy of the commons / free-rider:** Delhi blames Punjab in October; Punjab asks why Delhi runs **ACs** for **7–8 months** on a grid that is **>70% coal**, and why it will not use public transport. Blame is cheap; nobody owns the clean-up.

sections.heading: Update — 2 September 2026 (same GHG list; not a new topic)
sections.content:
Class closed the 30 August agri–GHG sequence, then started **features of Indian agriculture** (`06_Agriculture_Rainfed_Irrigation_and_Land.md`).

**Point 2 — livestock (already above):** **enteric fermentation** of feed → **CH₄**, released largely through **belching**. Keep the 30 August breed/diet / “non-veg milk” frame.

**Point 3 — in-situ combustion of agri residue:** stubble burning as a major reason for **winter smog in Delhi and nearby areas**; cheapest and most convenient residue management; GHGs **+ particulate matter**, worse in **stagnant** winter air. Four solutions dictated in class (adds machines not named on 30 Aug):

1. **Technological inputs:** decomposers, **mouldboard (MB) plough**, **Happy Seeder**, **Super Straw Management System (Super SMS)**
2. **Monetary incentives** for environment-friendly residue management
3. **Strict enforcement** of rules
4. **Change the cropping pattern** of the region

**Point 4 — land-use change due to agriculture (new on this note):** trees = **carbon sinks** (absorb CO₂, release O₂). Cut them → that CO₂ stays in the air. **Deforestation** is a major reason for global warming. **Large tracts of forest** have become agri fields → **loss of carbon sinks** → higher GHG concentration.

Class examples:

- **Shifting / slash-and-burn:** cut, burn, crop a few seasons without fertiliser, abandon when fertility falls, repeat. Primitive land-use change.
- **Partition refugees** given land in **Punjab**, **Ganganagar (Rajasthan)**, **Yamunanagar (Haryana)**, and the **Terai** belt (**Udham Singh Nagar, Uttarakhand**; **Lakhimpur Kheri, UP**) — once **dense sal jungle**, now fields. Many **Sikh** settlements in this Terai belt.

sections.heading: Update — 4 September 2026 (*The Hindu* — CAQM + ISRO; not a new topic)
sections.content:
**Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM)** in the National Capital Region (NCR) and Adjoining Areas has asked the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** for a **basic protocol** that goes beyond **fire counts**. Chairman **Rajesh Varma**: satellite-pass counts “may not be the most accurate picture.” Need better **ground-truthing**.

Satellites still struggle with **straw quantity, moisture, combustion efficiency, and per-pollutant emission factors**.

**Share (clip, not the class year-round 14%):** farm fires **≤15%** of winter particulate matter over the whole season; can spike to **~44%** in some **October–November** weeks.

**ISRO Space Applications Centre (SAC) study:** peak fire activity shifted from **1:30 p.m. (2020)** to **~5:00 p.m. (2024)** — after the **two polar-orbiting** day-time passes. That is why Punjab’s claimed **90% drop since 2021** is treated as **exaggerated** (same “sensor gap” the 30 August class already flagged via **IFEST 2025**).

---

sections.heading: UPSC Cues
sections.content:
- **Mauza = revenue village**; no population definition of village. **Statutory** = municipal / cantonment / town area committee. **Census town** = **5,000 + 400/km² + 75% males non-agri**.
- US/EU **>80% urban** is not India’s distress-migration problem. **Smart cities need smart villages.**
- **Census 2011 sex ratio 943 (or 940) / rural 949 / urban 929.** Feminisation = **rising female share**, not a female majority.
- **~60% agri workforce women, <15% land titles.** Machines follow male purchasing power (plough vs tea plucking).
- **NCRB 1995–2015 >3 lakh**; **2023: 10,786** cultivators + landless. **MH 35–40%**. South **TN** rain is **NE monsoon**; **2016** national SW normal, TN **~65%** deficit.
- **Bundelkhand** = specified **UP + MP** districts; **+3.5 °C by 2100** (class estimate). **2020 locusts** ← **2019 East Africa rain**.
- Land reform + **GR** + **OBC / bullock capitalists** (Rudolph & Rudolph). **Harela = Uttarakhand.**
- **FAO: 18% GHGs from agri + land-use change.** Paddy **~10% of world CH₄** — **transplantation**, not rice itself. **DSR + AWD**. **SRI ≠ DSR.**
- Livestock CH₄ **> paddy**; **enteric / belching**; **non-veg milk** = blood meal / meat in feed.
- Stubble: **15-day** rice–wheat window; **Pusa decomposer = 30 days**; **15 June ± 5** transplant ban (2009); **Pusa-44 vs PAU PR-12x**; **Happy/Super Seeder** opex; **Haryana cash > Punjab machines**; **evening fires vs satellite**; long-term = **leave rice**.
- **2 Sep add-on:** four-point stubble list includes **MB plough** + **Super SMS**; **land-use change** = slash-and-burn + **sal Terai** cleared for Partition settlement (**Ganganagar, Yamunanagar, Udham Singh Nagar, Lakhimpur Kheri**). Full rainfed/irrigation class → `06_...`.
- **4 Sep paper:** **CAQM** (Rajesh Varma) + **ISRO / SAC** protocol beyond fire counts; winter PM **≤15%** / weekly spike **~44%**; peak burn **1:30 p.m. (2020) → ~5 p.m. (2024)** vs two polar day-passes; Punjab **90% since 2021** = exaggerated.

---
