sections.heading: Lecture 3 — Features of Indian Agriculture — 2 September 2026
sections.content:
> **Date of Lecture:** 2 September 2026  
> **Date Added:** 2026-09-02  
> **Source:** Vajiram & Ravi class lecture + audio transcript + 5 handwritten notebook pages  
> **Continues:** 28 August (`04_Agriculture_Importance_Trade_and_Commodities.md`) and 30 August (`05_Agriculture_Society_Climate_and_Stubble.md`). Class opened by finishing the agri–greenhouse gas (GHG) list from Lecture 2, then moved to **features of Indian agriculture**.  
> **Also relevant for:** GS-I (physiography, monsoon, Purvanchal), GS-III (irrigation, farm size, land reforms, Farmer Producer Organisations), GS-II (Directive Principles / land), Essay  
> **Land reforms in depth:** Geography sir only *briefed* the four legs. Class said the full treatment sits with **Shyam Sundar Sir (SS Sir)** in Economy.

**How to read class shortcuts:** full form on first use, then the short form. Glossary at the end.

**Already in Lecture 2 — do not restudy as a new topic:** enteric fermentation / belching; stubble burning. Those got a dated patch on `05_Agriculture_Society_Climate_and_Stubble.md` (`### Update — 2 September 2026`). This file is the **rainfed–irrigation–mechanisation–land** block.

---

sections.heading: 1. Indian Agriculture Is Rainfed (GEO-08-01)
sections.content:
Even after decades of independence, **most farmers still depend on the monsoon**. Class line: Indian agriculture is a **gamble in the hands of the monsoon**.

| Figure (class) | Value |
|:---|:---|
| Share of **farm holdings** with **no irrigation** (fully rainfed) | **~60%** |
| Irrigation infrastructure on agri land (your sheet; audio garbled) | **~33%** |
| **Net Sown Area (NSA)** | **~142 million hectares (ha)** (sheet ~**140**) |
| **Arable** (fertile / cultivable) land | **~154 million ha** |
| Gap (arable but not sown) | **~12–14 million ha** (dispute, fallow / rest) |
| **Gross Sown Area (GSA)** | **~1.5 × NSA** |
| India’s **total geographical area** | **~328 million ha** |
| **Reported area** (under Indian control / measured) | **~302 million ha** (rest: Pakistan / China control, unmeasurable terrain) |

**NSA** = land that is **fit for cultivation *and* actually under cultivation**. Arable includes land that *could* be cropped but is not.

**Why GSA is only 1.5× NSA:** India is tropical — temperature allows **two–three crops** a year (kharif paddy → rabi wheat → a zaid crop such as watermelon on the same 100 ha would make GSA **3× NSA**). In practice the extra seasons need **irrigation**. Monsoon rain lasts **~4 months**. Without a canal or tubewell, the farmer crops **only kharif**. That is why average intensity stays **~1.5**.

**Rainfed vs irrigated logic:** **Punjab (PB)** and **Haryana (HR)** get **<75 cm/year** (semi-arid) yet grow basmati / non-basmati rice **because almost every field is irrigated**. Heavy-rain states can still be drought-prone if water **runs off** and there is no storage.

---

sections.heading: 2. Who Has Irrigation? (GEO-08-02)
sections.content:
Only a handful of states have built real irrigation support. **Class percentages of agricultural land irrigated:**

| Band | State | Share irrigated (class) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Very high | **Punjab** | **>98%** |
| Very high | **Haryana** | **~94%** |
| High | **Telangana (TG)** | **~86%** |
| High | **Uttar Pradesh (UP)** | **~84%** (class also said ~86% in one pass — use **~84–86%**) |
| Moderate–high | **Andhra Pradesh (AP)** | **~63–64%** |
| Around half | **Tamil Nadu (TN)** | **near 50%** |
| Around half | **Bihar (BR)** | **~60–62%** |
| Around half | **Madhya Pradesh (MP)** | **around 50%** (sheet grouped MP / BR / TN) |
| Very low | **Assam** | **~10%** |
| Very low | **Mizoram** | **~14%** |
| Very low | **Sikkim** | **~15–16%** |
| Very low | **Maharashtra (MH)** | **~18%** |

Large states that *look* well irrigated still have **non-uniform** coverage inside the state. That is the next section.

---

sections.heading: 3.1 Western UP vs Bundelkhand
sections.content:
**Western UP** (rice + India’s main **sugarcane** belt) is canal-and-groundwater rich:

- **Upper Ganga Canal** — operational since **1854**
- **Lower Ganga Canal** — operational since **1872**

Most of UP from **Haridwar** toward **Varanasi** is a **flat alluvial plain**. Class exception: parts of **Sonbhadra / Churkhi in Mirzapur**.

**Bundelkhand** (specified districts of **UP + MP** — already in Lecture 2) is different: **granitic hills** alternating with flats. Granite **does not let water through** except along fissures → **slow groundwater recharge**. Canal network is thin compared with western UP. Farmers dig **farm ponds** in the field; granite holds the rain for a while, but ponds **dry in the lean season** — not perennial irrigation.

**Ken–Betwa Link Canal:** **Yamuna** in the north; **Betwa** and **Ken** in this dry belt. Class: a dam on the **Ken** (**Dhodan / Daudhan Dam**) stores Ken water → **link canal** into the **Betwa** → drinking water + irrigation for the parched belt of **MP + UP**.

sections.heading: 3.2 Coastal Andhra vs Rayalaseema
sections.content:
**Coastal AP** (Srikakulam on the **Odisha** border down to **Nellore** on the **TN** border): **Godavari** and **Krishna** deltas have **almost merged**. For **~200 km** the **Eastern Ghats** are missing → fertile alluvium, groundwater, canals. Strong **agriculture + aquaculture**.

**Rayalaseema** (class: **Chittoor, Anantapur, Kadapa, Kurnool, Nandyal**): hilly, poorly irrigated except pockets (**Nandyal valley** — rice; some Chittoor / Anantapur — sugarcane). That is why Rayalaseema is poorer than coastal Andhra.

sections.heading: 3.3 Tamil Nadu: Kaveri delta vs the dry south-east
sections.content: **Kaveri** enters the plains after **Mettur Dam**. After **Srirangam** it splits into distributaries — the **delta**. Irrigated since the **11th century** (**Grand Anicut / Kallanai**, Cholas). **Thanjavur, Villupuram, Tiruchirappalli** — two rice crops. Contrast: **south-east TN** drought-prone, weak irrigation — the farmer-suicide belt from Lecture 2.

sections.heading: 3.4 North-East: rain without irrigation
sections.content: **Assam ~220 cm/year** vs **Punjab <75 cm** — yet Assam has **agricultural drought** news and **Punjab almost never does**. Punjab has canals + free/subsidised power to pump groundwater even if the meteorological monsoon fails. **Cherrapunji ~1,100 cm/year** — **NCERT still calls it drought-prone**: water **rushes down the slope**; little is stored. **Why canals were not built:** terrain. - **Arunachal Pradesh** hills named after tribes: **Dafla, Miri, Abor, Mishmi**. Himalaya from **Nanga Parbat (Kashmir)** to **Namcha Barwa (Arunachal)**; three parallel ranges (**Himadri / Himachal / Shiwalik**) continue — only the *names* change with the dominant tribe. - Hills bordering **Myanmar**, collectively **Purvanchal Hills**: **Patkai Bum, Naga, Manipur, Mizo / Lushai**, plus **Barail**. **Prelims trap:** **Dafla–Miri–Abor–Mishmi ≠ Purvanchal.** Those four are **Arunachal Himalaya** labels. **Purvanchal** = Patkai–Naga–Manipur–Mizo/Lushai (+ Barail), the Myanmar-border arc. - **Meghalaya**: **Garo, Khasi, Jaintia** — **flat-topped plateaus**, *not* Himalaya; class: part of the **peninsular plateau** family (with Deccan, Chota Nagpur). - **Brahmaputra** occupies a **narrow valley** between Himalaya (north) and the Meghalaya plateau (south). Hill water dumps into the river → **April–September floods** are perennial in Assam.

sections.heading: 3.5 Maharashtra: 18% irrigated, rain shadow, suicides
sections.content:
**Western Ghats** from southern **Gujarat** to **Kerala**. **South-West monsoon** hits the Ghats:

- **Windward** (Goa, Mumbai): air **rises → expands → cools → condenses** → heavy orographic rain.
- **Leeward / rain-shadow**: air **descends → compresses → warms** → higher moisture-holding capacity → **less rain**. **Vidarbha** (cotton) and **Marathwada** (sugarcane belt in class) sit here.

**MH ~18% irrigated** + rain-shadow + monsoon failure → crop failure. Same reason MH accounts for **~35–40% of India’s farmer suicides** (Lecture 2 NCRB map). MH also has the **largest number of large dams**, but they sit in **southern / western Maharashtra** — the dry interior is left out.

Class bicycle-pump analogy: compressing air **heats** it without an external flame; the reverse (rising air) **cools** it — that is orographic rainfall.

---

sections.heading: 4. Even Irrigated States Have a Water Problem (GEO-08-04)
sections.content: Class (and a **2024** mains-style prompt they flagged): major challenges of Indian irrigation.

sections.heading: 4.1 Low water-use efficiency
sections.content:
India uses **~80% of freshwater** in agriculture; **China ~60%**, with higher production — India **wastes** more. Canal irrigation is the worst: class **water-use efficiency as low as ~38%** (your sheet: **34%**). Water is lost at **storage, transport, and distribution**.

**Indira Gandhi Canal:** source **Harike Barrage** (where **Sutlej** meets **Beas**) → tail end **Barmer, Rajasthan**. Most Indian canals are **perennial** (water year-round), tied to a **dam / reservoir** (storage) or a **barrage** (diversion).

| Stage | Loss |
|:---|:---|
| Open reservoir | **Evaporation** |
| Long open canal | **Evaporation** again |
| **Unlined / kachcha** distribution channel | **Seepage** as well |
| **Lined / pakka canal** (concrete sides + bed) | Seepage cut; evaporation remains |

**Floating solar** on reservoirs: generates power **and** shades water → less evaporation; does not eat scarce land. **New** canal projects: class said they move toward **closed pipelines**, not open channels.

**Canal share of irrigated area:** early/mid-**1950s ~55–60%** → now **~25–26%** (sheet ~**20%**). **Groundwater / tubewells** are now the main system.

sections.heading: 4.2 Warabandi / Barabandi (rotational irrigation)
sections.content:
Head-reach farmers steal the canal; the **tail end** runs dry. State government therefore runs **Warabandi** (also **Barabandi**):

- **Bara / bari** = **turn**
- **Bandhi** = **bund / embankment**

Each farmer gets a **date**. On your turn you throw up a mud–sand–wood bund so the channel water is diverted into *your* field; the next farmer breaks it and builds his own. **Equitable in design.**

**Catch:** the state is **not legally bound** to release water in the main canal on that date. If the canal is dry, germinating seed dies and the farmer **cannot sue**. Canal irrigation = **dependency on someone else**. A **tubewell on your own field** = you water **at will**.

sections.heading: 4.3 Why tubewells won — and why that is unsustainable
sections.content:
Tubewells are **decentralised, convenient, cost-effective** because states give **highly subsidised or free farm power** (capital subsidy / construction support as well). Operational cost ≈ **zero**. Flooding a field is actually **faster with canal water**, but farmers still prefer the tubewell.

**Night-power trick:** daytime grid demand is high, so the farmer is told to irrigate **11 p.m.–5 a.m.** He switches the motor **on at 11, sleeps, off at 5** — the pump runs **all night**. Free power + a false sense of surplus → **over-extraction**.

**Punjab water table:** falling **70–110 cm/year** (~**1 metre a year**). Class: this is how an “easy” irrigation system makes agri **unsustainable**.

sections.heading: 4.4 Flood vs micro-irrigation
sections.content:
Most farmers still use **flood irrigation** — class: **obsolete and wasteful**. Government pushes **micro-irrigation (drip, sprinkler)**; **high cost** confines it to a **few regions**.

**Five challenges to recite (class wrap):** (i) still not monsoon-proof / not every farmer covered; (ii) **non-uniform** distribution; (iii) **low water-use efficiency** (80% freshwater, still behind China); (iv) **groundwater overuse** from cheap power; (v) **flood** technique, drip still expensive.

---

sections.heading: 5. Non-Mechanised: Small and Fragmented Farms (GEO-08-05)
sections.content:
Labour is **affordable and available** — that is *not* the main brake. The brake is **farm size**.

| Category | Holding |
|:---|:---|
| **Marginal** | **< 1 ha** |
| **Small** | **1–2 ha** (both ends included) |

**Agriculture Census** is meant to be **every 5 years**. Last release **2018**, carrying **2015–16** data. No newer full census yet.

| Year | Number of holdings | Average size |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **1970–71** | **~70 million** | **2.28 ha** |
| **2010–11** | **~138 million** | **~1.15–1.16 ha** |
| **2015–16** (Census 2018) | **~146 million** | **1.08 ha** |
| **2021–22** (provisional, process started) | — | **~0.92 ha** (class also said **~0.9**) |

**2015–16:** **86%** of farmers are **small or marginal** (holding **up to 2 ha**). **66%** are **marginal** alone.

**Why a tractor still does not pay:** small revenue → no purchasing power; even with a subsidy the machine **never recovers** its capital on 1–2 acres — bullocks are rational. **Fragmentation** (inheritance): 3 acres in **three parcels** means moving the machine between plots → high operating cost. Population + inheritance → **more farms, smaller farms**.

sections.heading: 5.1 India vs USA vs Japan vs China / Israel
sections.content:
**Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), last ~10 years:** largest arable land is **India or the USA**. Class now: **India ~154 million ha**, **USA ~151 million ha**. Population: India **~146 crore**, USA **<40 crore**. USA **>80% urban**; even rural Americans are mostly **not** on the farm. **USA average farm ~150 ha** vs India’s **~0.9 ha** — more than **150×**. Large farms → revenue → machines that actually get used.

**Japan:** tiny paddy plots (Hokkaido snowed under **4–6 months**). Still mechanised because **machines are designed for small fields**. India designs for **large-farmer purchasing power** (link to Lecture 2 feminisation). Uttarakhand **terrace**: you cannot put a tractor on a step — you need a **power tiller**. Class: **India–Japan agri** = copy *design to plot size*, not US scale.

**China:** bigger geographical area but west/north-west/south-west is **desert**; **NSA ~105 million ha** vs India’s **~142**. Population comparable (**India ~146 crore, China ~142–143 crore**). China still mechanises better. **Israel:** desert, high population pressure on agri land, still mechanised. Class reason: **collective farming worked** there; in India the state has pushed it since Independence and it **has not**.

Leave-the-class question: **should India emulate the USA?** US mechanisation is a **compulsion** (Civil War / slavery frame: South needed cheap cotton labour; today few rural workers, high living costs). India has cheap, available farm labour — mechanisation is **not** the same compulsion.

---

sections.heading: 6. Land Reforms (Brief — GEO-08-06)
sections.content:
Four legs (plus cooperatives). **SS Sir** will expand.

1. **Abolition of intermediaries**
2. **Tenancy reforms** — (i) **rent reduction**, (ii) **security of tenure**, (iii) **ownership rights** to tenants
3. **Land ceiling**
4. **Land consolidation**
5. **Development of agricultural cooperatives / collective farming** (became a *necessity* after the other four)

sections.heading: 6.1 Why zamindari existed
sections.content:
British wanted India as a **raw-material colony**, copying Britain’s **enclosures**: few capitalist farmers, the rest as urban industrial labour. Revenue collectors who already had men and horses were made **owners**. Class dated **zamindari / Permanent Settlement to 1790**. Revenue **fixed in perpetuity** (or for decades) so the zamindar would **invest** and behave as a capitalist farmer. In practice: **absentee landlords** — they did not till; they leased to cultivators, skimmed rent, paid the Raj. They were **intermediaries**.

Independence leadership (including **Nehru**) leaned socialist. **Directive Principles, Part IV** — class: this is the constitutional hook (Lecture 2 already had **Article 39(b)/(c)**).

sections.heading: 6.2 Tenancy: security → investment → yield
sections.content: A tenant who can be thrown out **will not put ₹1 lakh into the soil**. He **mines** fertility and leaves. **Security of tenure / ownership** is how you get investment and yield, not only how you stop exploitation. If a tenant has cultivated for a set period and paid the due, he should become **owner**.

sections.heading: 6.3 Ceiling vs abolition of intermediaries
sections.content:
**Late 1960s, Indira Gandhi:** eradicate poverty via a **socialistic pattern** — bank nationalisation, other nationalisations, words added to the **Preamble**. **Ceiling** = cap on land a **family of five** may hold. Class example: **20 ha** ceiling on that class of **irrigated** land; a **100 ha** holder loses **80 ha** to **landless agri workers**.

**Difference:** abolition of intermediaries — if a zamindar **proves he is the tiller**, he could **keep** even a huge holding. **Ceiling** does not care: **above the cap, land goes**, whether you cultivate or not.

sections.heading: 6.4 Consolidation = chakbandi
sections.content: **Chak** = plot, **bandhi** = tying together. Two farmers each own strips on **both** sides of a canal. Officer allots **one compact block to A, one to B** (same fertility, same distance from water). That is how you fight fragmentation.

sections.heading: 6.5 Why cooperatives after this
sections.content:
Abolition + ceiling **created an army of small/marginal farmers** with **no bargaining power**. A 100 ha landlord could not be squeezed by a middleman; **100 people with 1 ha each** can. Government: register under the **Societies Act**, pool, take the cooperative benefits. **China and Israel succeeded; India did not** — but the idea was not dropped.

---

sections.heading: 7. Collective Farming Today: Coop, SHG, FPC / FPO (GEO-08-07)
sections.content:
Three legal doors:

| Form | Who | Exam hook |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Agricultural cooperative** | Farmers as members | Ownership + **one member, one vote** (farm size does not buy extra votes) |
| **Self-Help Group (SHG)** | Often landless / same socio-economic peers | Bank will not lend to one landless tenant (no collateral, can abscond). **Six people cannot all run**; peer pressure = repayment |
| **Farmer Producer Company (FPC) / Farmer Producer Organisation (FPO)** | **≥10 farmers**, register under the **Companies Act** | **Hybrid:** coop *soul* + private-company *management* |

**Coop pluses:** sense of ownership (**Amul** — millions of 1–2 animal backyard dairy farmers, not one mega-herd). Profit → **dividends** + retained expansion (fodder plant, veterinary hospital). **Equality in voting.**

**Private-company plus:** **managerial / professional expertise**. Class school analogy: government schools have land, midday meals, better-paid teachers who cleared a competition — yet parents (including government teachers) still pick **private** schools for **professional management**.

**FPC / FPO:** owned by farmers; **one vote each**; cooperative-style subsidies; **professionally managed**. Amul’s success also credited to **Verghese Kurien**’s professional leadership.

Collective farming **raises produce size** → **bargaining power** (the 5 litres of surplus milk vs Amul moving the consumer price). It also lets a **machine be used on a large pooled field**.

---

sections.heading: 8. Custom Hiring Centres (GEO-08-08)
sections.content:
**Machine penetration (2020–21, class):** **~20 tractors per 1,000 ha** — too few if every farmer must *own* one. Ownership is the wrong test. **Paddy harvest** already **shares** machines: Punjab first, then the same combines move to **Haryana**.

**Custom Hiring Centre (CHC)** = a village / block / panchayat “shop” of **tractor, tiller, seeder, laser leveller, harvester**. Farmers **hire**. Can be set up by an **individual, an FPO, or a cooperative**. Rules vary by state.

**Class numbers (illustrative capital math, not a scheme gazette):** unemployed youth with **₹10 lakh** + bank loan **₹40 lakh**; **~25% capital subsidy** so he repays **₹30 lakh** not 40. **Gram Sabha** (all **18+** in the village) or a committee **caps the rent** — investor gets a return, farmer is not gouged.

**Stock:** **>40,000 CHCs** in India vs **>6 lakh villages**. They cluster in **developed agri belts** (**Haryana, western UP, Malwa plateau**). Missing in **tribal Jharkhand**, the **North-East**, remote tracts.

**Private “Uber for tractors”:** **Uber Tractor / Hello Tractor**; **Mahindra Tringo**; **EM3 Agri Services — Gold Farm** (Punjab) — this is the sheet box **“Bring Gold & Farm”**. Same as Ola/Uber in Delhi: the app **dies in Churachandpur, Manipur** if there is no nearby fleet. **Remote mechanisation still needs the state**, not only an app.

---

sections.heading: UPSC Cues
sections.content:
- **~60% holdings rainfed**; **GSA ≈ 1.5 × NSA (~142 million ha)** even though temperature allows 2–3 crops — irrigation is the missing season.
- Irrigation map: **PB >98 / HR ~94 / TG ~86 / UP ~84 / AP ~64**; **Assam 10 / Mizoram 14 / Sikkim ~16 / MH ~18**.
- **<75 cm** rain + irrigation = Punjab rice; **1,100 cm** Cherrapunji + runoff = drought. **Assam ~220 cm** still floods **April–September**.
- **Ken–Betwa:** Ken dam (**Daudhan**) → Betwa → Bundelkhand. **Purvanchal** = Patkai–Naga–Manipur–Mizo/Lushai (+ Barail). **Dafla–Miri–Abor–Mishmi** = Arunachal Himalaya names.
- Canal **WUE ~38%** (sheet 34%); agri takes **~80% freshwater** (China ~60%). Canal share **~55–60% (1950s) → ~25–26%**. **Warabandi** = turn + bund; **state not legally bound** to release water. Tubewell + free **night power** → Punjab WT **70–110 cm/year**.
- Census **2018 / 2015–16: 86% small+marginal, 66% marginal**; holdings **70 mn (2.28 ha) → 146 mn (1.08 ha)**; **2021–22 provisional ~0.92 ha**. USA **~150 ha**. India **largest arable (~154 mn ha)**.
- Land reforms: abolition / tenancy (rent, security, ownership) / ceiling / **chakbandi**. Ceiling ≠ abolition (tiller-zamindar could keep land). Detail → **SS Sir**.
- **FPC = coop ownership + private management**; **≥10** farmers, **Companies Act**. **CHC >40k vs >6 lakh villages**. **EM3 Gold Farm**, Tringo, Hello Tractor.

---

sections.content:
> **Date of Lecture:** 11 September 2026  
> **Date Added:** 2026-09-11  
> **Teacher:** **Rizwan Sir** (Geomorphology syllabus topic **IV**)  
> **Source:** Vajiram & Ravi — class notes (6 sheets dated **11/9/26**) + audio transcript

> **Parked:** classification of **endogenic** forces (folding / faulting / nappe) — next class; then volcanism and earthquakes. **Exogenic landforms** is on the portal (watch before that class).  
> **Do not:** Faraday / Maxwell / Lorentz for this paper — class said applied geography only.  
> **Yellow Book:** dynamo one-liner stays in `Yellow_Books/Concepts_of_Geography/03_Interior_of_the_Earth.md`. **This lecture is the exam default.**

---

sections.heading: 1. Density — three reasons it is not the same at two depths (GEO-12-01)
sections.content:
Sheet: average **5.5**, surface **2.7**, centre **13**. Density **increases with depth**, and the increase is **non-uniform**. If A sits higher than B, **A and B do not have the same density.** Three factors (class): | Factor | Why density can differ | |:---|:---| | **Composition** | Different material (SIAL vs SIMA vs NiFe) | | **State of matter** | Solid / semi-solid / liquid | | **Pressure** | Weight of overlying material compresses | These numbers already sat on A2 Model 2. Today’s lock is the **three-factor** trap, not a new 5.5.
---

sections.heading: 2. Temperature — increases, but not at one rate (GEO-12-01)
sections.content:
Temperature **increases with depth** and is **non-uniform**. Two governors: **radioactivity** (heat source) and **heat transfer**. Max class T ~**6,000°C** (both cores — already A3).

**Direct data** (mines / drilling — data collected):

| Rise | Depth |
|:---|:---|
| **1°C** | **30 m** |
| **5°C** | **150 m** |
| **30°C** | **1 km** |

If that **30°C / km** held for the whole radius **~6,400 km**, interior T would be ~**1.92 lakh °C**. Class: **impossible**. After a certain depth the rate **slows or becomes constant**, so the **max** stays around **6,000°C**.

- **Lower mantle:** increase is **very slow** — **absence of radioactivity** + **slow conduction** (silica is a poor conductor — A3 heat path).
- **Core:** temperature remains **uniform** (~6,000°C).
- **Pressure does not set temperature.** It sets **melting point** / how the material **responds** (why inner core is solid at the same T as liquid outer core). Interior = **closed system**.

---

sections.heading: 3. Geomagnetism and the magnetosphere (GEO-12-02)
sections.content:
**Geomagnetism** = the behaviour of Earth as a **giant magnet**, with poles and a magnetic field around it. **Magnetosphere** = the **envelope** of Earth’s magnetic field. It acts as a **protective shield**: it prevents **direct interaction** of **high-intensity solar and cosmic radiation** with the surface. Without it, that energy would hit the surface and raise temperature. Field of a bar magnet is **systematic / symmetrical** because the current in the coil is **continuous and consistent**. Earth’s field is **not**.
---

sections.heading: 4. Geodynamo — why Earth behaves as a magnet (GEO-12-02)
sections.content:
Class analogy: a **metallic bar** with **current** around it behaves as a magnet. **I ∝ B** (more current → stronger field). Reverse the current → reverse the polarity. **Inside Earth:** - **Inner core** = solid **metallic** basement (the “bar”). - **Outer core** = **liquid metallic** iron, **not at rest**. Rotation of the outer core over the inner core converts **heat → magnetic field**. That conversion is the **geodynamo** — a **self-sustaining engine**. Law of conservation of energy: heat is converted, not created. **Two reasons the outer core rotates:** | Driver | Role | |:---|:---| | **Thermal convection** (heat transfer; hot liquid iron jumping) | **Major**. If this stopped, the outer core would stop. | | **Rotation of the Earth** (Coriolis-type force on the liquid) | **Additional**, not primary. | **Trap:** “A non-rotating Earth would have no magnetism” is **incorrect**. Even if Earth stopped spinning, the outer core would still rotate from **thermal convection**. Earth continues as a magnet **as long as thermal convection and heat transfer go on in the outer core**. If current = 0 in the coil experiment, the bar **demagnetises**. Same logic: no heat transfer in the outer core → no dynamo. It is **movement of hot liquid iron**, not a flow of electrons. **Why not the asthenosphere?** There **is** convection in the asthenosphere. The basement under it is the **lower mantle** — **non-metallic** (SIMA / silica). Geomagnetism is an **endogenic** property caused by the **geodynamo effect of the core only**, not the whole interior.
---

sections.heading: 5. Irregular magnetosphere; poles, declination, inclination (GEO-12-03)
sections.content:
Outer core is **more than 2,000 km** thick. Thermal convection is **not the same speed / intensity everywhere**, so outer-core rotation is **inconsistent**. Therefore the magnetosphere is **irregular in shape and size**. **Height and extent** of the field **differ from one location to another**.

**Magnetic pole** = where the **intensity** of the field is **highest** (energy most concentrated). Geographic poles are a **geometrical** identity — they **do not shift** while Earth’s shape stays. Magnetic poles **can shift** when the place of maximum intensity moves.

| Line | What it is |
|:---|:---|
| **Geographic axis** | Imaginary line geographic N → geographic S. Perpendicular to the **geographic equator**. |
| **Magnetic axis** | Line joining the two magnetic poles. |
| **Magnetic declination (θ)** | Angle between **magnetic axis** and **geographic axis**. Present class value **11.5°**. Not fixed forever. |
| **Magnetic inclination** | Angle between **magnetic axis** and **geographic equator** = **90° − 11.5°**. |
| **Magnetic equator** | Line **perpendicular to the magnetic axis**. Angle between magnetic equator and geographic equator = **same θ (11.5°)**. |

**Present locations (class):**

- Geomagnetic pole of the **northern** hemisphere: **Ellesmere Island**, **northern Canada**.
- Geomagnetic pole of the **southern** hemisphere: **Southern Ocean** — **outside Antarctica**, **not** over the Antarctic continent.

sections.heading: Orientation trap (Prelims)
sections.content:
Energy **emerges** from the magnetic **north** of the dipole and returns to magnetic **south**. On **present** Earth the dipole is **flipped relative to geographic polarity**: - **Magnetic north of Earth is in the southern hemisphere.** - **Magnetic south of Earth is in the northern hemisphere.** So the field is oriented **geographic south → geographic north**. Reversals have happened; they are **not felt immediately**. For now, circulation is **S → N**.
**Equator vs poles (field height):** | Belt | Height of field | Strength | |:---|:---|:---| | Equatorial / tropical | **Greater height**; **not** attached to the surface; more **scattered** | **Weaker** | | Toward poles | Field **descends**; attached to the surface | **Maximum at the poles** | ---

sections.heading: 6. Atmosphere overlap → aurora (GEO-12-04)
sections.content:
Atmosphere = envelope of gases. Class mix: **nitrogen 78%**, **oxygen 21%**. Density **falls with height**. **~97%** of atmospheric gases sit in the **first 30 km** (class benchmark **30–40 km**). Source of oxygen is **photosynthesis**, so **highest O₂ is near the surface**. **Atmosphere and magnetosphere do not overlap at low latitudes** (field is high; gases hug the surface). They **overlap in the polar region** as the field descends. That overlap is the **essential condition** for aurora **as a pattern**. **Mechanism:** high-intensity solar energy (e.g. a **solar flare**) hits the magnetosphere → charges **absorb / deflect / divert** it (it does **not** go straight to the surface) → extra energy is **carried toward the poles** → at the overlap, energy is **dissipated** by lifting an electron off an atmospheric-gas atom and dropping it back → **light** = sparkling / lightning effect in the sky = **aurora**. | | North Pole | South Pole | |:---|:---|:---| | Name | **Aurora Borealis** | **Aurora Australis** | | Colour lock | **O₂ → green**; **N₂ → blue** | same gases | Green and blue **dominate** because N₂ and O₂ dominate. Colour **can differ with height** (composition and density change): closer to the surface → more **green** (more O₂); a few km up → more **bluish**; **40–60 km** may go **reddish / purple**. **Borealis is more common** because present field direction is **S → N**: added energy prefers **geographic north**. Australis needs energy **against** the field — rarer unless the hit is very strong. **Norway** / Scandinavia / northern Europe are the classic watch spots. **Not a seasonal solar event.** The Sun does not fire flares to match Earth’s seasons. **Visibility** rises in **winter** — **absence of insolation** at that pole. Watch **Norway in winter** (class: around Christmas). Southern watch would be **southern Argentina in June** — still less fruitful than Norway in December.
**Aurora vs lights (same mechanism, different scale):** | | **Aurora** | **Lights** (northern lights) | |:---|:---|:---| | Energy | Localised dump | **Continuous + large-scale** over the whole polar cap | | Who sees it | One place (Alaska **or** Greenland **or** Norway) | **All** polar locations at once (Alaska, Hudson Bay, Greenland, Norway, Siberia) | | Look | Curtain, **hours** | Green **circle** over the whole pole; can last **days** (class 5–7, even ~15 with wind) | | South | Australis less common | **Southern lights = rarest of rare** | ---

sections.heading: 7. Insolation, CME, storms (GEO-12-05)
sections.content:
Sun’s heat is from **thermonuclear** reaction; convection carries it to the **coronal layer**. Ordinary **insolation** from that layer is **not charged** (class also: mainly **protons**, weak). The magnetosphere is **transparent to insolation** — it is **not blocked**. **Solar hotspot** = a **heated patch** on the Sun’s surface where an enlarged convection has broken into the corona. Class treats **flare, wind, plasma** as **three types of Coronal Mass Ejection (CME)**. Online sources **merge** the terms — keep **class meanings**.
| Ejection | What the hotspot is doing | Typical Earth result | |:---|:---|:---| | **Solar flare** | Short **burst** from a hotspot | **Aurora** (sometimes lights if flares keep hitting) | | **Solar wind** | Hotspot **larger and hotter**; energy **continuous and intense** | **Lights** (can last a **week**); can **suppress** the field → **magnetic storm** | | **Plasma** | Whole convection **detached** and thrown off the Sun | **Highest-intensity magnetic storm**; random aurora | **Magnetic storm** = **suppression / distortion** of the magnetosphere by high-intensity solar radiation (class cyclone analogy: normal pattern is disturbed). Field is **brought down** toward the surface and may **fragment**. Energy then **cannot** ride the usual path to the poles. Dissipation happens **wherever** the crushed field meets the atmosphere → **random aurora at multiple latitudes**, including tropics. **Not permanent** — after the pulse passes, the **geodynamo reorganises** the field. Class also: more frequent CME → some extra heat is transferred, **especially to the polar / Arctic** side of the present field → glaciers melt → **sea-level** rise. Treat as the class **endogenic–exogenic link**, not an IPCC table. **Do not invent numbers.** ---

sections.heading: 8. Four features of geomagnetism (GEO-12-06)
sections.content: 1. **Magnetic field is inconsistent** — it fluctuates, because outer-core “current” is not steady. 2. **Average field intensity over geological time has declined.** Radioactivity (the “battery”) has **decayed**; Earth has **lost heat**; the magnet has **weakened** and will weaken further. 3. **Position of magnetic poles will shift** when the **orientation / tilt** of outer-core rotation changes. (Geographic poles do not.) 4. **Polar reversal** = **full reverse** of outer-core **direction** (clockwise ↔ opposite) → magnetic **N and S swap**. Last event **7–8 lakh years before present**. **Cyclic** (it keeps repeating) **but not periodic** (two reversals are **not** separated by equal time). Random outer-core behaviour. **Shift ≠ reversal.** A slight tilt moves the *place* of the pole. A complete reverse of rotation reverses **polarity**.

sections.heading: Update — 11 September 2026 (UPSC CSE Prelims 2018 / 2022)
sections.content:
`CSE-2018-Q57` **missed** (`MST-077`). **1 and 3.** Statement 1: the field has reversed every few hundred thousand years (class: last **7–8 lakh years**, cyclic ≠ periodic). Statement 3: when living organisms originated, they **modified** the early atmosphere (degassing first; photosynthesis oxygenated later — `02_Geomorphology`). Trap 2: Earth was **not** created with **54% oxygen and no CO₂**. He picked **1 only**.

`CSE-2022-Q40` **held**. A major solar storm **can** hit GPS / navigation, power grids, satellite orbits, polar shortwave radio, and produce intense aurora over much of the Earth (class: crushed field → random aurora, including tropics). **Tsunami** and **planet-wide forest fires** fail.

sections.heading: UPSC Quick Recall
sections.content:
1. Surface **2.7** / mean **5.5** / centre **13**. A ≠ B at two depths — **composition, state, pressure**.
2. Geothermal **1°C / 30 m** ≈ **30°C / km** is **only near-surface**. Cap ~**6,000°C**. Lower mantle slow; core **uniform**.
3. Magnetosphere = **shield** against **high-intensity solar and cosmic** radiation. **Transparent to insolation**.
4. Dynamo = **outer core rotating over solid inner core**. **Thermal convection is the major driver**; Earth rotation is extra. Asthenosphere **does not** make the field.
5. “Non-rotating Earth has no magnetism” = **false**.
6. Declination **11.5°**. N mag pole = **Ellesmere Island** (N Canada). S = **Southern Ocean**, **not** Antarctic land.
7. Present circulation **geographic south → north**. Magnetic **north** of the dipole sits in the **southern** hemisphere.
8. Aurora needs **overlap of field and atmosphere** → **poles as a pattern**. **Borealis more common**. Winter = **visibility**.
9. **O₂ green, N₂ blue.** Lights = **large-scale** aurora.
10. Class CME trio: **flare → aurora**; **wind → lights + storm**; **plasma → strongest storm**. Storm aurora can be **anywhere**.
11. Four features: **inconstant**; intensity **declined**; poles **shift**; reversal **cyclic not periodic**, last **7–8 lakh years ago**.

sections.content:

sections.heading: Topics Covered in Ancient India
sections.content:
1. **Stone Age** → Anthropology
2. **Indus Valley Civilization**
3. **Vedic Age** (1500 BC – 600 BC)
4. **Mahajanapada Age** (6th century BC to 4th century BC)
5. **Mauryan Age** (321 BC – 185 BC)
6. **Age of Commerce** (2nd century BC – 3rd century AD)
7. **Gupta Age** (240 AD – 550 AD)

---

sections.heading: Theories: Pre-history, Proto-history, History
sections.content:
| Category | Definition | Examples |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Pre-history** | That part of the past for which **no written records** are available | Palaeolithic Age, later Stone Age cultures |
| **Proto-history** | That part of the past for which **written records are available but could not be read** by us | Indus Valley Civilization (undeciphered script) |
| **History** | That part of the past for which **written records are available and could be read** by us | Vedic Age to present day |

---

sections.heading: Eras (Based on Fossil Evidence)
sections.content:
| Era | Dominated By | Approx. Period |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Palaeozoic Era** (Old Life) | Fish (water creatures) | ~500 crore yrs ago |
| **Mesozoic Era** (Middle Life) | Reptiles / Dinosaurs | ~25 crore yrs ago |
| **Cenozoic Era** (New Life) | Mammals (lion, elephant, whale, monkeys, humans) | ~6.6 crore yrs ago (66 million yrs ago) |

> **Key Transitions:** Single-cell organism (LUCA — Last Universal Common Ancestor) → Cambrian Explosion → Permian-Triassic (Gigantic) Extinction → Cretaceous-Paleogene (Big) Extinction → Mammals dominate → Primates → Homo sapiens (~2 lakh years ago)

sections.heading: Climatic Ages (Based on Rock/Sediment Evidence)
sections.content:
- Cambrian → Jurassic → Triassic → Pliocene → Oligocene → **Pleistocene** → **Holocene**
- 19th century classification: Primary (Fish) → Secondary (Dinosaurs) → Tertiary (Mammals) → **Quaternary (Humans)**

sections.heading: Pleistocene Epoch (25 lakh years ago → 10,000 BC)
sections.content:
- Earth entered **cycles of ice ages** (glaciation) and **warm periods** (inter-glaciation)
- Riss glaciation and Würm glaciation were the last two ice ages
- This epoch is characterized by the **cycle of ice ages**
- Human evolution and stone tool usage occurred during this epoch

sections.heading: Holocene Epoch (10,000 BC → Present)
sections.content:
- **Last ice age ended** → Earth entered a warming period
- "Hol" = Recent (Greek/Hindi); "Holocene" = Recent warming
- **Agriculture began** because of the warming of earth (warming came first → agriculture followed)
- Transition from **hunter-gatherer** to **food producer**

sections.heading: Anthropocene Epoch (Proposed)
sections.content:
Some scholars suggest that since the **19th century (Industrial Revolution)**, warming of earth is **unnatural** and climatic changes are **mainly due to human actions**.
- *Anthropo* = Human → "Human-dominated epoch"
- ⚠️ **Not universally accepted** — still a proposal, not in formal academics

> **Fascinating fact:** If Earth's entire history were compressed into one year:
> - Humans appeared on **31 December at 11:50 PM** (10 minutes of the year)
> - Agriculture appeared at **11:59:40 PM** (20 seconds of evolution!)

---

sections.heading: Palaeolithic Age (Stone Age → Anthropology)
sections.content:
> The **formation and use of stone tools** by humans marks the beginning of the Palaeolithic Age.

**Critical distinction:** Accidental use of stone ≠ Palaeolithic Age. **Conscious making** of uniform tools, keeping them for later use = true tool-making = Palaeolithic Age.

- If any animal achieves conscious tool-making, their Palaeolithic Age would start
- Humans are at least **25 lakh years ahead** of all other animals in this respect

sections.heading: Stratigraphy & Relative Dating
sections.content:
- If you dig up earth, **lower layers = older** (called **relative dating** or **stratigraphy**)
- Eras determined by **fossils/bones**; climatic ages determined by **rocks/sediments**

---

sections.heading: 1. Lower Palaeolithic Age (25 lakh years ago – 1.5 lakh years ago)
sections.content:
The **oldest stone tools** made by humans are found at the **lowest level** in archaeology; therefore it was named **Lower Palaeolithic Age**.

> This is the longest period: ~23.5 lakh years out of 25 lakh years total

sections.heading: Tool Tradition 1: Oldowan Tools
sections.content: - **First discovered in:** Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, Eastern Africa - These were **pebble tools** made by the process of **flaking** and used mainly for **chopping** - Therefore also called **chopper-chopping tools** - **Process:** Take a pebble (stone rounded by water action) → break into core + flake → discard flake → use core edges for chopping - **Chopping** = cutting by force (like a helicopter/chopper cuts air) - Used primarily for: breaking animal bones (for marrow), cutting skin - ~99% diet was vegetarian, only ~1% non-veg - **Human species associated:** **Homo Habilis** (first tool user)

sections.heading: In India — Oldowan/Soanian Tools
sections.content:
- Earliest Oldowan tools discovered on the **banks of Soan River** (tributary of Sutlej), **Potwar Plateau, West Punjab, Pakistan**
- Therefore called **Soanian Tools**
- Soan River tools dated to ~20 lakh years ago (Rawat, Pakistan)
- ⚠️ **No Homo Habilis fossil is found in India**

sections.heading: Tool Tradition 2: Acheulean Tools
sections.content: - The **second major tool tradition** of Lower Palaeolithic Age - Named after **Saint-Acheul, France** (first discovery site) - These tools were **triangular hand axes** used for various purposes like chopping, hammering, scraping, boring, etc. - Major improvement over Oldowan — hammer/axe-like action reduces jerk to head - **Human species associated:** **Homo Erectus** (first to walk straight)

sections.heading: Acheulean Tools in India
sections.content:
- **Majority of Lower Palaeolithic sites in India have Acheulean tools**
- Also called **Madrasian Industry** (after sites near Madras/Chennai)
- **Key Indian Sites:**
  - Didwana, Singi Talav (Rajasthan)
  - Belan Valley (Allahabad, UP)
  - Paisra, Munger (Bihar)
  - Bhimbetka (Raisen, MP)
  - Adamgarh (Narmadapuram/Hoshangabad, MP)
  - Sabarmati Valley (Ahmedabad, Gujarat)
  - Hunsgi (Karnataka)
  - **Attirampakkam, Pallavaram** (Tamil Nadu) — very famous
  - Kuliana (Odisha)

sections.heading: Oldest Human Fossil in India
sections.content:
- **Skull of Homo Erectus**, belonging to **6 lakh years ago**
- Discovered in **1982** at **Hathnora** (Sehore, MP), in **Narmada Valley**
- Named **Narmada Man** or **Narmada Human**
- Discovered by **Arun Sonakia**

> **Why so few fossils in India?** Indian soil is generally **acidic** → bones decompose. Also, frequent river movements expose and scatter remains. Animals may have taken bones. Tools found in great numbers, but fossils are scarce.

---

sections.heading: 2. Middle Palaeolithic Age (1.5 lakh years ago – 45,000 years ago)
sections.content: The **strata (depositional layer)** found above the deposits of Lower Palaeolithic Age is identified as **Middle Palaeolithic Age**.

sections.heading: Tool Tradition: Mousterian Tools
sections.content: - Named after **Le Moustier**, a site in France - Prepared by the process of **bifacial flaking** (**Levallois technique**) - Take a stone disc → hammer from both sides → entire tool has a sharp edge - Used mainly as **scrapers, points, triangles**, etc. - **Human species associated:** **Homo Neanderthalensis (Neanderthal man)**

sections.heading: Mousterian Tools in India
sections.content:
- First discovered in **Nevasa** (near Pune / Ahmednagar, Maharashtra)
- Therefore called **Nevasian Tools**
- ⚠️ **No Neanderthal fossil is discovered in India so far**

sections.heading: Neanderthals & Evidence of Religion
sections.content:
Sites of Neanderthal man are the **earliest to give evidence of religion**, including:
- **Respectful burial of dead**
- Burial in a **specific pattern** (e.g., feet southwards)
- **Grave goods** (objects kept with the dead body)
- **Food kept in non-habitational caves**

sections.heading: Emergence of Homo Sapiens
sections.content:
- **Homo Sapiens appeared either at the end of Lower Palaeolithic Age or in Middle Palaeolithic Age**
- *Sapien* comes from the Sanskrit word *Sapna* (dream/think) — "the one who thinks/dreams"
- Homo Sapiens are the species that create art, imagination, novels, paintings
- Only Homo Sapiens are **superstitious** and **religious** — sign of intelligence (obsessive pattern tracking)

---

sections.heading: Key Characteristics
sections.content:
- **All other human species went extinct**; only **Homo Sapiens survived**
- This age **coincided with the last phase of Pleistocene Epoch** (last ice age)

sections.heading: Tool Tradition: Parallel Blades & Bone Tools
sections.content:
- Major tools: **Parallel blades** — sophisticated, fragile, indicates better hand control
- For the **first time**, **substantial bone tools** were used
  - Scoops, sharp hunting knives (double-edged), kitchen knives (single-edged with blunt side)
  - Crisscross grip patterns — consciously designed
  - Example: **Kurnool Caves, Andhra Pradesh**

sections.heading: Art & Cave Paintings
sections.content:
- For the **first time**, **art forms were made by humans** — especially **carvings and paintings on cave walls**
- **Key Sites:**
  - **Bhimbetka** — Raisen, MP (local legend: Bheem used to sit here → Bheem-Bethak → Bhimbetka)
  - **Adamgarh** — Narmadapuram (Hoshangabad), MP
  - **Lakhudiyar** — Almora, Uttarakhand

---

sections.heading: Mesolithic Age (Middle Stone Age) — 10,000 BC to 8,000 BC
sections.content:
The **end of Pleistocene Epoch** (last ice age) and the **beginning of Holocene Epoch** (warming of earth) marks the beginning of the **transition of humans from hunter-gatherers towards food producers**. This **transitionary phase** is called the **Middle Stone Age** or **Mesolithic Age**.

> Mesolithic = Epi-Palaeolithic (peak of Palaeolithic) + Proto-Neolithic (earliest Neolithic)

sections.heading: Targeted Hunting of Smaller Animals
sections.content:
- In the beginning, humans started **targeted hunting-gathering of relatively smaller animals**
- Ice age mammals (mammoths) had gone extinct; ice sheets melted; river streams appeared
- Earlier mammoth-hunting strategies (chasing, pit traps, cliff drives) didn't work for small, fast animals
- **Solution:** Compound tools with stone tips on sticks → **microliths**

sections.heading: Tool Tradition: Microliths
sections.content:
- **Microliths** are **small stone tools** (1–4 cm) used mainly as part of **compound/composite tools**
- Tied to tops of sticks as arrowheads, spear tips
- Some had **back-to-back** binding — when removed, creates a bigger wound
- Shape of arrowheads same even today — only material has changed

sections.heading: Domestication & Surplus
sections.content:
- **Domestication of plants and animals began** in Mesolithic Age
  - ⚠️ Agriculture & livestock are **features of Neolithic Age**, but domestication **began** here
- **Surplus appeared for the first time** (although **irregular and unreliable**)
- **Pottery appeared** in some Mesolithic cultures
  - ⚠️ Pottery **appeared** in Mesolithic (exception) | Pottery is a **feature** of Neolithic (rule)

> **Terminology:** Microlith = small stone tool | Macrolith = large stone tool | **Megalith** = large stones kept on graves (e.g., Taj Mahal, Humayun's Tomb, Sanchi Stupa, Rajghat)

sections.heading: Key Indian Sites
sections.content:
- **Belan Valley** (Allahabad, UP) — Lekhania, Morana Pahad
- **Sarai Nahar Rai** (Pratapgarh, UP)
- **Lahuradev** (UP)

---

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: The practice of **agriculture and livestock as main activity** marks the beginning of Neolithic Age.

sections.heading: Settled Life & Villages
sections.content:
- Due to agriculture, humans started living **sedentary life (settled life)** in **villages** (houses built near agricultural fields)
- Although hunting-gathering continued, it became a **secondary activity**

sections.heading: Tool Tradition: Celts
sections.content:
- Main tools were **Celts** (C-E-L-T-S)
- Celts were **polished, finished, symmetric, and precision tools**
  - Axes, chisels (asymmetric — to produce fire), grinding stones (*silbatta*)
- **Microliths further evolved** and became **symmetric**
- These are the works of **specialized tool-makers** (part-time hunter-gatherers or full-time craftsmen)

sections.heading: Neolithic Revolution
sections.content:
- Due to **agricultural surplus and settled life**, population **greatly expanded**
- Due to large surplus, a **substantial part of population was now free from the obligation of food production**
- They took up **other professions**: tool-making, pottery, cloth making, masonry, etc.
- This led to **division of labour, specialization**, etc., greatly **improving the efficiency of society**
- Due to these **sudden and fundamental changes**, humans became the **prime species** who now **control all other species of plants and animals**
- Therefore it is now known as the **Neolithic Revolution**

> **Evolution vs Revolution:** If change is fundamental but slow = **Evolution**. If change is fundamental and sudden = **Revolution**. Neolithic Revolution = sudden & fundamental.

---

sections.heading: Human Speciation Summary
sections.content:
| Species | Key Feature | Associated Tools |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Australopithecus** | First to practice **bipedalism** (walk on two feet) | — |
| **Homo Habilis** | First **tool user** | Oldowan (chopper-chopping) tools |
| **Homo Erectus** | First to **walk straight** | Acheulean (triangular hand axes) |
| **Homo Neanderthalensis** | Mainly in Europe; earliest **evidence of religion** | Mousterian (Levallois technique) |
| **Homo Sapiens** | First to **think/dream**; art, imagination, religion | Parallel blades, bone tools, microliths, celts |

> **Key clarification:** Monkeys are NOT our ancestors — monkeys are our **cousins**. We and monkeys share a **common ancestor**. Homo Erectus is a true ancestor. Neanderthals (Europe) and Denisovans (Asia) interbred with Homo Sapiens.

---

sections.heading: Comparison Table — Stone Age Periods
sections.content:
| Feature | Lower Palaeolithic | Middle Palaeolithic | Upper Palaeolithic | Mesolithic | Neolithic |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Period** | 25 lakh yrs ago – 1.5 lakh yrs ago | 1.5 lakh yrs ago – 45,000 yrs ago | 45,000 yrs ago – 10,000 BC | 10,000 BC – 8,000 BC | 8th mill BC – 4th mill BC |
| **Epoch** | Pleistocene | Pleistocene | Pleistocene (last phase) | Pleistocene → Holocene | Holocene |
| **Tools** | Oldowan tools → Acheulean tools | Mousterian tools | Parallel blades, bone tools | Microliths | Celts (polished, symmetric) |
| **Technique** | Flaking (unifacial) | Bifacial flaking (Levallois) | Parallel pressure | Composite/compound | Polishing, finishing |
| **Lifestyle** | Hunter-gatherer | Hunter-gatherer | Hunter-gatherer; cave art | Transitionary (HG → food producer) | Agriculture, livestock, settled |
| **Human Species** | Homo Habilis → Homo Erectus | Neanderthal | Homo Sapiens (all others extinct) | Homo Sapiens | Homo Sapiens |
| **Indian Name** | Soanian (Oldowan) / Madrasian (Acheulean) | Nevasian | — | — | — |
| **Key Sites (India)** | Soan River, Hathnora, Attirampakkam, Bhimbetka | Nevasa (Pune) | Kurnool caves, Bhimbetka, Adamgarh, Lakhudiyar | Belan Valley, Sarai Nahar Rai | *(Chalcolithic next)* |



---

sections.heading: Uncanny Valley Theory
sections.content:
- Explains why we fear **human ghosts** but not animal ghosts
- During evolution, different human species (Homo Erectus, Neanderthals) **killed each other**
- Faces that are **~95% human** (almost-but-not-quite) trigger fear
- This evolutionary memory persists as our fear of "uncanny" faces

sections.heading: Selfish Gene & Survival
sections.content:
- Selfish mothers' children survived → selfish gene passed on
- Egoistic humans survived → ego is evolutionary
- Non-egoistic humans could not survive in hunter-gatherer age
- **All our weaknesses come from evolution**

sections.heading: Why Monkeys Didn't Evolve Further
sections.content:
- We did NOT evolve from modern monkeys
- Modern monkeys and humans **evolved from a common ancestor**
- "Monkeys are our cousins, not our grandparents"

---

sections.heading: 1. Chalcolithic Age (HIS-IVC-01)
sections.content:
**Dates (class):** **4th millennium BC → 2nd millennium BC.**

**When it starts:** **substantial** use of copper tools — **not** the first copper object. Metal appears in the **Neolithic** already. Class analogy: we are not in an “AI age” because a computer was invented; an age starts when the thing is **in substantial use**.

By the **mid-4th millennium BC**, various **Neolithic** villages / cultures started using substantial copper tools and **transitioned** to the Chalcolithic Age.

In this age they **greatly improved agriculture** to produce **enough surplus** to support **high-volume long-distance trade**. That grew **market centres** and centres of **industrial production**.

**Industry** here is **secondary production** — cloth, pots, *chattai* — **not** modern factories. Class: when the British came they ended India’s **rural industries**.

This is the **beginning of urbanization**, where the **earliest cities** appeared. Class example: **Indus Valley Civilization (IVC)**.

sections.heading: Bronze Age is not a separate age
sections.content:
**Worldwide**, the **developed phase** of the Chalcolithic Age is called the **Bronze Age**. It is **not** a separate age.

**Bronze** = alloy of **copper + tin**.

**India lock:** availability of **tin was limited**. Main source = mines of the **Afghanistan** region. Therefore a **true Bronze Age never appeared in India**. In the Indian Chalcolithic, **bronze tools and artifacts existed but were limited**.

**Stone tools continued** (class: they continue even today — *silbatta*).

| Age | Tools | Other |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Chalcolithic** (4th mill. BC – 2nd mill. BC) | **Copper** tools + **stone** tools | Trade and industry substantial; **urbanization** in **some** places (IVC) |

sections.heading: Iron Age (parked)
sections.content:
Iron Age **starts somewhere in the 2nd millennium BC**. Class: **do not** take a deep interest yet — features come with **Later Vedic**. Some anthropologists end it with the **Mauryas**; that is not your job here.

**Chalcolithic does not end** when this chapter heading ends. **IVC** and **Rig Vedic** still sit inside it.

---

sections.heading: 2. Board timeline (HIS-IVC-02)
sections.content: | Span | What | Metal age | |:---|:---|:---| | **2600–1900 BC** | **IVC** (Mature Harappan) | Chalcolithic | | **1900–1500 BC** | **Dark period** | opaque — **do not fill** | | **1500–1000 BC** | **Rig Vedic** | still Chalcolithic | | **1000–600 BC** | **Later Vedic** | **Iron Age** starts | **Dark period ≠ Dark Age.** Class word: **opaque**. Historians have not solved where Harappans “went” and where Aryans “appeared” (IVC: no horse / no warfare vs Aryans: horse / warfare — class contrast, not a theory to memorise today). **Do not cross the gap with fictional stories.** Class lock that **does** sit here: **people did not die; urbanization declined.** Traditions continued (houses around a **central courtyard**; **swastika**; **sindoor**; **dhoti**; **yoga** poses). Imagine a 50-year lockdown: Delhi-the-city declines; people survive in neighbouring villages with Delhi’s culture. ---

sections.heading: 4. Four names (HIS-IVC-03)
sections.content:
**Harappa is a city / site. IVC is the civilization.** They are not two different cultures.

| Name | Why | Class status |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Harappan Civilization** | First discovered site = **Harappa**, on the **Ravi**, Sahiwal district, **West Punjab, Pakistan**. Discovered by **Daya Ram Sahni**, **1920/21**. A new site is compared with **Harappa’s features**. | **Most scientific / technical** name. Archaeology names a culture from the **first** discovered site (Oldowan ← Olduvai). |
| **Indus Valley Civilization** | Majority of **early** sites were found on the **Indus river system**. | **Most used** name. Sir uses this in class. |
| **Sindhu–Saraswati Civilization** | Majority of sites prospered on the **Indus** and **Ghaggar–Hakra**. Indus = **Sindhu**. **Ghaggar–Hakra** is identified as **Saraswati**. | **UPSC uses “Saraswati.”** Debate of which river = Vedic chapter. |
| **Meluha** | **Mesopotamian** records (Iraq), **3rd millennium BC**: traders of Meluha came from the **east** with **cotton textiles and beads**. Description matches IVC traders. | **Could have been** their contemporary name. **Guess — no guarantee.** |

**Ghaggar–Hakra (class, not a Vedic essay):** two monsoon streams (north Rajasthan / Ghaggar, Sindh / Hakra) look separate because the middle is dry. Satellite: **one palaeo-channel**. Old channels of **Sutlej** and **Yamuna** once fed it → an enormous river. **Tectonic uplift / flood** created a watershed: Sutlej now joins the **Indus**, Yamuna the **Ganga**, Ghaggar–Hakra **declined**. Cultural memory at Allahabad / Prayag: Yamuna “brings Saraswati’s water” = **river capture**. For Prelims, **Saraswati** is the word UPSC used.

Sites now run **Iran → Uttar Pradesh (UP)** and **Afghanistan → Maharashtra**. So “Indus Valley” is geographically thin; **Harappan** is the feature-name.

---

sections.heading: 5. Geography — map secondary, features primary (HIS-IVC-04)
sections.content:
**Prelims lock:** a site on the Indus that is **contemporary** but **lacks Harappan features** is **not** Harappan. A site **far away** with the **core features** **is**. **Map is secondary; features are primary.** Map **changes** when a qualifying site is found.

Core features class listed (citadel, boundary wall, beads, seals, mother goddess, Harappan script, grid planning, sewage, covered drains). Sites are **not replicas** of each other; the **core** is the same.

sections.heading: Cardinal sites (class)
sections.content:
| | Site | Where (class) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **West** | **Sutkagendor** | **Balochistan–Iran** border; still in **Pakistan** |
| **North** (older textbook) | **Manda** | **Jammu**, Jammu and Kashmir |
| **East** | **Alamgirpur** | **Meerut** district, **western UP**, **between Yamuna and Ganga** |
| **South** | **Daimabad** | **Ahmednagar** district, **Maharashtra** |

**Ganga lock:** **no** Harappan site **on the Ganga banks** or **east of the Ganga**. Alamgirpur is **west of Ganga**, after crossing the **Yamuna**.

**Northernmost now:** **Shortughai** (northern **Afghanistan**) — **trading outpost** built by IVC traders. It has the **features**, so the map moved; **Manda is no longer northernmost**. The surrounding region has a **different** culture (**BMAC**); Shortughai is Harappan **because of features**.

sections.heading: Two surviving ports
sections.content:
A naval-trade civilization would have had **hundreds** of ports; most were wiped. **Two** remain because **tectonic uplift** lifted them — **today they are not on the coast**. 1. **Sukta Koh** (*koh* = mountain) near **Sutkagendor** / **Gwadar** (class: China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) place-name only). 2. **Lothal** — mouth of the **Sabarmati**, **Ahmedabad** district, **Gujarat**. **Artificial dockyard** (basin filled through one gate so waves do not smash boats while loading). Class: some say “swimming pool”; a pool on the coast is a weak story — the find has dockyard features.

Figure: Class geography board — cardinal sites, rivers, Lothal dockyard inset. Features decide the map, not the other way round.

Q&A extras (class): geographically **both** India and Pakistan; class order-of-magnitude **~500–600 sites each**. Harappan **baked brick** ratio **4 : 2 : 1** (why a “same as Egypt” brick PYQ fails — Egypt used **stone**). Intermediate Meluha trading stations → **trade map later**. Names thrown in passing (features later — **do not** treat as today’s list to mug): Mohenjo-daro, Amri, Kot Diji, Rehman Dheri, Ropar, Bhagwanpura, Banawali, Rakhigarhi, Kalibangan, Dholavira, Surkotada, Rangpur, Padri, Prabhas, Malwan. ---

sections.heading: Mesopotamian origin — **archaeology does not support**
sections.content: Some scholars (class: **do not write names**; spoken: Mackay / Wheeler) said IVC **urbanization** was **migration of Mesopotamian people** into the Indus region. **Mesopotamian elite** lived in the **cities**; **indigenous commoners** lived in neighbouring **villages**. “Proof”: **citadel + fortification wall** (Mesopotamia urbanised earlier).

sections.heading: Indigenous origin — **archaeology supports**
sections.content:
**Majority** of scholars: the developments needed for urbanization happened **where the cities are found** (Indus region) **for over 1,000 years**. That early layer is **proto-urbanization** (early / undeveloped urban features). It became the **basis** of Mature Harappan cities.

Harappan **city** (green) matches the **layer below it** (red) **more** than it matches Mesopotamian cities. Borrowing a citadel idea ≠ becoming Mesopotamian — class: Netflix / Apple in the house does not make you American.

**Lock:** urbanization of IVC was **gradual, successive, and indigenous**.

**Proto-** = early / undeveloped (proto-nationalism after 1857; proto-human before *Homo sapiens*). A highway *kasba* with a few pukka shops linking villages = proto-urban, not a city.

---

sections.heading: 7. Timeline of phases (HIS-IVC-06)
sections.content:
| Phase | Also called | Dates | Age |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **1. Food-producing** | **Mehrgarh** phase | **8th mill. BC → 4th mill. BC** | **Neolithic** |
| **2. Early Harappan** | Pre-Harappan / **regional cultures** / proto-urban | **3300–2600 BC** | Chalcolithic |
| **3. Mature Harappan** | **Integration** / urban phase / **IVC** | **2600–1900 BC** | Chalcolithic |
| **4. Late Harappan** | Disintegration / **deurbanization** | **1900–1300 BC** | Chalcolithic |

sections.heading: Food-producing / Mehrgarh
sections.content:
From the **8th millennium BC**, many **Neolithic** villages appeared in **north-western India** and built an **agrarian base** (food production) to support a **large population**. For millennia the main change is **villages growing**.

**Mehrgarh** = **one of the earliest villages** developed in India. **Quetta, Balochistan**, **south of the Bolan Pass** (Suleiman Range). Class: Upinder Singh gives it **three pages** — remember the site.

sections.heading: Early Harappan / regional Chalcolithic cultures (3300–2600 BC)
sections.content:
By the **mid-4th millennium BC** these villages used **substantial copper** → Chalcolithic. Surplus supported **high-volume trade**. Villages of a region built **trade networks** and, besides goods, exchanged **features** (pottery, tools, irrigation, crops, clothing, houses) → **regional Chalcolithic cultures**. **Four main pre-Harappan regional cultures** (recognise on a map; class: no need to mug every village): | Culture | Region (class) | |:---|:---| | **Amri–Nal** | **Sindh** and **Gujarat** | | **Kot Diji** | Main **Indus** — northern Sindh and western Punjab (Multan belt) | | **Sothi–Siswal** | **Haryana**, north **Rajasthan**, south **Punjab** — between present **Sutlej** and older **Saraswati**. Class: **Ropar** northern end of this culture, **Kalibangan** southern | | **Damb Sadaat** | **Balochistan** |

Figure: Four pre-Harappan cultures on the class map. They merge at 2600 BC into one urban IVC. Ropar is the north of Sothi–Siswal; Kalibangan is the south.

**Proto-urban features already here:** straight roads, boundary wall, houses in a line, **baked bricks**, bead production, seal production. These become the **basis** of Mature urbanization → again: **gradual, successive, indigenous**.

sections.heading: Mature Harappan / IVC (2600–1900 BC)
sections.content:
By **2600 BC** the regional cultures produced enough surplus for **high-volume long-distance trade**, exchanged **best features**, and **merged** into one **large, integrated, uniform, urban** civilization — **IVC**. Class analogy: metro / more communication → Delhi–Gurugram–Noida feel like one culture.

**Next sitting (14 Sep):** town planning through trade — Lecture 2 below. Religion still parked.

---

Statement 3 (horse) is **not** accepted in the official key — class contrast “IVC no horse / Aryans horse” does **not** beat the key. He picked **all three**.

sections.heading: Lecture 2 — 14 September 2026
sections.content:
> **Date of Lecture:** 14 September 2026  
> **Date Added:** 2026-09-14  
> **Source:** Vajiram & Ravi (Vijender Singh) + audio transcript + 8 handwritten sheets (dated **14/9/26**)  
> **Paper:** **GS-I**. Class flagged **CSE 2025** Mains (town planning / architecture) — reproduce these keywords, not a pretty sentence.  
> **Continues:** Lecture 1 — 11 Sep (names, map, origin, phases). Cluster **HIS-IVC2**.  
> **Parked:** **religion**; decline / Late Harappan; artifacts as a separate art-forms sitting (beads sketched only as industry).

**How to read class shortcuts:** full form on first use. **GJ** = Gujarat; **HR** = Haryana; **RJ** = Rajasthan; **OCP** = Ochre Coloured Pottery. Glossary at the end.

Cities of the **Indus Valley Civilization (IVC)** had **some basic similar features**. They were **not exactly the same**. Class: “similar” ≠ replica (Indian films generally end happy — *Tere Naam* is the exception).

**Exceptions named today**

| Site | Where (class) | What is different |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Dholavira** | **Kachchh, Gujarat (GJ)** | City in **three** parts: **citadel, middle town, lower town** (usual picture is citadel + lower town). Height difference = **flood management**, not hierarchy. Main building material here = **stone**. |
| **Banawali** | **Fatehabad, Haryana (HR)** | **Radial** town planning (streets radiate from the citadel), not the usual grid. |

---

sections.heading: 8. Town planning (HIS-IVC2-01)
sections.content: Figure: Class city plan. Citadel is a raised platform of public architecture, not a palace or an army fort.

sections.heading: 8.1 Fortification wall
sections.content: Cities had a **fortification wall** around them. The wall **lacks defensive features** — no added batter / slope, no warrior’s post, no loopholes. **Not built for warfare.** Built for **protection against flood and wild animals** (also a **demarcation**). Inner and outer walls are about equally thick (**3–4 bricks**). Anyone from the city could stand on it — not an army fort (contrast Jaipur / Mehrangarh: palace-fort **above**, city **below**).

sections.heading: 8.2 Citadel and lower town
sections.content: Cities were divided into **two parts** — **citadel** and **lower town**. **Citadel** = a **raised platform**. It **lacks large rooms and halls** → **not a king’s palace**. It **lacks defensive features** → **not an army fort**. It had **public architecture**: granaries, water tanks, **meeting rooms**, **fire altars** (*havan kund*). Class: perhaps **administrative blocks** or **ceremonial buildings**, or **protection against extreme flood**. Equal seats in the meeting hall → **not** a king’s court. **Lower town** was divided into **two parts by the main road**. **Subsidiary streets** meet the main road at **90°** → a **grid** that cuts the city into **rectangular blocks**. Houses sit in those blocks and **open on subsidiary streets**. **Rarely** any house opens on the **main road**.

sections.heading: 8.3 Bricks and houses
sections.content:
**Main building material** of the city = **baked / burnt bricks**. Dimensions in the ratio **1 : 2 : 4**, **uniform in the entire IVC**. Mortar = **mud**. **Gujarat region:** main material = **stones** (Dholavira lock).

Houses were built around a **central courtyard**; **all rooms open into the courtyard**. **Rarely** any room has a door or window opening **outside**. The courtyard is **hidden** (not the European “open the gate into the yard”). Houses had their own **kitchen, bathroom and toilet**. Bathroom and toilet were **separate**.

**Two types of toilet**

1. **Flush toilets** — connected to the **sewage system**.  
2. **Pit toilets** — connected to **soak pits** (modern name: **septic tank**) via **terracotta ring wells** (*terra* = earth; *cotta* = burnt — a brick is terracotta). Rings stacked vertically so the waste goes **down**. First finders thought they were wells to draw water **up**.

Houses were generally **single storey**. **Double** and **triple** storey houses are also found. In cities on **large rivers** (**Harappa, Mohenjo-daro**) **about half** the houses had their **own wells**.

sections.heading: 8.4 Sewage
sections.content:
The **sewage system runs along the network of streets**. Drains were **covered** by **bricks or stone slabs**. **Manholes** for regular cleaning. The **main drain** takes waste out into a **river, the sea, or a cesspool**.

**Lothal:** **terracotta cylinders** were buried **horizontally** and joined to form the sewage line.

sections.heading: 8.5 Character of the city
sections.content:
Town planning was **utilitarian** (for **use**, not decoration), **egalitarian**, and **symmetric** (every part of the city equally developed — not Chanakyapuri vs a slum).

Harappan cities **lack a king / ruling class** — **absence of palaces**, **absence of warfare and armies**, **absence of forts**. Weapons **lack a midrib** (the central thickening that lets a blade survive a twist in bone) → they are **hunting and agricultural tools**, not war weapons. **Copper Hoard** culture weapons **have** a midrib — the contrast is the lock. Class colour: “priest-king” statue at Mohenjo-daro is now a **bearded nobleman**; the **priest-king theory is dead**.

**Even the smallest house** built on the **edge of the city** was connected to the network of **roads and drains**.

---

sections.heading: 9. Pottery — Harappan ware (HIS-IVC2-02)
sections.content:
Harappan pottery is now identified as **Harappan ware**. **Two main variants:**

1. **Red pottery** with **black paintings** of natural figures (plants, animals) **and geometric patterns**.  
2. **Grey pottery** with the **same** black paintings (plants, animals, geometric patterns).

**Humped bull** on pots: huge **hump**, huge **horns**, loose skin under the throat = the **desi** bull they wanted (exaggeration in art = a desired feature).

**Varied pottery** indicates a **complex and developed economic system** (different pots for different uses). **Perforated ware** — use still unclear (class guesses: washing vegetables / brewing). John Marshall once said Harappans were not artistic because towns look utilitarian; class: geometric patterns **are** aesthetics. Optional 2026 colour only — not a Prelims lock.

---

sections.heading: 10. Technology (HIS-IVC2-03)
sections.content:
1. **Developed metallurgy.** Five metals: **copper, tin, lead, gold, silver**, plus one alloy — **bronze**.  
2. **Uniform weights and measures.** Two variants:  
   - **Hexadecimal** weight system (**based on 16**). Class audio said *hexahedron*; the lock is **base-16**. Side lock: till **1957** India had this in **currency** (1 rupee = **16 anna** = **64 paise**); **1957** adopted the **decimal** rupee (1 = **100 paise**).  
   - **Decimal** weight system (**based on 10**).  
3. **Land transport:** **wheeled carts** pulled by **ox or buffalo** (terracotta cart models). **Water transport:** **boats powered by sail** (wind) — seals show two poles with cloth between.  
4. **Bead making** was a **prominent industry**; beads at a **majority of sites**. In **Chanhudaro** (**Sindh, Pakistan**) **more than half** the houses were in bead making — class: **city of bead makers**. Beads = a **major export**. (Artifacts sitting later; lipstick evidence at Chanhudaro is colour, not a drill.)  
5. **Dentistry:** various **teeth** with **uniform holes**, **semi-precious stones**, or **copper wires**. Similar **uniform holes on skulls** → **some efforts of surgery**. Do **not** write “brain surgery.”  
6. Town planning indicates knowledge of **geometry, trigonometry, arithmetic** (uniform bricks; drain **slopes**).

---

sections.heading: 11. Script (HIS-IVC2-04)
sections.content:
Class: UPSC is **unlikely** to ask a political “Dravidian vs Sanskrit” current-affairs stem. Cover the topic; do not pick a side.

So far **more than 400 letters** of Harappan script are known, written mainly on **seals**. Sentences are generally **6–10 letters**; the **longest** is **26 letters**. The most famous sentence is the **Dholavira signboard (10 letters)** — about **1-foot** signs fallen near the main gate. A signboard is a **city** feature (strangers need names). Script **could not be deciphered**. Theories (no scholar names except where class locked):

1. Written **right to left** — **crowding of letters on the left**.  
2. Written **left to right** — **seals are mirror images**.  
3. **Boustrophedon** (class / R.S. Sharma) — one line L→R, next R→L, like a snake; **based on frequency of letters**.  
4. Language and script = early **Dravidian**. Side lock: **Brahui** (Dravidian family) is **still spoken in Balochistan**.  
5. Language and script = early **Sanskrit** and **Brahmi** script.  
6. These characters are **not letters of any script**; they are **unreadable signs** (emoji-like). Class colour: Michael Witzel — 400 signs + short strings do not behave like a spoken script.

---

sections.heading: 12. Agriculture (HIS-IVC2-05)
sections.content:
IVC was **self-sufficient**; **majority of production was indigenous**. **Majority of granaries** sit in **inner / central cities**. It is certain that the **majority of the population** lived in **villages surrounding the cities** and farmed — but **archaeological evidence** for those villages is **not found / insufficient**.

**Single crop** a year; the **major season was the winter crop**. They also practised **multi-cropping** (more than one crop in the **same field**).

**Main crops:** wheat, barley, lentil (pulses), millet, peas, chickpea. **Rice was added in the Mature Harappan phase.** **Cotton** was the **main cash crop**.

**Main sowing tool:** **wooden ploughshare**. Models at **Banawali** and **Kalibangan** (**Hanumangarh, north Rajasthan**). At **Kalibangan** a **ploughed field** is discovered (early Harappan). **Main harvest tool:** **copper sickle** (not iron).

sections.heading: Four methods of irrigation (class map)
sections.content:
| Method | Where (class) | Main crop on that sketch | |:---|:---|:---| | **Bund irrigation** | **Balochistan** (small bunds on a slope; Sahara colour only) | **Millet** | | **Flood irrigation** | **Indus** belt (sow on the bank; wait for the flood) | **Wheat** | | **Canals** | **Haryana / Rajasthan** | **Barley** | | **Water tanks** | **Gujarat / Maharashtra** | **Rice** |
---

sections.heading: 13. Water management (HIS-IVC2-06)
sections.content:
IVC prospered in a **semi-arid** region with **monsoon dependence**, so they practised **rainwater harvesting**. At the **lowest level in a city**, **wells and tanks** stored **excess** water (class: store surplus, not only draw groundwater). **Most elaborate** rainwater harvesting = **Dholavira**. A **rampart** keeps river flood out of the city. **Reservoirs** sit inside. **Underground water channels** cut under the rampart to fill those reservoirs. Three-tier city (citadel / middle / lower) = **flood management**. Stone is the Gujarat building material. Small rooms here are read as a **market**, not houses. (G20 photo-op at the tanks is colour, not a fact to drill.)
---

sections.heading: 14. Trade (HIS-IVC2-07)
sections.content: **Majority of Harappan trade was internal** (among IVC cities). **No coin** of IVC is discovered → trade was **barter**.

sections.heading: Imports (class map)
sections.content:
| From | What (class) | |:---|:---| | **Oman** | Copper | | **Bahrain** | Pots and utensils | | **Mesopotamia / Persian Gulf** | Trade is certain (**Harappan seals**; **Failaka hoard**). What they *bought* there is not locked. | | **Iran** | **Turquoise** or **lapis lazuli** (sky blue / dark blue) | | **Afghanistan** | **Tin** and **lapis lazuli** | | **Central Asia** | **Tin** and semi-precious stones | | **Burzahom** (Srinagar) | **Wool** and **wood / timber** | | **Ganeshwar** (Sikar, Rajasthan) | **Copper** (UPSC has asked this) | | **Ahar** (Udaipur / Rajsamand, **Banas** → Chambal) | **Copper** — class: majority of their copper; **Aravalli** / **Khetri** colour | | **Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP)** culture | **Copper** | **Lapis lazuli is not found in India** — they **import the stone** and can **export it as beads**.
**Western-flowing rivers of India** served as **natural highways** of this (Persian Gulf) trade network. **Therefore a majority of cities appeared on the banks of those rivers.** **Less-dense forest** in the north-west played the **most important** role in **first urbanisation**; the trade network is the **secondary** reason (Ganga–Yamuna is richer land, but it opens **east**).

sections.heading: Exports
sections.content:
**Two major:** (1) **cotton textile** (2) **beads**. Also: copper tools and implements; pots and utensils; **faience** (glazed ware); jewellery (gold, silver, ivory, pearls, shells, stones); perfume and cosmetics (some perfume-making pots). **Semi-precious stones in the form of beads** (carnelian, chert, agate, jasper, lapis lazuli, turquoise).

---
