sections.heading: 6. Qutbuddin Aibak (1206–1210) (HIS-MED-08)
sections.content:
| Aspect | Detail |
|:---|:---|
| **Court historian** | **Hasan Nizami** — wrote **Taj-ul-Maasir** (*"crown of glorious deeds"*) |
| **Title** | **Lakh Baksh** — "giver of lakhs" (famed for charity) |
| **Qutub Minar** | **Began** its construction — and **dedicated it to a Sufi saint**, **Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki** (Chishti order) |
| **Mosques (2)** | **Adhai Din ka Jhopra** (Ajmer) and **Quwwat-ul-Islam** (Delhi) |
| **Death** | **1210, at Lahore**, while playing **chaugan** (polo) — fell from his horse |
| **Succession** | **Aram Shah** (1210) → killed by **Iltutmish** (1211) |

---

sections.heading: 7. Sultan Iltutmish (1211–1236) — The Real Founder of the Delhi Sultanate (HIS-MED-09)
sections.content:
> Ten points — this is the single most examinable list of the Slave Dynasty.

| # | What he did | Why it matters |
|:---:|:---|:---|
| **1** | Took **formal permission (investiture) to become SULTAN** from the **Abbasid Caliph Al-Mustansir** | He is no longer merely a *ghazi* or a governor — he is a **legally recognised Sultan**. Islam now enters India **legally** → India becomes **Dar-al-Islam** ("land of Islam", where Islamic law runs) → hence Iltutmish, not Aibak, is the **real founder of the Delhi Sultanate** |
| **2** | Issued the **Tanka** — the **silver coin** | Once you are Sultan, you issue coin. First Sultanate silver currency |
| **3** | **Completed the Qutub Minar** | Kept Aibak's **dedication to Bakhtiyar Kaki** unchanged |
| **4** | Created the post of **Chief Religious Minister** and appointed a **Sufi — Bahauddin Zakariya** (Suhrawardi) to it | A Sufi religious minister ⇒ the state now formally adheres to **Sharia** |
| **5** | Formally **extended Dar-al-Islam** | The legal-religious basis of the Sultanate |
| **6** | Created **two administrative posts**: **Wazir** (Prime Minister) and **Ariz-i-Mamalik** (Defence Minister) | The first ministries of the Sultanate |
| **7** | Created **two systems**: **(a) IQTA** — land assigned as **salary/revenue assignment**; **(b) an audit system — Naqib** | Iqta is the backbone of Sultanate finance (see section 14). Audit was built in from day one |
| **8** | Bought his own corps of slaves — the **CHAHALGANI** (*Turkan-i-Chihalgani*, "The Forty") | The **first military elite** of the Sultanate — and the force that will later make and unmake Sultans |
| **9** | Appointed **Razia as Sultan-in-absentia** whenever he left Delhi | Unprecedented — a woman formally on the throne of Delhi |
| **10** | Brought the **Gupta iron pillar from Udayagiri (Madhya Pradesh)** and installed it **in front of the Qutub Minar** | It still stands in the Qutub complex |

*   **Source for the whole reign:** **Minhaj-us-Siraj Juzjani** — **Tabaqat-i-Nasiri** (Persian). *Tabaqat* = biography; *Nasir* = Nasiruddin Mahmud, the ruler under whom he wrote.

sections.heading: 7.1 Reading Medieval Names, Titles and Book-Names — The Cue System (HIS-MED-10)
sections.content:
> UPSC medieval questions are overwhelmingly **book–author** questions. Even if you don't know the book, the *word pattern* gives the answer away.

| Cue in the word | What it tells you | Example |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **bin** | "son of" | **Muhammad bin Qasim** = Muhammad, son of Qasim |
| **binte** | "daughter of" | Azman **binte** Afzal |
| **al- / -i** (place) | "of that place" | **Al-Biruni** = the man from Beruni |
| **Tarikh** | history — **Sultanate** period | *Tarikh-i-Firozshahi* |
| **Tawarikh** | history — **Mughal** period | *Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh* |
| **Tuzuk** | **Turkic** (not Persian) | *Tuzuk-i-Baburi* |
| **-nama** | **Persian (Farsi)** | *Shahnama*, *Akbarnama* |
| Hard, difficult-to-pronounce words | usually **Arabic** | *Kashf-al-Mahjub* |
| Title **"Mian"** | conferred by **non-Mughals / Arabic-speaking patrons** | **Mian Tansen** — *UPSC has asked who gave Tansen the title "Mian"; the trick was that three options were Mughals* |
| Title **"Mirza"** | **Mughal** | Mirza Man Singh |

sections.heading: 7.2 Successors of Iltutmish — and Which Source Covers Whom (HIS-MED-11)
sections.content:
* **You are NOT required to memorise this list.** Only **four** names of the Slave Dynasty matter: **Aibak, Iltutmish, Razia, Balban**. The list is worth one look because it tells you **which historian is the source for which reign**.

Figure: One book (Minhaj's Tabaqat-i-Nasiri) is enough for the entire Ilbari family up to Nasiruddin Mahmud; from Ulugh Khan/Balban onwards the source shifts to Barani's Tarikh-i-Firozshahi.

* **Bahram Shah** created the post of **Naib** (Deputy Sultan) — and the **first Mongol invasion** falls in his reign. * **Nasiruddin Mahmud** was the **last member of the Ilbari family** to sit on the throne — but the **Slave Dynasty did not end**, because his **Naib, Ulugh Khan, killed him and became Sultan Balban**. * The 3-year-old **Kayumars** was beheaded one night by his own staff officer, **Jalaluddin Khalji**, who threw the head into the Yamuna and took the throne. ---

sections.heading: 8. Razia (1236–1240) (HIS-MED-12)
sections.content:
*   **First ruler of the Sultanate to issue a GOLD COIN — the *dinar***.
*   On her coins she called herself **"JALAL" (Jalalat-ud-din)** — *she never called herself Razia*. We know Jalal = Razia **only because of Minhaj-us-Siraj's book**.
*   **Wore male attire** and **sat openly on the throne**. *(Flagged in class as a UPSC 2026 question.)*
*   **First Islamic religious revolt in India — the Revolt of Nur Turk.** The orthodox **ulama** could not accept a woman on the throne; she crushed the revolt.
*   **Razia vs the Chahalgani** — she realised the real threat was not the orthodox clergy but her father's forty slaves, who had become too powerful:
    *   **Removed the Chahalgani** from important posts and gave those posts to **non-Chahalgani** men.
    *   **Bought her own set of slaves** — deliberately **NOT** from Central Asia or the Middle East (they would be kin to the Chahalgani), but from **Africa**.
    *   These African slaves appear in the sources under a chain of names: **Africans → Ethiopians → Abyssinians → Habshis → Siddis**. Their descendants are counted today as **Siddis** in the Census — found in **Gujarat, Bengal (mostly Muslim)** and **Karnataka (mostly Christian)**.
*   **The end:** The Chahalgani revolted under **Altunia**, who **imprisoned Razia**. Razia then played her best card — she **offered him marriage**; they married and became one team. Together they marched on Delhi, but the Chahalgani **intercepted and killed them both just short of Delhi, at Kaithal (Haryana), in 1240**. Her original mausoleum still stands beside the Kaithal highway.

---

sections.heading: 9. Ulugh Khan / Sultan Balban (1266–1287) (HIS-MED-13)
sections.content:
> Balban was **himself a Chahalgani** and the **Naib** of Nasiruddin Mahmud. Everything he did follows from that one fact: a Chahalgani who took the throne cannot afford another Chahalgani above or beside him.

| # | Measure | Explanation |
|:---:|:---|:---|
| **1** | **Abolished the post of Naib** (Deputy Sultan) | Only a Chahalgani could become Naib — so the post itself had to go |
| **2** | **POLICY OF BLOOD** | Killed the other Chahalgani and anyone who could be a probable threat to the throne |
| **3** | **POLICY OF IRON** | The **Mongols** were the standing external problem → he answered it by **consolidating** the Sultanate (creating the departments — see section 13) |
| **4** | **DIVINE THEORY OF KINGSHIP** | The first Sultan to claim divinity. Consequences below |

**Elements of the Divine Theory of Kingship:**

*   **Fixed a law of succession** for the first time — note that a fixed hereditary succession law is **not** an Islamic principle.
*   Called himself **ZIL-I-ALLAH** — *zil* = shadow (Persian), *i* = of, *Allah* = God → **"Shadow of God on Earth"**. Only **two** rulers in Indian history used this: **Balban** and **Akbar** (as *Zil-i-Ilahi*).
*   Introduced **court etiquette** for approaching a divine king: **SIJDA** (prostration, forehead to the ground) and **PAIBOS** (kissing the Sultan's feet).
*   Introduced the **Iranian New Year festival — NAVROZ**.
*   Claimed to be the **great-grandson of AFRASIYAB**, a mythical hero of Iranian legend.

*   **Source:** **Fatawa-i-Jahandari** by **Zia-ud-din Barani** — who therefore wrote **two** books: *Tarikh-i-Firozshahi* and *Fatawa-i-Jahandari*.

---

sections.heading: 10. The Four Pillars of the Sultanate (HIS-MED-14)
sections.content:
> Just as a democracy has four pillars, the Sultanate rests on four.

| # | Pillar | Root word | Who they were |
|:---:|:---|:---|:---|
| **1** | **SULTAN** | *sult* = **wielder of the sword** | The analytical point is not the etymology — it is that **anyone could become Sultan**, because **Islam had no caste hierarchy** |
| **2** | **ULAMA** | *alim* ← *ilm* = **knowledge** | The intellectual class that **interprets Sharia** — Maulana, Qazi, Sadr-us-Sudur |
| **3** | **UMARA** | *amir* | The **bureaucracy** |
| **4** | **KHUT** | — | The **local landed chiefs** — the **Indian** pillar. A tiny minority of outsiders could not rule India without them. Called **Thakur** in inscriptions; **Amir Khusrau later coined the word "ZAMINDAR"** for them |

**How Sanskrit inscriptions describe the newcomers** (pillars 1–3, who came from outside):

| Sanskrit term | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| **Mlechha** | outsider, impure |
| **Turushka** | Turk (also used for "slave") |
| **Pahlava** | Persian |

---

sections.heading: 11. What Changed with the Advent of Islamic Rule in India? (HIS-MED-15)
sections.content:
> A big Mains-type question. Answer in four heads: **economic, social, scientific-technological, political-administrative**.

| Head | Change |
|:---|:---|
| **1. Economic** | The invaders came from the **Arabian peninsula, Central Asia and the Middle East** → **overland trade routes opened** → trade grew → **urbanization**; new demand (dates, carpets, paper) created **workshops = KARKHANAS** |
| **2. Social** | **Conversion — welcomed by many**, especially **lower castes and untouchables**, because Islam had no caste hierarchy. It was **not forced**; it followed **occupational and economic logic** (which is why whole occupational groups converted together). Plus **language and cultural exchange** |
| **3. Science & Technology** | **(i) Manufacturing:** paper, carpets, soap (from the 12th century). **(ii) Metallurgy:** wrought iron + silver (to resist oxidation) → **WOOTZ steel**. **(iii) Building:** **mortar and lime** (*chuna*) enter India for the first time → makes the **true dome** possible. **(iv) Irrigation:** the **Persian wheel** |
| **4. Political & Administrative** | **Feudal → NON-FEUDAL, centralized state.** The **iqta is not a feudal grant** and the **iqtadar is not a bhogika**. Administratively, a full structure of **departments (diwans)** appears. **This single shift is why Early Medieval ends and Medieval begins with the Sultanate** |

> **Class aside — what a "masjid" actually is:** *Masjid* means a **congregation standing shoulder to shoulder in prayer** — Islam does not require a **building**; wherever people stand and pray together is a masjid. Related vocabulary from the same digression: Prophet Muhammad's migration from **Mecca** to **Yathrib** = *hijra* (start of the Islamic calendar); Yathrib became **Madinat-un-Nabi** → **Madina**; those who welcomed him = **Ansari** ("welcomers"); those who kept faith through everything = **Siddiq** (the first being Abu Bakr); *Rasool* = the one who brought a holy book, *Nabi* = prophet.

---

sections.heading: 12. Water Management across 1,500 Years — South vs North India (HIS-MED-16)
sections.content: > **Why the South is different:** the South's advantage is the coast; its **disadvantage is fresh water** (saline coast + old, hard crystalline rock = poor groundwater). Fresh water therefore becomes the **most precious resource** — and it is deliberately kept **out of the king's hands** (a corrupt or casteist Raja would ruin everyone). Instead it is controlled by the **temple** (tanks) and by **Brahmin assemblies** (canals) — which is exactly why **temples became economic centres / proto-banks and temple towns grew in the South first**.

sections.heading: 12.1 South India
sections.content:
| # | Structure | Who controlled it | Names in the sources |
|:---:|:---|:---|:---|
| **1** | **Water tanks** | the **temple** | **Eri, Keri, Tataka, Kulam** — a place-name ending in *-kulam* or *-eri* usually means a town that grew around a tank |
| **2** | **Canals** | **Brahmin villages** (*agraharam*) — a **committee**, never one man | **Kal, Vaykkal, Aruvaykkal** — e.g. in Thanjavur the agraharams control Brihadeshwara, which controls the **Grand Anicut** |
| **3** | **"Wells"** | — | **Kinaru / Kanvai** — but the South has no true wells: the hard old rock means these are really **catchment / percolation pits** holding still water |
| **4** | **PICOTAH** | — | The **lever-lift**, which came **from the Arabs** (who had the same desert water problem) through the South Indian trade contact |
| **5** | **Dams** | — | The defining part of a dam is its **sluice gate**: **horizontal flap → Tumpu / Madagu / Kalingu** (used on the sloping **Coromandel** side — Tamil Nadu, Andhra, Odisha, where pressure opens the flap); **vertical shutter → Kumizhi** (used on the **Malabar** side) |

> **Geography decides technology:** the slope of the Coromandel gives you enough pressure for a flap-type sluice; the Malabar does not, so it needs a shutter. The same lesson repeats across Indian water history.

sections.heading: 12.2 North India (HIS-MED-17)
sections.content:
| # | Structure | Detail |
|:---:|:---|:---|
| **1** | **Caste wells** | The North had **plenty of water — so it made water casteist**. Separate wells for Brahmins, Kayasthas and others |
| **2** | **Reservoirs — Tadaga** | For genuinely dry regions: Rajasthan, Gujarat, Rann of Kutch |
| **3** | **Dykes — Kulya** | Embankment channels |
| **4** | **Step-wells — Vav / Vapi / Baoli** | Reserved for **royalty and for gods** — e.g. **Rani ki Vav**, **Agrasen ki Baoli** |
| **5** | **Irrigational wells** | Developed in **three stages** — see below |

sections.heading: The Three Stages of the Irrigational Well
sections.content:
| Stage | Period | Name | Lifting power |
|:---:|:---:|:---|:---|
| **S1** | **7th–9th century** (Early Medieval) | **NORIA** | **Men** pull the water |
| **S2** | **9th–11th century** (just before the Turks) | **GHATI-YANTRA** | A **lever**, pulled by an **animal** |
| **S3** | **11th–13th century** (arrival → establishment of the Sultanate) | **Arhat / Rahat / Dhenkli**, best known as **ARAGHATTA** (the Persian wheel) | **Pulley + animal** |

*   In the **araghatta**, a horse or bullock is tied to a wheel and the leather bucket on the other side is called the **CHARAS** — made of leather by the **CHARANS**, an untouchable community of Rajasthan.
*   The same Charans held an important wartime job in the Sultanate: carrying water in leather bottles to quench the army's thirst.

> **The irony worth remembering:** the community whose hands Hindu society would not accept water from was the community that **made the buckets that lifted everybody's water**.

---

sections.heading: 13. The Central Departments — Diwans (HIS-MED-18)
sections.content:
> "Consolidation" is not a vague word. It means exactly this: **Balban created the departments**, and later Sultans only **added** to his list. *Diwan* = department.

| Created by | Post / Department | Portfolio (modern equivalent) | Goes to |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Iltutmish** | the post of **SULTAN** itself (+ Wazir, Ariz-i-Mamalik) | — | — |
| **Bahram Shah** | **NAIB** (Deputy Sultan) | — | *abolished by Balban* |
| **Balban** | **Diwan-i-Wizarat** | PMO / finance | **Umara** |
| **Balban** | **Diwan-i-Arz** | Defence | **Umara** |
| **Balban** | **Diwan-i-Insha** | Correspondence, *farman* (Information & Broadcasting) | **Umara** |
| **Balban** | **Diwan-i-Risalat** | Foreign affairs — i.e. **expansion of Dar-al-Islam** | **Ulama** |
| **Balban** | **Sadr-us-Sudur** *(no "diwan" prefix)* | Chief religious officer | **Ulama** |
| **Balban** | **Qazi-ul-Quzat** *(no "diwan" prefix)* | Chief Justice **+ Education** | **Ulama** |
| **Alauddin Khalji** (1296–1316) | **Diwan-i-Riyasat** *(under Wizarat)* | **Commerce** | — |
| **Alauddin Khalji** | **Diwan-i-Mustakhraj** *(under Wizarat)* | **Income tax / arrears** | — |
| **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** (1325–51) | **Diwan-i-Kohi** *(under Riyasat)* | **Agriculture** — gave **pre-harvest loans** called **SONDHAR** | — |
| **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** (1351–88) | **Diwan-i-Bandagan** | Department for **slaves** | — |
| **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** | **Diwan-i-Khairat** | **Charity** | — |
| **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** | **Diwan-i-Istihqaq** | **Pensions** | — |

> **Why three departments went to the Ulama:** to run **Risalat** (spreading Islam), **Sadr-us-Sudur** (religion) or **Qazi-ul-Quzat** (justice and education) you must know **Sharia, Quran and Islamic law** — so those three necessarily go to the **Ulama**, while the other three go to the **Umara**. Three each = **division of power with checks and balances**. *That* is what "consolidation" means.
>
> **These are ALL the departments the Sultanate ever created**, from Iltutmish to the Lodis. There is no other department to learn.

---

sections.heading: 14.1 Slave Dynasty (1192–1290): the land is one circle in three slices
sections.content:
Figure: Under the Slave Dynasty the Sultanate's land is a circle in three slices; Alauddin Khalji melts the three into one taxed core and rules everything beyond it as one giant tribute-paying district.

| Slice | What it is | Taxable? | Notes | |:---|:---|:---:|:---| | **KHALSA** | *khalis* (Arabic) = **pure** → **crown land**, the **personal property of the Sultan** | Not taxed — it **is** his income | The **WAZIR** collects it and gives it **directly to the Sultan** — it goes to the **imperial treasury**, not the state treasury | | **IQTA** | Land assigned as **salary / revenue assignment** to an **iqtadar** | Yes — **75% of the Sultanate's revenue** | **NON-FEUDAL**: an iqtadar is **not** a *bhogika* and an iqta is **not** a *bhog* (land grant). This is the political change from Early Medieval feudalism | | **MADAD** | Grants — three types below | See below | — | **The three kinds of Madad:** | Type | Meaning | Hereditary? | Taxable? | |:---|:---|:---:|:---:| | **MILK** | Land of the **original inhabitants** of India (Brahmin, Vaishya, Shudra — anyone). A Sultan can **never** take it from you, provided you pay tax on time. From this Arabic word come **maalik, malikana, milkiyat** | Yes | **Yes** | | **INAM** | A **gift** of unclaimed land by the Sultan | Yes | **Yes** (once you start using it) | | **WAQF** | **Religious endowment** — used for the upliftment of the poor within that land: housing, a Hajj office, a school, a hospital | Yes | **NO** | > **UPSC definition trap:** *Waqf* is an **endowment** — **not** a religious *grant*, **not** a religious *charity*, **not** an extension of land. In law its **owner is God**.

sections.heading: 14.2 Khalji period (1290–1320): Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316) — expansion
sections.content:
*   **Abolished the iqta.** Khalsa + Iqta + Madad are melted into **one single core area** — his **political core** — and everything in it is taxed:

| Tax | On what | Rate |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **KHARAJ** | Produce (land revenue) | **50%** |
| **GHARAI** | Houses | house tax |
| **CHARAI** | Goats, sheep, milch animals | grazing tax |

*   Because Madad is now part of the core, **WAQF also became taxable** — **Alauddin is the only Sultan of Delhi ever to tax the waqf** (including Hajj offices). *This is the single most examinable exception of the topic.*
*   **Outside the core:** he expanded from Delhi to **Madurai** (Malik Kafur **defeated** — deliberately not killed — **Jatavarman Pandya**), taking Gujarat, Andhra, Telangana; **not Kashmir, not Bengal**. Defeated rulers **kept their kingdoms and paid tribute**.
*   That whole tribute belt was treated as **one giant district (SIQQ)**, which was impossible to administer — so it was broken into **HAZARI** (packets of 1,000 units) → **SADI** (100 units) → each with a tribute collector, the **AMIR-I-SADAH**, sent by Alauddin. *(Hence place-names like Hazaribagh.)*
*   **Net effect:** a **centralized core** plus a **decentralized, quasi-feudal tributary periphery**.

sections.heading: 14.3 Evolution of the Landed System (HIS-MED-20)
sections.content:
| Ruler / dynasty | Crown land | Assignment | Grant | Waqf |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---:|
| **Iltutmish & Balban** | Khalsa | **Iqta** *(non-feudal)* ✔ | Madad | non-taxable |
| **Alauddin Khalji** | Khalsa (enlarged core) | *iqta abolished* | Siqq (tribute belt) | **TAXED** ⚠ |
| **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** | Khalsa only (kills rulers, takes the land) | — | — | non-taxed |
| **Firoz Shah Tughlaq & Sayyids** | Khalsa | **Bhog** — iqta became **hereditary**, i.e. it started behaving as **feudal** property | — | non-taxable |
| **Lodis** | **Khalisa** *(non-feudal)* | **Iqta** *(non-feudal)* ✔ | **Madad-i-Maash** | non-taxable |

> **The question UPSC can ask:** *when did the Sultanate have a proper iqta system?* Only twice — under the **Slave Dynasty** and under the **Lodis** (✔ above). In between, it was either abolished (Alauddin, MbT) or had degenerated into hereditary, feudal *bhog* (Firoz Shah, Sayyids).

---

sections.heading: 15. Provincial and Local Administration (HIS-MED-21)
sections.content:
Figure: The Sultanate's administrative ladder, Balban's parallel audit-and-spy arm on the left of the class sheet, and the Lodi-era renaming on the right.

* **Check and balance by recruitment:** the **Muqti** and the **district officers** are picked by the **Sultan**; the **village-level juniors** are picked by the **Muqti**. Exactly the modern **UPSC vs State PCS** logic applied to medieval public administration. * **Balban's audit layer** (flowing from his policy of blood — the governors were themselves powerful Chahalgani): * **KHWAJA** — one per province, an **auditor** who audits the governor **on the governor's own authority, without his knowledge**. * **MUTASARRIF** — **one** auditor at the local level, given **two clerks (KARKUNS)**. * **Why two clerks?** So they check each other — and to make sure they can never collude, **one knows only Sanskrit and the other only Persian**. * **Therefore: Sanskrit was one of the working languages of the Delhi Sultanate's administration**, even though **Persian was the official court language**. This is a favourite statement-type question. * **BARID** — the **spy** who carries the reports to the Sultan. **Balban introduced the spy system.** * **Lodi expansion:** by the Lodi period the Sultanate is too big for the old ladder → **Vilayat becomes SUBA** (under a **Subadar**), the district becomes **SARKAR**, and for the first time a **block-level tier — the PARGANA** — is inserted above the **Gram**. → **Suba → Sarkar → Pargana → Gram.** ---

sections.heading: 16. Land Revenue System — MASAHAT (HIS-MED-22)
sections.content:
> **Masahat** = the Persian term for the **land revenue system**. *UPSC has asked directly: "What is Masahat?"* All the administration above exists for exactly one purpose — collecting this revenue.

| # | Ruler(s) | Method | Share | Mode | Machinery / innovations |
|:---:|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **1** | **Iltutmish & Balban** | **Crop-sharing method** — simply continued the old **Hindu** system | **1/3 of gross produce** (*ushr*) | share of the standing crop | Village officials inspect the crop before harvest and take the state's share |
| **2** | **Alauddin Khalji** | **Measurement method** — the **most scientific** of the three | **50% — kharaj** | **in kind only** (grain, not money) | **(a)** unit of measurement: the **BISWA** (a sub-unit of the bigha, still used in western UP and Rajasthan); **(b)** two **granaries** — **Delhi** and **Jhain** (Rajasthan); **(c)** to let people buy that grain he minted **fractional copper coins** of the **JITAL** (½, ¼, ⅙, ⅛) called **GHANI** |
| **3** | **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** | **Tax farming method** | **1/3 of gross produce** | **cash only** | The land goes to the **highest bidder** — the **khut**, hence **KHOTI** — who keeps a fixed **10% commission** for collecting |

*   **Why the ghani matters today:** the *chavanni* and *athanni* were ghani coins (withdrawn from circulation around 2005), and "**Kachchi Ghani**" mustard oil still carries **Alauddin Khalji's measurement word**.
*   **Link to Modern India:** the **auction of revenue collection to the highest bidder** is *not* a British invention. The **term** *ijaradari* comes from **Warren Hastings**, but the **concept is as old as Firoz Shah Tughlaq**.

---

sections.heading: 17. The Khaljis (1290–1320) — Expansion (HIS-MED-23)
sections.content:
> **One-word cue for the whole dynasty: EXPANSION.** Whatever the question — political expansion, expansion on land, expansion in monuments, expansion of cities — the answer word is *expansion*.
>
> **Second cue: "Khalji" always means a FREE MAN**, never a slave. So with the Khaljis, the **slave elite is thrown out of Indian administration** for the first time. **Expansion + removal of the slaves = the "KHALJI REVOLUTION".**

sections.heading: 17.1 Jalaluddin Khalji (1290–96)
sections.content:
*   Founder of the dynasty — he was the staff officer of the 3-year-old Kayumars and killed him to take the throne.
*   A revolution implies fights — his reign is a **period of revolts**:

| # | Revolt | Nature |
|:---:|:---|:---|
| **1** | **Sidi Maula** | **Religious** |
| **2** | **Khusrau Khan** *(as named in class)* | **Political** |
| **3** | **Ali Gurshasp** | The successful one — **he killed Jalaluddin Khalji** and took the throne as **Alauddin Khalji** |

> *Cross-check for accuracy:* standard textbooks name the political revolt of Jalaluddin's reign as that of **Malik Chhajju** (the displaced governor of Kara); **Khusrau Khan's** coup belongs to **1320**, against **Mubarak Shah Khalji**, and is what ends the dynasty. Keep both names in mind if a statement-based question turns on the date.

*   **Ali Gurshasp was Jalaluddin's own nephew** (and son-in-law) — he killed him at Kara and changed his name to **Alauddin Khalji**.

sections.heading: 17.2 Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316)
sections.content:
| # | Achievement | Detail |
|:---:|:---|:---|
| **1** | **Defeated the Mongols decisively** — threw them out | The **most successful Sultan of Delhi against the Mongols** |
| **2** | Brought **new military technology** to India | — |
| **3** | Introduced the **best breeds of horses** | Created **horse-breeding centres — PAIGAH**; started the **branding system (DAGH)** and the **descriptive roll (CHEHRA)**; introduced **DO-ASPA** — two horses per soldier as a rule; also created a **central postal system** |
| **4** | **Market reforms and price regulation** | The famous experiment — it **ran for about 25 years** |

> **Standing exam line:** *after Balban, the most successful Sultan of Delhi is Alauddin Khalji.*

---

sections.heading: UPSC Cues & PYQ Connections — Delhi Sultanate (Lecture A4)
sections.content:
*   **Iltutmish, not Aibak**, is the **real founder** of the Delhi Sultanate (Abbasid investiture → Dar-al-Islam).
*   **Firsts:** first silver **tanka** (Iltutmish) · first **gold dinar** (Razia) · first **Islamic religious revolt** — Nur Turk (Razia) · first **Mongol invasion** (Bahram Shah) · first **spy system** (Balban) · first **fixed law of succession** (Balban).
*   **Book–author pairs:** *Taj-ul-Maasir* — Hasan Nizami · *Tabaqat-i-Nasiri* — Minhaj-us-Siraj Juzjani · *Tarikh-i-Firozshahi* **and** *Fatawa-i-Jahandari* — Zia-ud-din Barani.
*   **Definition questions:** *Masahat* = land revenue system · *Waqf* = religious **endowment** · *Iqta* = **non-feudal** revenue assignment.
*   **The one exception to memorise:** **Alauddin Khalji is the only Sultan who taxed the waqf.**
*   **Proper iqta system existed only under the Slave Dynasty and the Lodis.**
*   **Zil-i-Allah** was used by only two rulers in Indian history — **Balban** and **Akbar** (*Zil-i-Ilahi*).
*   **Sanskrit was a working language of the Sultanate's administration** (Balban's two karkuns) even though **Persian** was the court language.
*   **Title cue:** "Mian" ≠ Mughal (asked for **Mian Tansen**); "Mirza" = Mughal.
*   **Revenue-farming to the highest bidder** begins with **Firoz Shah Tughlaq**, not Warren Hastings.

---

sections.heading: Topics Covered in These Lectures
sections.content:
1. **Nationalism:** A brief definition → Origin in Europe & America
2. **Nationalism in India:** When, where, among whom → Factors responsible for emergence of Indian Nationalism (+ debate on whether India is "real" or "imagined" nation)
3. **Formation of INC** — Safety Valve Theory vs Nationalist Theory
4. **The Moderate Phase of INC: 1885–1905** — Demands, methods, contribution & criticism
5. **Swadeshi Movement (1905)** — Partition of Bengal, course, features, Surat Split, Moderates vs Extremists
6. **Indian Councils Act 1909** — Background, clauses (CLC 69, separate electorate), critique
7. **Three Delhi Durbars (1877 / 1903 / 1911)** — Lytton famine, Curzon, Hardinge II
8. **1911 announcements** — Bengal reunited; capital Calcutta → Delhi
9. **Home Rule Leagues, 1916** — Tilak (Pune) & Besant (Madras); urban limit; Gandhi’s critique
10. **Lucknow Pact, 1916** — INC–Muslim League; 1/3 seats; 3/4 Muslim veto
11. **Lucknow Pact (C) — significance** — communal harmony; Rowlatt 1919; Khilafat–NCM 1920–22; Montagu–Chelmsford → Government of India Act 1919
12. **The Making of Mahatma** — Gandhi in South Africa (1893–1914/15); Satyagraha named; religious thought
13. **Lecture 6 — Mass Mobilizations and the Dialogues (part taught 6 Sep)** — Gandhian political thought; Satyagraha as method; Gandhi & Tagore on nationalism and education.
14. **Lecture 7 — 8 Sep** — **Wardha Scheme / Nai Taleem (1937)**; Gandhi vs Nehru (state, trusteeship, religion); Gandhi vs Ambedkar (untouchability, caste, Hinduism). **1917–48 movements** still later.

---

sections.heading: What is Nationalism?
sections.content:
**Nationalism is a modern political thought based on a feeling of oneness — real or imagined.**

It is an idea in which people of a **defined territory** believe that they share:

- **Common origin** — ancestral roots, racial stock
- **Common ethnicity** — physical appearance, racial characteristics (e.g., Proto-Australoid, Mediterranean, Mongoloid)
- **Common culture** — food, dress, way of life, marriage customs, music, architecture, painting, festivals
- **Common history & heritage** — monuments like Harappa, Ajanta, Taj Mahal, Konark Temple evoke a shared pride
- **Common value system** — e.g., *Atithi Devo Bhava*, respect for elders, parental obedience
- **Shared aspirations** — collective vision for the future

sections.heading: The "Us vs Them" Boundary
sections.content:
Nationalism creates a distinction between **"us" and "them"** based on:
- Origin & ethnicity
- Culture & language
- History & heritage
- Value systems & aspirations

This consciousness leads to the creation of a **Nation-State**: first, a belief that "we are one nation" (nation = people), then, a defined boundary → common government, parliament, constitution, currency, tax system.

sections.heading: "Real or Imagined" — The Scholarly Debate
sections.content:
Some historians (e.g., **Yuval Noah Harari** in *Sapiens*) argue nationalism is **imagined, not real**:
- Globally, a community truly knows each other by name and face to about **250 families** (international average; India ~500)
- In a huge country like India — from Kashmir to Kanyakumari — you cannot personally know most fellow "nationals"
- The feeling of oneness is therefore a **constructed belief**, not a lived reality

**Ancient & Medieval Period — No Nationalism:**
- People lived under **empires** (Roman, Mauryan, Gupta, Mughal) — ruled from top by emperor/king
- Communities at the bottom had **tribal/community pride**, not national consciousness
- When empires collapsed, communities became independent again → cycle repeats
- Mauryans conquering Kalinga → Kalinga people saw Magadha as "outsiders"
- Rajendra Chola attacking North → Northerners saw Cholas as "outsiders"
- 36 Rajput clans fighting each other — no concept of "Indian unity"

**Key Insight:** Nationalism is a **modern concept** (18th century Europe, 19th century India). The idea that "we are all Indian" was absent in ancient and medieval times.

---

sections.heading: Chronology
sections.content:
| Event | Year | Significance |
|:---|:---:|:---|
| **American Revolution** | 1776 | First assertion of modern national self-determination |
| **French Revolution** | 1789 | Liberty, Equality, Fraternity — basis of modern nation-state |
| **European Revolutions** | 1830, 1848 | Gave birth to modern nation-states across Europe |

sections.heading: Why Nationalism was Easier in Europe
sections.content:
European countries (England, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Denmark, etc.) found it **easier** to create nation-states because they were:
- **Relatively homogeneous** — in race, language, religion, culture
- **Smaller in size** — Most European countries (minus Russia) smaller than Indian states; some smaller than Indian districts
- **~50 countries in Europe** — an area smaller than undivided India (including Pakistan & Bangladesh)

**Example:** If you travel from Poland to Portugal, you enter a new country every ~30 minutes. In India, UP alone takes an entire night by Rajdhani Express. Israel's size = half of Ghaziabad; its population (25 lakh) is a fraction of Delhi's (2.5 crore).

sections.heading: Birth of Nation-States
sections.content:
Through revolutions, wars, and movements, European communities created nation-states by asserting:
- "We share common race, language, religion, culture"
- "We need our own government, parliament, constitution"
- Even small groups fought for statehood → Czechoslovakia split into Czech Republic & Slovakia

---

sections.heading: When, Where, Among Whom?
sections.content:
> **"India is a nation in the making."**  
> — S.N. Banerjee or Gopal Krishna Gokhale (c. 1903)

**In India, nationalism was first born or emerged in Bengal, Bombay, and Madras regions, among the middle educated class, during the period of 1860s, 1870s, and 1880s (late 19th century), which continued to grow later on.**

sections.heading: Key Characteristics
sections.content:
- **Not a single event** — nationalism is a **feeling** that emerges gradually, not born on a specific date
- **First emerged among small elite** — educated, upper-middle-class professionals in three presidency towns
- **Grew in two dimensions:**
  1. **Deepening** — becoming stronger over time
  2. **Widening** — spreading to new sections of society and new regions

sections.heading: India's Unique Challenges for Nationalism
sections.content:
Unlike European countries, India faced **two massive obstacles**:

| Challenge | Details |
|:---|:---|
| **Giant Size** | Undivided India (with Pakistan & Bangladesh) was bigger than entire Europe minus Russia |
| **Enormous Diversity** | Multiple races, 750+ languages (Census 2011: 101 scheduled; Linguistic Survey: 750), each with multiple dialects (UP alone has 16); multiple religions with sects within (Vaishnavism, Shaivism, Shaktism, Shia, Sunni); 4 Varnas but 8,000+ Jatis (including 400+ Muslim Jatis) |

sections.heading: Pre-Existing Consciousness vs. National Consciousness
sections.content:
Indians had **strong consciousness** of:
- ✅ **Caste** — hierarchy, position, rules (since ancient times)
- ✅ **Sect within religion** — Vaishnavism vs Shaivism, Sunni vs Shia
- ✅ **Language & region** — strong regional identities

But they **lacked consciousness** of:
- ❌ **Indian-ness** — the idea that "we are all Indian" regardless of caste, religion, language

**This national political consciousness started emerging only in the late 19th century** — which is where the UPSC syllabus on Modern India begins.

sections.heading: Contemporary Perspective — Ramachandra Guha (c. 2015)
sections.content:
- **Two-thirds** of Indians have accepted the idea of India (i.e., feel proud to be Indian beyond caste/religion/language identity)
- **One-third** have not fully accepted — separatist feelings persist in:
  - Parts of **North-East** (especially Nagaland)
  - **Punjab** (Khalistan movement — subdued but revived in Canada, UK)
  - **Kashmir** (not fully resolved)
  - **Tamil Nadu** (1960s–70s anti-Union protests)
  - **Naxal belt** (central India) — against the very idea of the Indian state
- Integration of India — physically and emotionally — is **still an ongoing project**
- ~35% Indians today live outside their birth-state → strengthens national integration

sections.heading: Two Types of Struggle in Freedom Movement
sections.content:
1. **Indian vs. British** — the anti-colonial struggle
2. **Indian vs. Indian** — the struggle to unite diverse Indians under one national identity

The freedom struggle became **very long** precisely because the first challenge (uniting Indians) itself took decades.

---

sections.heading: 4. Factors for the Emergence of Indian Nationalism (MOD-B1-04)
sections.content: > **Question (Mains-type, 250 words, 15 marks):** *"Discuss the various factors that contributed to the emergence of Indian nationalism in the late 19th century."*

sections.heading: Factor A: Administrative Unification of India (1772–1858)
sections.content:
- British completed administrative unification of India between **1772 and 1858**
- Created **uniform administrative structure** across the country:
  - **Office of District Magistrate** — first established in **1772** (under Warren Hastings)
  - **Office of Superintendent of Police** — first established in **1793** (under Cornwallis)
  - **Office of Commissioner** — established across regions
- These offices exist in every district of India even today
- **Impact:** Gave a **sense of oneness** to different parts of India — same administrative framework from Bengal to Punjab to Madras
- **Note:** British did it for **their own sake** (governing India, collecting revenue, exploiting resources) — but it helped create a unified administrative identity (*blessing in disguise*)

sections.heading: Factor B: Uniform Legal System — IPC, CrPC & Judicial Institutions
sections.content:
- **Uniform IPC (Indian Penal Code)** — since **1862**
- **Uniform CrPC (Code of Criminal Procedure)** — since **1890** (originally 1861/1872)
- **Uniform Judicial Institutions — High Courts** — since **1865** (first three: Calcutta, Bombay, Madras)
- **English language** as medium of higher education helped in uniting Indians across diverse customs and practices

**Impact:**
- Before IPC, India had **no common criminal law** — customs of marriage, inheritance, property varied from community to community
- IPC sections like **302 (Murder), 307 (Attempt to Murder), 420 (Cheating/Forgery), 144 (Assembly restriction/Curfew)** became pan-India
- Uniform law bound Indians together under one legal identity
- **Note:** Again, British purpose was colonial governance — positive impact on Indian unity was a **spin-off benefit**

sections.heading: Factor C: Social-Religious Reform Movements of 19th Century
sections.content:
- Movements like **Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, Ramakrishna Mission** and others:
  - Gave birth to **cultural consciousness** — the awareness that Indians share a **common Hindustani culture**
  - *Hindustani culture* = neither pure Hindu, nor pure Islam, nor pure Buddhist — but a **unique mix**; not pure Aryan or Dravidian; not pure Hindi or Tamil
  - Often described as **"Unity in Diversity"**
- Reform leaders **travelled, met each other** — Bengalis and Punjabis, Marathis and Tamils — agitating for same social causes (education, superstition removal)
- This cultural consciousness **further helped** in the emergence of **national political consciousness**

**Progression:** Community consciousness → Cultural consciousness → **National Political consciousness**

sections.heading: Factor D: Economic Exploitation of India by the British
sections.content:
British economic policies brought:
- **Poverty** — widespread impoverishment
- **Famines** — recurring and devastating
- **De-industrialization** — destruction of traditional Indian industries (textiles, handicrafts)
- **Unemployment** — loss of livelihood for millions
- **Drain of Wealth** — transfer of Indian resources to Britain (theory given by **Dadabhai Naoroji**)

**Impact:**
- The **educated class** became conscious of the impact of colonial rule
- They started **writing and talking** about the misadventure of British rule
- Economic historians wrote series of articles from **1860s to 1890s** in Calcutta, Bombay, Madras, and London
- **Common grievance unites victims** — a Bengali victim and a Madrasi victim, a Punjabi farmer and a UP farmer, were all suffering the same colonial exploitation
- This common economic suffering helped develop a **national consciousness**

**Key Figures:** Dadabhai Naoroji (Drain Theory), R.C. Dutt, and other economic nationalists of the late 19th century

sections.heading: Factor E: Modern Liberal Political & Scientific Thought
sections.content:
**Modern Liberal Political Thought** such as:
- **Liberty, Equality, Fraternity, Justice**

**Modern Scientific Thought** such as:
- **Observation, Questioning authority, Reasoning, Scientific temper**

**How it spread:** Through modern **schools, colleges, books, journals, and newspapers** established during British period

**Impact:**
- Educated Indians adopted ideas of **reasoning** and **questioning the state** — the mother of all modern knowledge
- Led to questioning of feudal/monarchical claims (e.g., divine right of kings: Mughal *Zillellahi* = Shadow of God; Rajput rulers claiming to be *Avatars* of Vishnu)
- These ideas are enshrined in the **Indian Constitution** (Article 14 — Equality; Preamble — Liberty, Equality, Fraternity, Justice)
- **Key Pioneers:** Raja Ram Mohan Roy (established girls' school in Calcutta in 1820s; died 1833), Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Surendranath Banerjee

**Important Distinction:**
- **Westernization** = adopting Western dress, gadgets, lifestyle (superficial)
- **Modernization** = adopting modern values — equality, liberty, scientific temper, questioning authority (substantive)
- India became **westernized quickly** but has been **slow to modernize**
- This paradox continues — people living in "two centuries" simultaneously (11th century values + 21st century technology)

sections.heading: Factor F: Modern Means of Transportation & Communication
sections.content: - **Roadways, Railways, Ports, and Telegraph services** helped in **integrating Indians not only physically but also emotionally** **How it worked:** - Before railways/roadways: people of Bengal never met Marathis; North Indians never met South Indians; India's peasant majority didn't travel beyond a few kilometers - Railways and roads enabled **criss-crossing** of the subcontinent → physical meetings, exchange of ideas, handshakes - **Broke stereotype images** — Bengalis realized Tamilians are not so different; North Indians realized South Indians share many similarities - **Post & Telegraph** further enabled communication across vast distances **Impact:** - Similarities between Indians were found to be **greater than differences** - This realization gave birth to **national consciousness** - **Note:** British built railways for **economic exploitation & military transportation** — the positive spin-off on national unity was unintended **Factor G: Reactionary Colonial Policies & Racial Arrogance (Lytton & Ilbert Bill)** - **Reactionary Viceroyalty of Lord Lytton (1876–1880):** - **ICS Examination Age Reduction (1876):** Lowered the maximum age limit for Indian Civil Service examinations from **21 to 19 years** to deliberately handicap and exclude Indian candidates (who had to travel to London and write in English against native British graduates). - **First Pan-Indian Agitation (Civil Service Agitation):** **Surendranath Banerjee** and **Ananda Mohan Bose** organized the **Indian Association (1876)** in Calcutta and launched an all-India campaign, with Banerjee touring northern, western, and southern India to mobilize public opinion and present a mass memorial to the British Parliament against the ICS age reduction — considered the **first pan-Indian political agitation**. - **Vernacular Press Act (1878):** Known as the *"Gagging Act"*, specifically targeted vernacular newspapers (like *Amrita Bazar Patrika* which switched to English overnight) to suppress nationalist criticism while exempting English-language press. - **Arms Act (1878):** Imposed racial discrimination by mandating licenses for Indians to carry firearms while exempting Europeans and Anglo-Indians. - **Imperial Delhi Durbar (1877):** Lavish imperial grand durbar organized to proclaim Queen Victoria as *Kaiser-i-Hind* while millions were dying in the catastrophic Great Famine of 1876–78 (*"Nero was fiddling while Rome was burning"*). - **Ilbert Bill Controversy (1883) under Lord Ripon:** - Law Member **C.P. Ilbert** proposed granting Indian District Magistrates and Sessions Judges jurisdiction to try European British subjects. - White European community launched a virulent, racially charged agitation (*European and Anglo-Indian Defence Association*), forcing Ripon to compromise (allowing Europeans to claim trial by a jury comprising 50% Europeans). - **Impact:** Shattered any illusion of British "racial equality" or fair play, proving to the educated middle class that organized pan-Indian political agitation was the only path forward, directly paving the way for the **Indian National Congress (1885)**. ---

sections.heading: Key Concept: *Zama & Makan* (Time & Space in History)
sections.content:
> **Persian:** *Zama* = Time | *Makan* = Space

- When studying history, **erase present-day consciousness** and transport yourself to the time period being studied
- You cannot judge Akbar by 21st-century standards — compare him with **16th-century rulers** of India and the world
- **Common mistake:** Non-history background people judge historical figures from current point of view — this is a fundamental error
- **Analogy:** You cannot compare Don Bradman (1920s–40s cricket, no helmet, 8-ball overs) with Virat Kohli (2010s cricket, modern equipment) — different eras, different contexts

---

sections.heading: Summary Table — Factors for Emergence of Indian Nationalism
sections.content: | Factor | Key Elements | Timeline | British Intent vs. Indian Impact | |:---:|:---|:---:|:---| | **A** | Administrative Unification (DM, SP, Commissioner) | 1772–1858 | Colonial governance → Sense of oneness | | **B** | Uniform IPC, CrPC, High Courts, English Education | 1862–1890 | Law & order → Common legal identity | | **C** | Social-Religious Reform Movements (Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, etc.) | 19th century | Cultural consciousness → National political consciousness | | **D** | Economic Exploitation (poverty, famine, de-industrialization, drain of wealth) | 1860s–1890s | Revenue extraction → Common grievance → National consciousness | | **E** | Modern Liberal & Scientific Thought (liberty, equality, reasoning, scientific temper) | 1820s onwards | Western education → Questioning authority → Constitutional values | | **F** | Modern Transportation & Communication (railways, roads, post, telegraph) | Mid-19th century | Military/economic transport → Physical + emotional integration | | **G** | Reactionary Colonial Policies (Lytton's Acts 1878, Ilbert Bill 1883) | 1876–1883 | Racial arrogance & repression → Pan-Indian political organization (INC 1885) | ---

sections.heading: A. Safety Valve Theory
sections.content: **In December 1885, Indian National Congress was founded at Bombay** and the first session was held at **Sir Tej Pal Sanskrit Mahavidyalaya**. - **Attended by:** 100 people, **72** of them were delegates/members - **Presided by:** **Womesh Chander Banerjee (W.C. Banerjee)** **UPSC Fact & Delegate Breakdown:** While approximately 100 people were present in the hall (including non-voting official observers, journalists, and sympathizers), exactly **72 official delegates** (representatives) registered from different provinces (38 from Bombay, 21 from Madras, 3 from Bengal, 7 from North-Western Provinces and Oudh, and 3 from Punjab). In standard UPSC Prelims questions and textbook sources (Bipan Chandra, NCERT), it is officially characterized as *"attended by 72 delegates"*.

sections.heading: First Four Sessions (Deliberately Planned Diversity)
sections.content:
| Year | City | President | Significance |
|:---:|:---|:---|:---|
| **1885** | **Bombay** | W.C. Banerjee (Bengali, Hindu) | First session (72 delegates) |
| **1886** | **Calcutta** | Dadabhai Naoroji (Parsi) | 2nd session (434 delegates) |
| **1887** | **Madras** | Badruddin Tyabji (Muslim) | 3rd session (607 delegates) |
| **1888** | **Allahabad** | George Yule (Anglo-Indian/Christian) | First non-Indian president (1,248 delegates) |

**Three Deliberate Patterns (NOT accidental — all planned):**

1. **Geographic Diversity (Caste → Region):** Bombay (West), Calcutta (East), Madras (South), Allahabad (North) — represented all India geographically → because it was *Indian National Congress*, not a regional body
2. **Religious Diversity:** Hindu → Parsi → Muslim → Anglo-Indian/Christian — represented all major religions
3. **Cross-Regional Presidency:** President was NEVER from the host city's region (Bengali presided in Bombay, Parsi in Calcutta, etc.) — deliberately breaking caste, religion, and regional identity

**Purpose:** India had 3 strong pre-existing identities — **Caste, Religion, Region**. The founders wanted to strengthen a NEW identity: **Indian**. Since only ~0.5% of the population had this political consciousness, the founders knew transmitting this idea to the remaining 99.5% would take decades.

sections.heading: The Safety Valve Theory — Evidence & Logic
sections.content: Some historians believe INC was founded by some Indians and British **together**, but the **idea came from British**. This group of writers (both English and Indian) rely heavily on **correspondence/exchange** between: - **Lord Dufferin** — Viceroy & Governor-General of India - **Allan Octavian Hume (A.O. Hume)** — a retired civil servant Their letters have been **preserved in Shimla** (Shimla was the summer capital of British India — British rulers governed from Shimla for 5–6 months because the heat of Delhi, Agra, and Calcutta was unbearable for them). **The Safety Valve Logic:** - They desired to form an organization that would work as a **link between the people of India and the Government** - They believed the **absence of such an organization** had led to the rise of **uprisings like the Revolt of 1857** - 1857 was the biggest upheaval in Indian history till then — it shook the British Empire like a Richter-8 earthquake - The British fear: 50,000 angry Indians outside → dangerous. Better to have 20 gentlemen from Congress who would talk **in English, peacefully, with tea and coffee** **Who named it "Safety Valve"?** — **Lala Lajpat Rai** coined and popularized the term *"Safety Valve"* in 1916 in his book *Young India* to criticize Moderate methods as "political mendicancy". Later, Marxist historian **R. Palme Dutt** (*India Today*, 1940) articulated the "conspiracy theory" that the Congress was brought into existence through a conspiracy hatched by Dufferin and Hume to abort a popular revolution. **The Pressure Cooker Analogy:** Just as a pressure cooker releases accumulated steam through a safety valve to prevent explosion, INC was designed to release the political heat/anger of the people before it reached the government directly. > **Key Insight:** Any theory in social science is **subject to scrutiny** — both sides have facts and logic. The competition in UPSC is between **"two truths, not between truth and false."**

sections.heading: B. Nationalist Theory
sections.content: **Indian nationalists and recent/present-day Western historians** did NOT agree with the Safety Valve Theory. They argued that INC was the **"brain child"** of **Indian nationalists**. Their argument was based on the following points: **(a) Pre-INC Political Organizations Already Existed:** Before INC (going back 3 decades), many political organizations had been established in Bengal, Bombay, and Madras regions: | Organization | Year | Region | Key Founders | |:---|:---:|:---:|:---| | **Landholders' Society (Zamindari Association)** | 1838 | Bengal | Dwarkanath Tagore, Radhakanta Deb | | **British Indian Association** | 1851 | Bengal | Debendranath Tagore, Radhakanta Deb | | **East India Association** | 1866 | London / India | Dadabhai Naoroji | | **Poona Sarvajanik Sabha** | 1870 | Bombay / Pune | M.G. Ranade, G.V. Joshi, S.H. Chiplunkar | | **Indian Association of Calcutta** | 1876 | Bengal | Surendranath Banerjee, Ananda Mohan Bose | | **Madras Mahajan Sabha** | 1884 | Madras | M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer, P. Anandacharlu | | **Bombay Presidency Association** | 1885 | Bombay | Pherozeshah Mehta, K.T. Telang, Badruddin Tyabji ('The Triumvirate') | The **members of these political organizations regularly met Dadabhai Naoroji** (in London) and **A.O. Hume** (in India). They felt the **need of an all-India political organization**. These people shared common political thoughts and ideas. **Rallying Points:** The houses of Dadabhai Naoroji and A.O. Hume became *adda* (rallying points) for like-minded Indians — since Dadabhai was nationalist, highly educated, senior, and rich. **Modern connectivity made this possible:** Railways (1853), Post & Telegraph (1853), Transatlantic cables (1870), newspapers — ideas from Bengal could now travel to Madras, Bombay, and London. Like-minded people converge naturally. **(b) Why English Were Included in INC & The "Lightning Conductor" Theory:** These nationalists **deliberately** included some English (like A.O. Hume) in INC because: - Those English were **retired civil servants** with good networks - Their **presence in Congress would NOT have invited suspicion** in the minds of British authorities - If only Indians were in Congress, British would be suspicious ("What are these Indians planning?") — 1857 was recent memory - **Gopal Krishna Gokhale's "Lightning Conductor" Theory (1913):** As Gokhale famously put it: *"No Indian could have started the Indian National Congress... If an Indian had come forward to start such a movement, the officials would not have allowed it to come into existence. If the founder of the Congress had not been an Englishman and a distinguished ex-official, such was the distrust of political agitation in those days that the authorities would have at once found some way or the other of suppressing the movement."* Early nationalists thus used Hume as a 'lightning conductor' to catalyze the national movement without immediately inviting colonial repression. **(c) Congress Leaders Did NOT Demand Freedom:** They demanded **reforms** — legislative, administrative, social, and judicial in nature: - The British were bringing some positive changes (education, infrastructure, social laws) - These Congress leaders were themselves a **product of the British system** - Many hoped British would bring positive change — but after 15–20 years, **nothing changed** - This **disillusionment** is why the extremist group emerged within INC by late 1890s > **Dadabhai Naoroji** wrote *"Poverty and Un-British Rule in India"* (1901) — called it "Un-British" because British brought development in England but destroyed Indian economy.

sections.heading: C. Formula for Remembering INC Sessions (25–26 out of 60+)
sections.content:
| # | Formula Category | Details |

> **ICS Exam History:** Competition introduced by Charter Act 1853 → First exam in 1856 → Held ONLY in England (Haileybury) from 1856–1922 → First held in India at **Delhi and Allahabad** in **1923** → Lord Cornwallis (1793) excluded Indians from services with salary ≥ ₹500/annum (corrected by Charter Act 1833)

sections.heading: A. Objectives / Demands
sections.content:
Initially, Congress raised **few demands** through its **resolutions, articles, representations, and interviews**. Their demands were mostly **centered around reforms:**

| # | Demand | Key Details |
|:---:|:---|:---|
| **(a)** | **More Indians in Legislative Bodies** | Greater Indian representation in councils |
| **(b)** | **Separation of Powers** | Executive should be separated from Judiciary — Earlier, the DM (District Magistrate) was also the District Collector: he would commit atrocities while collecting revenue, and the farmer's complaint would go to the same DM sitting as magistrate → no justice |
| **(c)** | **Civil Services Reforms** | Exam should be held in India also + Exam papers should change (papers were English literature, history of England/Europe — unfair to Indians) |
| **(d)** | **Reduction in Land Revenue** | Reduce the burden on peasants |
| **(e)** | **Reduction in Military Expenditure** | Reduce expenditure on arms & ammunition, army & administration + Utilize public money in **public welfare** programs |
| **(f)** | **Protection of Indigenous Industries** | Protection and promotion to indigenous Indian industries |
| **(g)** | **Press Freedom** | Demanded freedom of press |
| **(h)** | **Implementation of Famine Code (1883)** | The government had made a code but was NOT implementing it on the ground |

sections.heading: Famine Code — 6 Key Provisions (Key Words to Remember)
sections.content:
| # | Key Word | Provision |
|:---:|:---:|:---|
| 1 | **Food** | Government should provide food to affected people |
| 2 | **No Tax** | Government should NOT collect tax from famine-affected areas |
| 3 | **Data Collection** | Collect data on land, water, animals, humans for better future administration |
| 4 | **Rehabilitation** | Government should rehabilitate affected people |
| 5 | **Loan** | Government should provide loans to affected people |
| 6 | **Fodder** | Government should provide fodder to affected animals |

sections.heading: The Critical Analysis Sentence (Worth 4+ extra marks in Mains)
sections.content:
> **"These Congress demands were nationalist, secular, meant for all the classes, and they hoped for reforms."**
>
> — This single sentence contains 5 analytical keywords: (1) Nationalist — not regionalist, (2) Secular — for all religions, (3) For all classes — not just elites, (4) Reformist — not revolutionary, (5) Hopeful — they still had faith in British

sections.heading: B. Nature of Struggle / Method of Struggle (1885–1905)
sections.content:
| # | Method | Details |
|:---:|:---|:---|
| **(a)** | **Annual Sessions** | Congress leaders would meet in **annual session**, held in the **last week of December** in different cities. Before Gandhi, politicians were **part-timers/ad hoc leaders** — busy in professions. Gandhi made politics **24×7×365** from 1920s |
| **(b)** | **President by Consensus** | They would choose a president through **consensus** (possible because size was small — initially 72, then 200, then 2000). They would discuss various public issues: **poverty, famine, high taxation, unemployment, atrocities of authority, restrictions on press, drain of wealth** |
| **(c)** | **Resolutions by Consensus/Voting** | They would adopt a resolution through consensus; if needed, through voting. Officials (president, secretary) would draft, others would debate and amend |
| **(d)** | **Petitions & Representations** | Resolutions presented before authorities in the form of **prayers, appeals, petitions, and through representation**. The **language and tone** in their letters were **soft, humble, and submissive**: "His Excellency," "I beg to say you, sir," "Yours most obedient servant" |
| **(e)** | **Publishing in Media** | Proceedings of Congress sessions and adopted resolutions would be **published in newspapers, magazines, and journals**. Many nationalist leaders were **themselves editors or journalists** |

> **Why "Moderate"?** — Not because of their demands (which were the same as extremists), but because of the **way they demanded** — soft, submissive, through petitions. Compare: Bhagat Singh threw a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly with a letter saying *"to make the deaf hear"* vs. Moderates writing *"I beg to say you, sir."*

sections.heading: Achievements (4 Key Points)
sections.content:
**(a) First All-India Political Platform:**
The moderates created an **all-India political platform for the first time in Indian history**. They developed a **new political culture** in India which was both **democratic and secular** — in a society which was **undemocratic and religious**.

> **The Indian Paradox:** Indian society was (and still is) deeply hierarchical, caste-based, patriarchal, and religious. But Indian politics became democratic and secular — the reverse of Europe, where social democracy was achieved first. Congress in its first 20 years introduced: (1) Democracy, (2) Secularism — which survive to this day.

**(b) Raised National Issues & Sensitized Indians:**
They raised important national issues and **sensitized Indians** with those issues, **made them aware**. Common people thought their poverty and suffering was "destiny." The moderates told them: *"You are poor because of bad government policies, not destiny. These are social constructs made by men — you can change them."*

**(c) Pressurized Government for Reforms:**
- In **1892**, **Indian Councils Act** was passed — more Indians were included in legislative bodies
- In **1909**, another **Indian Councils Act (Morley-Minto Reforms)** was passed — expanded the size of legislative bodies

**(d) Aroused Patriotic Feeling:**
The activities of early moderates helped in **arousing patriotic feeling among a section of urban Indians**. Leaders **travelled, met diverse people, and inspired by their thoughts and persona**.

> **Integrity + Intelligence:** These early leaders (Tilak, Gokhale, Dadabhai, Pherozeshah Mehta) had both high integrity AND high intelligence — a combination rarely found together. Today, intelligence is mostly outside politics and integrity is mostly outside politics.

sections.heading: Criticism
sections.content:
**(e) Product of Urban India:**
- The moderate Congress was a **product of urban India**, led by **upper-caste males**
- They **failed to penetrate villages** where **over 90% of Indians lived**
- Under Moderates: **Led by few, for few**
- Under Gandhi (post-1920): **Led by all, for all** — women, Dalits, tribals, peasants, workers included
- Gandhi's concept of **Swaraj** (self-rule) = *"You should be master of yourself — your body, soul, and mind"*
