sections.heading: Indian Polity & Constitution
sections.content:
> **Source:** Vajiram & Ravi Class Lectures 01, 02, 03, 04 & 05 & Notes
> **Date:** 3–5, 16–17 August 2026
> **Last Updated:** 2026-08-17

---

sections.heading: Lecture 01 — What is Polity? & Laws of Land
sections.content: > **Date:** 3 August 2026

sections.heading: 1. What is Polity?
sections.content:
**Definition:** Polity is the **art of who gets what, when, and where**.

*   **Core Idea:** Resource Redistribution — the job of polity is to make sure that resources (tangible or intangible) are not concentrated at one point, but are redistributed across the entire society.
*   **Mechanism:** For redistribution, you need the **interaction of institutions** (both formal and informal). Formal institutions (bureaucracy, civil services) have the force of the state; informal institutions (NGOs, civil society) do not.
*   **The Problem:** Formal institutions are more powerful → they tend to dominate informal ones → unfair interaction → unfair redistribution.
*   **The Solution:** Empower the lesser powerful; regulate the more powerful → establish a **level playing field** → fair interaction → fair redistribution.
*   **How?** Through **laws** that regulate these interactions. The most important set of laws = the **Constitution of India (COI)**, the supreme law of the land.

---

sections.heading: 2. Laws of Land
sections.content: **Definition:** The summation of all the laws which are used in the administration of a country is called **Law of Land**.

sections.heading: 8 Types of Laws
sections.content:
| # | Type | Made By | Key Features | Example |
|---|------|---------|--------------|---------|
| 1 | **Constitutional Laws** | Constituent Assembly (COI) | Supreme Law; highest legitimacy; written in the Constitution itself | Article 21 — Right to Life |
| 2 | **Ordinary Laws / Statutory Laws / Legislation** | Higher Legislature (Parliament at Centre; State Legislature at State level) | Permanent laws; enacted by legislative bodies | RTI Act, RTE Act, Hindu Marriage Act |
| 3 | **Ordinances** | Executive — President (Art. 123) & Governor (Art. 213) | **Temporary** laws (max life: 6 months & 6 weeks); issued during extraordinary/emergency situations when legislature is not in session | Ordinance increasing SC judges (2026) |
| 4 | **Court's Judgments** | Constitutional Courts (Supreme Court & High Courts) | Verdicts/rulings having force of law; interpretation of existing provisions | *Puttaswamy Case (2017)*: Right to Privacy under Art. 21; Right to Hygiene Health under Art. 21 |
| 5 | **Applicable Provisions of International Laws** | International agreements/treaties | Only those international laws **applicable to India** become part of Indian Law of Land | *Indus Water Treaty (1960)* between India & Pakistan is part of Indian law; CPEC is NOT |
| 6 | **Bye-laws** | Lesser Legislature — Municipalities (Urban) & Panchayats (Rural) | Made by third-tier/ground-level bodies; local governance rules | Road construction norms, drainage rules, grazing ground regulations |
| 7 | **Orders / Directives / Notifications / Rules & Regulations** | Government — at Centre, State, or Local level (Executive bodies) | Administrative orders; executive in nature | UPSC notification, COVID-era social distancing norms |
| 8 | **Personal Laws** | **Non-state actors** — based on religious beliefs & customs | Deal with 4 subjects: **Marriage, Divorce, Adoption, Inheritance**; under the control of Legislature, Executive & Judiciary | *Triple Talaq* — was personal law under Sharia 1937; struck down by SC as unconstitutional (violating equality of Muslim women) |

**Key Distinction:**
*   Laws **1 to 7** → Made by **state actors** (executive, legislature, judiciary).
*   Law **8** → Made by **non-state actors** (religious communities, customs).
*   Because law 8 is made by non-state actors, the state (legislature, executive, judiciary) exercises **control** over it.
*   **If UCC (Uniform Civil Code) is passed**, personal laws will cease to exist as separate laws.

**Difference between Bye-laws (6) and Orders/Directives (7):**
*   Bye-laws → made by **legislative bodies** at the local level.
*   Orders/Directives → made by **executive bodies** at centre, state, or local level.

sections.heading: Statutory Law vs. Constitutional Law (Lecture 3 Recap)
sections.content:
| | Statutory / Ordinary Law | Constitutional Law |
|---|---|---|
| **Made by** | Parliament / State Legislature | Constituent Assembly (COI) |
| **Provision** | Written in ordinary Acts/statutes | Written in the Constitution itself |
| **Example** | Right to Education **Act** 2009 (how you get education — procedure) | [Article 21A](../Articles/Article_21A.md) (right to education itself) |
| **Hierarchy** | Subordinate to Constitutional Law | Supreme — cannot be challenged by statutory law |

> **Key Distinction (from Lecture 3):** Right to Property was a **Fundamental Right** (Art. 19(1)(f)) → **44th Amendment Act, 1978** (Janata Party Govt) converted it from a Fundamental Right to a **Constitutional Right** ([Art. 300A](../Articles/Article_300A.md)) — i.e., reduced its status.

---

sections.heading: Feature 1: Supreme Law of the Land
sections.content:
*   **Supreme** = a comparative term → comparing one entity (Constitution) with other entities (all other laws).
*   **Law** = the collective conscience (value system) of a society. Core values the society will never compromise = Constitutional laws.
*   **Land** = the territory of India (will be detailed under Part 1, Article 1).
*   The Constitution is the **highest law** of the land → none of the laws from 2 to 8 can challenge it. It has the **highest legitimacy** in the country.

sections.heading: Feature 2: Fundamental Law of the Land
sections.content:
*   The Constitution is the **basic law** of the land. No other law can compromise it.
*   If any law from 2 to 8 would compromise or challenge the Constitution → the Constitution **remains intact** while the other law is declared **Null & Void**.
*   *(See [Article 13](../Articles/Article_13.md) — Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void)*

sections.heading: Feature 3: Organic Law of the Land
sections.content: > ⚠️ **UPSC Critical Distinction:** "Organic Law of the Land" ≠ "Organic in Nature"

sections.heading: (a) Organic in Nature (Living Document)
sections.content:
*   **Organic** = life-giving → most visible symbol of life = **growth / change**.
*   **Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru** in the Constituent Assembly: *"Stagnancy leads to irrelevancy"* (inspired by Napoleon's *"Stagnancy is death"*).
*   **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** legally codified this under **Article 368** → process of amendment + Parliament's power to amend.
*   **Parliament** has two legislative powers:
    1.  **Ordinary Legislative Power (OLP):** Make ordinary laws under point 2 (everyday job of Parliament worldwide).
    2.  **Constituent Legislative Power (CLP):** Under Article 368 — Parliament can **modify, add, or delete** anything in the Constitution. When using Art. 368, Parliament behaves like the Constituent Assembly.
*   **106th Amendment** (most recent): Reservation for women in legislative bodies.
*   **Example — Evolution of Article 21 (Right to Life):**
    *   Text of Article 21 has **never changed** since 1950 ("No person shall be deprived of life and liberty except by procedure established by law").
    *   But the **SC's interpretation** evolved with changing value system:
        *   **1950s:** Protected Life (state must protect your life from arbitrary deprivation)
        *   **1970s:** Dignified Life (not mere animal existence; human dignity)
        *   **1990s:** Educated Life (education as a component of dignity → eventually led to RTE)
        *   **2017:** Right to Privacy (*Puttaswamy Case* — digital life must also be protected)
    *   ∴ The Constitution is a **Living Document** that represents the **Spirit of the Age** (the current value system of society).
    *   Living things are organic → Constitution of India is **organic in nature**.
    *   *(UPSC Mains 2021 — 15 marks: "Write how the Indian Constitution is a living document representing the spirit of the age with special focus on judicial interpretation of Article 21.")*
*   **Law** is changed by two organs:
    *   **Parliament** (Legislature) → via **Article 368** amendments.
    *   **Courts** (Judiciary) → via evolving **interpretation** (most changes to the Constitution actually start in court chambers).
*   Why is interpretation given to the judiciary and not legislature/executive? Because judiciary is **not based on voting/elections** → no populistic pressure → can be fair and independent.

sections.heading: (b) Organic Law of the Land (different meaning)
sections.content:
*   **Definition:** Any law that **meticulously provides the details of administration** of a country is called the organic law of the land.
*   The Constitution of India provides the meticulous detail of governance under **3 tiers**:

| Level | Executive | Legislature | Judiciary | Subjects |
|-------|-----------|-------------|-----------|----------|
| **Centre** | President + PM & Council of Ministers | Parliament (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha) | Supreme Court | **99 subjects** (Union List) |
| **State** | Governor + CM & Council of Ministers | State Legislature (Vidhan Sabha + Vidhan Parishad in some states) | High Courts | **61 subjects** (State List) |
| **Local** | Chairman/Mayor & Vice | Gram Sabha / Ward Committees | District Courts / Gram Nyayalayas | **29 subjects** (PRIs) + **18 subjects** (ULBs) |

sections.heading: Feature 4: Special Legal Sanctity
sections.content:
*   **Sanctity** = power / authority / position.
*   The Constitution derives its power **directly from the People of India** (Preamble: *"We the People of India..."*).
*   All other laws (2 to 8) derive their power **from the Constitution itself**.
*   ∴ Constitution has **special** legal sanctity; other laws have **mere** legal sanctity.

sections.heading: Feature 5: Aspirational Document
sections.content:
*   The Indian Constitution acts as a **platform for individuals to realize their potential**.
*   Under the colonial government → laws were majorly used for **regulation** and **punishing** persons.
*   Our founding parents ensured that the Constitution **not only regulates but also empowers** individuals to have a **dignified life** under independent India.
*   ∴ The Constitution is **not a mere transactional document** but rather a **transformative document** comprising **liberal and progressive values** like **Liberty, Equality, Democracy, Justice**, etc.

---

sections.heading: Examples
sections.content:
*   **Written:** All constitutions except UK, NZ, Israel (India, USA, etc.)
*   **Unwritten:** UK, New Zealand, Israel

> **Key Concept:** Unwritten ≠ "not written down". Both are printed/published. The difference lies in **codification** (systematic/logical arrangement into a single document).

sections.heading: 9 Points of Difference
sections.content:
| # | Written Constitution | Unwritten Constitution |
|---|---------------------|----------------------|
| **1** | Provisions **are codified** (systematically arranged: Land → People → Rights → Duties → Government → …) | Provisions **are not codified** (scattered across multiple documents) |
| **2** | **Enacted** constitution — brought into existence by a **single entity** (Constituent Assembly); has an **identifiable beginning** (India: 26 November 1949) | **Evolved** constitution — brought into existence by **multiple entities** (Magna Carta 1215 + Parliamentary laws + historical events); **no identifiable beginning** |
| **3** | **Constitution came first** → then Parliament was created by the Constitution | **Parliament came first** → laws made by Parliament became part of the Constitution |
| **4** | **Constitution is supreme** | **Parliament is supreme** |
| **5** | Judiciary has **wider powers** — Judicial Review is **well established** (judiciary can check both Executive and Legislature against the Constitution) | Judiciary has **limited powers** — Judicial Review is **partially established** (can only check Executive, NOT the supreme Parliament/Legislature) |
| **6** | Can be **Unitary or Federal** (will be covered under Salient Features) | **Always Unitary** |
| **7** | Can be **Rigid, Flexible, or Both** (depending on provisions in the Constitution) | **Always Flexible** (Parliament doesn't share power → only one institution involved in amendment) |
| **8** | Constitution is an **easily identifiable document** (special setup; **complex** treatment — e.g., two-thirds majority needed for amendment) | **Not an identifiable document** (all laws are ordinary; **simple** treatment) |
| **9** | Governed **majorly by Provisions**, less by Conventions | Governed **majorly by Conventions**, less by Provisions |

---

sections.heading: Magna Carta (1215 CE)
sections.content:
*   **King John** of England — hated for: (a) compulsory military service, (b) arbitrary taxation.
*   People of Britain, funded by **local barons** (business entities), revolted → raised a people's army → defeated the King's army.
*   King compelled to sign the **Magna Carta** (Great Charter) → **financial regulation**: King cannot levy taxes without **consensus of the people** (through Parliament).
*   This gave Parliament an additional job: representing people's consensus on taxation.
*   Over 800 years, Parliament made thousands of laws → King went from **absolute authority** to **ceremonial rubber stamp**; people went from **powerless** to **legitimate rulers**.

sections.heading: Act of Settlement (1701) & The Origin of the Prime Minister
sections.content:
*   **Act of Settlement:** Only a **Protestant Christian** of **royal blood** can become King of Britain (Catholics excluded).
*   **1714:** Queen Anne died without a legitimate male heir → no qualifying person found **inside Britain**.
*   They searched outside → found **Hanover** in Prussia (today's Germany), ~45 years old, Protestant, royal blood, but a **local mayor** in a Prussian municipality.
*   **1720:** Hanover crowned as **King George I** of Britain.
*   **Problem:** Hanover never visited Britain, **didn't speak English** (only German/Prussian).
*   **Solution:** One minister in the cabinet knew **both English and German** → became indispensable as translator between King and Cabinet, and King and Parliament.
*   This minister → without him, neither Cabinet nor Parliament could function → everyone started calling him the **most important (prime) minister** → that's how the world got its **first Prime Minister**.
*   That minister was **Robert Walpole** — never knew in his lifetime he was the world's first PM; recognized only long after his death.
*   **Key UPSC Insight:** The most powerful office in UK (PM) has **no law** backing it — it emerged purely from a **historical accident/convention**.

sections.heading: Rigid vs Flexible vs Both (Amendment Process)
sections.content:
| Type | Definition | Example |
|------|-----------|---------| 
| **Rigid** | Amendment process involves **more than one institution** | **USA:** CAB → passed by **2/3 Congress** + **3/4 States (38 of 50)** → CAA |
| **Flexible** | Only **one institution** involved in amendment | **Sri Lanka:** CAB → passed by **2/3 Parliament** → CAA |
| **Both** | Some amendments rigid, some flexible, depending on subject | **India:** (a) *Federal subjects:* CAB → **2/3 Parliament** + **1/2 States** → CAA (Rigid); (b) *Non-federal subjects:* CAB → **2/3 Parliament** → CAA (Flexible) |

*   **Flexible does NOT show power** — Parliament doesn't share power with any other institution.

sections.heading: Conventions
sections.content:
**Definition:** Practices which are **not enacted** and have been **followed since some time**. They represent the **democratic spirit** of the country.

**Indian Examples of Conventions:**
1.  **Three sessions of Parliament per year** — Constitution only says max gap = 6 months (so even 2 sessions is legal). But by convention, 3 sessions have been held since independence. Breaking it isn't illegal, but questions the government's **democratic spirit**.
2.  **Deputy Speaker from opposition** — Speaker comes from ruling party (by provision); since **1967**, Deputy Speaker has come from the opposition (by convention). Not legally binding.
3.  **Resignation after No-Confidence Motion** — Provision says COMs' confidence lies in Lok Sabha. If NCM is passed, by convention the government **resigns**. No provision forces resignation — but not doing so questions democratic credentials.

---

sections.heading: 5. Study Resources (As Advised by the Teacher)
sections.content:
1.  **Class Notes** (foundational; thematic note-making; creates eidetic/picture-based memory)
2.  **Standard Books:** Vajiram & Ravi Yellow Book (Polity 1 & Polity 2) — both Prelims + Mains oriented
    *   M. Laxmikant = good **Prelims** book but insufficient for Mains
    *   *Golden Rule: Minimum books, maximum revision*
3.  **Newspaper** (The Hindu or Indian Express) + **Monthly Magazine** (Recitals — Polity section)
4.  **Bare Act of Constitution of India** (or Constitution of India app on phone) — read parallelly with class
5.  **PYQ Book** — Prelims: last 20 years; Mains: last 7-10 years (**theme-wise**, not year-wise)

**How to Study:**
1.  Come to class → make notes (eidetic memory through writing)
2.  **Revise notes immediately** after class (same day)

sections.heading: Lecture 02 — Salient Features of the Indian Constitution
sections.content:
> **Date:** 4 August 2026 (Pages 9–17)

> [!NOTE]
> There is **no exhaustive list** of Salient Features. Whatever is taught across the entire Polity syllabus is, in essence, a Salient Feature. Many features (FR, DPSP, Emergency, etc.) will become full-fledged chapters and are only noted here — not expanded.

---

sections.heading: Feature ① — Lengthiest Written Constitution
sections.content: **The Constitution of India (COI) is the lengthiest written constitution in the world.**

sections.heading: Structure of COI
sections.content:
| Component | Original (1950) | Current (2026) |
|---|---|---|
| **Preamble** | 1 | 1 (amended by 42nd Amendment, 1976) |
| **Articles** | ~395 | ~470 (added via [Art. 368](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_368.md) amendments) |
| **Schedules** | 8 | 12 |
| **Word Count** | ~90,000 words | Even larger |

**Hierarchy within Provisions:** COI → **Parts** → Chapters → **Articles** → Clauses → Sub-clauses → Sub-sub-clauses

**Article** = A **stand-alone provision** in the Constitution. Self-sufficient — no prerequisite reading of another article needed to understand it. (e.g., [Article 21](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_21.md) is complete in itself.)

**Schedules** = Quantitative appendices at the end (like appendices in a book).

sections.heading: 4 Reasons Why the Constitution is Bulky
sections.content:
| # | Factor | Explanation |
|---|--------|-------------|
| 1 | **Historical** — GOI Act, 1935 | The entire structural part of COI was borrowed from the Government of India Act 1935, itself the bulkiest British law. We took a bulky base and added more aspirations to it. |
| 2 | **Geographical** — Vastness + **Diversity** | India is vast, but USA is vast too (yet has a short constitution). The real factor is **diversity** — diversified people = diversified aspirations = more provisions needed to cater to all sections. |
| 3 | **Single Constitution** | Unlike USA's dual constitution model (one at centre + one per state), India chose a **single constitution** covering Centre, States, and (after 73rd & 74th Amendments) Local Government — all three tiers under one document. |
| 4 | **Legal Luminaries** | Most Constituent Assembly members were lawyers. A lawyer's job = convert subjective situations into objective reality through detailed definitions. This lawyerly mindset produced extensive sub-clauses. *"A document made by lawyers, for lawyers."* — Shakespeare: *"For justice to be there, kill all the lawyers."* |

---

sections.heading: Feature ② — Blend of Rigidity & Flexibility
sections.content:
*   At **certain parts** of the Constitution, amendment requires a **complex process** involving more than one institution (rigid — e.g., requiring state ratification under [Art. 368](file:///c:/Users/nitee/OneDrive/Desktop/UPSE_Syllabus/Articles/Article_368.md)).
*   At **most places**, amendment uses a **simple process** involving only Parliament by special majority (flexible).
*   Hence, our Constitution is a **blend** of rigidity and flexibility — not purely one or the other.

---

sections.heading: Feature ③ — Neither Parliamentary Sovereignty nor Judicial Supremacy → Constitutional Supremacy with Checks & Balances
sections.content:
> [!IMPORTANT]
> This was a **favourite UPSC question** for ~10 years. Understand the distinction between Supremacy (comparative) vs. Sovereignty (absolute).

sections.heading: Two Models We Rejected
sections.content:
| Model | Country | Who is Most Powerful? | Type of Term |
|-------|---------|----------------------|-------------|
| **Judicial Supremacy** | USA (Written) | **Judiciary** — can question both L and E via Judicial Review | **Supremacy** = comparative (more powerful than the other two) |
| **Parliamentary Sovereignty** | UK (Unwritten) | **Parliament** — all-powerful; can do anything except change a man to a woman (i.e., except challenging nature) | **Sovereignty** = absolute (all-powerful, not just comparatively) |

sections.heading: Key Definitions
sections.content:
*   **Parliamentary Sovereignty** = The **primacy of Parliament in the law-making domain** in comparison to the other two organs (Judiciary & Executive). In the law-making domain, Parliament's laws have more legitimacy, more acceptance, more primacy than laws made by Executive or Judiciary.
*   **Supremacy** = a **comparative** term (more powerful *than* others).
*   **Sovereignty** = an **absolute** term (all-powerful in itself). Used for territorial entities (India is sovereign, not India is supreme).

sections.heading: India's Model: Constitutional Supremacy with Checks & Balances
sections.content:
*   India rejected both the US and UK models. We wanted **neither** one organ to be burdened with excessive power, **nor** one organ to be so powerful it cannot be questioned.
*   In India, **all three organs** (L, E, J) are placed on the **same pedestal** — none is more powerful than the other two.
*   All three derive their power from a **single source: the Constitution of India** → hence **Constitutional Supremacy**.
*   Additionally, **each organ checks the other two** → hence **Checks & Balances**.

> [!NOTE]
> Why not "Constitutional Sovereignty"? Because sovereignty belongs to **"We the People of India"** (Preamble). The Constitution derives its authority FROM the people. Also, sovereignty as a term is used for territorial entities (countries), not documents.

---

sections.heading: Feature ④ — Single Citizenship
sections.content:
*   The Constitution defines the **relationship between the State and its people** → that relationship is **Citizenship**.
*   In India, there is a **single political identity**: **Citizen of India**.
*   **No model of dual citizenship** — **neither internal nor external**:
    *   *No internal dual citizenship:* Unlike USA (where you are a citizen of both the US and your state, e.g., citizen of California), India does not recognize state-level citizenship. You are NOT a "citizen of Gujarat" or "citizen of Tamil Nadu."
    *   *No external dual citizenship:* Unlike many European countries, you cannot hold citizenship of India and another country simultaneously.
*   Irrespective of multiple social identities (caste, class, race, religion, state of origin), there is only **one political identity** for the State vis-à-vis its people: **Citizen of India**.

sections.heading: Update — 9 September 2026 (Test 1 — borrowed features + Assembly machinery)
sections.content:
Test extras on this class note. **No extra Day-1.**

**Answer drop (GS-2 salient features / “borrowed but Indian”):** India took the **parliamentary** engine, **FPTP**, **rule of law**, **Speaker** and **lawmaking** from **Britain**, but **single** citizenship (not the US dual model). **Fundamental Rights**, **judicial review** and **independence of the judiciary** are **US**. **DPSP** is **Irish** — do not park it on Canada. **Canada** is the **strong-Centre federation** plus **residual powers**. Preamble **Liberty, Equality, Fraternity** is **French**. **Concurrent List** is **Australian**; **Fundamental Duties** are **USSR**. Close the paragraph: borrowed bricks, Indian architecture (GOI Act 1935 + diversity + one Constitution + lawyers’ drafting).

**Drafting Committee (7):** Ambedkar (Chair), N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, K.M. Munshi, **Syed Mohammad Saadullah**, **N. Madhava Rau** (replaced B.L. Mitter), T.T. Krishnamachari (replaced D.P. Khaitan). **Not** Gopinath Bardoloi. **Not** J.B. Kripalani.

**Constituent Assembly lock:** seal = **elephant**, not lion. Constitutional Advisor = **B.N. Rau**. Chief draftsman = **S.N. Mukherjee**. Calligraphy / decoration = **Nandalal Bose** (Shantiniketan).
