sections.heading: 1. Strategy — The "How" of UPSC
sections.content:
> The "What" is never the difficult question. The difficult question is the **How**.

- You must develop your **own strategy** — a road map from A (today) to B (La Paz = selection).
- Create a **Strategy Page** → paste it on the wall → review it on the **last day of every month** (15 min self-evaluation).
- Every time you receive an advice (teacher, topper talk, cousin), **write it on the Strategy Page**.

sections.heading: 2. Four Non-Negotiable Daily Priorities (Discipline Building)
sections.content:
These 4 activities are **first priority** — do them **every single day**, no matter what:

| # | Activity | Details |
|---|----------|---------|
| 1 | **Read the News** | Paper / digital — first priority; cannot sleep without doing this; if you skip 5–6 days, you pile up a monster; initially 2–3 hours is okay |
| 2 | **Attend All Classes** | Build discipline; don't bunk even if subject seems boring |
| 3 | **Revise the Same Day** | Revise = complete the topic (class notes + handouts + book + PYQs); not just re-reading |
| 4 | **Read in Advance** | Read the next day's topic beforehand; go **ahead** of the class, not behind it |

> **Key Insight:** If you can do only these 4 and nothing else, you are still making progress. First gear must be right.

sections.heading: 3. Build Command — Knowledge → Understanding → Application → Analysis → Synthesis → Success
sections.content:
```
Knowledge → Understanding → Apply → Analysis → Synthesis → Success
     ↓              ↓                                    ↓
  Prelims        Prelims                              Essay
              (mostly)                              (Mains)
```

- **Prelims** ≈ Understanding + little Knowledge (15–20 questions are pure knowledge; rest are understanding-based)
- **Mains** ≈ Application + Analysis + Synthesis
- **Essay** = Synthesis of all subjects (no History, Geography, Polity silos — everything is connected)
- **Example of Synthesis:** Dandi March (History) + Right to Walk on Footpath = Fundamental Right (Polity, 2026 SC judgment)

---

sections.heading: Part B — Sources for Polity
sections.content:
| # | Source | Nature | Notes |
|---|--------|--------|-------|
| 1 | **Constitution of India (COI)** — Actual text | **Reference** (most authentic source) | Download from india.gov.in; any version/language; always have it accessible; author (jokingly): Dr. Ambedkar |
| 2 | **Textbook** — Yellow Book (Vajiram) | **Textbook** (read page 1 to last page, 5 times) | Written with flow → useful for Mains answer writing |
|   | **Laxmikant** (Blue Book) | **Textbook** | Great for Prelims; pinpointed info; practically useless for Mains |
| 3 | **Class Notes** | Notes from class | Write everything |
| 4 | **NCERT** — Class 11 & 12 | **Base building** | Class 11: Political Theory; Class 12: Indian Constitution at Work; go back to Class 8 → Class 6 if needed |
| 5 | **Current Affairs** | Ongoing | Link with static topics |

sections.heading: Gap-Filling Approach (Two-Book Strategy)
sections.content:
1. **Start with Book A** (recommended: Yellow Book for non-FOMO candidates; Laxmikant for FOMO candidates).
2. After finishing one chapter in Book A → Open same topic in **Book B**.
3. Flip through headings → cross out what's already covered → **assimilate additional info** (recent judgments, analysis, events) into Book A.
4. **Bare minimum:** At least read ONE book. Better to read one than none.

---

sections.heading: Two Fundamental Questions for Building Understanding:
sections.content:
| Question | Purpose | Natural/Active? |
|----------|---------|-----------------|
| **"What is ___?"** | Define the concept | Natural for new words; requires **active effort** for familiar words |
| **"Why ___?"** | Understand the reason/purpose | Kids ask this naturally; adults must force this curiosity |

> **Key Skill:** Focus on **words** — terms, terminologies, ideas. Don't assume you know just because the word is familiar.

sections.heading: Demonstrated Examples from Class:
sections.content:
| Word | Common Answer | Problem | Deeper Understanding |
|------|--------------|---------|---------------------|
| What is Constitution? | "Supreme law of the land" / "Set of laws" | — Not universal (UK has no "supreme law"); IPC is also law but not Constitution | Purpose = **to limit the powers of government** (constitutionalism) |
| Why Constitution? | Often re-answers "what" | Students conflate "what" and "why" | **Limited Government** — UK 1215 AD: Magna Carta (Great Charter); King John → free men revolted → document limiting King's powers → modern equivalent: controlling government |
| What is Polity? | "Art of governing state" | Mugged-up definition | System of rules & regulations used to **implement policy** — the HOW of governance |
| What is Politics? | "Struggle for power" (NCERT) | Surface-level | Power to do what? → **Distribution of resources**; "Who gets what, when, and where"; Example: Bullet train Mumbai–Ahmedabad (not Varanasi–Patna) — someone decided that |
| Polity vs Politics | Often confused | — | Politics = WHAT to do (decision-making, policy); Polity = HOW to do it (system, machinery, implementation) |
| What is Government? | "Make policies" / "Ruling" | Incomplete | **Any organization** (India, Delhi Police, Vajiram, your family, even you individually) that performs 3 functions: (1) Goal-setting, (2) Execution, (3) Corrective Action |

> **Polity = It is a system of rules & regulations used to implement policy.**

---

sections.heading: Top-Level Architecture
sections.content:
| Component | Numbering System | Count | Details |
|-----------|-----------------|-------|---------|
| **Parts** | Roman numerals (I, II, III…) | **25 total** (numbered till XXII; 3 extra: 9A, 9B, 14A etc.) | Major divisions |
| **Schedules** | Words (First, Second… Twelfth) | **12** (original 8 + 4 added) | Supplementary provisions |
| **Chapters** | Within Parts (may or may not exist) | Varies | Sub-divisions of Parts |
| **Articles** | Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3…) | Numbered till **395** (total count is more due to sub-articles like 21A) | Smallest self-contained provision |
| **Clauses** | Circular brackets → (1), (2), (a), (b) | Within Articles | Further breakdown |
| **Sub-clauses** | Nested brackets | Within Clauses | Further sub-division |

> **Article** = The smallest self-contained provision of the Constitution.

sections.heading: Logical Flow of Parts
sections.content:
| Part | Content | Logic |
|------|---------|-------|
| Part I | **Union & its Territory** | Define WHAT is India (geography) |
| Part II | **Citizenship** | Define WHO are the people of India |
| Part III | **Fundamental Rights** | Constitution GIVES rights to people |
| Part IV | **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)** | Government WILL give more with time |
| Part IVA | **Fundamental Duties** | People must give something in RETURN |
| **Part V** | **The Union (Government)** | Define the government at the TOP |
| Part VI | **The States** | Government at next level down |
| … | … | Continues logically |
| Part XIV | **Services under the Union & States** | Civil servants (servant quarters — at the back!) |

> **Learning Strategy:** Always go **Top → Down** (forest first, then trees). Never start bottom-up from individual articles.

---

sections.heading: Structure of Part V — Chapters
sections.content:
| Chapter | Subject | Equivalent in Part VI (States) |
|---------|---------|-------------------------------|
| **Ch. 1** | **Executive** | State Executive (Governor) |
| **Ch. 2** | **Legislature** (Parliament) | State Legislature |
| **Ch. 3** | **Legislative Powers of President** (Ordinances) | Legislative Powers of Governor |
| **Ch. 4** | **Judiciary** (Supreme Court) | High Courts |
| Ch. 5 | Comptroller & Auditor General (CAG) | — |
| Ch. 6 | — | — |

sections.heading: Three Functions of Government (Governance = Goal + Execution + Correction)
sections.content:
| Function | Wing | Role |
|----------|------|------|
| **Goal-setting** (What to do) | **Legislature** | Make laws, set policy direction |
| **Execution** (Doing it) | **Executive** | Implement laws, day-to-day governance |
| **Corrective Action** (Fixing mistakes) | **Judiciary** | Interpret laws, check violations |

> Government = Whoever performs these 3 functions for an organization. Not limited to territorial context.

sections.heading: Two Meanings of "Government"
sections.content:
1. **Broad/Technical:** All three — Legislature + Executive + Judiciary
2. **Common/Practical:** Only the Executive (what comes to mind when we say "Government of India" — PM, Modi, etc.)
3. **Contextual:** In newspaper: "SC directed the government" → means judiciary directed the **executive**

---

sections.heading: Hierarchy of Union Executive
sections.content:
| Position | Constitutional Reference | Notes |
|----------|------------------------|-------|
| **President** | Art. 52, 53 | Head/Big Boss — top of the hierarchy |
| **Vice President** | — | "Useless boss" — no independent salary; gets paid as ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha |
| **PM + Council of Ministers** | — | Real Boss — PM is part of CoM |
| **Attorney General of India (AGI)** | — | Law officer / Lawyer of the government; part of executive team |

> **Civil Servants** (You!) → Part XIV (servant quarters, behind the house) — Policy implementation, NOT policy making. Master decides rice/jeera rice → servant decides how much jeera, flame, water, salt.

sections.heading: Prohibitory Orders — Section 163 BNSS / Section 144 CrPC (Example)
sections.content:
- **Who issues?**
  - In **Commissionerate system** (e.g., Delhi): ACP (police officer, DANIPS — Delhi, Andaman & Nicobar Islands Police Service — Group B)
  - In **IG system** (rest of India): District Magistrate / SDM (IAS officer)
- **S-163 BNSS** replaced **S-144 CrPC** (old law)
- Police cannot use weapons without orders → order flows down the hierarchy
- Crowd management example (Bangladesh protests) → Administration's job = control (not dialogue/politics)

---

sections.heading: Article 52 — Existence
sections.content:
> "There **shall** be a President of India."
- Mandatory office; not optional
- Current President: **Droupadi Murmu**

sections.heading: Article 53(1) — Executive Power
sections.content: > "The executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President and shall be exercised by him either **directly** or through officers **subordinate** to him in accordance with this Constitution."

sections.heading: Key Derivations from Art. 53:
sections.content:
| Point | Explanation |
|-------|-------------|
| President = **Head of Union Executive** | Like CEO of a company; no one has more power above |
| Power is **vested** in President | All executive power belongs to President constitutionally |
| Can act **directly** or through **subordinates** | Constitution gives both options; "directly" is listed first |
| **In practice:** Acts only through subordinates | President acts on **aid and advice of Council of Ministers** (Art. 74); WHY → will be covered in next 2 classes |
| All executive decisions taken **in the name of President** | Officers exercise delegated power → it remains President's power → decisions bear President's name |
| PM is NOT the head | PM is powerful practically, but constitutionally not even second in line; HEAD = President |

sections.heading: Powers of the President
sections.content: > **Task:** Read the full list of powers by self (Swadhyay) from your textbook before next class. Write them as a numbered list (1, 2, 3… ~20 powers).

sections.heading: Election of the President
sections.content: > **PYQ Alert!** Presidential election years: 2012, 2017, 2022 → question appeared on election of President in all three years. **Next election: 2027** (July) — exam also in May 2027. High-priority topic!

sections.heading: Article 58 — Eligibility Conditions
sections.content:
| # | Condition | Detail |
|---|-----------|--------|
| 1 | **Citizen of India** | Requirement for all constitutional offices |
| 2 | **Age ≥ 35 years** | "Completed the age of 35 years" → means **35 or above** (not "more than 35") |
| 3 | **Eligible to be a member of Lok Sabha** | NOT Rajya Sabha — WHY? (Question to think about; books won't tell you directly) |
| 4 | **Must NOT hold any office of profit** under Union / State / Local government | Cannot be serving in a government job |

> **Focus on words BEFORE and AFTER the factual number.** Everyone remembers "35" but the key is "completed the age of" — meaning ≥ 35. In exam, you can't change your answer — come back next year.

sections.content:
| # | Task | Details |

| 2 | **Download COI** | From india.gov.in → have it on phone/book at all times |

sections.heading: Important Terms & Definitions
sections.content:
| Term | Definition / Meaning |
|------|---------------------|
| **Polity** | A system of rules & regulations used to implement policy |
| **Politics** | Struggle for power → power to distribute resources → "Who gets what, when, and where" |
| **Constitution** | Set of rules to **limit the powers of the government** (constitutionalism) |
| **Constitutionalism** | The belief/practice of being governed by a constitution; limiting government power |
| **Government** | Whoever performs 3 functions for an organization: Goal-setting, Execution, Corrective Action |
| **Article** | Smallest self-contained provision of the Constitution |
| **Clause** | Sub-division of an Article (marked by circular brackets) |
| **Magna Carta** | "The Great Charter" — 1215 AD, UK — first document limiting King's powers; oldest constitution |
| **BNSS** | Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (replaced CrPC) |
| **DANIPS** | Delhi, Andaman & Nicobar Islands Police Service (Group B) |
| **Ex-officio** | By virtue of holding another office (e.g., VP is ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha) |
| **Synthesis** | Ability to connect knowledge from different subjects into a unified understanding |

sections.heading: Lecture 2 — President of India
sections.content:
> **Source:** Vajiram & Ravi — Polity Class Lecture 02 (Abhey Kumar) + Handwritten Notes  
> **Date:** 14 August 2026  
> **Last Updated:** 2026-08-14

---

sections.heading: Origin — Separation of Powers (SoP)
sections.content:
- **Legislature controls Executive** → Legislature must NOT come under Executive's control
- Members of Parliament should **not hold any office of profit under the Government**
- "Under the Government" = under the Executive → **Executive posts are offices of profit**
- **Rule of Thumb:** Is the post an executive post? → If yes, it is an Office of Profit

sections.heading: Key Clarification — Is the President an Office of Profit?
sections.content:
- **Yes.** President = Head of the Executive → biggest executive office in India
- Art 59(2): President "shall not hold any **other** office of profit" → The word **"other"** proves the President's office is itself an OOP
- This distinction is critical:
  - **For candidates (Art 58):** Shall not hold **any** office of profit
  - **For sitting President (Art 59):** Shall not hold **any other** office of profit

> **Key Insight:** If exceptions are given (Art 58), it means the offices ARE OOP. Otherwise, why would exceptions be needed?

sections.heading: Session Start at Parliament
sections.content:
- **11:00 AM** — Session begins → **Question Hour** (Q&A)
- **12:00 PM** — Zero Hour (also Q&A)
- Most parliamentary time = Executive accountability (asking questions), NOT law-making
- Legislature's primary function = **keeping a check on the Executive** (accountability)
- Law-making is one part of this larger accountability function

---

sections.heading: Basic Qualifications:
sections.content:
1. Citizen of India
2. Minimum age: **35 years**
3. Eligible to become a member of Lok Sabha
4. Should not hold any **office of profit under the Government**

sections.heading: Four Exceptions to OOP Rule (Art 58):
sections.content:
| # | Exception | Logic |
|---|-----------|-------|
| 1 | **President** (sitting) | Re-election allowed; already holds OOP but exempted |
| 2 | **Vice President** | Like a promotion; VP is also executive but exempted |
| 3 | **Governor** of any State | Similar executive head; allowed to become President |
| 4 | **Any Minister** (Central or State) | Any minister of any level is exempted |

> **Trap:** Exception is given BECAUSE they ARE offices of profit. Exception ≠ "Not OOP." Exception = "OOP but allowed anyway."
> This exception is **ONLY for the election of President** — not for any other purpose.

sections.heading: Application Examples:
sections.content:
- **Can PM Narendra Modi contest for President?** → **Yes.** He is a Minister (PM), exempted under Art 58.
- **Can Rahul Gandhi (LoP) contest?** → **Yes.** He is NOT executive; just a member of Parliament. No issue at all. If he wins, his Lok Sabha seat **auto-vacates** on taking oath as President (Condition under Art 59, not eligibility).

---

sections.heading: 3. Conditions of Office of President — Article 59
sections.content: > **Eligibility vs. Conditions:** Eligibility = to contest the election. Conditions = after becoming President.

sections.heading: Key Conditions (Art 59):
sections.content:
1. **Shall not hold any other office of profit** (Clause 2) → Proves President's own office IS an OOP
2. **Shall not be a member of any legislature** — Parliament or State Legislature
   - If an MP/MLA wins presidential election → seat **auto-vacates** on taking oath (not resignation, not disqualification — **automatic**)

---

sections.heading: 4. Returning Officers (RO)
sections.content:
| Election | Returning Officer |
|----------|-------------------|
| **Lok Sabha election** | District Magistrate (DM) |
| **State Assembly election** | Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM) |
| **Presidential election** | Secretary General of **RS/LS** (turn by turn) |

- Last election (2022): Rajya Sabha Secretary General was RO
- Next election (2027): Logically → Lok Sabha Secretary General

---

sections.heading: 5A. Electoral College of President (Art 54)
sections.content:
**Members of Electoral College:**
- **Elected** MPs (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha)
- **Elected** MLAs of States

> **Critical Keywords:**
> - **"Elected"** — Nominated members of RS/Puducherry Assembly do NOT vote (no link to "people of India")
> - **MLCs excluded** — Not elected by the people (elected by special groups — teachers, graduates, etc.)
> - Only **MLAs** from state legislatures are included (not MLCs)

sections.heading: Union Territories & Electoral College:
sections.content:
| UT | Participates? | How? |
|----|---------------|------|
| **Delhi** | ✅ Yes | 70th Constitutional Amendment Act, **1992** |
| **Puducherry** | ✅ Yes | 70th CAA, 1992 |
| **J&K** | ❌ No (as of 2022 election) | Constitution says only "Delhi & Puducherry"; J&K became UT in 2019 but not added to Art 54 |

- **Original Constitution** said "States" only → UTs didn't exist (UT concept came in **1956** — reorganization)
- Delhi got assembly in **1992** → 70th Amendment added Delhi + Puducherry to Art 54
- J&K: Assembly was dissolved (President's Rule) during 2022 election → no MLAs anyway
- **2027 election:** J&K now has MLAs, but Constitution still doesn't include J&K → **amendment needed** or make J&K a state again, or SC judgment

> **Possible Solutions for J&K (2027):**
> 1. Amend Constitution → add J&K to Art 54
> 2. Make J&K a state again (Omar Abdullah's demand) → automatic inclusion
> 3. SC judgment → spirit of Constitution, representatives of people should vote

---

sections.heading: 5B. Proportional Representation (PR) System
sections.content:
**Two components:**
1. **System** = Proportional Representation
2. **Method** = Single Transferable Vote (STV)

sections.heading: Why "Proportional"?
sections.content:
- Representatives (MPs + MLAs) represent **different populations**
- An MLA representing 200 people should have more vote value than one representing 100
- Vote value is **in proportion to population represented**

sections.heading: First Assumption: MPs and MLAs are Equal as Groups
sections.content:
- Both groups represent the **same people of India** (largely)
- Exception: Chandigarh has an MP but no MLA → not exactly same people
- But **fair assumption** → no better alternative
- Also justified because President has **dual role**: Head of the Union (MPs participate) + Head of State/Federal Union (MLAs participate)

sections.heading: 5C. Value of Vote of MLA
sections.content:
**Formula:**
```
Value of Vote of 1 MLA = Population of State / (No. of Elected MLAs × 1000)
```

- **Population** = as per **1971 Census** (frozen until first census after 2026)
- ÷ 1000 → simplifies calculation; doesn't change proportion
- Originally: last available census was used (1951 → 1961 → 1971)
- **Frozen at 1971** → to prevent rewarding states with high population growth (poor governance) and punishing states with good family planning (good governance)
  - North India = faster population growth → value would keep increasing
  - South India + NE = controlled population → value would stagnate
  - Freezing = fairness to southern & NE states

> **Until when frozen?** → Until **first census AFTER 2026** (not "until 2026")
> - Census 2021 started late (COVID), reference date = **1 March 2027**
> - So next year's (2027) election will STILL use **1971 census** (data not available yet)
> - Delimitation dispute (Vijay et al.) = related but different issue

sections.heading: Update — 10 September 2026 (UPSC CSE Prelims 2023)
sections.content:
`CSE-2023-Q80` **missed** (`MST-071`). How many statements = **only two** (3 and 4):

| Statement | Hold? |
|:---|:---|
| 1. Nominated MPs / MLAs also in the Electoral College | **No.** Art 54 = **elected** only (articles tab held this). |
| 2. Higher elective Assembly seats → higher vote value of **each** MLA | **No.** Value = **population / elected seats** (÷ 1000). More seats **lower** each MLA’s value if population is similar. |
| 3. MLA vote of Madhya Pradesh **>** Kerala | **Yes** (UPSC key). |
| 4. Puducherry MLA value **>** Arunachal because population / elective seats is greater | **Yes** — that **is** the formula. |

He picked **only three** — the extra tick is statement 2.

sections.heading: Update — 11 September 2026 (Ghost Recall)
sections.content: `MST-071` **held**: nominated MPs/MLAs **out**; MLA vote value **will not increase**. Formula lock: **Population / (elected MLAs × 1000)**. Mechanism: more seats sit in the **denominator**. The **1971 census freeze** is a different lock (the **numerator** does not grow).

sections.heading: Real Values (2022 Election):
sections.content:
| State | MLA Vote Value | Notes |
|-------|---------------|-------|
| **UP** (highest) | **208** | 403 MLAs |
| **Sikkim** (lowest) | **7** | 32 MLAs |
| **Jharkhand = Tamil Nadu** | Equal | Ratio works out same |

> **Key Questions & Answers:**
> - Two MLAs from **same state** → Equal value? **Yes** (assumption within state)
> - Two MLAs from **different states** → Always unequal? **Not necessarily** (may be equal, e.g. JH = TN)
> - Total value of all 32 Sikkim MLAs (32 × 7 = 224) ≈ Value of 1 UP MLA (208)

sections.heading: 5D. Value of Vote of MP
sections.content:
**Assumption:** All elected MPs are **equal** (within Parliament → same house → same people of India → no discrimination)

**Formula:**
```
Value of Vote of 1 MP = Total Value of Votes of All Elected MLAs / No. of Elected MPs
```

- Total MLA votes ≈ 5,43,000 → Total Electoral College value ≈ 10,86,000
- MP value (2022 election) = **700**

**Why indirect method?**
- Cannot calculate MP value directly from population → would make MPs unequal
- First calculate all MLA values → sum them → equate to total MP value → divide equally
- This ensures: Total MLA votes = Total MP votes (both groups equal in aggregate)

> **MP value is always higher than MLA value of same state** → MP constituency is larger (more population) than MLA constituency

---

sections.heading: 5E. Single Transferable Vote (STV) — The Method
sections.content: Also called: **Preferential Voting System / Order of Choice System**

sections.heading: How It Works:
sections.content:
1. **Ballot Paper:** Candidates listed (A, B, C, D...) → Voters write preference numbers (1st, 2nd, 3rd...)
2. **Secret Ballot** — like all elections (exception: Rajya Sabha election = open ballot)
3. Preferences written in **any Indian language** (must write, no thumb impression)
4. **Minimum preferences:** 1 → **Maximum:** Number of candidates (not mandatory to exhaust all)

sections.heading: Winning Condition:
sections.content:
- **Majority of valid votes polled** → i.e., >50% of actual votes cast (not total members)
- If 100 members, 5 don't vote → need majority of 95 (i.e., 48+)

sections.heading: Counting Process:
sections.content:
1. **Round 1:** Count **first preferences** only
   - Value of ballot = value of that voter's vote (e.g., UP MLA = 208, not 1)
   - If someone gets majority → **Winner declared**
2. **If no majority → Round 2:**
   - **Least preferred** candidate **eliminated**
   - Their ballots reopened → look at **next available preference**
   - Transfer vote value to next preferred candidate still in race
   - If no next preference available → ballot set aside
3. **Repeat** until:
   - Someone achieves majority, OR
   - Only **one candidate left** (wins even without majority)

sections.heading: STV Example (Simplified: 100 members, value = 1 each):
sections.content:
```
Round 1:  A=40, B=30, C=20, D=10 → No majority (need 51+)
          D eliminated → 10 ballots reopened → 6 to A, 2 to B, 2 to C
Round 2:  A=46, B=32, C=22 → Still no majority
          C eliminated → 22 ballots reopened → transfer by next preference
Round 3:  Continue until majority or 1 candidate left
```

sections.heading: Why STV?
sections.content:
- Elects the **most preferred** candidate (not just plurality winner)
- Unlike FPTP (Lok Sabha): candidate with 40% can win even if 60% hate them
- In STV: preferences ensure broader acceptability

sections.heading: Historical Facts:
sections.content:
| Event | Year | Details |
|-------|------|---------|
| **Only 2nd round of counting** | **1969** | V.V. Giri (Varahagiri Venkata Giri) became President |
| **Elected unopposed** | **1977** | Neelam Sanjiva Reddy — no other candidate |
| All other elections | — | Winner declared in 1st round itself |

---

sections.heading: Principle: There is a term → Two possibilities
sections.content:
**Term of President = 5 years**

| Scenario | When is election held? |
|----------|----------------------|
| **Term completed** | Election held **BEFORE** completion of term |
| **Term NOT completed (Vacancy)** | Election held **AFTER** vacancy, **within 6 months** |

sections.heading: New President takes oath on the **next day** of outgoing President
sections.content: - Unlike PM (PM takes oath before the outgoing PM's term ends)

sections.heading: Vacancy = only 3 things:
sections.content:
1. **Death** (e.g., Zakir Hussain — 1969, Fakhruddin Ali Ahmad)
2. **Resignation**
3. **Removal** (Impeachment / Court order)

> Nothing else can happen. Either complete the term or one of these three. Be convinced — no fourth possibility.

---

sections.heading: Succession Order:
sections.content:
| Priority | Who? | Role |
|----------|------|------|
| 1st | **Vice President** | Acting President (NOT President) |
| 2nd | **Chief Justice of India (CJI)** | If VP also unavailable |
| 3rd | **Senior-most Judge of SC** | If CJI also unavailable (37 judges available) |

sections.heading: Vice President's Dual Role:
sections.content:
- **Primary purpose:** Backup for President (that's why the office was created)
- **Secondary (routine):** Ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha
  - **Ex-officio** = "by virtue of the office" → whoever is VP automatically gets RS chairmanship
  - No separate appointment needed; if VP changes, RS Chairman changes automatically
- VP salary: Gets salary as **Chairman of RS** (no separate VP salary); when acting as President → gets **President's salary**
- When VP acts as President → **Deputy Chairman of RS** handles RS

sections.heading: Historical Usage of Backup:
sections.content:
- Only **2 Presidents died in office** (Zakir Hussain 1969, Fakhruddin Ali Ahmad)
- Total backup usage ≈ **1 year** out of ~80 years → "very useless backup"
- 1969: Justice **M. Hidayatullah** (CJI) was Acting President briefly (V.V. Giri had resigned as VP to contest)

---

sections.heading: Key Provisions:
sections.content:
1. **Only Supreme Court** can hear and dispose disputes (highest office → highest court; High Courts have NO role)
2. Applies to both **President and Vice President** elections

sections.heading: If SC Invalidates the Election:
sections.content: - All decisions taken and **completed prior** to invalidation → **NOT invalid for this reason alone** - Invalidation is **prospective** (from now onwards), NOT retrospective - **Principle:** What happened, happened. Now it won't happen. - Same principle as triple talaq invalidation, any law struck down, etc. - **Article 71(2) Text:** "If the election of a person as President or Vice-President is declared void by the Supreme Court, acts done by him in the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of the office of President or Vice-President, as the case may be, on or before the date of the decision of the Supreme Court shall not be invalidated by reason of that declaration."

sections.heading: Cannot Dispute on Ground of:
sections.content:
- **Vacancy in Electoral College** — some MLA/MP died/resigned → doesn't matter
- President is the highest office → can't remain vacant for such operational issues
- Election will happen regardless

sections.heading: Who Can Dispute?
sections.content:
- **Principle (applies to ALL elections):** Only **interested parties** can dispute
  - = **Voters** of that election + **Candidates** of that election
  - For President: Members of **Electoral College** + Candidates
  - Random citizen CANNOT challenge (you didn't vote directly)
  - Even PM's Lok Sabha election → only voters of that constituency + candidates of that constituency

sections.heading: Governing Law:
sections.content:
- **Presidential and Vice Presidential Elections Act, 1952**
  - "Act" (capital A) followed by year = statute/legislative act of Parliament

---

sections.heading: 9. Impeachment of President — Article 61
sections.content:
- **Never happened** in India → no case law, no interpretation, no real examples
- Simple process → read from Constitution/handout directly
- Will be connected indirectly to other topics later

---

sections.heading: Journey of a Bill:
sections.content:
```
Bill (Proposal of Law)
  → Parliament (Both Houses pass it)
    → President (Assent)
      → Act (Law)
        → Notified in Gazette (Rajpatra)
          → Enforceable
```

- **Gazette (Rajpatra)** = official mode of government communication
  - Contains: notifications, orders, names of gazetted officers, Acts
  - Unless notified in Gazette → Act exists but is NOT enforceable

sections.heading: Veto = Power of Chief Executive to prevent enactment of legislation, either temporarily or permanently
sections.content:
- Not a word in the Constitution — a scholarly/academic term

---

sections.heading: 10A. Types of Bills (Classification by Subject Matter)
sections.content:
| Type | Definition | Key Points |
|------|-----------|------------|
| **Ordinary Bill** | Bill that is NOT money, NOT financial, NOT constitutional amendment | Defined by exclusion; "ordinary things have no definition" |
| **Money Bill** | Bill dealing **ONLY** with money matters | Keyword: **ONLY** money. Defined in Art 110 |
| **Financial Bill** | Bill dealing with money **AND** non-money matters | Money + Ordinary combined |
| **Constitutional Amendment (CA) Bill** | Bill that amends Constitution **under Article 368** | Keyword: **under Art 368**. Ordinary bills can also amend Constitution (e.g., Art 3 — rename state) |

> **Critical Distinctions:**
> - **Money Bill** = category, not an actual bill name. Actual bills: Appropriation Bill (expenditure), Finance Bill (revenue/taxation)
> - **Budget = 2 Money Bills:** Appropriation Bill + Finance Bill
> - **Appropriation** = allocation of funds for spending (not just "expenditure")
> - **Finance Bill ≠ Financial Bill** — Finance Bill = revenue/tax proposal (money bill); Financial Bill = a category (money + non-money)
> - "Money bill" and "financial bill" are **categories** → no bill becomes "Money Act" or "Financial Act"

sections.heading: 10B. President's Three Choices (Art 111)
sections.content:
When a bill is presented for assent, President has **3 choices** (first time):

| Choice | Action | Effect | Type of Veto |
|--------|--------|--------|-------------|
| 1 | **Declare Assent** | Bill → Act | No veto |
| 2 | **Withhold Assent** | Bill **dies** — comes to an end permanently | **Absolute Veto** |
| 3 | **Return for Reconsideration** | Bill sent back to Parliament with/without recommendations | **Suspensive Veto** |

---

sections.heading: 10C. Absolute Veto (Withholding Assent)
sections.content:
**What it means:**
- President says **NO** → Bill is **dead**. Permanently finished. No revival.
- "Withholding **assent**" (NOT "withholding the bill") — Assent is President's to withhold; Bill is Parliament's
- **No = No.** Move on. Make a new proposal.

**Four-Point Framework:**

| Aspect | Answer |
|--------|--------|
| **What does it do?** | Brings the bill to a **permanent end** |
| **On whose advice?** | **Advice of Council of Ministers** (President doesn't act on own here) |
| **Which bills?** | Ordinary ✅ Money ✅ Financial ✅ CA Bill ❌ |
| **Examples** | PEPSU Appropriation Bill, 1954 (Rajendra Prasad) + Salaries/Allowances/Pension of MP Amendment Bill, 1991 (R. Venkataraman) |

> **Major Misconception Debunked:**
> - Many books/sources wrongly say "money bills cannot be rejected"
> - **BOTH examples of absolute veto in India are MONEY BILLS:**
>   - PEPSU Appropriation Bill (1954) = expenditure bill = **money bill**
>   - MP Salaries Bill (1991) = salary/allowance = **money bill**
> - **Money bills CAN be rejected.** Generally President gives assent (because COM recommended the bill in the first place), but rejection is legally possible.

**Why generally assent to money bills?**
- Money bill requires **President's recommendation** to introduce (Art 110)
- President's recommendation = Council of Ministers' recommendation
- Same COM unlikely to later advise rejection
- But: Government can change, private member's bill possible, etc.

---

sections.heading: 10D. Suspensive Veto (Return for Reconsideration)
sections.content: **What it means:** - President returns bill to Parliament with recommendations/suggestions - Parliament may accept, modify, or ignore recommendations - If Parliament passes bill **second time** (with or without changes) → President **SHALL declare assent** (no choice) - Effect: **Delay** + opportunity for reconsideration, discourse, media attention **Four-Point Framework:** | Aspect | Answer | |--------|--------| | **What does it do?** | **Delays** enactment; cannot permanently kill the bill | | **On whose advice?** | **Own discretion** (understood, not written) — President's own suggestions/wisdom | | **Which bills?** | Ordinary ✅ Financial ✅ Money ❌ (can't delay money) CA Bill ❌ | | **Example** | MP Prevention of Disqualification Amendment Bill, **2006** (Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam returned; Parliament re-passed without changes → Kalam gave assent) | > **2006 Case — Sonia Gandhi & NAC:** > - NAC (National Advisory Council) chairperson = Sonia Gandhi (MP) > - Allegation: NAC chair = Office of Profit → Sonia would be disqualified as MP > - Congress govt passed bill adding NAC chair to exempted list → Dr. Kalam returned it > - Parliament re-passed same bill without changing a single comma → Kalam had to give assent > - Significance: Kalam's principled stand got recorded in history; discourse happened **Why no suspensive veto on Money Bills?** - Money bills deal with government's immediate financial needs → delay not allowed - President must decide: either give assent or withhold (reject) — no return option - **UPSC Trap Mandate (Article 111 Proviso):** The proviso to Article 111 explicitly states that the President may return the bill *"if it is not a Money Bill"*. Therefore, the President has **NO power to return a Money Bill for reconsideration** under any circumstances. If a Money Bill is presented, the President can only give Assent or Withhold Assent. ---

sections.heading: 10E. Pocket Veto (No Time Limit to Choose)
sections.content:
- Constitution gives **no time limit** for President to make a choice
- If President simply **does not choose** (neither assent, nor withhold, nor return) → bill stays in "pocket"
- **Not written in Constitution** — arises from the absence of a time limit
- Effectively: bill **neither dies nor becomes law** — indefinite limbo

> **To be discussed in Lecture 3** along with Mercy Powers and Constitutional Position of President.

---

sections.heading: 10F. Veto Powers — Applicability Summary Table
sections.content:
| Veto Type | Ordinary Bill | Money Bill | Financial Bill | CA Bill (Art 368) |
|-----------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Absolute** (Withhold Assent) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ (shall assent — 24th CAA, 1971) |
| **Suspensive** (Return) | ✅ | ❌ (no delay) | ✅ | ❌ |
| **Pocket** (No time limit) | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |

> **For CA Bills:** President **shall declare assent** — no choice, no veto. Written in Constitution after **24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971** (earlier it was convention/practice, now mandated written rule).
> **For Money Bills:** Can reject (absolute) but cannot delay (no suspensive/pocket).

---

sections.heading: 11. Key Constitutional Articles — Quick Reference
sections.content:

|---------|---------|

sections.heading: Lecture 3 — Mercy Powers & Constitutional Position of President
sections.content:
> **Source:** Vajiram & Ravi — Polity Class Lecture 03 (Abhey Kumar) + Handwritten Notes + Audio Transcript  
> **Date:** 18 August 2026  
> **Last Updated:** 2026-08-18

---

sections.heading: Recap: How Pocket Veto Arises
sections.content:
- Article 111 gives President **3 choices** (Assent / Withhold / Return) but provides **no time limit** to choose
- If President simply **does not choose** for an indefinite period → bill lies on the table → **Pocket Veto**
- **Not a power to do something** — it is a **power to do nothing**

sections.heading: Pocket Veto = Discretionary Power
sections.content:
- Since it is **not written** in the Constitution, nobody can advise the President to exercise it
- The President is **thinking** which option to choose → discretion of the President
- Applies only to **Ordinary and Financial Bills** (not Money Bills, not CA Bills)
- Both **Suspensive Veto** and **Pocket Veto** are discretionary powers of the President

sections.heading: The Only Example: Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986
sections.content:
| Detail | Fact |
|--------|------|
| **Bill** | Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill |
| **Government** | Rajiv Gandhi (PM) — 424 seats, youngest PM ever |
| **President** | Giani Zail Singh |
| **Year Introduced** | 1986 |
| **Controversial Provision** | Government could legally intercept any postal communication |
| **What Happened** | President kept the bill on the table indefinitely — did nothing |
| **Duration** | ~4 years (1986–1990) |
| **Resolution** | President R. Venkataraman (new President) **returned** the bill in 1990 on advice of PM Chandrashekhar |
| **Parliament's Response** | Never re-passed the bill — it disappeared |

> **Key Insight:** Technically, the final act was a **Suspensive Veto** (return), but the case is cited as the example of **Pocket Veto** because the bill was kept idle for 4 years. Pocket veto has been observed only **once** in Indian history.

sections.heading: Background Context
sections.content:
- 1984 election: Congress won **424 seats** (highest ever majority, even more than present BJP's 240)
- Rajiv Gandhi: Youngest PM, enormous power
- Giani Zail Singh: Old-school, loyal to Indira Gandhi, differences with Rajiv after her assassination
- Bill was widely criticized as an attack on citizens' privacy

sections.heading: Important Distinction: Parliamentary Bills vs State Bills
sections.content:
- SC ruling on pocket veto for **Governor on state bills** = **different** issue (SC said no pocket veto for Governor)
- This case is about **Parliamentary bill coming to President** — completely separate

---

sections.heading: Constitutional Framework
sections.content:
| Article | Authority | Scope |
|---------|-----------|-------|
| **Article 72** | **President** | Union law offences + Court Martial + **Death sentences** (even under State law) |
| **Article 161** | **Governor** | State law offences only |

> **Critical Terminology:** Call them **Mercy Powers** or **Clemency Powers** — NOT "Pardoning Powers" (because pardon is only ONE of the powers). Constitution itself never uses the heading "Pardoning Powers."

sections.heading: Types of Mercy Powers
sections.content:
| Power | What Changes? | Effect | Example |
|-------|--------------|--------|---------|
| **Pardon** | Conviction + Sentence | **Both removed** — person treated as if crime never committed | Rarely used in India; very common in USA (Joe Biden pardoned Hunter Biden, preemptive pardons) |
| **Commutation** | **Nature** of sentence | Substitutes harsher punishment with a lighter one | Death → Life imprisonment |
| **Remission** | **Quantum** of sentence | Reduces the period without changing character | Life → 20 years (then released) |
| **Respite** | Nature **temporarily** | Temporary relaxation of the nature of punishment | Rigorous → Simple imprisonment for 4 weeks (due to injury/pregnancy) |
| **Reprieve** | **Delays execution** | Nothing changed — same punishment, just later | Execution delayed by 3 weeks to allow mercy petition filing |
| **Suspension** | Indefinite delay | Courts suspend sentences on appeal — **not exercised by President/Governor** | Higher court suspends lower court's sentence during appeal |

> **Suspension** is written in Art 72 but practically used only by **courts**, not by President/Governor. It gets covered by reprieve for the executive.

sections.heading: Criminal Justice System — Foundation for Understanding Mercy Powers
Nature of Sentence (Severity Hierarchy — Highest to Lowest)
sections.content:
1. **Capital Punishment** (Death penalty — "hanged by the neck until death")
2. **Imprisonment**
   - **Rigorous Imprisonment (RI)** — hard physical labour required
   - **Simple Imprisonment (SI)** — no hard labour
3. **Fine** (monetary penalty — amount = quantum)
4. **Community Service** (NEW — introduced under BNS/BNSS)
   - e.g., 50 hours at old age home — for petty offences
   - Philosophy: Reform over revenge

> **Life imprisonment = Life** → person dies in jail. NOT 14 years or 20 years. There is NO such thing as "life imprisonment = 14 years."

sections.heading: Key Mapping: Which Power Changes What?
sections.content:
| What Changes | Power Used |
|-------------|-----------|
| Conviction removed + Sentence removed | **Pardon** |
| Nature changed (harsher → lighter) | **Commutation** |
| Quantum reduced (amount/years) | **Remission** |
| Nature changed temporarily | **Respite** |
| Execution delayed (nothing changes) | **Reprieve** |

sections.heading: President vs Governor — Key Differences
sections.content:
| Aspect | President (Art 72) | Governor (Art 161) |
|--------|-------------------|-------------------|
| **Law** | Union law offences | State law offences |
| **Territory** | Anywhere in India | Within the State |
| **Court Martial** | ✅ Yes (Supreme Commander) | ❌ No |
| **Death Penalty** | ✅ Can pardon (even under State law) | ❌ **Cannot pardon** death sentence |
| **Commute Death** | ✅ | ✅ (can commute death → life, but cannot pardon) |

> **UPSC Trap:** "Governor cannot pardon" does NOT mean Governor has NO mercy powers. Governor can **commute**, **remit**, **respite**, **reprieve**. Governor cannot **pardon** — which is only ONE power. Governor specifically cannot pardon death sentence but can commute it.

sections.heading: Successive Application of Mercy Power
sections.content:
- **Yes**, mercy power can be applied successively (one after another)
- Example: Death → Life imprisonment (commutation by President) → Life → 20 years (remission by State/President)
- Same person, different powers applied at different times

sections.heading: Pardon — The Highest Form of Mercy (Detailed)
sections.content:
**What Pardon Does:**
- Removes **conviction** AND **sentence**
- Also removes **all other disqualifications** attached to conviction
- Places the person in the **same legal position as before committing the crime** (innocent)
- e.g., A convict barred from contesting elections → after pardon, can contest again

**Timeline of Legal Status:**
```
Birth → [Innocent] → Crime → [Accused] → Trial → [Convict] → Pardon → [Innocent Again]
```

**When Can Pardon Be Granted?**
- ✅ After trial (typical)
- ✅ During trial (trial stops)
- ✅ Before trial (no trial starts — **Preemptive Pardon**)
- ❌ Before crime (would be license to commit crime)

**Preemptive Pardon (USA Practice):**
- Very popular in USA — Presidents pardon people before trial/charge
- Example: Joe Biden pardoned Hunter Biden, his sister, brother-in-law on his **last day in office** (4:45 PM before leaving at 5 PM)
- Protects from prosecution for **past actions** only, not future crimes
- Not practiced in India — in our system, President acts on COM advice (not absolute power like USA's Presidential system)

sections.heading: Why Do Mercy Powers Exist?
sections.content:
| Reason | Explanation |
|--------|-------------|
| **Tradition/Legacy** | Kings historically had power of mercy ("Maharaj, maaf kijiye") — philosophy continued |
| **Philosophy** | State should have a bigger heart; reform over revenge |
| **Humanitarianism** | Courts examine only law + facts; cannot consider humanitarian factors (small children, special circumstances) |
| **Correcting Errors** | Even SC can err — executive provides a final safety valve |
| **Executive Implementation** | Court gives order; executive implements it — executive can say "for these reasons, I won't fully implement" |

sections.heading: Nature of Mercy Power — Key Constitutional Points
sections.content:
| Statement | True/False | Explanation |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| Mercy power is an **Act of Grace** | ✅ True | Executive's compassion, not convict's right |
| Convict has **Right to Hearing** | ❌ False | No right to hearing — executive may give, but convict cannot demand |
| It is a **Judicial Function** of President | ❌ False | President does not examine evidence, call witnesses, follow judicial procedure |
| It is a **Judicial Power** of President | ✅ True | The power is judicial in nature but exercised as **executive** |
| President overrides Supreme Court | ❌ False | President only modifies **implementation** of court order, not the judgment itself |
| President is superior to SC | ❌ False | SC remains highest court of justice; President is not a court |

> **Key Distinction:** A power of the President may be **judicial in nature** (mercy) or **legislative in nature** (ordinance), but the President always **functions as executive**.

sections.heading: Judicial Review of Mercy Power
sections.content:
- **Yes**, judicial review is possible — but courts examine only **whether the decision was malafide (bad faith)**
- Courts do NOT re-examine evidence or guilt (that's already established)
- **Malafide** = bad faith, wrong intention (e.g., pardoning because person is minister's daughter)
- **Bona fide** = good faith, genuine reason (e.g., India signed international treaty against that punishment)
- **ICOM/MHA** handles mercy petitions (delegated from President to Ministry of Home Affairs)
- **Shatrughan Chauhan case:** SC directed that mercy petitions must be decided **expeditiously** — unexplained delay of 20+ years = mental torture → SC itself commuted death to life in bulk
- No specific time limit, but "timely" decision expected

---

sections.heading: The Foundation: Article 53
sections.content:
- **Text:** "Executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President, who shall exercise it either directly or through officers subordinate to him"
- **Constitution says:** President can act directly
- **Reality:** President acts on aid and advice of Council of Ministers

sections.heading: Article 74 — Aid & Advice of Council of Ministers
sections.content:
**Article 74(1)** (as amended by **42nd CAA, 1976**):
> "There shall be a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to aid and advise the President, who **shall** act according to such advice."

- **Original provision** (pre-1976): Only said "to aid and advise the President" — NO "shall act according to advice"
- **42nd Amendment (1976)** added: "who shall act according to such advice" → made it **constitutionally binding**

**Proviso to Article 74(1)** (inserted by **44th CAA, 1978**):
> "The President may require the Council of Ministers to **reconsider** their advice, either generally or otherwise, and the President **shall** act according to the advice tendered after such reconsideration."

- This is a **totally new power** (inserted, not substituted) — didn't exist before 1978
- President can ask COM to reconsider **once** → after reconsideration, must act on the advice
- This is a **discretionary power** of the President (though not written as discretionary)

sections.heading: Art 74(1) Proviso ≠ Suspensive Veto (Important Distinction)
sections.content:
| Feature | Suspensive Veto (Art 111) | Art 74(1) Proviso |
|---------|--------------------------|-------------------|
| **What is sent back?** | A **Bill** | **Advice** |
| **Sent back to?** | **Parliament** | **Council of Ministers** |
| **Relationship** | Executive ↔ Legislature | Within the Executive team |
| **Second time** | President **declares assent** | President **acts** on advice |

sections.heading: Supreme Court Judgments on Position of President
sections.content:
| Case | Year | Key Ruling |
|------|------|-----------|
| **Ram Jawaya v. State of Punjab** | 1955 | India follows parliamentary system → President should work on advice of COM |
| **Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab** | 1974 | President cannot exercise executive power against or without COM advice (most important — remember this one) |
| **U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi** | 1971 | "There **shall be** a Council of Ministers" = always, even when LS dissolved (caretaker government) |

sections.heading: Court's Two Key Conclusions (Shamsher Singh):
sections.content:
1. President **cannot** exercise executive functions **without** the advice of COM
2. President **cannot** exercise executive functions **against** the advice of COM
- All President can do: ask COM to **reconsider once** → after that, must act

sections.heading: There Shall **Always** Be a Council of Ministers
sections.content:
- Art 74(1) begins: "There **shall be** a Council of Ministers..."
- "Shall be" = always, at all times
- Even when Lok Sabha is **dissolved** → **Caretaker Government** exists
- **U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971)** confirmed this
- Example: 2024 — Modi resigned after election → became caretaker PM → took oath again as new PM after ~5 days. In between = caretaker COM existed.

sections.heading: Three Principles of Parliamentary System
sections.content:
| # | Parliamentary System (India) | Presidential System (USA) |
|---|------------------------------|--------------------------|
| **1st (Primary)** | Head of State is **Nominal** (just a name) | Head of State is **Real** |
| **2nd** | Real executive power with **Council of Ministers** (headed by PM) | — |
| **3rd** | COM is collectively responsible to **Legislature** (Lok Sabha) | Not responsible to Legislature |
| **Corollary** | Members of COM **derived from** Legislature | Members **cannot be** from Legislature |

> **Duality of Heads:** Parliamentary system has TWO heads — **Head of State** (President = de jure, formal, legal) and **Head of Government** (PM = de facto, practical, real). In Presidential system (USA), both = same person (Trump is both Head of State & Head of Government).

sections.heading: Ambedkar's Comparison: President of India ≈ Crown of England
sections.content:
| Aspect | President of India | Crown (King/Queen) of England |
|--------|-------------------|-------------------------------|
| Status | Head of State | Head of State |
| Real power | No (with COM) | No (with PM & Cabinet) |
| Ambedkar's words | **"More or less a ceremonial office"** | "They **reign** but do not **rule**" |

> **Critical Phrase:** Ambedkar said "**more or less** ceremonial" — NOT "ceremonial." The words "more or less" imply that while 99.9% ceremonial, there exists 0.1% discretionary space. This is what makes India's President a **Constitutional Head**, not a **Figurehead**.

sections.heading: Figurehead vs Constitutional Head
sections.content:
| Feature | Figurehead | Constitutional Head |
|---------|-----------|-------------------|
| **Office of** | Respect, dignity, ceremony | Respect, dignity, ceremony |
| **Real authority** | ❌ **None whatsoever** | Generally ❌, but **sometimes ✅** |
| **Acts on advice** | **Always** — no exceptions | **Generally** — but not in extraordinary circumstances |
| **Exceptional circumstances** | Still no authority | Has **own authority** (discretionary) |
| **Example** | King of England | **President of India** |

> **Conclusion:** India's President is a **Constitutional Head** (not a mere figurehead) because discretionary powers exist, even if implicit and rare.

sections.heading: President's Evolved Role
sections.content:
- Over the years, President has evolved into the role of **friend, philosopher, and guide** to the government
- President is **apolitical** (detached from politics) → can give unbiased advice
- COM has the mandate of the people but is politically motivated (next election concerns)
- President can give objective, non-partisan advice because of distance from electoral politics
- In practical terms, the **President is the real advisor** to COM (not the other way around)
  - COM's "advice" is actually a **decision** (binding on President)
  - President's suggestions/returns are actual **advice** (not binding on COM)

---

sections.heading: Key Characteristics of Presidential Discretion
sections.content:
- **NOT explicitly mentioned** in the Constitution — they are **implicit** (understood)
- The word "**discretion**" does NOT exist in any provision for President
- Contrast: For **Governor**, "discretion" is explicitly written (Art 163) — at least 3-4 times
- **Same Constitution makers** used "discretion" for Governor but NOT for President → **intentional** omission
- President's discretion is **not intentional** but **situational** — arises from extraordinary circumstances
- Governor's discretion is **intentionally** provided

sections.heading: List of Discretionary Powers (Discussed So Far — 7 points, 8th onwards in next lecture)
sections.content:
| # | Discretionary Power | Article/Provision | Why Discretionary? |
|---|--------------------|--------------------|-------------------|
| 1 | **Suspensive Veto** (Return of Bill) | Art 111 | President's own suggestions — not on COM advice |
| 2 | **Pocket Veto** (Inaction on Bill) | Not written — emerges from absence of time limit | Unwritten power; no advice possible for something not written |
| 3 | **Reconsider Advice** (Art 74 Proviso) | Art 74(1) Proviso (44th CAA, 1978) | President asks COM to rethink — obviously on own initiative |
| 4 | **Seek Information** from PM (Art 78) | Art 78(b) | If President wants information from PM, PM must furnish — President asks on own |
| 5 | **Summon Parliament** (if 6 months lapsed) | Art 85 | If COM hasn't advised summons and 6 months gap exceeds → President protects Constitution by summoning on own |
| 6 | **Dissolution of Lok Sabha** (minority situation) | Art 85 | COM advice to dissolve is binding **only when COM has majority**; if minority, President decides independently |
| 7 | **Appoint PM in Hung Parliament** | Convention | No party/coalition has majority → President decides who gets first chance (convention: largest pre-poll alliance leader) |

sections.heading: Hung Parliament — President's Most Important Duty
sections.content:
**President's Primary Real Duty:** Provide India a **stable government**
- If majority clear → appoint leader of majority party → done
- If **Hung Parliament** (no party has majority):
  1. Try coalition government
  2. If no coalition has clear majority → President's discretion:
     - Call leader of **largest pre-poll alliance** first
     - **Pre-poll** (not post-poll) because pre-poll alliances are more **ideological** and likely **stable**
     - **Largest** because highest probability of proving majority
  3. That leader becomes PM → must prove majority on floor of House
  4. This practice → repeated → becomes **convention**

> **Convention Formation:** 1st time: President thinks and decides → 2nd time: follows precedent → 3rd time: media predicts outcome → Convention established. Conventions derive force from being **followed over time** — breaking them invites massive criticism even though not legally enforceable.

---

sections.heading: 5. Key Constitutional Articles — Quick Reference (Lecture 3)
sections.content:
| Article | Subject |
|---------|---------|
| **Art 53** | Executive power vested in President (directly or through subordinates) |
| **Art 72** | President's Mercy/Clemency Powers (Pardon, Commute, Remit, Respite, Reprieve) |
| **Art 74** | Aid & Advice of Council of Ministers (42nd CAA, 1976 + Proviso: 44th CAA, 1978) |
| **Art 78** | Duties of PM — furnish information to President |
| **Art 85** | Sessions of Parliament — 6-month gap rule, summoning & dissolution |
| **Art 111** | President's Assent to Bills (3 choices + Pocket Veto) |
| **Art 161** | Governor's Mercy Powers (parallel to Art 72 but narrower) |

---

sections.heading: 6. Important Cases & Names
sections.content:
| Person/Case | Role/Event |
|-------------|-----------|
| **Giani Zail Singh** | President who exercised Pocket Veto (1986 — Indian PO Amendment Bill) |
| **R. Venkataraman** | President who returned the bill in 1990 (on Chandrashekhar's advice) |
| **Rajiv Gandhi** | PM during Pocket Veto incident (1986); 424 seats — highest majority ever |
| **Chandrashekhar** | PM who advised R. Venkataraman to return the bill (1990) |
| **Ram Jawaya v. State of Punjab (1955)** | SC: President should work on advice of COM |
| **Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974)** | SC: President cannot act without or against COM advice (landmark — remember this) |
| **U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971)** | SC: There shall **always** be a COM, even when LS dissolved |
| **Shatrughan Chauhan case** | SC: Mercy petitions must be decided expeditiously — unexplained delay (20 yrs) = mental torture → SC commuted death to life |
| **Joe Biden / Hunter Biden** | Example of preemptive pardon in USA (not India) |
| **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** | President is "more or less a ceremonial office" (not "ceremonial") |

---
