sections.heading: Lecture 4 — VP, Council of Ministers, Cabinet System & PM
sections.content:
> **Source:** Vajiram & Ravi — Polity Class Lecture 04 (Abhey Kumar) + Handwritten Notes + Audio Transcript  
> **Date:** 19 August 2026  
> **Last Updated:** 2026-08-19

---

sections.heading: 1. Convention: President's Right to Encourage & Warn (Continued from Lecture 3)
sections.content:
- **Convention from England**, observed in India also
- President has the right to **encourage** or **warn** the Council of Ministers
- Only for discharge of **executive functions** — not other matters
- **Practically does nothing** — but when the President speaks, people listen
- Presidents are very **polite and docile** in their demeanour
- It is purely a **conventional practice**, not written anywhere

---

sections.heading: Definition & Nature
sections.content:
- A **temporary government** that runs during the gap between resignation of PM and appointment of new PM
- **Not a constitutional term** — purely conventional
- Lasts only a few days to weeks
- Exists because the **parliamentary system mandates** there must always be a CoM (UNR Rao v. Indira Gandhi, 1971)

sections.heading: Update — 10 September 2026 (evening articles)
sections.content: `MST-075`: *U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi* (**1971**) — there **shall** be a Council of Ministers **always**, even when Lok Sabha is **dissolved** (caretaker). He picked the inverse. Caretaker is a **convention**, not a constitutional word. Labels caretaker-under-Constitution vs interim (`MST-046`) already held. **Held 11 Sep evening.**

sections.heading: What Can a Caretaker Government Do?
sections.content:
| ✅ Should Do | ❌ Should NOT Do |
|:---|:---|
| Decisions **necessary for day-to-day administration** | **Major policy decisions** |
| Routine governance & continuity | New policy initiatives |

sections.heading: President's Discretionary Power in Caretaker Period
sections.content:
- Both terms ("major policy" and "day-to-day decision") are **highly subjective**
- **President decides** which decisions are necessary and which are not — with **discretion**
- President **cannot take a 6th decision** on their own — can only filter from CoM's advice
- **Discretion is in NOT taking action**, not in taking independent action
- Example: If CoM advises 5 things, President can decide: Advice 1 & 2 = necessary → action; Advice 3, 4, 5 = not necessary → wait for next PM

> **Key Statement:** "In case of a caretaker government, since it is not expected to take major policy decisions, only necessary decisions for day-to-day administration, it is the President who decides which decisions are necessary or not."

sections.heading: Not Cast in Rigid Mode — Only Restricted Mode
sections.content:
- What a caretaker government can/cannot do is **not fixed**
- It depends entirely on **circumstances** and **President's discretion**
- **1999 ABV Example:** Vajpayee resigned in April 1999 (lost majority); Kargil war happened in May → caretaker PM had to fight a war → major decision but **necessary** → President supported, Sonia Gandhi rallied behind PM
- Books may say "can do this, cannot do that" — but remember it's always **"may"**

sections.heading: 3 Situations When CoM is Dissolved
sections.content:
1. **PM Resigns** → pivot gone, CoM dissolved → same PM becomes caretaker
2. **PM Dies** → pivot gone, CoM dissolved → senior-most cabinet minister becomes caretaker (convention since 1964, Nehru's death)
3. **Lok Sabha Dissolved** → mother of CoM died → same PM becomes caretaker

sections.heading: Convention for Caretaker PM (when PM dies)
sections.content:
- **1964 (First Instance):** Nehru died → Congress still had majority → party needed time to choose new leader
- President appointed the **senior-most cabinet minister** → became convention
- Managed entirely by **conventions** — nothing written

---

sections.heading: 3. R. Venkataraman's Emergency Lamp Analogy
sections.content:
- R. Venkataraman was VP (1982–87) → President (1987–92) → 10 years at the top
- In his farewell speech, he described the **role of the President** as that of an **"emergency lamp"**:
  - When political power supply is proper (clear majority) → nobody bothers about the President
  - When political power supply is disrupted (no clear majority / hung parliament) → President's role becomes critical
  - The role **ceases** the moment a PM emerges with parliamentary majority
- **1989 election** during his tenure was the first time Centre saw no clear majority → President became crucial
- Tamil Nadu Governor example: all over news during hung assembly → invisible after clear majority emerged

---

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
- Second in line after the President
- Functions: **Acting President** (when vacancy arises) OR **Ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha**
- **As Vice President, there is virtually no work** — nothing to discuss

sections.heading: Election of VP
sections.content:
| Feature | Detail |
|:---|:---|
| **Elected by** | **All members of Parliament** (both elected AND nominated) |
| **Contrast with President** | President = only elected members of Parliament + State Legislatures |
| **Method** | Proportional Representation by Single Transferable Vote (PR-STV) — same as President |
| **Rationale** | VP is just a backup for President's office — no need to involve states |

sections.heading: Removal of VP
sections.content:
- **Parliament removes** (Parliament elects, Parliament removes)
- **Key condition:** Proposal to remove must be **introduced in Rajya Sabha only** (since VP is Chairman of RS)
- If RS passes → goes to LS → if LS also passes → VP stands removed
- Majority requirements will be covered in Parliament chapter

sections.heading: Timing of Election & Vacancy
sections.content:
| Situation | Rule |
|:---|:---|
| **Regular election** | Must be held **before completion of term** |
| **Vacancy (death/resignation/removal)** | Election must be held **as soon as possible** |
| **Unique feature** | **No fixed time limit** (unlike President's 6 months rule) — only office where this is possible |

---

sections.heading: What is "Government" — 3 Levels of Meaning
sections.content:
| Level | Meaning | Example |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Broadest** | Legislature + Executive + Judiciary | "Government of India" |
| **Narrow** | Executive only | Administrative machinery |
| **Narrowest** | Council of Ministers | "Modi Sarkar" / "Modi Government" |

sections.heading: Appointment Chain
sections.content:
```
President --(?discretion)--> appoints PM ---(PM's advice)---> President appoints Ministers
```
- **President appoints PM** → discretion may or may not exist (depends on majority clarity)
- **President appoints other ministers** on the **advice of PM** → no discretion here
- **× = No discretion** | **? = May or may not** | **A = On advice**

sections.heading: Individual Responsibility of Ministers
sections.content:
- **Minister is responsible to the President** (objectively/formally — President appointed, President removes)
- **Practically responsible to the PM** (because President removes on PM's advice)
- Both statements are correct — depends on context (objective vs subjective/practical)
- **Responsibility** means: for your action/inaction, who takes action against you?
- Ultimate meaning: **Who can remove the minister?** → President (on PM's advice) → hence responsible to both

sections.heading: Collective Responsibility of CoM
sections.content:
- **Collectively responsible to Lok Sabha** (Article 75(3))
- They came to power because of **majority in Lok Sabha** → will lose power by **losing majority in Lok Sabha**
- If Lok Sabha is not an option in MCQ → next most suitable answer = **Parliament** (not PM, since PM is part of CoM)
- **"Mark the most suitable answer"** — first instruction in UPSC exam

---

sections.heading: 3 Ranks of Ministers (Currently)
sections.content:
| Rank | Description | Number (Current ~) | Cabinet Meeting |
|:---|:---|:---:|:---|
| **Cabinet Ministers** | Senior leaders, important portfolios, manage ministry **independently** | ~29 | **Regular members** |
| **MoS (Independent Charge)** | Manage their own ministry independently but **not part of cabinet** | ~5 | **May be invited** when their ministry is discussed |
| **MoS (Minister of State)** | Work **under** a Cabinet Minister — assistants/lieutenants | ~34 | **Not invited** (their boss is already there) |

> **Current total CoM strength = ~69** (29 Cabinet + 5 MoS-IC + 34 MoS + 1 PM = ~69 but 5 MoS-IC are also MoS for something → overlap counted once)

sections.heading: Key Points About Cabinet Ministers
sections.content:
- Manage their ministries **independently** — PM is NOT their boss
- PM's role = **coordination and leadership** only
- Day-to-day decisions in Ministry of Finance → Finance Minister decides (PM may not even know)
- Cross-ministry decisions (e.g., Operation Sindoor) → need coordination → PM leads

sections.heading: Key Points About MoS (Independent Charge)
sections.content:
- Also manage their ministry independently → very similar to Cabinet Minister
- **Not part of Cabinet** → PM decided to keep them out of the core team
- Example: Dr. Jitendra Singh → MoS (IC) for Science & Technology + MoS for DoPT
- **May be invited** to cabinet meetings only when their ministry's issue is being discussed → consulted → then leave

sections.heading: Key Points About MoS (without IC)
sections.content:
- Work under Cabinet Ministers — assist them with large ministries
- Example: MoS Finance assists Nirmala Sitharaman
- Work allocation decided by the **Cabinet Minister** they serve under
- **Not invited** to cabinet meetings — their boss (Cabinet Minister) is already present

sections.heading: Deputy Ministers (Historical — No Longer Appointed)
sections.content:
- Used to exist as assistants → lollipop for alliance-building
- **91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003** → imposed **15% of Lok Sabha strength** cap on total CoM size
- Deputy Minister post stopped being used — redundant since MoS already exists
- **Deputy CM** = not a constitutional post (CM is constitutional; Deputy CM, Senior Minister, etc. = internal nomenclature)

sections.heading: Constitutional Position on CoM
sections.content:
- Constitution only says: **"There shall be a Council of Ministers"**
- Doesn't mention Cabinet Minister, MoS, MoS-IC, Deputy Minister etc.
- **All nomenclature is internal** to the government — Constitution doesn't care
- Key rule: Total CoM **cannot exceed 15% of Lok Sabha strength** (91st CAA, 2003)

---

sections.heading: Cabinet vs CoM Relationship
Cabinet ≠ Council — Key Differences
sections.content:
| Feature | Council of Ministers | Cabinet |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Size** | ~69 | ~30 |
| **Constitutional mention** | Article 74, 75 | **Only in Article 352** (added by 44th CAA, 1978) |
| **Meetings (per 5-year term)** | **Zero** (practically never meets) | **Weekly** (sometimes more than once/week) |
| **Decision-making** | Does nothing — a formal/legal entity | **All real decisions are taken here** |

sections.heading: Cabinet in the Constitution — A Special Story
sections.content:
| Timeline | Status |
|:---|:---|
| **1947 (Pre-Constitution)** | Cabinet existed (Nehru had a cabinet of 13) — word was "Cabinet" not "Council" |
| **1950 (Constitution enacted)** | Cabinet word **NOT in Constitution** — but Cabinet still functioned |
| **1978 (44th CAA)** | Cabinet word **added** — but only in Article 352 (National Emergency) |
| **State Constitutions (today)** | Cabinet word **still not in state articles** — but every state has a cabinet |

> **Insight:** Cabinet has always existed, with or without constitutional mention. It is so fundamental that it preceded the Constitution itself.

sections.heading: Why a Separate Cabinet? (Reasons)
sections.content:
1. **Ease of conducting business** — smaller body = easier to hold meetings, conduct government work
2. **Ease of decision-making** — lesser divergence of opinion in 30 than in 69 (but not one person → avoids dictatorship)
3. **Maintenance of secrecy** — fewer people = better secret-keeping (first rule of secrecy: don't tell anyone)
4. **High workload** — government's workload is massive
5. **Not every decision requires all ministers** — e.g., JS appointment doesn't need 69 people

sections.heading: Decision Flow in Government
sections.content:
```
Cabinet Committee takes decision
    → treated as Cabinet's decision
        → treated as Council's decision
            → presented as President's decision
```
- What citizens see: **"President is pleased to appoint..."**
- What actually happens: A cabinet committee decided it far away from the President
- **President does not even know** who was appointed — only their name is used
- **Council does nothing** — from now on, even Council is a myth (just like President)

---

sections.heading: Types
sections.content:
| Type | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| **Standing Committees** | Long-term purpose — can go beyond one government |
| **Ad Hoc Committees** | Short-term, specific purpose — once purpose is over, committee dissolved |

sections.heading: Current Status
sections.content:
- **8 Standing Committees** (was 12, then 10 under Modi — now 8)
- **0 Ad Hoc Committees** currently
- Numbers can change — not critical to memorize exact count

sections.heading: Most Important Committee: Appointments Committee of Cabinet (ACC)
sections.content:
- **Members:** Only **2** — PM + Home Minister
- **Function:** All appointments of **Joint Secretary and above** in Government of India
- JS+ level = **mid-career** (~17-19 years of service) → point where you enter **policy road**
- Before JS level: you're a worker/implementer (800 district collectors)
- From JS level: **policy input, monitoring, evaluation** → work closely with Cabinet → hence Cabinet decides appointments

sections.heading: GoS (Group of Secretaries)
sections.content: - JS and above (after ~17 years of service) start taking part in **policy decisions**

sections.heading: Homework: Find the Other 7 Standing Committees
sections.content:
- Go to **Cabinet Secretary website** (cabsec.gov.in or similar .gov.in)
- Look at **Transaction of Business Rules** (TOBR) — all committee details are there
- Spend 10 minutes — scan history of office, present cabinet secretary, etc.

---

sections.heading: Constitutional Basis: Article 77(3)
sections.content: > *"The President shall make rules for the convenient transaction of the business of the government and the allocation among the ministers of that business."*

sections.heading: Two Sets of Rules
sections.content:
| Rules | Content |
|:---|:---|
| **Transaction of Business Rules (TOBR)** | How decisions are taken — committees, process, decision-making machinery |
| **Allocation of Business Rules (AOBR)** | Who does what work — which minister handles which ministry |

- All cabinet committee details are in **TOBR**
- Who made these rules? **Cabinet** (not President, not Council — President's name is used but Cabinet decides)

---

sections.heading: PM Comes First
sections.content:
- PM appointed **before** Council → Council created on PM's advice
- **Council cannot exist without PM** → if PM vacates office (resignation/death) → Council **automatically dissolved**
- **PM is the pivot** which holds the Council in power/office → pivot gone = Council gone

sections.heading: PM as Residual Legatee of the Government
sections.content:
- **Residual Legatee** = all leftover responsibilities are delegated to the PM
- PM allocates portfolios to ~70 ministers → after allocation, some work is **left over** (known and unknown)
- All leftover work = PM's responsibility
- **Even allocated work** → PM is also responsible for it
  - If Nirmala Sitharaman's policy fails → history won't remember her → **"Modi did it"**
  - Nehru did it, Indira Gandhi did it, Vajpayee ji did it → PM = face of government
- **PM = face of the government, name of the government**
- Elections fought in PM's name: "Ghar ghar Modi, har har Modi" — not "Ghar ghar Gadkari"

sections.heading: Primus Inter Pares vs Inter Stellas Lunar Minoris
sections.content:
| Phrase | Meaning | Source |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Primus Inter Pares** | First among equals | Traditional description — PM is leader but all ministers are at par |
| **Inter Stellas Lunar Minoris** | Moon among lesser stars | William Harcourt (UK MP) — PM is special, not just first among equals |

- **Primus Inter Pares:** PM is not boss → Cabinet ministers manage independently → PM's role = coordination + leadership → "they swim together and they sink together"
- **Inter Stellas Lunar Minoris:** Harcourt argued PM has special status → PM is like the bright moon among lesser stars
- **Teacher's Critique:** Highly unscientific — moon is NOT a star → comparing apples to oranges → don't be a fan of fancy phrases → focus on real arguments

---

sections.heading: When Does It Emerge?
sections.content:
- **Single party** wins **majority** in lower house elections
- Party led by an **undisputed** and **charismatic** leader
- Party members know: "we won because of THIS leader" → subservient nature
- People know it, party knows it, **the person also knows it**
- CoM/Cabinet reduced to **"shadows of the PM"** — no real debate/discussion

sections.heading: Advantages
sections.content:
1. **Stability** — government is stable with clear majority
2. **Timely decisions** (NOT "fast" — fast is actually a negative)
3. **Strong/Bold decisions** — e.g., Article 370 abrogation → only this kind of government could do it

sections.heading: Disadvantages / Challenges
sections.content:
1. **Fundamental principle of parliamentary democracy (collective decision-making & collective responsibility) may be undermined** — always use **probabilistic language** ("may be")
2. **Kitchen Cabinet / Coterie** can emerge (see below)
3. **Influence may be more by political interest and less by public interest** — one person deciding → easier to be influenced
4. **Higher chances of misuse of power** — power concentrated without proportional accountability

sections.heading: Phases of Indian Politics
sections.content:
| Period | Nature |
|:---|:---|
| **1947–1964** | Nehru era — strong PM form |
| **1966–1984** | Indira Gandhi era — PM form (except 1977–79) |
| **1989–2014** | Coalition era — Cabinet form |
| **2014–present** | Strong PM form again |

sections.heading: When Does It Emerge?
sections.content:
- **Coalition era** — no single party majority
- Even charismatic PM (e.g., Vajpayee 1999) cannot dominate because coalition partners resist
- **Cabinet is more powerful** than PM — able to control the PM collectively

sections.heading: Merits
sections.content:
1. **Collective decision-making** — debate and discussion happen
2. **Kitchen cabinet is less likely** to emerge

sections.heading: Demerits
sections.content:
1. **Less stability** — coalition may break
2. **Decisions may be delayed** — e.g., Dr. Manmohan Singh's government → "policy paralysis" (decisions not just delayed but government stopped taking decisions because every coalition partner objected)

---

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
- **Extra-constitutional power centres** that exercise power **without any accountability towards Parliament**
- People **outside the constitutional system** who can influence PM and get decisions in their favour

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.content:
- In PM form of government → easier to influence **one person** (PM) than convince entire cabinet
- Route 1 (through PM) is easier than Route 2 (through Cabinet)
- These people may have personal connections (friendship, business, school ties, political favours)
- PM decides → Cabinet just agrees (shadows) → decision made

sections.heading: Problems
sections.content:
1. **Power without accountability** → recipe for disaster in democracy
2. Not accountable to Parliament → cannot be questioned
3. Decision may be good or bad — **the problem is the process, not the outcome**
4. Even if they take a good decision → if process allows unaccountable power → future misuse is inevitable

sections.heading: Terminology
sections.content:
| Term | Formality |
|:---|:---|
| **Kitchen Cabinet** | Informal/popular phrase — widely used but too casual |
| **Coterie** | More formal/technical term — preferred in academic writing |

---

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
- **Does NOT exist in India** — exists in countries with **two-party political systems**
- In UK: opposition party **behaves as a cabinet** — mirrors the ruling government's structure

sections.heading: Structure
sections.content:
| Ruling Side | Opposition Side |
|:---|:---|
| PM | **Leader of Opposition (LOP)** = "PM in waiting" |
| Minister of Home Affairs | Shadow Minister A |
| Minister of Finance | Shadow Minister B |
| Minister of Defence | Shadow Minister C |

sections.heading: Purpose — Two Arguments
sections.content:
1. **Channelized effort by opposition** → each shadow minister studies one specific ministry's policies, schemes, budget, expenditure → systematic scrutiny of every ministry (not just big ones like Defence/Finance)
2. **Training of portfolio** → if voted to power, **cabinet is ready** → quick transition → "Cabinet in waiting"

sections.heading: Why Not in India?
sections.content:
1. **India is NOT a two-party system** — opposition is fractured
2. India is moving towards **two-alliance system** (NDA vs INDIA) but not stabilized yet
3. Parties switch alliances between elections
4. With India's diversity, unlikely to become two-party → maybe two-alliance system eventually

sections.heading: Answer Writing: Opinion-Based Questions (Critical Skill)
sections.content:
**Framework for Balanced Answers (Madhya Path — Buddha's Middle Path):**

**If Supporting the Proposal:**
1. State the positives (reasons for support)
2. Acknowledge challenges that come as "free gift" with positives
3. Recommend solutions to handle those challenges

**If Opposing the Proposal:**
1. State the negatives (reasons for opposition)
2. Acknowledge the positives you'd be letting go
3. Suggest reforms in the existing system to achieve those positives without the proposal

> **Key Insight:** "The most important word in 'middle path' is not 'middle' — it is 'PATH'." Just listing plus/minus is not an answer. You must show a path forward.

- **Never make blanket statements** — especially when criticizing
- **Always use probabilistic language** — "may be undermined," "higher chances," "less likely"
- **Criticize on principles**, not on outcomes — e.g., collective decision-making principle being violated
- **Write positives first** — shows positive frame of mind (negatives come naturally; finding good things requires effort)

---

sections.heading: Why Caretaker Government Exists
sections.content:
- **Parliamentary system requires** there must always be a CoM
- **UNR Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971):** SC held there must always be a CoM
- Without CoM → President would have to take decisions alone → presidential system → unconstitutional
- Managed **only by conventions** — nothing written

sections.heading: Who Becomes Caretaker PM?
sections.content:
| Situation | Caretaker PM |
|:---|:---|
| PM resigns | Same PM |
| Lok Sabha dissolved | Same PM |
| PM dies | Senior-most Cabinet Minister (convention since 1964) |

sections.heading: Caretaker Government Restrictions
sections.content:
- Should only take decisions **necessary for day-to-day administration**
- Should NOT take **major policy decisions** — both terms subjective
- **President decides** what is necessary → discretionary power
- **Not cast in rigid mode** — only in **restricted mode**

---

sections.heading: Key Articles Referenced in This Lecture
sections.content:
| Article | Subject |
|:---|:---|
| **Art 74** | Aid & Advice — CoM to advise President |
| **Art 75** | Appointment & Collective Responsibility of CoM |
| **Art 75(3)** | CoM collectively responsible to Lok Sabha |
| **Art 77(3)** | President to make TOBR and AOBR |

sections.heading: Lecture 5 — 5 September 2026
sections.content:
> **Date of Lecture:** 5 September 2026 (continues Lecture 4 — `Polity_Lec4_AbheyKumar_VP_COM_PM_CabinetSystem.md`)  
> **Date Added:** 2026-09-05  
> **Faculty:** **Abhey Kumar** (sheet: *Abbey*). Vajiram & Ravi GS Polity.

> **Also relevant for:** Prelims (Attorney General of India, articles, majority arithmetic); **GS-II** (Parliament, Union executive, Centre–State via Articles 249 / 312)

**How to read class shortcuts:** full form on first use. Glossary at the end. Do not invent a number the sheet / class did not give.

Class paused after **special majority / Article 61**. Second class the same day: Lecture 6 — `Polity_Lec6_AbheyKumar_Houses_Motions_Speaker.md`.

---

sections.heading: 1. Interim (provisional) government vs caretaker (POL-06-01)
sections.content:
Neither word is a **constitutional** term. Books mix them; the idea is different.

| | **Caretaker government** | **Interim / provisional / transitional government** |
|:---|:---|:---|
| When | Gap after a Prime Minister (PM) resigns / dies, or Lok Sabha (LS) is dissolved — until a new PM is sworn | A **historical transition** of the polity: institutions / elections / sometimes a constitution are being created or have been **sidelined** |
| System | Works **under a system** — Constitution of India is still there (outgoing / incoming / caretaker PM, all three) | Works under **no (or a sidelined) system** |
| India | Routine after every LS term | **Once** in our story: **15 August 1947 → first LS 1952**. No Constitution yet, no Election Commission, no LS / Rajya Sabha (RS). Government ran on the **Government of India Act, 1935** (British-era law) |

**Recent neighbours (class):**

- **Bangladesh** — after Sheikh Hasina was removed, an interim set-up until elections announced **March 2026**. Head: **Muhammad Yunus**, designation **Chief Advisor** (not a named constitutional PM/President post — they **created** it). They **sidelined** their existing constitution; class: they restarted it after the election. Do **not** formula-write “interim = always writing a new constitution.”
- **Nepal** — also had an interim government recently (class: mention only).

Caretaker detail stays in Lecture 4. Trap: **interim ≠ caretaker**.

---

sections.heading: 2. Minority government ≠ coalition (POL-06-02)
sections.content:
**Misnomer:** a government must still **prove majority** on the floor. It is called **minority** because the **Council of Ministers (CoM)** itself does not have the numbers. Extra votes come from parties **outside** the CoM.

**Coalition ≠ minority.** Two different axes. All **four** combinations are possible:

| | **Minority** (CoM needs outside / issue-based votes) | **Majority** (partners inside the CoM are enough) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Coalition** | **United Progressive Alliance (UPA) I, 2004** | **National Democratic Alliance (NDA)** today |
| **Single party** | **Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), Delhi 2013** (Arvind Kejriwal, first term — class example) | **Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) 2019** *could have* governed alone (**303** seats) — they still took allies (class: do not drop friends in good times) |

sections.heading: 2004 UPA I (class worked example)
sections.content:
No party won a majority. **Indian National Congress (INC)** led UPA. Alliance parties **form** the government = they put some members into the CoM (there is a size cap). They are **not** themselves “the government.”

- UPA parties together in LS: about **218**.
- Need **more than half** of total membership. **Today** total LS = **543** → **272**. **Then** LS had **545** (Anglo-Indian nominated seats still existed) → **273**.
- **218 < 273** → cannot form on alliance seats alone.

**Outside / issue-based support:** Samajwadi Party, Bahujan Samaj Party, **Left Front** (Communist Party of India; Communist Party of India (Marxist); Communist Party of India (Marxist–Leninist) — class: names starting with CP). They **did not take ministries** → **no collective responsibility** (“not swimming / not sinking”). Class: often good politics — influence without accountability.

They survived **five years**, returned in **2009**. Support can vanish any day.

**2008 India–United States of America (USA) civil nuclear deal:** needed parliamentary approval. Left would not back a deal with a capitalist USA. Government proposal failed in LS → question on majority → Dr **Manmohan Singh** brought a **confidence motion**. Left then supported **majority of the government** but not **that issue**. Class label: **issue-based support** / *muddon par samarthan*.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph CoM["CoM = the government (~218)"]
    INC[INC + UPA ministers]
  end
  OUT["Outside: SP / BSP / Left"] -->|vote, no ministry| INC
  INC -->|must cross 273 then / 272 now| FLOOR[Floor majority]
```

Sheet 2×2: **S** / **C** (single / coalition) × **min** / **maj**.

sections.heading: NDA today (class contrast) — coalition **majority**
sections.content:
BJP alone **240** — not enough. Partners (class named Shiv Sena, Shiromani Akali Dal — “names not important”). Sheet / class: NDA **293** at the start of this term → about **318** after party changes. Already a majority; **no outside support needed**.

---

sections.heading: 3. Attorney General of India — last entity in Part V, Chapter 1 (POL-06-03)
sections.content: **Attorney General of India (AGI)** = **first law officer** of India = **lawyer / advocate of the Government of India (GoI)**. **One article: Article 76.**

sections.heading: Appointment, term, pleasure
sections.content:
- Appointed by the **President**. President is the name on the file. Real recommendation: **CoM**, in practice **Prime Minister + Ministry of Law and Justice (MoLJ)** via **Allocation of Business Rules** (Article **77(3)** — President makes rules for convenient transaction of business). Even the Cabinet as a body does not sit on this file.
- **Constitution:** **no term**. Holds office during the **pleasure of the President**.
- Context trap (Lecture 4): for a **minister**, Article **75(2)** pleasure ≈ pleasure of the **PM**. For AGI, pleasure ≈ pleasure of the **government of the day** (they hired the lawyer).
- **Convention (not a must):** when the CoM is **dissolved / leaves office**, AGI **resigns**. Client is going; the incoming party will remove a previous government’s lawyer anyway. Class: they **need not** resign — it is practice.

sections.heading: Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1987
sections.content:
**Rules** = **executive** (President / government), not an Act of Parliament. **Acts** = legislature.

Any law officer: appointed for **not more than 3 years at a time**, extendable again by **not more than 3 years at a time**. Government may appoint for 6 months / 1 year / 2 years — ceiling is 3 + 3.

**Current holders (class / sheet):**

| Post | Name | Class fact |
|:---|:---|:---|
| AGI | **R. Venkataramani** (sheet: Venkat Ramani) | Completed **3 years**; government gave a **2-year** extension (**2025**) |
| Solicitor General of India (SGI) | **Tushar Mehta** | SGI since **2018** — extension after extension |

---

sections.heading: 4. Eligibility = Supreme Court judge (POL-06-04)
sections.content:
Article 76: person shall be **eligible to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court (SC)**.

SC judge (class, not a judiciary lecture):

1. **Citizen of India**
2. **Any one** of:
   - Judge of a **High Court (HC)** for **5+** years, **or**
   - **Advocate** of an HC for **10+** years, **or**
   - **Distinguished jurist** (expert in the **theory of law** — jurisprudence). Who counts is the **government’s opinion**.

**Trap:** distinguished-jurist route is **only for the SC**, **not** for HCs. Class: **no jurist has ever been appointed** as an SC judge so far.

---

sections.heading: 5. Duties — Constitution 3 + 1950 notification 3 (POL-06-05)
sections.content: Class meta-pattern: **3 + 3 + 3** (duties in text / extra duties / rights).

sections.heading: In the Constitution (three)
sections.content:
1. **Advise GoI on legal matters** when the matter is **referred by the President** → in practice **MoLJ, Department of Legal Affairs (DoLA)**. A ministry secretary writes to Secretary, DoLA; DoLA writes to AGI; reply returns the same path. Class: **~53 ministries** cannot queue at one office.
2. **Any other duty assigned by the President** (legal nature).
3. **Any other function conferred by the Constitution or by Parliament by law.** Window for the future. **No such Act** has been made.

sections.heading: 1950 Presidential notification (three extra)
sections.content:
1. Represent GoI in the **SC** (when required).
2. Represent GoI in **HCs** (when required — AGI cannot physically cover every HC; other law officers go).
3. Represent GoI in the SC on a **Presidential reference under Article 143** (**advisory jurisdiction** of the SC). Class: last year’s Tamil Nadu Governor / withheld-bills reference. **Minimum 5 judges.** Advocates argue; AGI puts the government’s doubt.

---

sections.heading: 6. Rights / powers (POL-06-06)
sections.content:
Three in the Constitution:

| Source | Right |
|:---|:---|
| **Art 76(3)** | **Right of audience** in **any court in the territory of India** (SC, HC, district, taluk, **tribunal / quasi-judicial**). Ordinary advocates cannot walk into every court. |
| **Art 88** | Ministers **and** AGI may **take part** in proceedings of **Parliament**: any House, **joint sitting**, or a **committee if made a member**. **Attend + speak. No vote** (vote is for members). PM (LS member) can speak in RS but votes only in LS; External Affairs Minister (if RS) can speak in LS, votes in RS. |
| **Art 105(4)** | Does **not** name AGI. Says **any person** who can take part in Parliament enjoys **privileges and immunities of Members of Parliament (MPs)**. Combined with Art 88 → AGI gets MP privileges. **Example only:** during a session, **40 days before and 40 days after**, no MP (hence AGI) can be **arrested in a civil matter**. |

**United Kingdom (UK) comparison (class):** in the UK the Attorney General is a **minister**. In India, AGI is **not** a minister — an **extension of the executive**, not a CoM member.

---

sections.heading: 7. Limitations, private practice, retainer (POL-06-07)
sections.content:
**Idea:** **principal–agent**. AGI **is** the government in court. Must not hurt the client’s interest.

| Not allowed | Gloss |
|:---|:---|
| Advise / hold a **brief against GoI** | Cannot be on Alpha’s side in *Alpha v. Union of India* |
| Advise / hold a brief in a case **where GoI has already called for advice** | Even *A v. B* (GoI not a party): once DoLA asked AGI, **secrecy** — do not advise A or B |
| **Defend an accused in a criminal case without GoI permission** | Civil = A v. B. Criminal = **three parties** (A, B, **State**). Defending the accused is against the State unless government **permits** (false case / trap possible) |
| Accept **directorship** in any **company** without permission | Leadership / other clients — government wants to know. **Not a total ban** |

**Boxed sheet line:** **AGI can have private practice.**

AGI is **not a government employee / civil servant** → **no salary**. Paid a **retainer** (keeps the lawyer on call even if no brief for 10 days) **+ hearing fees** when they appear. Service-provider relationship: unhappy → change the lawyer.

---

sections.heading: 8. Other law officers & pre-audience (POL-06-08)
sections.content:
**Law Officers (CoS) Rules, 1987** hierarchy (only AGI is **in the Constitution**; the rest are **rules**):

1. **AGI** — **1**
2. **SGI** — **1**
3. **Additional Solicitor General (Addl. SG)** — **many** (class: floated **~38**, many vacant; government can add tomorrow; typically 1–2 per HC as regional advocates; bigger team in Delhi)
4. **Advocate General** — **State** (same *idea* as AGI, for the State)
5. Other advocates by **seniority**

GoI may send AGI, SGI, or any Addl. SG — **nothing fixed**. Class: “generally AGI in the SC, but whoever we wish.”

**Advocates Act, 1961, Section 23 — right of pre-audience** (first hearing), distinct from Art 76 **audience**:

1. AGI  
2. SGI  
3. then Addl. SGs (class listed SGI again, then State Advocate General)  
4. **Advocate General of the State**  
5. other advocates by seniority  

---

sections.heading: 9. Part V Chapter 2 — Parliament begins (POL-06-09)
sections.content:
Pivots class wants you to keep:

| Chapter | What | First / last article (class) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | Union Executive | … **Art 76** AGI; **Art 78** = **duties of the PM** (furnish information the President may call for) |
| 2 | Parliament | **Art 79** → last **Art 122** |
| 3 | Ordinance | **Art 123** only |
| 4 | Supreme Court | **Art 124** |

sections.heading: Article 79 — three components
sections.content:
Parliament of the Union = **President + Council of States + House of the People**.

- President is **not a member** (Article **59** — cannot sit in a legislature) but is an **integral part** of Parliament: **inseparable**. Without a **summon**, the Houses cannot sit. President also **prorogues** (ends a **session**). Houses cannot pass a **law** without **assent**; the President **can** make a law without them = **ordinance (Art 123)**.
- **Separation of Powers (SoP)** is **partial**: entire political executive sits in the legislature; President sits in **both** executive and legislature — but as **part**, not as an MP.

| Term | Meaning | Who |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Summon** | Call a session | President |
| **Prorogue** | End a **session** | President |
| **Adjournment** | End a day’s **sitting** | House (every day; class: can happen several times a day) |

**Session clock (class):** **11:00–18:00**. **11:00 Question Hour**, **12:00 Zero Hour** (discussion; “zero” = unlisted). Do not invert.

sections.heading: Functions of Parliament (overview; not exclusive boxes)
sections.content:
1. **Legislative** — **Art 245** territorial (India) + **extra-territorial** (only Union; States cannot). **Art 246** + **Seventh Schedule**: List I **Union**, List II **State**, List III **Concurrent**. Concurrent conflict → **Union law prevails**, **except** if the **State law has Presidential assent** — then that State’s law prevails *in that State*. Class example: **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) Act, 2023**, **Section 1** — extra-territorial reach for Indian citizens’ offences abroad.
2. **Keep a check on the Executive** (class: this is the real job; law-making is one tool). **Administrative:** make / break government — **Confidence Motion (CM) / No-Confidence Motion (NCM)**; also **Censure Motion**, **Adjournment Motion**. Oversight of institutions (annual reports of **Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)**, National Commissions for Scheduled Castes / Scheduled Tribes / Backward Classes, Finance Commission, etc.) **to Parliament**.
3. **Financial** — custodian of public money. **No tax / no expenditure without Parliament.** **Annual Financial Statement** = Budget.
4. **Deliberative** — debate for its own sake, not only to pass a law. Class: **Raghav Chadha** on **gig workers (Zomato)** — no bill that day; discussion still moved companies off “10-minute delivery” branding.
5. **Informative** — questions → ministerial statistics become **public**; MPs write; Parliament sets the country’s **discourse**.

---

sections.heading: 10. House strength & quorum (POL-06-10)
sections.content:
| Term | Lok Sabha | Rajya Sabha | Use |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---|
| **Maximum strength** (Constitution allows) | **550** | **250** | Theoretical. Class: a Budget-session proposal to take the *maximum* toward **850** — **543 is not becoming 850**. **Not** used in majority maths |
| **Total strength / membership** (what we have) | **543** | **245** | Used in calculations |

**Quorum — Article 100:** minimum members **present** to **transact business** = **1/10 of total membership** of that House. Below quorum → House is **adjourned** until quorum is met. Majority is a **voting** idea; quorum is a **sitting** idea.

---

sections.heading: 11. Absolute, simple, effective majority (POL-06-11)
sections.content: These **names are not in the Constitution**. Text says “agreed by the House” / “ratified” / “majority of the then membership.” Always **explain the fraction**.

sections.heading: (1) Absolute majority = **> ½ of total membership**
sections.content:
| House | Class number |
|:---|:---|
| LS | **272+** (543). Sheet also **273** = old **545**-seat / Anglo-Indian maths |
| RS | Teacher **123+**. Sheet **125+** |

**Not required alone for any purpose inside the House.** **Immense political significance:** this is the number that **forms a government**. Miss it → **hung Parliament** (coalition, relatively unstable) or a **minority government**. Number is largely **fixed**.

sections.heading: (2) Simple majority = **> ½ of members present and voting**
sections.content:
Also called **functional / working majority**. Day-to-day work.

**Class / sheet drill (LS):** total **543** − absent **23** (teacher first said 20) = present **520** − abstain **10** = present-and-voting **510** → need **256**.

Used for:

- **Ordinary, Money, Financial bills** (not Constitution Amendment Bills)
- **Election** of Speaker & Deputy Speaker (LS / Legislative Assembly); Deputy Chairman (RS); Chairman & Deputy Chairman (Legislative Council). RS **Chairman** is the Vice-President — elected elsewhere
- **CM / NCM / Censure** (and like motions)
- **Approval** of **President’s Rule** and **Financial Emergency**
- **Discontinuance** of **National Emergency** — **LS, special sitting**. **Approval** of National Emergency is the **tougher** majority (below). Logic: imposing must be harder than lifting (rights are hit)
- Wherever the Constitution is **silent** (“agreed by the House”) → treat as simple

sections.heading: (3) Effective majority = **> ½ of effective strength**
sections.content:
**Effective strength = total − vacancies** (death, resignation, removal). Constitution language: **majority of the then membership** — members **at the time of voting**, not “present.” Sleeping at home still counts; a dead / resigned member does not.

**Only one use:** **removal** of **presiding / deputy presiding officers** — **eight posts** (LS + Legislative Assembly Speaker & Deputy; RS + Legislative Council Chairman & Deputy).

**Vice-President / RS Chairman:** removal **introduced in RS** by **effective** majority; **LS only agrees** → **simple** majority. Same proposal, **two different majorities**. Rare.

---

sections.heading: 12. “Special majority” = anything that is not half (POL-06-12)
sections.content: Class: the phrase **has no meaning** until you write the **exact fraction**. Four kinds today:

sections.heading: (i) Article 249 — **not less than 2/3 of members present and voting**
sections.content: RS resolution **in national interest** authorising **Parliament to legislate on the State List**. “Not less than” → **equality is enough**. Same fraction: **Article 312** — RS resolution to create a new **All India Service**. Both are **RS-only** and both are cases where the **Centre will affect the States** — so the **House of States** must pass a **tougher** bar.

sections.heading: (ii) Article 368 — Constitution Amendment Bills
sections.content:
**Not less than 2/3 present and voting AND > ½ of total membership.** Meet the **higher** of the two numbers. Floor can never drop below **absolute majority**; if attendance is high, the 2/3 number rises.

**Class / sheet LS drill:** 543; abs 23; present 520; abstain 10; voting **510** → 2/3 = **340**. Absolute floor **272**. Practically need **340**.

**RS drill:** 245; abs 50; present 195; abstain 12 (class: “all 12 nominated may abstain someday”); voting **183**. Absolute floor **123**. Need the **higher** of 2/3 of 183 and 123.

Same majority also for: **approval of National Emergency**; **removal** of **SC / HC judges**, **Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)**, **Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)**.

**Legislative Council create / abolish:** State **Legislative Assembly** resolution by this **tough** majority → **Parliament by law** → **simple** majority (Constitution silent = simple).

sections.heading: (iii) Article 61 — impeachment of the President
sections.content:
**Not less than 2/3 of total membership** (not present-and-voting). **Only this purpose.** **Never used.**

| House | Sheet | Class arithmetic |
|:---|:---|:---|
| LS | **363** | 543 × 2/3 = 362 → **round up** (less would fail “not less than”) → **363** |
| RS | **167** | Students split **163 / 164**; **round up**. Sheet **167** looks like **250 × 2/3**. Do not mix the two |

---

sections.content:

sections.heading: 1. How the two Houses are made (POL-07-01)
sections.content:
| | **Rajya Sabha** | **Lok Sabha (LS)** |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Total now | **245** = **233 elected + 12 nominated** | **543 elected**. **No nominated** members now (old Anglo-Indian nominated seats gone) |
| Who elects | **Elected** Members of the Legislative Assembly (MLAs) of **States + Union Territories (UTs) that have a legislature** — class: **Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir** | **Direct** election from **territorial constituencies** |
| Method | **Proportional Representation (PR) + Single Transferable Vote (STV)** | **First Past the Post (FPTP)** = **maximum** votes. **Not** a majority. Class: election of **popularity**, not majority |
| Label | Council of States — **indirect** people | **Popular House** — **direct** people |
| Seat list | **Fourth Schedule** (233) | **Parliament by law** — **RPA 1950**. Changes with population / new states. Has moved since 1950 |

**Trap:** both Houses represent **the same people**. LS = direct; RS = people of the States via MLAs. Do not write “RS does not represent the people.”

**PR here ≠ Presidential PR.** President: vote **value** ∝ State **population**. RS: all **403** Uttar Pradesh (UP) MLAs elect UP’s **31** RS seats — **no extra vote-value**. PR+STV is used because the electoral college must pick **more than one** member (top-five FPTP would collapse if everyone first-preferences the same name). Class will not drill the arithmetic in the room.

**Class numbers (do not invent more):** Delhi **7 LS / 3 RS**. UP **80 LS / 31 RS**. Tamil Nadu **39 LS**.

sections.heading: Why two RPAs? (class prompt — do not invent the split)
sections.content:
Both Acts together regulate **LS / Assembly / Council / RS** elections. **Only statute named in the GS-II syllabus** (*salient features of the Representation of the People Act*). Class hint after the 2003 ballot change: **1950 has the seats; 1951 has the process.** Confirm from the **index pages** yourself.

---

sections.heading: 2. Open ballot, *Kuldip Nayar*, anti-defection, NOTA (POL-07-02)
sections.content:
| | RS election | LS election |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Ballot | **Open** (only such election in India) | **Secret** — **free and fair** (no force) |
| Since | Originally **secret**. **Open from 2003** (RPA **1951**) | Always secret |

**Open** = a party **observer** may **see** the MLA’s preference sheet. The MLA is still free to vote as they like. The **system** will not punish them.

***Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India, 2006*** (class: renowned journalist; now deceased). Challenge: open ballot kills free voting. Court / government logic class stressed: **secret** RS polls hid **cross-voting** and **corruption**; **indirect** election + party representation was being gamed.

**Anti-Defection Law (ADL)** applies only to a **proceeding of the House**. President / Vice-President / RS **elections are not House proceedings** → **ADL does not apply**. Same logic: **None of the Above (NOTA)** is for **direct** free voters only — **no NOTA** in President / VP / RS elections.

---

sections.heading: 3. Continuous House vs dissolvable House (POL-07-03)
sections.content:
| | RS | LS |
|:---|:---|:---|
| House term | **None** — **continuous House** | **5 years**, then **auto-dissolved** |
| Members | **6 years**; **1/3 retire every 2 years** | Whole House goes together |
| Age (class) | **Same RS since 1952** — **74 years** old | This is the **18th LS**, about **2 years** old. **17** LS have come and gone |

**Early dissolution — 1971:** after 1952–57–62–67 the next poll was due **1972**. Indira Gandhi called it a year early on a “good vibe” (*India is Indira…*). **Second-highest** majority ever; beaten only by **1984**.

**Extension beyond 5 years** (only during **National Emergency**):

1. Emergency proclaimed in the country **or any part**.
2. **Parliament by law**.
3. **≤ 1 year at a time** (3 / 6 / 9 months fine; not more than 12). Can repeat while Emergency lasts.
4. When Emergency is **revoked**, leftover extension **cannot go beyond 6 months** (time to hold a poll).

**1971 cycle:** next poll due **1976** → extended to **1977**, approved again to **1978** but the **second year was not used** — election held in **1977**.

**Bye-election** (any House, any vacancy): winner gets only the **leftover** term, not a fresh 5 / 6 years. Class: a bye-election today → new LS member sits till **2029**.

---

sections.heading: 4. RS is federal — minus / plus / equal (POL-07-04)
sections.content:
**Why an RS at all?** **Federalism** = **division of power** between **two layers** (Centre and States; names differ abroad). Centre’s Union-list law hits every State → States need a House in the conversation. **Seventh Schedule** is the map.

Do **not** write “RS is useless / less useful.” Visibility (LS elections, government formation, money) ≠ relevance.

sections.heading: Minus (LS stronger) — finance + administration
sections.content:
1. **Make / break government** — Confidence Motion (CM), No-Confidence Motion (NCM), Censure Motion, Adjournment Motion. **Collective responsibility to LS** (parliamentary principle 2 — Lecture 4 / Article **75(3)**). **United States of America (USA) House is also direct-elected** and still cannot make/break the executive — so “direct election” is **not** the reason. Reason: **parliamentary democracy**.
2. **Money Bills** — introduce **only in LS**. RS may **recommend within 14 days**; LS may **override**. Reason: **no taxation without representation** — people’s money → **House of the People**.

sections.heading: Plus (RS only / RS unique)
sections.content:
- **Article 249** (national-interest State-list law) and **Article 312** (new All India Service) — **RS resolutions**. Class: **249 used zero times**. **312:** only **Indian Forest Service** created after Independence (Indian Administrative Service / Indian Police Service inherited from the British). Put this **later** in an answer — rare.
- **Removal of the Vice-President** — introduced in RS (Lecture 5: effective in RS, simple in LS).
- **National Emergency / President’s Rule / Financial Emergency** normally need **both Houses**. If **LS is dissolved**, **RS alone** can approve. **LS alone can never** — RS is always there. **Significance of a continuous House:** it **assists continuity of administration**. Class: President’s Rule when an LS poll is due.

sections.heading: Equal — legislation + deliberation
sections.content:
- **Ordinary Bills, Financial Bills, Constitution Amendment Bills (CABs)** need **both Houses**.
- **Deadlock** on ordinary / financial → **joint sitting, Article 108** (detail next class). Class: **three** joint sittings in ~80 years. LS is roughly **double** RS, so LS would dominate the room — **not** an argument that RS is useless.
- **No joint sitting for Article 368.** Both Houses sit **separately**. One House’s no = dead.

**42nd / 44th story (class):** Emergency **42nd** = **mini-Constitution** (strengthen the executive). Janata **45th Constitutional Amendment Bill** → became **44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978**. RS still Congress-controlled; it **diluted** the rollback; LS had to **accept RS changes** or lose the Bill. **House of Elders** = **experience / link to the past** (2/3 still sitting), **not** because members are older. **Temperance** vs LS “change everything in one election.”

**Numbering trap:** CAB numbers and CAA numbers are **two pipelines**. Class: **106** CAAs so far. This year’s Budget-session **131st CAB** (delimitation / **850** seats) **failed** — that bill number is used up; next bill **132** would become Act **107** if it passed.

**Deliberation:** both have Question Hour, Zero Hour, debates. **LS: Question Hour then Zero Hour. RS inverted** (class: RS switched ~**10 years** ago to get more Zero-Hour time). **Starred** = oral in the House; **unstarred** = written papers. Zero Hour = on the spot; Question Hour needs advance notice.

---

sections.heading: 5. Committees — RS is inside Parliament’s work (POL-07-05)
sections.content:
**Estimates Committee** = **LS only** (not a “Parliament” committee in class’s sense).

| Body | Size (class) | Split |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Public Accounts Committee (PAC)** | **22** | **15 LS + 7 RS** |
| **Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU)** | **22** | **15 LS + 7 RS** |
| **Department-Related Standing Committee (DRSC)** | **31** each; class **24** DRSCs cover the ministries | **21 LS + 10 RS** |
| **Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC)** | **31** (this LS’s first JPC — current affairs; class did not name the subject) | **21 LS + 10 RS** |

**PAC:** examines the **Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)** audit of government accounts (report to Parliament **through the President**). Overspend / underspend / fraud. **COPU:** same idea for **public sector undertakings**. **DRSCs:** schemes, policy, and the **budget** of their departments. Class news hook: **DoPT** DRSC chair **Brij Lal** on **Civil Services Aptitude Test (CSAT)** — read the paper, not only daily-news videos.

A parliamentary committee **cannot run without RS members**. Many **ministers** sit in RS (class: **S. Jaishankar**). Indirect election is a **window for talent** that may not win an FPTP popularity contest. **About one-third** of India’s PMs have come from RS.

**PMs from RS (class four):** **Indira Gandhi**, **I.K. Gujral**, **H.D. Deve Gowda**, **Dr Manmohan Singh**. Sheet listed the first three + Manmohan. **Narendra Modi = 15th PM** → 4 of the previous 14.

**Line to hold:** **RS is not a secondary House; it is the second House.** (State **Legislative Councils** *are* secondary to Assemblies — later topic.)

---

sections.heading: 6. Motion vs resolution; three LS special powers (POL-07-06)
sections.content:
**Motion** = a **proposal to transact business** (*prastav*). Introduction of a bill, a discussion, anything. It **moves** through stages.

**Resolution** = a **motion that is voted** — a House **decision**.

**Every resolution is a motion; every motion is not a resolution.** Raghav Chadha / gig workers (Lecture 5) = motion to **discuss**, no vote.

Make-or-break tools sit on **Article 75(3)** (collective responsibility to LS). Procedure lives in the **Rules of Procedure of the Lok Sabha**, not the Constitution.

**Three rules to remember (gap of 7):**

| Rule | What |
|:---|:---|
| **184** | General **motions** |
| **191** | **Voting** on motions |
| **198** | **NCM** specifically |

**CM** and **Censure** are **not** in the rules — **convention**. Adjournment has its **own** block: **Rules 56–63** (**8** rules).

**Three special powers of LS** (class count):

1. Make / break (CM / NCM / Censure / Adjournment).
2. Money Bills — introduce + override.
3. **Discontinue National Emergency** — **special sitting of LS** (sessions class next).

sections.heading: Update — 10 September 2026 (UPSC CSE Prelims 2022)
sections.content: `CSE-2022-Q15` **missed** (`MST-070`). Exclusive power of Lok Sabha = **no-confidence against the Council of Ministers** only. **Ratifying a declaration of Emergency** is **not** LS-exclusive — class already: National Emergency / President’s Rule / Financial Emergency need **both Houses**; if LS is dissolved, **RS alone** can approve; **LS alone never**. **Impeachment of the President** (Art 61) is **not** LS-exclusive. He kept Emergency ratification + NCM.

sections.heading: Update — 12 September 2026 (evening paper)
sections.content:
`MST-070` **held** (option c). LS exclusive = **NCM only**. Emergency ratification and impeachment stay **not** LS-only. 15-day **27 Sep**.

---

sections.heading: 7. NCM vs Censure Motion (POL-07-07)
sections.content:
| | **No-Confidence Motion** | **Censure Motion** |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Home | **Rule 198** | Convention under **184 + 191**. Word *censure* = **criticise** — not in the rules |
| Against | **Entire Council of Ministers (CoM)** only | **One / group / entire CoM** |
| Point | **Want of confidence** of LS. **Reason not required** (“This House does not have confidence in the CoM” is enough) | An **act, failure to act (omission), or policy**. **Reason required** |
| Leave | **Leave of the House** — **≥ 50 members** stand to **introduce** (passage is still **simple majority**) | **No leave**. Speaker + **Leader of the House** + **Business Advisory Committee (BAC)** slot the discussion — government can **delay** |
| If it passes | Entire CoM must go. **PM’s resignation is enough** (pivot). **Never passed** in independent India. **1999:** Vajpayee resigned after a **confidence** test, not after an NCM *passed*. Last NCM **introduced 2023** (BJP **303** — class: it was never going to pass) | Official record + **political** hit. **Never passed** against a minister. If it ever did, an NCM would follow |

**NCM clock (Rule 198):** notice to the **Speaker’s office**. **Before 10:00** (sitting starts **11:00**) → taken up **the same day** (Speaker picks the hour). **After 10:00** → **next working day**. After leave: dispose within **≤ 10 days**. Marshal counts those standing.

**Why bring a motion that will fail?** Debate. Class: 2023 NCM; recent proposal to **remove the Speaker** — not to win the numbers, to put **partisan chair** on the record. **Seven bills in 36 minutes** is the opposite of that democracy.

---

sections.heading: 8. Adjournment Motion (POL-07-08)
sections.content:
**Adjournment** (everyday) = Speaker ends a **sitting** (lunch, 18:00). **Adjournment Motion** = a **member** proposes to **stop today’s listed work** to discuss an **urgent matter of great public importance**.

- **Leave ≥ 50.**
- After discussion the House **votes**. If passed → **rest of the day adjourned**.
- **Element of censure:** majority slaps the **government’s agenda**. Same reason it exists **only in LS**, **not in RS**.

---

sections.heading: 9. Presiding officers — both Houses (POL-07-09)
sections.content:
| | LS | RS |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Presiding | **Speaker** | **Chairman** (Vice-President) |
| Deputy | **Deputy Speaker** | **Deputy Chairman** |
| Panel if both absent | **Panel of Chairpersons ≤ 10** (Speaker appoints) | **Panel of Vice-Chairpersons ≤ 6** (Chairman appoints) |

Deputy **works only when the chair is empty**. Otherwise they are an ordinary member.

Chair **does not participate** like a member (no ordinary speech / motion / vote) except a **casting vote** on a **tie**.

They **regulate**: who speaks, how long, *baith jaiye*. **Interpret** the Constitution and the **rules** for the sitting — that interpretation is written down for later Speakers. **Discipline:** suspend a member for at most **the end of the session**. **Face of the House** (not of the government), inside and outside — President’s message (e.g. return of a bill) arrives **to the chair**; a result is official when the chair **announces** it.

---

sections.heading: 10. Three special powers of the LS Speaker (POL-07-10)
sections.content:
Same count as LS’s three special powers:

1. **Certify a Money Bill.** Certificate is **final** for the House to **proceed**. **Final ≠ unreviewable in court.** Class: even an SC judgment can be overruled by a larger bench.
2. **Preside at a joint sitting:** **Speaker → Deputy Speaker → Deputy Chairman of RS** (**not** the RS Chairman) → a **member decided by the Houses**.
3. **Article 94 proviso:** when LS is **dissolved**, the Speaker **does not vacate** until **immediately before the first meeting** of the next LS. **Institutional continuity** — 17th → 18th LS. One person, no law-making; members are gone; the **face** stays. Vacates **automatically** the night before the new House meets.

sections.heading: Speaker Pro Tem (convention)
sections.content:
**Member-elect** ≠ member until the **oath**. Chicken-and-egg: need a Speaker to oath members; need members to elect a Speaker.

**President** administers the oath to **one** member-elect and names them **Speaker Pro Tem** (temporary). That person (1) oaths the rest (540+ , days) and (2) conducts the election of the Speaker. Class: House then chose **Om Birla**. Pro Tem’s job ends when the new Speaker sits.

**Article 93:** House shall choose **one** Speaker and **one** Deputy Speaker **as soon as possible**. **No clock.** **No Deputy Speaker** for the **entire 17th LS + 2 years of the 18th** = **7 years**. Government hides behind *asap*; class: **spirit** of the article + **convention** (Speaker = ruling; Deputy = **opposition**) + democracy. **Public Interest Litigation (PIL)** pending.

**Homework split:** **Absence** of S + DyS + panel ≠ **vacancy** (death / resignation / removal). **Panel is appointed by the Speaker** — if the Speaker’s office is **vacant**, the panel has **no role**. Answers differ; you find them.

---

sections.content:

sections.heading: Lecture 1 — 24 August 2026 — S&T Syllabus Overview & Public Health (Virology)
sections.content:
> **Date of Lecture:** 24 August 2026 | **Subject:** GS Science & Technology | **Lecture:** 01

sections.heading: Prelims — General Science
sections.content:
- **Foundation:** Physics, Chemistry, Biology
- **NCERT Level:** Class 8, 9, 10 (PHY + CHE + BIO); Class 11 & 12 (Biology only)
- **Key Rule:** 90% of Prelims S&T questions come from the chapters listed below (not from basic physics/chemistry)
- **S&T is highly contemporary** — no fixed syllabus unlike History/Polity/Geography. Questions are driven by current affairs + PYQ patterns

sections.heading: Reading Resources
sections.content:
1. **NCERT Textbooks** — 8th, 9th, 10th (PHY/CHE/BIO) + 11th, 12th (BIO)
2. **Class Notes** — Primary reference
3. **PYQs** — 10 years for Prelims, 6 years for Mains
4. **Current Affairs** — The Hindu & Indian Express (newspaper reading is the **most important** resource — "journey starts with the newspaper and ends with the newspaper")

sections.heading: 1. Biotechnology
sections.content:
- Tool of BT = **Recombinant DNA Technology** (also called **Genetic Engineering**)
- Applications in agriculture, medicine, industry

sections.heading: 2. Space & Astrophysics
sections.content:
- Study of universe = **Cosmology**
- Composition of universe → Stars, **Black Holes**, **Gravitational Waves**
- **Only 4% of the universe** is visible matter (known/observable)
- Remaining **96% unknown** — yet to be explored (dark matter + dark energy)

sections.heading: 3. Nanoscience & Nanotechnology
sections.content:
- Significance of **nanoscale: 1 nanometer to 100 nanometer**
- Extraordinary properties at nanoscale
- **Graphene** — key nanomaterial (properties and applications)

sections.heading: 4. Robotics & Artificial Intelligence
sections.content:
- Components of robots, robotic sensors
- **Humanoid robots** vs **Industrial robots**
- AI started in 1960s (WWII era) but prominence is recent
- **Intelligence = Algorithm** (set of instructions to perform a task)

##### Fixed Algorithm vs Learning Algorithm
| Feature | Fixed Algorithm | Learning Algorithm (Machine Learning) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Instructions | Pre-defined, rigid | Adaptive, learns from data |
| Output | Yes/No answers | Complex decisions with feedback |
| Adaptability | None | **Adapts based on data** |
| Error Correction | Cannot self-correct | **Learns from mistakes** (hit & trial) |
| Core Function | Rule-based execution | **Data-driven decision making** |

##### Deep Learning
- **Artificial Neural Network (ANN)** — inspired by human brain's biological nervous system
- **Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)** — handles images, videos
- **Machine Learning + ANN/CNN = Deep Learning**
- Deep Learning: Processes **vast amounts of data** quickly; no pre-programmed instructions needed; learns autonomously through trial & error

##### Large Language Models (LLMs)
| LLM | Company | Backed By |
|:---|:---|:---|
| ChatGPT | OpenAI | Microsoft |
| Gemini | Google | Google |
| Claude | Anthropic | Amazon |
| **Sarvam AI** | Sarvam (India) | **India's first indigenous LLM** |

- **Sarvam AI** — focuses on **Indic language translation**; works with local accents; can read documents in natural human language with local dialect accuracy
- LLMs are applications of Deep Learning — require vast data processing

sections.heading: 5. Information Technology
sections.content:
- **Evolution of Internet**
- **Internet of Things (IoT)** — interconnecting both physical & virtual devices through internet (cars, refrigerators, not just laptops/tablets)
- **Cloud Computing** — data collection, storage, processing happens **online** (e.g., Gmail, web conferencing); requires internet connection; server located remotely
- **Edge Computing** — data collected, stored, processed **on the spot** by the device itself or nearby local server (e.g., self-driving car making immediate decisions); does NOT send data to remote server
- **Blockchain Technology** — ecosystem where data once stored **cannot be changed/manipulated**; ensures data accuracy, fidelity, security; applications include electronic voting, supply chain
- **5G vs 6G** — digital wireless mobile communication; differences in data speed, volume, latency

sections.heading: 6. Indigenization of Technology
sections.content:
- India's efforts in innovation, R&D
- **Dual Advantage:**
  1. **Creates new economic opportunities** — boosting manufacturing through innovation
  2. **Serves national/strategic interest** — reducing dependence on other nations
- Areas: Space technology, Defense, Vaccine development
- Key metric: India's proportion of GDP spent on R&D/Innovation
- Goal: **Self-reliance** (Atmanirbhar)

sections.heading: 7. Public Health
sections.content: - Diseases, Vaccines, Types of vaccines, Vaccine-induced immunity - COVID-19 reference - **Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR)** - Key diseases/viruses: - HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis (TB) - Polio, Malaria - Influenza virus — Swine Flu & Bird Flu - Dengue virus - Nipah virus - Ebola virus ##### Medical Device Regulation Architecture & 2026 Reforms - **Statutory Base:** Regulated as statutory "drugs" under the **Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940** and governed by the **Medical Devices Rules, 2017** under the **CDSCO** (headed by DCGI, MoHFW). - **4-Tier Risk Classification:** - **Class A (Low Risk):** Surgical dressings, thermometers (State Licensing Authority). - **Class B (Low-to-Moderate Risk):** Hypodermic needles, suction pumps (State Licensing Authority). - **Class C (Moderate-to-High Risk):** Hemodialysis catheters, ventilators (Central Licensing Authority / DCGI). - **Class D (High Risk):** Heart valves, coronary stents, implantable pacemakers (Central Licensing Authority / DCGI). - **2026 Ease of Doing Business Amendments:** - **Rule 44 (Sterilisation):** Removed separate loan licence mandate for outsourced sterilisation (facility's licence number must be printed on device label; 6-month transition). - **Rule 63 (Clinical Investigation Waiver):** Added **European Union (EU)** to Stringent Regulatory Jurisdictions (US, UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, EU) to fast-track market approval for novel devices without predicate in India. ---

sections.heading: Immunity
sections.content:
- **Definition:** Ability of the body to fight against **infection or diseases**
- Role of **White Blood Cells (WBC)** — specifically **B-cell lymphocytes**

sections.heading: Pathogen / Pathogenic Microbe
sections.content:
- **Disease-causing microorganisms**, including bacteria and virus
- Can also include fungi and protozoa

sections.heading: Antimicrobial Medicine
sections.content:
- Used to **prevent growth & multiplication** OR **kill** pathogenic microbes
- **Antibiotic** = Anti-**bacterial** medicine → prevents growth/multiplication or kills **bacteria**
  - ⚠️ **Antibiotics do NOT act against viruses**
- **Antiviral drugs** = Anti-**viral** medicine → acts against viruses
  - Needed specifically because antibiotics are ineffective against viruses

sections.heading: Inflammation
sections.content:
- When there is **injury or infection** to the body → triggers **immune response**
- Body increases blood flow to the affected area → brings more WBCs to fight infection
- **4 signs of inflammation:** Redness, Swelling, Heat, Pain
- Even **fever** is a form of inflammation — body raises temperature to make it difficult for bacteria/virus to multiply
  - ⚠️ Too high fever can damage the body → need to control with antipyretics

sections.heading: Antipyretic
sections.content: - **Reduces body temperature** / **reduces/controls fever**

sections.heading: Analgesic
sections.content: - **Reduces pain** / acts as **pain reliever**

sections.heading: Paracetamol — The Dual-Action Drug
sections.content:
- Acts as **BOTH** antipyretic AND analgesic
- ⚠️ **Paracetamol is NOT an antimicrobial medicine**
- Cannot act against any pathogenic microbe (neither bacteria nor virus)
- Only manages symptoms (fever + pain), does NOT treat the infection itself

---

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content:
> **Virus = Obligate Intracellular Parasite**

Each word carries a specific meaning:

| Word | Meaning | Implication |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Obligate** | Compulsory / Mandatory | Virus **MUST** use a living host cell — cannot complete life cycle without it |
| **Intracellular** | Inside/Within the cell | Virus infects & multiplies **inside** a living cell |
| **Parasite** | Organism dependent on another for life processes | Virus is completely dependent on host cell for reproduction |

- Virus **infects and replicates** inside a living cell called its **host cell**
- **All viruses are parasites** — correct statement for Prelims
- Host cell types: **Plant cell, Animal cell, Bacterial cell, Fungal cell**

sections.heading: Virus is Acellular
sections.content:
- Virus **lacks any cellular structure** → called **acellular** (without cell)
- This is why we say "bacterial cell" but NEVER "viral cell"
- No nucleus, no organelles, no ribosomes

sections.heading: Composition of Virus — Nucleocapsid
sections.content:
```
Nucleocapsid = Nucleic Acid + Capsid
                    |              |
          Genetic Material    Protein Coat
          (Viral Genome)    (Protects genome
                             from environment)
```

- **Nucleic acid / Genetic material / Viral genome** — Complete set of biological instructions (software) to make new copies of the virus; contains **genetic code** → genes encoding viral proteins
- **Capsid** — Protein coat/covering that **protects** the genetic material from the outside environment

sections.heading: DNA vs RNA Virus
sections.content:
| Feature | DNA Virus | RNA Virus |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Genetic Material | Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA) | Ribonucleic Acid (RNA) |
| Structure | Double-stranded DNA | Single/double-stranded RNA |
| Examples | HPV, HBV, **adenovirus** | SARS-CoV-2, Dengue, Nipah, Ebola, Influenza, HIV (**retrovirus**) |

sections.heading: Critical Prelims Rule
sections.content: > **A virus can have EITHER DNA OR RNA as its genome — NEVER BOTH**

sections.heading: All Living Systems vs Virus — Genome Rule
sections.content:
| | Plants | Animals | Bacteria | Fungi | **Virus** |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Genetic Material | DNA only | DNA only | DNA only | DNA only | **DNA OR RNA** (never both) |

- In ALL other living systems, the genome is **always only DNA**
- Only viruses can have RNA as their genetic material

sections.heading: Update — 8 September 2026 (UPSC CSE Prelims 2021)
sections.content:
Class never named **adenovirus**. `CSE-2021-Q70` extra (held that night; now on this page):

| UPSC statement | Fact |
|:---|:---|
| 1. Adenoviruses have **single-stranded DNA**; retroviruses have **double-stranded DNA** | **False — inverted.** Adenovirus = **double-stranded DNA**. Retrovirus **packaged genome = RNA** (HIV is already a class RNA virus). Do not treat the DNA copy made **inside the host** as the viral genome. |
| 2. Common cold is **sometimes** caused by an adenovirus; AIDS is caused by a retrovirus | **True.** AIDS = HIV. Class lock: HIV kills **Helper T-cells**. |

---

sections.heading: Part D: Virus Tropism (Host Cell Specificity)
sections.content:
- Virus develops **specific preference** for a particular host cell
- Not every virus infects every type of cell
- **Virus tropism** = host cell specificity
- Example: **Polio virus** → infects **only human cells** (not plants, not other animals)

sections.heading: Examples of Virus Tropism
sections.content:
| Virus | Target Host Cell | Disease |
|:---|:---|:---|
| SARS-CoV-2 | Human lung cells (ACE-2 receptor) | COVID-19 / Severe Pneumonia |
| Hepatitis B | Human liver cells | Liver cancer |
| Polio virus | Human motor neurons | Paralytic polio |
| HPV | Human genital cells | Genital cancer |

---

sections.heading: 1. Human Papilloma Virus (HPV)
sections.content:
- Causes **genital cancer** in **both males AND females** — Prelims trap
  - Example: **Cervix cancer** in females
- **Mode of transmission:** Sexual transmission
- **Remains asymptomatic** — person may not show symptoms but can transmit
- **HPV Vaccine:**
  - **Gardasil** — a type of **Subunit / Peptide vaccine** (protein-based)
  - Injects only **virus protein fragment** (NOT full virus) → therefore "subunit"
  - Current India drive: Females aged **9-11 years** (before sexual maturity)
  - Can be given to males too (developed countries already do this)
  - India's current focus: Females first, males later

sections.heading: 2. Hepatitis B Virus (HBV)
sections.content: - **UPSC Trap Alert (MST-028):** Hepatitis B is a **DNA virus**. (In contrast, Hepatitis A, C, D, and E are RNA viruses). - Infects **only liver cells** — best example of virus tropism / host specificity - Can cause **liver cancer** (virus-induced cancer) - **Preventable** using **HBV vaccine** - **Remains asymptomatic for many years** → major threat - Person unknowingly transmits infection for years - May suddenly develop liver cancer symptoms - Prelims statement: "Number of HBV cases can be more than HIV" — **CORRECT** (because HBV is asymptomatic for years, HIV shows symptoms within months)

sections.heading: Modes of Transmission (Blood-borne virus):
sections.content:
1. Contaminated blood transfusion
2. Unsterilized medical instruments / infected needles
3. Sexual transmission
4. Infected mother → child transmission during pregnancy
5. **Tattooing** (dual risk: both HBV and HIV)

- Can cause **common cold** (UPSC: “sometime”).

sections.heading: Part F: RNA Virus Examples
sections.content:
| RNA Virus | Key Association |
|:---|:---|
| **SARS-CoV-2** (Coronavirus) | COVID-19 pandemic (Dec 2019 onwards) |
| **Dengue virus** | Dengue fever (mosquito-borne) |
| **Nipah virus** | Zoonotic; high mortality |
