sections.heading: 1. What the universe is, and how the picture changed (GEO-11-01)
sections.content:
- The universe = planets, stars, galaxies, space and time. Book: observable universe ≈ **93 billion light-years** across.
- **Geocentric:** ancient Greek picture — motionless Earth at the centre.
- **Aristarchus (312–230 BC):** Sun much farther and larger than the Moon; pushed against a simple Earth-centre model.
- **Eratosthenes (276–194 BC):** first successful measure of Earth’s size (class Fundamentals already uses him as the coiner of *geography*).
- **Ptolemy — *Almagest*:** **Ptolemaic system** — refined geocentric model.
- **Nicolaus Copernicus:** **heliocentric** — Sun at the centre of the solar system.
- **Galileo Galilei** and **Johannes Kepler** refined heliocentrism. Galileo: first telescope used for astronomy; evidence for Copernicus.

---

sections.heading: 2.1 Traditional (mostly *solar system*, not the whole universe)
sections.content:
| Theory | Who (book) | Picture |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Nebular hypothesis** | **Immanuel Kant (1755)**; refined by **Pierre-Simon Laplace** | Cloud of gas and dust (**nebula**) contracts under gravity → spinning disc → planets and moons |
| **Planetesimal theory** | **Chamberlin and Moulton** (early 20th century) | Planets grow by accumulation of tiny orbiting **planetesimals** |
| **Tidal / wandering-star picture** (book continues this as a traditional line) | — | A wandering star approaches the Sun → **cigar-shaped** filament of material is pulled out → later condenses into planets |

sections.heading: 2.2 Later: revised nebula, then the universe itself
sections.content:
- **Revised nebular hypothesis:** **Otto Schmidt** and **Carl Weizsäcker** (book spelling: Weizaskar). Sun already there, wrapped in a solar nebula of **hydrogen (H)** and **helium (He)**.
- **Accretion:** friction and collisions in a disc → material fuses into planets. Asteroids where gas rings converged.
- Scientists then asked not only “how planets?” but “how the **universe**?”

---

sections.heading: 3. Big Bang / expanding universe (GEO-11-01)
sections.content:
- Also called the **expanding universe hypothesis**.
- Book body: universe began as a **singularity** (tiny ball, infinite density and temperature) ≈ **13.7 billion years** ago; chapter recap also writes **13.8 billion years**. Same order of magnitude — not two theories.
- That event starts **time, space, matter and energy**. Rapid expansion continues.

sections.heading: Update — 9 September 2026 (Test 1 — Big Bang vs nebular)
sections.content:
**Both** statements in the paper hold with this chapter: (1) Big Bang = origin from a **singularity**. (2) **Nebular hypothesis** = accumulation of **interstellar gas** (and dust) → star / planetary system (Kant–Laplace disc → planets and moons). Do not treat nebular as a rival to the Big Bang for the *whole universe*.

- **Edwin Hubble (1920):** galaxies recede; farther galaxies recede **faster**. Evidence = **redshift**. This recession rule is **Hubble’s Law** — main observational support for the Big Bang.

sections.heading: Update — 10 September 2026 (Ghost Recall)
sections.content: `MST-067`: singularity held. Hubble’s evidence is **redshift**, not clouds. Nebular = **solar-system disc**, **not** a rival of the **whole universe**. He marked nebular **True**.

sections.heading: Update — 10 September 2026 (evening paper)
sections.content:
`MST-067` **held**: redshift, not clouds; nebular ≠ whole-universe rival.
- Early universe: energy → matter; first atoms in the **first three minutes**; expansion cools the mix.
- **Four fundamental forces** (book order): **gravity** (weakest, infinite range) · **weak nuclear** · **electromagnetic** · **strong nuclear** (strongest, short range).
- Other evidence the book lists: **cosmic microwave background (CMB)** radiation, large-scale structure, abundance of light elements.

**Arguments the book records *against* the Big Bang (know the headings, not a Mains essay):**

| Objection | Book’s line |
|:---|:---|
| First law of thermodynamics | Scientific laws “break down” at the creation event |
| Entropy | If the early universe was fully homogeneous / isotropic, today’s clumpy universe is hard to square with entropy |
| Speed of light | Early **inflation** looks as if it outran the speed-of-light rule |

---

sections.heading: 4. Galaxies (GEO-11-02)
sections.content:
- Gravity-bound systems of stars. Book: formation **300–500 million years** after the Big Bang; ~**100 billion** galaxies.
- **Hubble’s Law** again: as space expands, galaxies move apart; distance ↑ → speed ↑.
- Collisions: **stars almost never hit** (too far apart). Interaction is through **dark-matter halos**. Gravity redistributes stars; spiral arms can smear into **elliptical** shapes; starbursts and bigger bulges; some leftovers are **irregular**.

| Type | Shape / stars | Book traps |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Irregular** | No distinct shape; often collision products | Gas + dust + **hot blue** (young) stars; smaller; relatively rare |
| **Elliptical** | Round / oval / cigar; **most abundant** | **Old red and yellow** stars; little gas/dust; **no new star formation** (book) |
| **Spiral** | Flattened disc + trailing arms | Arms trigger **young bright** stars. Examples: **Milky Way**, **Andromeda**. Some galaxies are hybrids / in transition |

sections.heading: Milky Way
sections.content:
- **Barred spiral**; contains our solar system.
- Age ~**13.6–14 billion years**. Diameter ~**100,000 light-years**.
- ~**100–400 billion** stars + planets, gas, dust (**nebulae**).
- Central bulge + flat disc + spiral arms. Sun ~**26,000 light-years** from the centre.
- Centre: supermassive black hole **Sagittarius A\*** (~**4.1–4.5 million** solar masses).
- One solar-system lap around the centre ≈ **250 million years**.
- Name: Greek “river of milk” — the hazy band across the night sky. Dark matter shapes the rotation curve.

**Nebula (box):** giant cloud of gas and dust **inside** a galaxy; mostly H and He; gravity collapse → new stars. Prelims: **nebulae ≠ Cepheids** (see PYQs).

---

sections.heading: 5. Stars (GEO-11-03)
sections.content:
- Hot, luminous spheres of gas (mostly H and He), held by gravity. Examples in the book: **Pollux, Sirius, Vega, Polaris**, the **Sun**.
- Source of heavier elements. Same *kind* of life cycle; mass decides lifespan and death.

**Star clusters**

| Kind | Where | Age / look |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Open** | Disc of a galaxy | Loose, relatively young; often still forming stars |
| **Globular** | Halo | Tight; very old; mostly red and yellow giants |
| **Young clusters** | Still in nebulae | Less than a few million years; still assembling |

sections.heading: Life cycle (book diagram)
sections.content:
Common start: **nebula / giant gas cloud** → gravitational collapse → **protostar** → **T-Tauri** phase. Then **nuclear fusion:** core ~**10 million K** → hydrogen nuclei fuse to helium. Gravity ↔ radiation pressure = **main-sequence** star (longest phase). Small stars (red dwarfs) burn slowly; massive stars burn fast.
- **Chandrasekhar limit:** maximum mass of a **white dwarf** ≈ **1.4 solar masses**. Above it the remnant cannot stay a white dwarf; collapse can give a **Type Ia supernova**. **Black hole (later in the chapter):** region from which not even light escapes; massive-star collapse to a **singularity**. Invisible — inferred from nearby stars / specialised telescopes. **Event horizon** is the PYQ phrase (2017). ---

sections.heading: 6. The Sun (GEO-11-04)
sections.content:
- Central star of the solar system. Book age ≈ **5 billion years** (Earth in class geomorphology is **4.6 billion years** — do not force them into one number).
- Diameter ≈ **1,392,000 km**.
- Core ≈ **15 million °C**; surface ≈ **5,500 °C**. Entirely **plasma** (not solid / liquid / gas).
- Composition pie (book): **73% hydrogen · 25% helium · 2% other**. Energy = core **nuclear fusion**.

**Inner layers:** core → **radiative zone** → **convective zone**.  
**Outer layers:** **photosphere** → **chromosphere** → transition region → **corona**.

| Layer / feature | Book details |
|:---|:---|
| **Core** | Fusion H → He; ~**15 million °C**; hottest |
| **Radiative zone** | Core to convection zone; energy as **photons**; ~**2–7 million °C** |
| **Convection zone** | Hot plasma rises, cool sinks; base ~**2 million °C** |
| **Photosphere** | Visible surface; book table **3,700–6,200 °C** |
| **Chromosphere** | Just above photosphere (~**2,000–3,000 km**); **3,700–10,000 °C**; reddish glow in eclipse |
| **Corona** | Outermost; **1–3 million °C**; seen in **total solar eclipse** |
| **Solar flares** | Magnetic-energy bursts; space weather; satellites / comms |
| **Sunspots** | Darker, cooler patches; strong magnetic fields; **11-year** cycle |
| **Solar wind** | Plasma streaming from the corona along radial field lines |
| **Solar cycle** | ~**11 years** for the magnetic poles to flip; another 11 to original polarity |
| **Solar maximum** | Many sunspots, flares, auroras; can hit power grids, satellites, GPS |
| **Solar minimum** | Quiet sunspots; wind still blows |
| **Sun halo** | **Not** a solar layer — optical: sunlight through **hexagonal ice crystals** in Earth’s air; **22° circular halo** (Sun or Moon) |
| **Alfvén critical surface** | Where solar material breaks free of gravity + magnetic binding. **Parker Solar Probe** crossed it in **2021** |

---

sections.heading: 7. What is a planet? Solar system (GEO-11-05)
sections.content:
**International Astronomical Union (IAU), 2006 — three tests for a planet**

1. Orbits a star (in our system: the Sun).
2. Enough mass for a nearly **spherical** shape (hydrostatic equilibrium).
3. Has **cleared** its orbital neighbourhood.

Fail (3) but pass (1)–(2) and **not a satellite** → **dwarf planet**.

sections.heading: How planets grow (book)
sections.content: Nebula → local lumps collapse to a star + rotating disc → **planetesimals** by cohesion → collisions + **accretion** → planets that dominate their orbits.

sections.heading: Our solar system
sections.content:
- Formed ≈ **4.5 billion years** ago from the **solar nebula**.
- Book overview list: Sun + **8 planets** + **63 moons** + asteroids, comets, dust and gas. **Use the planet table below for moon counts** — **63** is the old stock phrase; the same chapter later prints **Jupiter 95** and **Saturn 146**.
- **Inner / terrestrial** (inside the asteroid belt): **Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars** — rock + metal, higher density.
- **Outer / Jovian (gas giants)** (beyond the belt): **Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune**.
- Diagram also marks **asteroid belt** (Mars–Jupiter), **Kuiper Belt** (beyond Neptune), **Oort Cloud** (much farther envelope).

| Planet | Book facts |
|:---|:---|
| **Mercury** | Smallest; closest; **57.9 million km**; year **88 days** |
| **Venus** | ~**108 million km** (Earth ~**150 million km**); **Earth’s twin** (size, mass, density) |
| **Earth** | Only known life; one moon |
| **Mars** | Fourth; dark patches; book flags plant-life / colonisation talk |
| **Jupiter** | Largest; H, He, methane; light/dark bands; **95 satellites**; very cold at its distance |
| **Saturn** | Second largest; thousands of ringlets in **7** major rings; **146** confirmed moons; orbit **29.5 years** |
| **Uranus** | ~**50×** Earth’s volume, **15×** mass (book); **27** satellites; telescope discovery, late 18th century; book: orbit one way, **clockwise (retrograde) rotation** |
| **Neptune** | Similar to Uranus; **14** known satellites; likely colder |

**Why terrestrial ≠ Jovian (book three lines)**

- Terrestrial: born **close** in; too warm for gases to condense; **strong solar wind** stripped gas; **small + low gravity** could not hold what escaped.
- Jovian: born **far**; winds too weak to strip gas; **larger**, so they kept atmospheres.

---

sections.heading: 8. Dwarf planets, Moon, small bodies (GEO-11-06)
sections.content:
**IAU dwarf planet:** orbits the Sun · nearly round · **has not cleared** its path · **not a moon**.

| Body | Book placement |
|:---|:---|
| **Pluto** | Reclassified **2006**; Kuiper Belt; **5** moons, largest **Charon** |
| **Eris** | Scattered disc; slightly smaller than Pluto, **more massive**; found **2005**; moon **Dysnomia** |
| **Haumea** | Kuiper; elongated because it spins fast; moons **Namaka**, **Hiʻiaka** |
| **Makemake** | Kuiper; found **2005**; moon found **2016** (book: **MK2**) |
| **Ceres** | Largest in the **asteroid belt**; found **1801**; water ice / possible subsurface ocean talk |

sections.heading: Moon (extras beyond class Theia)
sections.content:
- Earth’s only natural satellite. Book name for the impact story: **Big Splat** (~**4.44 billion years**; class **~4.5**).
- Mean distance **384,000 km** (book also **238,900 miles**). Sidereal month **27.32 days**.
- **Tidal locking:** rotation period = orbital period → about **59%** of the surface is ever seen from Earth.
- Atmosphere extremely thin.
- **Super Moon** = perigee **356,500 km**; **Micro Moon** = apogee **406,700 km**. Book mentions a “Super Pink Moon.”

sections.heading: Comets, asteroids, meteors
sections.content:
- **Comets:** “cosmic snowballs” — frozen gases + rock + dust. Near the Sun they grow a glowing head and a tail (can stretch millions of miles). Many in the Kuiper Belt / farther reservoirs.
- **Asteroids:** rocky leftovers, mostly **Mars–Jupiter** main belt. **Trojans** share Jupiter’s orbit (ahead and behind). **Near-Earth Objects (NEOs)** come close to Earth.
- **Kuiper Belt:** disc from Neptune ~**30 astronomical units (AU)** to ~**50 AU**; ices, dwarf planets, comets, **trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs)**.

| Term | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| **Meteoroid** | Fragment of comet/asteroid **still in space** |
| **Meteor** | The **streak** (“shooting star”) as it burns in the atmosphere |
| **Meteorite** | The piece that **hits the ground** |

---

sections.heading: 9. Space stations in this chapter (GEO-11-07)
sections.content:
Vinay Sir’s S&T class is still at **Skylab / Mir**. These are **Yellow Book extras**, copied onto `04_Space_Technology_Introduction.md` as a dated update — **no extra S&T Day-1 cluster**.

| Station | Book facts |
|:---|:---|
| **International Space Station (ISS)** | Largest man-made object in space; launched **20 November 1998**; inhabited since **2000**; ~**400 km**; ~**28,000 km/h**; orbit ~**90 minutes**. Partners: **NASA** (USA), **Roscosmos** (Russia), **ESA** (Europe), **JAXA** (Japan), **CSA** (Canada) |
| **Tiangong** (China) | Operational since **2022**; ~**450 km**; **three** astronauts |
| **Bhartiya Antariksh Station** (India; book spelling **Bhartiya Antriksh Station**) | Planned **2035**; ~**400 km**; **15–20 days**; up to **20 tonnes** |

Book: stations exist for space knowledge, **microgravity**, research.

---

sections.heading: 10. UPSC Previous Year Questions printed in the chapter
sections.content:
**2023 — how many pairs are correctly matched?**

1. Cepheids — giant clouds of dust and gas  
2. Nebulae — stars that brighten and dim periodically  
3. Pulsars — neutron stars after a massive star collapses  

**Trap:** (1) and (2) are **swapped**. Cepheids = pulsating variables; nebulae = gas/dust clouds; pulsars = spinning neutron stars. **Only one** pair is right → **(a) Only one**.

**2017 — ‘Event Horizon’, ‘Singularity’, ‘String Theory’, ‘Standard Model’**

Context = **observation and understanding of the Universe** (not eclipses, not satellite parking, not origin of life).

**2012 — evidence for continued expansion**

1. Microwaves in space (CMB)  
2. Redshift  
3. Asteroid motion  
4. Supernova explosions  

Book-consistent answer: **1 and 2 only**.

**2011 — asteroids vs comets** (book prints **Answer: (b)**)

1. Asteroids rocky planetoids; comets frozen gases + rocky/metallic material — **correct**  
2. Asteroids mainly Mars–Jupiter; comets mainly **Venus–Mercury** — **wrong** (comets are not a Venus–Mercury belt)  
3. Comets show a glowing tail; asteroids do not — **correct**  

**1 and 3 only.**

---

sections.heading: Knowledge graph (GEO-11)
sections.content:
```
Geocentric / Ptolemy → Copernicus heliocentric → Galileo telescope
Kant–Laplace nebula → Chamberlin–Moulton planetesimals → Schmidt–Weizsäcker accretion
Hubble redshift = Hubble’s Law → Big Bang ~13.7 BY + CMB
Galaxy types: irregular (blue, collisions) / elliptical (old, no new stars) / spiral (MW, Andromeda)
MW: barred spiral · Sgr A* · 26,000 ly from centre · 250 million year orbit
Star mass → white dwarf (≤1.4 M☉ Chandrasekhar) vs supernova → neutron star / black hole
IAU 2006: sphere + clear orbit = planet; no clear → dwarf (Pluto 2006)
Terrestrial inside belt (wind + small gravity) vs Jovian outside
Meteoroid (space) → meteor (streak) → meteorite (ground)
ISS 1998/400 km · Tiangong 2022 · BAS 2035
```

---

sections.heading: UPSC Quick Recall
sections.content:
- Hubble **redshift** + **CMB** = expansion / Big Bang evidence. Asteroids are **not** that evidence (2012).
- **Elliptical** = old, little gas, **no new stars** (book). **Irregular** = young blue + collisions.
- **Chandrasekhar 1.4 M☉** = white-dwarf ceiling.
- IAU planet vs dwarf = **cleared the orbit** or not. Pluto **2006**.
- **Ceres** = asteroid belt; **Pluto / Haumea / Makemake** = Kuiper; **Eris** = scattered disc.
- Meteor**oid** / meteor / meteor**ite** = location (space / sky / ground).
- Asteroids **Mars–Jupiter**; comets are **not** “between Venus and Mercury” (2011).
- Cepheids ≠ nebulae (2023 swap).
- Sun halo = **ice crystals in air**, not a photosphere feature.
- Parker Probe **Alfvén surface 2021**.
- ISS ~**400 km / 90 min**; Tiangong **2022**; Indian station **2035**.

sections.heading: Yellow Book — Concepts of Geography, Chapter 2 — 8 September 2026
sections.content:
> **Date added:** 8 September 2026 (Yellow Book ingest, not a class)  
> **Source:** Vajiram & Ravi, *General Studies — Concepts of Geography 2027*, Chapter 2, pp. 18–27  
> **Class twin:** almost the whole chapter is already in `GS_Geography_VR_Notes/01_Fundamentals_of_Geography.md` (shape, grid, great circles, seasons, local/standard time, IDL, DST). **Do not treat this as a new Ghost Recall cluster.**  
> **AWP 9 Sep:** this *is* the Geography paper (Physical vs Human is class; Earth = this chapter + Fundamentals). Read **VR extras** first, then this file if a list is missing.  
> **Geomorphology overlap:** early Earth / lithosphere / Moon impact — extras patched on `02_Geomorphology.md`, not a second origin lecture.

**How to read shortcuts:** full form on first use. Book figures only.

---

sections.heading: 1. Origin theories and early Earth (class already has nebula + Theia)
sections.content:
Same names as Ch 1, slightly different wording. **Use Ch 1 + Geomorphology as the master.** This page’s extras:

| Book line | Keep / caution |
|:---|:---|
| Kant nebular; Laplace **1796** | Laplace year is extra vs Ch 1 |
| **Chamberlin and Moulton (1900)** — wandering star ejects solar material → planets | Ch 1 listed them as **planetesimal** theory. Same names, two pictures. Do not merge in an MCQ |
| **Sir James Jeans** and **Sir Harold Jeffreys** backed the wandering-star / tidal picture | Extra names |
| **Binary** theories: Sun had a companion star | Extra heading |
| Otto Schmidt + Carl Weizsäcker (**1950s**, book: Weizscar) — solar nebula H, He, dust → disc → **accretion** | Same as Ch 1 |
| Early Earth: barren, rocky, hot; thin **H + He** atmosphere; molten; light stuff rises and hardens; cooling crust **wrinkles** into ridges and basins | Extra vs class Hadean |
| Further cooling → gas released → clouds → rain for **thousands of years** → basins fill = **oceans** | Extra hydrosphere picture |
| Giant impact heats Earth → **differentiation** into crust, mantle, outer core, inner core; density ↑ toward the centre | Same idea as Theia + density adjustment |
| Fe + Ni sink; silica + aluminium toward the surface; Earth cools, solidifies, **contracts** | Matches SIAL / SIMA / NiFe class chain |

---

sections.heading: 2. Shape of the Earth (GEO-01 extras)
sections.content:
- **Eratosthenes** (2nd century BC): early accurate size (Fundamentals already: he coined *geography*).
- Diameters match class: equatorial **~12,756 km**, polar **~12,714 km** (book also **7,900 miles** for polar).
- Rotation → bulge at equator, flatten at poles.
- Book term: **oblate ellipsoid**, commonly called **geoid** (“Earth-like”). Class sequence is **oblate spheroid → geoid**. Same exam idea: not a perfect sphere; treat as sphere for most sums.
- **UPSC / Test 1 (9 Sep):** geoid = model of **global mean sea level** for precise elevations — **not** “perfectly spherical.”

sections.heading: Evidence of sphericity (not in class — learn this list)
sections.content:
1. **Circumnavigation** — Magellan’s crew **1519–1522**; no “edge.”
2. **Circular horizon** — expands as you go higher.
3. **Ship:** mast first on approach; hull first to vanish on departure. On a flat Earth the whole ship would pop in/out at once.
4. **Sunrise / sunset** at different longitudes (Earth rotates **west → east**; east sees sunrise first).
5. **Lunar eclipse** — Earth’s shadow on the Moon is **circular**.
6. Other planets/Moon/Sun look circular in a telescope (analogy).
7. Equal poles in a line on curved ground: middle pole sits slightly **higher**.
8. **Aerial / satellite** photos show the curved limb.

---

sections.heading: 3. Rotation and revolution (GEO-01 / seasonality)
sections.content:
| Motion | Book | Effect |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Rotation** | Spin on axis, ~**24 hours** (**solar day**) | Day / night; daily temperature; winds and currents that move heat |
| **Revolution** | Around the Sun, ~**365.242 days** | Seasons (with tilt). **Leap year** every four years (29 Feb) for the extra fraction |
| Distance | Average **93 million miles** = **1 astronomical unit (AU)** | — |

**Axis:** **23.5°** from the **normal** to the orbital plane = **66.5°** to the **ecliptic** (orbital plane). Class Theia already locked **23.5°**.

**Circle of illumination:** great circle, day vs night. Tilt → day length varies with latitude and season. If the axis were **vertical**, day and night would be **equal everywhere all year**.

**Three reasons the book gives for why rotation matters:** (1) geographic grid; (2) measure of time; (3) physical processes and life.

**Dawn / twilight (extra):** dawn = sky lighting just **before** sunrise (reds/oranges). Twilight = Sun still **below** the horizon but sky lit by **scattered** sunlight (before sunrise and after sunset). Class already: twilight **lengthens** with latitude (DST logic).

sections.heading: Perihelion and aphelion (extra — seasons are **not** from this)
sections.content:
| | When (book) | Distance |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Perihelion** (closest) | **2–4 January** (~14 days after December solstice) | **147.1 million km** (91.4 million mi) |
| **Aphelion** (farthest) | **3–6 July** (~14 days after June solstice) | **152.1 million km** (94.5 million mi) |

Elliptical orbit → small distance change; book: **minimal** effect on seasons. **2013 PYQ trap:** variations of day length are **not** “elliptical revolution” alone.

sections.heading: Solstices and equinoxes (book dates)
sections.content:
| Event | Date (book) | Overhead / pole |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **June solstice** (NH summer) | ~**21 June** (also 20–22) | Tropic of **Cancer**; Arctic **24 h** day; Antarctic **0 h** |
| **December solstice** (NH winter) | ~**21–22 December** | Tropic of **Capricorn**; Arctic **0 h**; Antarctic **24 h** |
| **Vernal equinox** | ~**20–21 March** | Equator; Sun crosses celestial equator **S → N**; NH spring |
| **Autumnal equinox** | ~**22–23 September** | Equator; Sun crosses **N → S**; NH autumn |

Equator: **12 h** day **every** day (class). Arctic Circle: Sun **does not set** ~21 June; **does not rise** ~22 December.

sections.heading: Five reasons for seasons (book list — 2013 key)
sections.content:
1. Revolution around the Sun  
2. Daily rotation  
3. Tilted axis  
4. **Parallelism** — axis keeps pointing the same way (**Polaris**) all year  
5. **Sphericity** (different angles of incidence)

**Do not pick** “elliptical orbit” as the cause of seasonal day-length change.

---

sections.heading: 4. Location of places (mostly class)
sections.content:
- Rotation W→E gives two natural ends: **North and South Poles** → grid of **parallels** and **meridians**.
- Degrees, then **60 minutes**, **60 seconds** (angular; extra vs class).
- **Parallels at 1°:** 89 N + 89 S + equator = **179**. Extra.
- Meridians: **semi-circles**, **equal length**, meet at poles, cut the equator at **right angles**. Prime Meridian through **Greenwich Observatory**.
- **1° latitude ≈ 111 km (69 miles).** **1° longitude** shrinks toward the poles; at **60°** ≈ **55.5 km** (class ≈ **56 km**).

---

sections.heading: 5. Standard time and IDL (GEO-01-02 extras)
sections.content:
- 360° / 24 h → **15° = 1 hour**; **1° = 4 minutes**. Earth W→E: **east = later** (add); **west = earlier** (subtract).  
  **Ignore** any line that says time *falls* as you go east — the same chapter’s worked sums use the class rule.
- Standard meridians usually multiples of **15°** or **7°30′**.
- **Indian Standard Time (IST):** **82°30′ E**, book: through **Mirzapur**. IST = **GMT + 5 hours 30 minutes** because \(82.5 \times 4 = 330\) minutes. (Class had 82½° E and the 7½° rule; **Mirzapur** is the extra name.)
- **City lock (Test 1, 9 Sep):** **Raipur** is nearest that meridian among Bengaluru / Delhi / Kolkata / Raipur.
- Wide countries: several meridians. Book records: **France 12** time zones (overseas territories), **USA 11**. Class assignment was to list multi-zone countries — these two numbers are the book’s.

**Worked example (book):** Greenwich **7:30 PM**; find local time at **112.5° W**.  
\(112.5 / 15 = 7.5\) hours west → 7:30 PM − 7 h 30 min = **12:00 noon**.

**IDL:** ~**180°**. Clock is **12 hours** from Greenwich either way. Line **bends** (Aleutians etc.).  
Class rule (keep this, not a muddled “eastward = Wednesday” sentence):

| Travel across the IDL | Calendar |
|:---|:---|
| **East → West** (towards Asia / “add a day” on the book diagram) | **Lose / skip** a calendar day |
| **West → East** (towards the Americas / “subtract a day”) | **Gain / repeat** a calendar day |

---

sections.heading: 6. PYQs printed in the chapter (AWP-useful)
sections.content:
**2024 — 21 June, sunlight *more than* 12 hours?** Equator · Tropic of Cancer · Tropic of Capricorn · Arctic Circle.  
Equator = **exactly 12 h**. Capricorn = NH winter, **< 12 h**. Cancer and Arctic **> 12 h**. **(d) 2 and 4.**

**2019 — 21 June the Sun**  
**(a)** does not set at the **Arctic Circle**. Not Antarctic; not overhead at Equator or Capricorn.

**2013 — seasonal day/night length**  
**(d) Revolution of the Earth on a tilted axis.** Not rotation alone; not “elliptical manner” alone; not “latitudinal position” as the *cause* (latitude only *modulates* it).

---

sections.heading: UPSC Quick Recall
sections.content:
- Sphericity: Magellan, horizon, ship hull/mast, eclipse **circular** shadow.
- Seasons = **tilt + revolution + parallelism + sphere**, not perihelion.
- Perihelion **early January** / aphelion **early July**.
- 21 June: Cancer + Arctic long day; Arctic **no sunset**; Equator still 12 h.
- **179** parallels at 1°.
- IST **82°30′ E Mirzapur** = **+5:30**.
- France **12** zones (book), USA **11**.
- East = add time. IDL: westbound skip a date.

sections.heading: 1. Picture of the interior (already in class)
sections.content:
- Layers by depth: crust, mantle, **liquid outer core**, **solid inner core** (iron; magnetic field).
- **Lithosphere:** rigid crust + uppermost mantle = **plates**. Book thickness **7–200 km** (class average **~100 km**).
- **Asthenosphere:** under the lithosphere; hot rock that can **flow**. Book diagram splits it oddly (partially molten 100–200 km, “solid asthenosphere” 200–400 km, transition 400–**670** km). **Class: asthenosphere is semi-solid, often to Repetti ~700 km, entirely inside the upper mantle.** Do not replace class with the book wedge.
- Book radius to centre **6,370 / 6,378 km**; class **6,400 km**. Same order.

---

sections.heading: 2. Direct sources (GEO-04-07 extras)
sections.content:
Class: rocks, volcanic material ~40–250 km, mining 3–8 km, drilling ~13–14 km, **Kola ~13.7 km**, **Koyna** planned.

| Book extra | Figure |
|:---|:---|
| **Mponeng** gold mine, South Africa | deepest mine ~**4 km** (still nothing vs radius) |
| **Kola Superdeep Borehole**, Russia | book **12.2 km** (class **~13.7 km**) — do not fight over the decimal |

sections.heading: 3. Indirect sources (class list + extras)
sections.content:
Class: seismic waves, geomagnetism, meteorites, gravity anomaly.

Book also lists: **T / P / density** with depth; gravity **stronger at poles, weaker at equator** (shape + mass); gravity **anomalies** from crustal mass (mountains, ore); magnetic field from **molten outer core** (plates / volcanoes as applications). Class still **parks geomagnetism** — book’s **dynamo** line is below under core.

---

sections.heading: 4. Seismic waves (not in class — learn this)
sections.content:
**Focus / hypocentre** = underground origin. **Epicentre** = surface point **perpendicularly above** the focus. Recorded on a **seismograph / seismometer**.

Waves also from volcanoes, magma, big landslides, explosions.

sections.heading: Body waves (through the interior)
sections.content:
| | **P (primary)** | **S (secondary)** |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Arrive | **First** | Second |
| Motion | **Longitudinal / compressional** — particles **to-and-fro along** the travel direction (sound-like) | **Transverse / shear** — particles **perpendicular** to travel |
| Medium | Solid, **liquid and gas** (slower in liquid) | **Solid only** — **cannot** cross the outer core |
| Speed | Fastest | Slower than P |
| Interior use | Velocity shifts with elasticity and density | Absence through the core → **liquid outer core** |

sections.heading: Surface / L waves (along the surface; slower; more damage)
sections.content:
| | **Love** | **Rayleigh** |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Motion | Horizontal **side-to-side**, perpendicular to travel | **Elliptical rolling** (ocean-wave like), vertical + horizontal |
| Speed | Faster of the two surface types | Slightly slower than Love |
| Medium | Near-surface solid | Surface of solids |

**2023 PYQ (book answer (c) both):** (1) seismograph records **P before S**; (2) P = to-and-fro along the path; S = at **right angles**. Both correct.

---

sections.heading: 5. Shadow zones (not in class — high-yield)
sections.content:
Book uses **103°** and **105°** on the same page. Treat as **~105°** (NCERT-style), with P-shadow to **142°** (some books **145°**).

| Zone (from epicentre) | What arrives | Meaning |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Within ~**103–105°** | **Both P and S** | Crust + mantle behave as **solid** for S |
| **~105° to 142°** | **Neither** P nor S (shadow for **both**) | P **refracted** at mantle → liquid outer core; S **stopped** by liquid |
| Beyond **142°** | **P returns**; **no S** | P has gone through / around the core; S still blocked → **liquid outer core** |
| Entire far side beyond ~105° | **No direct S** | S-wave shadow is a **whole cap**, not just the 105–142 band |

---

sections.heading: 6. Structure — composition vs state (class models stay)
sections.content:
**Suess-style (composition)** — book densities on the disc diagram: SIAL **2.7**; SIMA **2.9–4.7**; NiFe **11**. Class Model 2 used crust **2.7** / mantle **5.4** / core **13**. Different generations of numbers — **do not mix in one MCQ**.

SIAL = granite-ish, silica + aluminium. SIMA = basalt, source of magma. NiFe = nickel + iron.

sections.heading: Crust (book extras vs GEO-09-09)
sections.content:
Class already: continental granite **2.7**, 60–70 km vs oceanic basalt **3**, 15–20 km; Conrad trap.

| Book extra | |
|:---|:---|
| Share | **0.5–1%** of volume; **less than 1%** of mass |
| Mean density | **2.7 g/cm³** vs whole Earth **5.51** |
| Thickness | Oceanic **5–30 km** (table **~7 km**); continental **50–70 km**, **70–100 km** under Himalaya (class 20 or 70–80) |
| Geothermal gradient | ~**30°C per km**; **200–400°C** at Moho |
| Oceanic age | **Not older than ~200 million years** (created and destroyed) |
| Continental age | ~**4 billion years** |
| P-wave speed | **Higher** in oceanic crust than continental |
| Tectonics | Oceanic thinner → more magma intrusion |

Moho: seismic velocity **jumps**. Oceanic crust subducts; continental more buoyant.

sections.heading: Lithosphere / asthenosphere / mantle (extras)
sections.content:
- Lithosphere = crust + uppermost **solid** mantle; **plates**; folding and faulting when they move.
- Asthenosphere (*astheno* = weak): book **~80–200 km**; viscous, weak, ductile; **isostatic** adjustment; **magma** source for eruptions. Class depth to ~700 at many places — keep class for placement, book for **isostasy + magma** uses.
- Mantle: Moho → **2,900 km**; ~**83%** volume, **~67%** mass. Upper density **2.9–3.3**; lower **3.3–5.7** (book). Lower mantle **solid** because of pressure (class).
- Mantle mix (book): oxygen **45%**, magnesium **23%**, silicon **21%**, Fe–Mg silicates. T from ~**1,000°C** near crust to ~**4,000°C** at core–mantle boundary → convection.
- **Mesosphere** here = mantle **below** lithosphere + asthenosphere, **above** the outer core (upper boundary ~**660 km**). **Not** the atmospheric mesosphere in Climatology.
- **Barysphere** (diagram) = core.

sections.heading: Core (extras; class already liquid outer / solid inner at ~6,000°C because pressure)
sections.content:
| | Outer core | Inner core |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Depth (book) | **2,900–5,100 km** (class Lehmann **5,150**) | **5,100 km** to centre |
| State | **Liquid** (not enough pressure to freeze) | **Solid** under crushing pressure |
| Density (book) | **9.9–12.2** g/cm³ | **12.6–13** |
| T (book) | **4,400–6,000°C** | ~**6,000°C** |
| Mix | NiFe + lighter traces | ~**80%** iron + nickel |
| Extra | Convection + **Coriolis** → **dynamo** → magnetic field | Same as class: pressure keeps it solid. **Class default for the dynamo is now A4** (`07_Geomagnetism.md`): thermal convection is the **major** driver; Earth rotation is additional. |

Volume ~**16%**, mass ~**one-third**.

---

sections.heading: 7. Discontinuities (class table is master)
sections.content:
Book names match class. **Conrad:** book = jump **inside continental crust** (A2: upper ↔ lower ~15–20 km). **A3 dictated Conrad = continental ↔ oceanic.** Keep **A3** for GEO-09; know the book/A2 sense for an “inside the crust” MCQ.

| Name | Book / class |
|:---|:---|
| **Conrad** | Inside continental crust (book) vs C ↔ O (A3) |
| **Moho** | Crust ↔ mantle |
| **Repetti** | Upper ↔ lower mantle; book mesosphere starts ~660 |
| **Gutenberg** | Mantle ↔ outer core **2,900 km** |
| **Lehmann** | Outer ↔ inner core |

---

sections.heading: 8. PYQ in the chapter
sections.content:
**2023** — P recorded **before** S; P particles along the path, S at right angles. **Both** → **(c)**.

---

sections.heading: UPSC Quick Recall
sections.content:
- **S cannot cross liquid** → outer core liquid. **P shadow 105–142°**; **S shadow** the whole far side beyond ~105°.
- Love = **sideways**; Rayleigh = **rolling**. Surface waves = damage.
- Focus **below**; epicentre **above**.
- Mponeng **~4 km**; Kola book **12.2** / class **13.7**.
- Oceanic crust **not older than ~200 million years**; continental ~**4 Ga**.
- **Mesosphere** in this chapter = lower mantle, **not** climatology’s mesosphere.
- Dynamo = outer-core convection + Coriolis (book). **Class A4:** thermal convection **major**; Earth rotation extra; asthenosphere does **not** make the field.

---

sections.heading: Abbreviations
sections.content:
| Short | Full |
|:---|:---|
| P / S | Primary / Secondary (body) waves |
| L / R | Love / Rayleigh (surface) |
| Moho | Mohorovičić discontinuity |
| SIAL / SIMA / NiFe | Silica–Aluminium / Silica–Magnesium / Nickel–Iron |
| PYQ | Previous Year Question |
